title: grind: a work-spec parse failure in the machine run dispatches a correction the worker can only satisfy by editing the frozen packet
description:
## Why

Run 3, issue ortus-u3ue: the machine run reported 'work-spec failure: AC-1: expected exactly one backticked command, found 3' — a defect in the packet, not the candidate — yet the FAIL verdict dispatched a correction round like any candidate defect. The correction worker correctly diagnosed the spec as the problem, and the only action that could satisfy the finding was bd update --acceptance on the claimed issue. The AC-6 acceptance-hash guard then rejected the run ('the acceptance criteria changed after claim'). The pipeline handed the worker a finding it was forbidden to fix: a designed-in trap.

## What

(1) When the machine run reports packet_failures (unparseable criterion checks), do not dispatch a correction: no worker edit to the candidate can change the packet. Park the candidate and escalate as a spec defect — comment naming the unparseable criteria, human label, claim kept — the same shape as correction exhaustion. (2) The worker and correction prompts gain an explicit prohibition: never edit the claimed issue's packet (acceptance, design, description); a spec defect is report-and-stop, the operator or planner repairs it before re-claim.
acceptance_criteria:
## Observable criteria
- AC-1: `uv run pytest tests/test_grind_recovery.py -k spec_defect_parks_without_correction -q` — a claim whose claim-time criterion checks cannot be parsed escalates (human label, escalation comment, claim and branch kept) with no correction worker spawned; the acceptance-hash and packet-drift rejections carry the same spec-defect escalation so a first-attempt rejection can never halt into a resume that fails identically.
- AC-2: `uv run pytest tests/test_grind_prompt_content.py -k packet_edit_prohibition -q` — the work-issue condition and the correction footer both forbid editing the claimed packet, state the frozen-by-hash mechanism, and name the report-and-stop route.
close_reason: Landed as a7795f5. Frozen claim-time defects (unparseable checks, post-claim packet edits, unreadable claim artifacts) escalate as spec defects with no correction rounds; worker and correction prompts forbid packet edits and name report-and-stop.

title: grind: journal resume bypasses EXCLUDED_LABELS while every snapshot gate applies them, so a resumed human-flagged claim silently drops its finished candidate
description:
## Why

Run 3 of 2026-08-12 (logs/grind-20260812-230721.log): the harness resumed the journal-owned issue via bd.show(resume_issue_id) — which ignores labels — while the issue still carried the 'human' label its own correction escalation had applied two runs earlier. The worker ran 68 minutes, validated its candidate green under two bd binaries, amended it to a proper commit, posted the completion comment, and exited 0. Then the verification gate ('issue_id in mid.in_progress_ids', where _snapshot applies EXCLUDED_LABELS) could not see the claim, verification was silently skipped, the delta read 0/0, the console said 'WARN no bd-state change', and the next iteration abandoned the journal. Same observable signature as the 2026-08-11 invisible-claim escape, this time armed by the harness's own escalation label rather than a worker flag.

## What

Two visibility regimes exist: journal-based resume is label-blind; every bd-snapshot gate is label-aware. Make them one regime: the startup/iteration resume path must refuse to resume a journal whose issue carries an excluded label, halting with a message that names the issue, the label, and the adjudication step (read newest comment, decide, relabel). And the post-worker verification gate must never skip silently — when the claimed issue is missing from the snapshot, log and print WHY (excluded label vs status change) before routing to the no-op branch.
acceptance_criteria:
## Observable criteria
- AC-1: `uv run pytest tests/test_grind_recovery.py -k resume_refuses_excluded_label -q` — a journal-owned issue carrying an excluded label is never fed to a worker: the startup resume is skipped with a loud warning naming the issue id, the label, and the relabel instruction; its claim, journal, and work stay parked and the queue continues past it.
- AC-2: `uv run pytest tests/test_grind_recovery.py -k verification_skip_names_its_cause -q` — when the claimed issue vanishes from the mid-iteration snapshot, the log and console name the cause (excluded label or status change) instead of only 'no bd-state change'.
close_reason: Landed as a7795f5. Journal resumes skip excluded-label issues loudly (claim/journal/work parked, queue continues); the verification-gate fall-through names its cause. Full gate 1040 passed.

title: grind: a resumed candidate makes every later iteration skip its implementation worker
description:
## Objective

Reset the resume-at-verification flag when an iteration claims a different issue, so only the inherited candidate skips its implementation worker and every issue claimed afterwards gets one.

## Behavioral context

Before. `resume_candidate_ready` is set once at startup from the handoff and never cleared when a later iteration claims a different issue. The implementation branch reads it every iteration, so a run that began by resuming a captured candidate skips the implementation worker for the whole run. The new-transaction block that detects the claim change and calls `CandidateJournal.start()` does not clear it.

Observed 2026-08-10 in a downstream repository. Iteration 1 legitimately resumed a captured candidate and skipped its worker. Iteration 2 then claimed a different issue and logged both lines together:

    transaction handoff: journal owned <first> but this iteration claimed
      <second>; starting a new transaction
    iter 2: harness selected+claimed <second>
    iter 2: implementation already captured; resuming at verification

No worker ran for the second issue, and verification was handed the seventeen paths belonging to the first. Had that verdict passed, finalization would have committed one issue's work under the other's id and closed the wrong issue. The run was saved only by an unrelated rejection.

The bug predates the handshake fix that made it reachable. Before that fix the run aborted at the first implementation handshake gate, so no second iteration ever ran.

After. The flag is cleared whenever a new transaction starts for a different issue. The inherited candidate keeps its resume, and any issue claimed after it runs a real implementation phase.
design:
## Readiness schema

v1

## Scope

Clear `resume_candidate_ready` in the block that starts a new transaction because the claimed issue differs from the one the journal owns, and add regression coverage that runs a second iteration rather than stopping at the resumed one.

## Non-goals

Do not change the resume itself: an iteration continuing the issue its journal owns must still skip the implementation worker, which is the whole point of resuming from a captured candidate. Do not touch the handshake guard, the seal, the finalization sequence, or the orphan policy. Do not alter which paths a candidate carries.

## Concrete locations

- `src/ortus/commands/grind.py` — the flag is assigned from the handoff at line 2936, read by the implementation branch at line 3481, and already cleared at lines 3766 and 4075 on other paths. The new-transaction block at line 3320 calls `CandidateJournal.start()` and is the site that must clear it.
- `src/ortus/core/transaction.py` — `CandidateJournal.start()`, the constructor that marks the boundary between one issue's transaction and the next.
- `tests/test_grind_recovery.py` — where resume behavior is covered today.

## Resolved decisions

1. Clear the flag where the new transaction is created, not at the top of the loop. That block is already the single place that decides the claimed issue differs from the journal's, and it already logs that decision; the flag is part of the same fact.
2. Clear it unconditionally there rather than recomputing it from the new journal. A journal that has just been constructed by `start()` has no captured candidate by definition, so any value other than false would be wrong.
3. Keep the two existing resets. They cover different paths and removing them is a separate question that this bug does not answer.
4. The regression test must run at least two iterations. A test that asserts only the resumed iteration passes today and would have passed before this bug existed, which is exactly why the bug shipped.

## Compatibility constraints

An iteration that resumes the issue its own journal owns keeps its current behavior exactly, including the handshake exemption and its log line. Journals on disk are untouched, so a run interrupted before this change resumes identically after it. No log line changes for the single-iteration case, so existing assertions on that text keep passing.

## Ordered steps

1. Clear `resume_candidate_ready` inside the new-transaction block in `src/ortus/commands/grind.py`, beside the existing handoff log line.
2. Add a regression test driving two iterations: the first resumes an inherited captured candidate, the second claims a different issue and must spawn an implementation worker.
3. Assert the second iteration does not emit the resuming-at-verification line and does invoke the runner.
4. Run `uv run pytest -m "fast or integration" -q` and confirm the suite is green.

## Dependencies

None. The handshake exemption this interacts with is already in place.

## Edge cases

A run whose every iteration works the same issue keeps resuming, which is correct. A run that starts with no handoff has the flag false throughout and is unaffected. An iteration whose claim fails before a journal is created must not leave the flag set for the next attempt. A resumed candidate that is finalized on its own iteration must not leave the flag set for the following one. A journal rebuilt from bd and the worktree, rather than loaded, must clear the flag the same way when the claim differs.

## Plan-gap guidance

Stop and report rather than improvising if clearing the flag at this site turns out to break a legitimate resume — that would mean the flag is carrying two meanings and needs splitting, which is a larger change than this packet describes. Never widen the resume exemption to make a test pass, and never make the implementation phase optional for a freshly claimed issue.
acceptance_criteria:
## Observable criteria

- AC-1: An iteration that claims an issue the journal does not own spawns an implementation worker.
- AC-2: That iteration does not log the resuming-at-verification line.
- AC-3: An iteration continuing the issue its own journal owns still skips the implementation worker and keeps its handshake exemption.
- AC-4: A run with no inherited candidate is unaffected in every iteration.
- AC-5: The regression test drives at least two iterations, so a fix that only satisfies the resumed one fails it.
- AC-6: A verification phase never receives a candidate whose paths belong to an issue other than the one claimed.

## Criterion checks

- AC-1: `uv run pytest tests/test_grind_recovery.py -k second_claim_runs_an_implementation_worker -q`
- AC-2: `uv run pytest tests/test_grind_recovery.py -k second_claim_does_not_log_resuming_at_verification -q`
- AC-3: `uv run pytest tests/test_grind_recovery.py -k resumed_issue_still_skips_implementation -q`
- AC-4: `uv run pytest tests/test_grind_recovery.py -k no_handoff_runs_every_worker -q`
- AC-5: `rg -n "iters_run|iteration" tests/test_grind_recovery.py` shows the new test asserting two iterations, and it fails when the fix is reverted
- AC-6: `uv run pytest tests/test_grind_recovery.py -k candidate_paths_belong_to_the_claimed_issue -q`

## Targeted tests

`uv run pytest tests/test_grind_recovery.py tests/test_grind.py -m fast -n auto --test-timeout=30 -q`

title: A resume from candidate-captured always fails the implementation CodeGraph handshake, because no worker turn ran
description:
## Objective

Stop requiring an implementation-phase CodeGraph handshake on a resume that
deliberately skips the implementation worker. A run resuming from
`candidate-captured` runs no worker turn, so it can never produce a CodeGraph
tool event, and under the default `required` mode the handshake gate aborts it
every time. Every such resume is currently unrunnable, and the error blames the
operator's MCP configuration.

## Behavioral context

Observed 2026-08-10 in a downstream repository (logicfirst) on
`ortus grind --integration-branch master`:

    [ortus grind] CodeGraph probe (mode=required)
    [ortus grind] CodeGraph child registration ready; awaiting handshake
    [ortus grind] resuming lf-ch2c from candidate-captured with 17 inherited path(s)
    [ortus grind] initial state: open=2 in_progress=0 closed=472
    [ortus grind] implementation CodeGraph handshake requested
    [ortus grind] implementation CodeGraph fallback: agent MCP capability handshake not observed
    error: CodeGraph required but the implementation agent reported no CodeGraph MCP
    tool capability. Configure the MCP server for this backend and retry.

The whole run took eight seconds, and `handshake requested` and the fallback
landed on the same second — no agent turn happened between them.

The mechanism: `resuming ... from candidate-captured` sets
`resume_candidate_ready`, and the resume branch reuses the prior returncode
instead of calling `runner.run(...)`, so the implementation worker never
executes. But `phase_offset` was already captured as the current log size just
above that branch, and the handshake check then parses the transcript from that
offset. Zero new bytes are appended, so the parse yields zero events,
`parse_transcript` appends `agent MCP capability handshake not observed`,
`capability_observed` stays false, and `require_handshake` raises because the
mode is `required`.

The operator's MCP server is correctly configured — the outer probe succeeded
and printed `CodeGraph child registration ready`. The diagnosis in the error
message points at the one thing that is not wrong, which is how the incident
was initially investigated.

Consequences: any resume from `candidate-captured` is unconditionally fatal
under the default mode, and re-running reproduces it identically because the
journal stays on that phase. The verification agent, which does run and would
perform real CodeGraph queries, is never reached. The only workaround is
`--codegraph auto`, which silently downgrades the policy for the verification
phase too.

After this change, a resume that skips the implementation worker proceeds to
verification without asserting a handshake that no agent was asked to perform,
and says so in the log rather than reporting a fallback.
design:
## Readiness schema

v1

## Scope

Skip the implementation-phase handshake assertion, and the misleading fallback
progress line that precedes it, on an iteration where `resume_candidate_ready`
is true and therefore no implementation worker ran. Log that the handshake was
not required and why. Keep the phase summary itself being parsed and recorded,
because later code consumes it.

## Non-goals

Do not weaken the handshake gate for an iteration that actually runs a worker —
that gate is the whole point of `required` mode and must stay fatal there. Do
not touch the verification-phase handshake, which runs a real agent on every
iteration including resumes. Do not change `require_handshake()` or
`parse_transcript()` in `src/ortus/core/codegraph.py`; the defect is that grind
applies a correct check to a phase that did not happen, not that the check is
wrong. Do not change the resume mechanics or what `candidate-captured` means.
Do not make the implementation worker run on resume just to satisfy the gate.

## Concrete locations

`src/ortus/commands/grind.py:3651` — the `require_handshake(implementation_summary)`
call that raises, inside the `try` whose `except CodeGraphUnavailable` sets the
issue back to open and exits 1.

`src/ortus/commands/grind.py:3640` — the `elif codegraph_mode is not CodeGraphMode.OFF`
branch that emits `implementation CodeGraph fallback: ...`; it needs the same
guard so a skipped phase is not reported as a degraded one.

`src/ortus/commands/grind.py:3481` — the `if resume_candidate_ready:` branch
that reuses the prior returncode instead of calling `runner.run(...)`; this is
where the worker turn is skipped.

`src/ortus/commands/grind.py:3470` — `phase_offset = log.stat().st_size if log.exists() else 0`,
captured before the branch, which is why the later parse sees an empty segment.

`src/ortus/commands/grind.py:3629` — `parse_transcript(...)` building
`implementation_summary`, which must keep running.

`src/ortus/core/codegraph.py:280` — where `parse_transcript()` appends
`agent MCP capability handshake not observed` for an empty segment.

`src/ortus/core/codegraph.py:310` — `require_handshake()`, unchanged by this issue.

`tests/test_grind_codegraph.py` — home for the regression tests, alongside
`test_required_child_missing_halts_at_handshake_gate`, which must keep passing.

## Resolved decisions

Guard at the call site in grind rather than inside `require_handshake()`.
The core helper has no notion of resume state, and threading one in would make
a general-purpose predicate carry grind's loop bookkeeping; the caller already
holds `resume_candidate_ready` in scope.

Keep parsing and appending `implementation_summary` unconditionally.
It is read later at `grind.py:3715`, `grind.py:3760`, and `grind.py:4083`
(where it becomes `verification_summary`), so skipping the parse would break
those. Only the assertion and the operator-facing fallback line are skipped.

Log the skip explicitly through `write_log`, in the same shape as the adjacent
`implementation already captured; resuming at verification` line. A silent skip
would leave no trace that a `required`-mode run completed without an
implementation handshake, which is exactly the kind of gap this gate exists to
surface.

Do not treat `--codegraph auto` as the fix. It downgrades the policy for the
verification phase as well, so it trades a false abort for a real loss of
enforcement on the phase that does run.

## Compatibility constraints

An iteration that runs a worker and observes no CodeGraph event must still
abort with the existing message and exit code, and must still set the issue
back to open when `harness_select` is on — `test_required_child_missing_halts_at_handshake_gate`
covers this and must not need editing. Behavior under `auto` and `off` is
unchanged in both cases. The journal format is untouched, so journals written
before this change resume without migration. Both backends reach this code
through the same path, so the fix must not depend on `resolved_backend`. The
recorded phase summary keeps its current shape, including the
`agent MCP capability handshake not observed` fallback string, so anything
reading the transaction journal keeps parsing.

## Ordered steps

1. Add a failing test in `tests/test_grind_codegraph.py` that drives an
   iteration with `resume_candidate_ready` true under `required` mode and
   asserts the run reaches verification instead of exiting 1.
2. Guard the `require_handshake(implementation_summary)` call at
   `grind.py:3651` so it only runs when a worker turn ran this iteration.
3. Guard the fallback progress line at `grind.py:3640` the same way.
4. Emit a `write_log` line recording that the implementation handshake was not
   required because the candidate was inherited and no worker turn ran.
5. Confirm `implementation_summary` is still parsed and appended on the resume
   path, and that its later consumers still receive it.
6. Run the regression tests plus the existing handshake-gate test.

## Dependencies

No issue dependency. Introduced with the CodeGraph phase-contract work that
added `require_handshake()` and the per-phase transcript offsets. Related to
ortus-9ljd only in that both are resume-path defects in the same loop; neither
blocks the other.

## Edge cases

An iteration where the worker ran but timed out must keep the gate active —
`implementation_timed_out` is a different condition from
`resume_candidate_ready` and must not be conflated. A resume that later clears
`resume_candidate_ready` mid-loop (`grind.py:3750`, `grind.py:4059`) must
re-arm the gate for the next iteration rather than staying permanently exempt.
A resume under `off` mode must produce no handshake log line at all. A resume
whose journal carries no evidence entries still resolves a returncode of 0 and
must take the same skip path. A run that resumes and then performs a correction
attempt with a fresh worker turn must have the gate enforced on that turn.

## Plan-gap guidance

If the loop turns out to skip the implementation worker under any condition
other than `resume_candidate_ready`, record PLAN-GAP naming that condition and
the line, and cover it in the same guard rather than adding a second ad-hoc
exemption. If the phase summary's later consumers cannot tolerate a summary
built from an empty segment, record PLAN-GAP rather than deleting the parse.

title: CI red on all six matrix legs: test_dashboard_reports_missing_textual asserts a substring split by ANSI codes
description:
## Objective

Restore a green `test` workflow by fixing the ANSI-styling assumption in the textual-absence tests, and stop help-text assertions from depending on whether Rich emits color.

## Behavioral context

Before. Every leg of the `test` workflow matrix — ubuntu-latest and macos-latest across Python 3.10, 3.11 and 3.12 — fails on exactly one test: `tests/test_dashboard.py::test_dashboard_reports_missing_textual`. Runs report `1 failed, 671 passed, 9 skipped, 4 deselected`. The suite passes locally, so eight consecutive commits were verified, committed and pushed onto a red `main`.

After. The same assertions hold regardless of whether the child process emits ANSI escapes, the full matrix is green, and a colorized help renderer cannot break a substring assertion again.
design:
## Readiness schema

v1

## Scope

Fix `tests/test_dashboard.py::test_dashboard_reports_missing_textual` and harden `_run_without_textual()` so assertions on CLI output are insensitive to ANSI styling. Audit the sibling test and the later assertions in the same body for the same defect. Confirm the full matrix returns to green.

## Non-goals

No change to `src/ortus/commands/dashboard.py` or to the lazy-import behavior it implements — that behavior is correct and its runtime contract is unchanged. Not altering the CI matrix, the marker selection, the duration budget, or the workflow file. Not addressing the separate process question of why eight commits were pushed onto red CI.

## Concrete locations

- `tests/test_dashboard.py` — `_BLOCK_TEXTUAL` (line 1973), `_run_without_textual()` (1992), `test_cli_imports_without_textual()` (2008), `test_dashboard_reports_missing_textual()` (2032), and the outer assertion that reports the child failure (2060).
- The failing assertion is line 27 of the composed child script, which maps to `assert "--replay" in helped.stdout, helped.stdout` inside the body at `tests/test_dashboard.py:2044`. `_BLOCK_TEXTUAL` contributes 16 lines before the body.
- `.github/workflows/test.yml` — the matrix (lines 22-25) and the `Run comprehensive hermetic pytest gate` step (81-86).
- `src/ortus/commands/dashboard.py` — the `--replay` option and the missing-textual message under assertion; read-only reference for this fix.
- Evidence: `gh run view 31295729122`, job 93200404123 logs; the first failing run is 31290629581 (`ortus-27uu`, 2026-08-09T02:34:52Z) and the last green is `ortus-apmf` at 02:25:47Z, matching commit 80b8fb2 which rewrote `dashboard.py` and added these tests.

## Resolved decisions

1. Root cause is ANSI styling, not the dashboard code. In the captured CI output the option renders as `ESC[1;36m-ESC[0mESC[1;36m-replayESC[0m` — Rich styles the option's leading dash separately, so the literal substring `--replay` never appears. `"--replay" in helped.stdout` is therefore False whenever color is on.
2. It reproduces only in CI because Rich enables terminal mode when it detects a GitHub Actions environment, while the same run under a local non-TTY pipe emits plain text. The fix must not depend on the precise detection rule, which is a Rich implementation detail that can change.
3. Disable color for the child rather than loosening the assertions. `_run_without_textual()` already sets `COLUMNS=400` to defend against line wrapping breaking a phrase; forcing color off is the same class of defense, fixes every assertion in every body at once, and keeps the assertions strict.
4. Strip ANSI defensively at the assertion sites as well, so a future renderer that ignores the environment cannot silently reintroduce this.
5. This is a test defect, not a product defect. `ortus dashboard` behaves correctly with textual absent; only the assertion about its help output is fragile.

## Compatibility constraints

`COLUMNS=400` must stay — it guards a different failure mode (phrase straddling a wrap) and removing it would trade one flake for another. The child must still run with textual genuinely unimportable, so `_BLOCK_TEXTUAL` semantics cannot change. The tests must keep passing on both ubuntu-latest and macos-latest across Python 3.10-3.12, and must not depend on a TTY. Any env var added to the child must not leak into the parent process or other tests.

## Ordered steps

1. Reproduce locally by forcing color on in the child, confirming `test_dashboard_reports_missing_textual` fails the same way as CI.
2. Set a color-disabling environment variable for the child in `_run_without_textual()`, alongside the existing `COLUMNS=400`.
3. Add ANSI stripping at the assertion sites in both `test_cli_imports_without_textual()` and `test_dashboard_reports_missing_textual()` so the assertions hold under either setting.
4. Re-check the later assertions in the same body — `pip install textual`, `Traceback`, `ModuleNotFoundError` — for the same substring fragility, since a styled message would break them identically.
5. Run the CI gate selection locally with color forced on and confirm green.
6. Push and confirm all six matrix legs pass.

## Dependencies

No issue dependencies. The failing tests were introduced by commit 80b8fb2 for `ortus-27uu`, which is closed; this issue does not reopen it. Code consumers: none — `_run_without_textual()` has two callers, both in `tests/test_dashboard.py`. Blocks nothing formally, but a red `main` obscures regressions in every other issue's verification, so it should be taken before further merges.

## Edge cases

- macOS and Linux runners may differ in color detection; the fix must hold on both, which is why it forces the setting rather than relying on detection.
- A future Rich release changing its CI detection: the ANSI-stripping assertion from step 3 keeps the test correct regardless.
- A colorized message where the asserted phrase is split mid-word by a style boundary, as happened to `--replay`: stripping must occur before substring matching, not after.
- The negative assertions (`"Traceback" not in message`) can only become weaker under stripping, never stronger, so they cannot start passing spuriously — confirm this rather than assume it.
- `COLUMNS` and the new variable must both reach the child through the copied `os.environ`, not replace it, or the child may lose `PATH` and fail to start.
- The child imports `ortus.cli`, so an env var that changes Typer or Rich behavior globally must not alter what the CLI actually prints, only how it is styled.

## Plan-gap guidance

Stop and record PLAN-GAP if step 1 cannot reproduce the failure locally under forced color, since the root cause in Resolved decisions 1 would then be unconfirmed and any fix would be speculative. Stop if disabling color changes the CLI's actual message text rather than only its styling, since the assertions would then be testing different output than users see.
acceptance_criteria:
## Observable criteria

- AC-1: `test_dashboard_reports_missing_textual` passes when the child process emits ANSI escape sequences.
- AC-2: `test_cli_imports_without_textual` passes under the same forced-color condition.
- AC-3: `_run_without_textual()` disables color for the child while retaining `COLUMNS=400`.
- AC-4: Assertions on child output strip ANSI escapes before substring matching.
- AC-5: The negative assertions (`Traceback`, `ModuleNotFoundError` absent) still fail when those strings are genuinely present.
- AC-6: The full hermetic gate selection passes locally.
- AC-7: Post-merge only. After the candidate is committed and pushed, all six `test` workflow legs (ubuntu-latest and macos-latest, Python 3.10/3.11/3.12) report success on the resulting commit. This criterion is not decidable during read-only pre-commit verification, where no workflow run exists for the candidate yet; a verifier records it as deferred and does not count it as a failure.

## Criterion checks

title: Verdict schema errors name the wrong problem, so a verifier cannot self-correct and burns every attempt
description:
## Objective
Make every verdict-envelope rejection state precisely what is wrong with the payload, so a correction attempt can fix it instead of re-emitting the same shape.

## Behavioral context
`src/ortus/core/verdict.py:135` rejects a criterion with `set(item) != {"id", "status", "evidence"}` and reports `each criterion needs id, status, and evidence`. That message describes a missing-field problem, but the check is exact set equality, so it also fires when every required field is present and one extra field is added.

Observed 2026-08-08 in a downstream repository. A verifier emitted eight criteria, each with keys `evidence`, `id`, `status` and `verdict`. Nothing was missing; the only defect was the extra `verdict` key. The run reported that each criterion needed the three fields it already had, so the verifier could not tell what to change, re-emitted the same shape, and failed identically on the initial attempt and both corrections. Eighty-five minutes, three model sessions, zero issues closed, and the candidate left uncommitted.

The message is not merely vague, it is false: the fields it names were all present. A correction loop cannot converge on a diagnosis that describes a condition which does not hold.

`criterion values are malformed` on the following line has the same defect: it names no criterion, no field, and no value.

After this change a rejection names the offending criterion, the missing keys and the unexpected keys separately, so the next attempt has something actionable.
design:
## Readiness schema
v1

## Scope
Replace the criterion-shape and criterion-value error messages with diagnostics that identify the criterion and the specific keys or values at fault.

## Non-goals
Do not relax the schema to accept unknown keys. The extra key observed was named `verdict`, which is plausibly where the model placed its real per-criterion decision; silently discarding it could accept a verdict whose status field means something other than what the author intended. Strictness is correct here and the defect is the diagnosis, not the rule. Do not change the required key set, the pass and fail vocabulary, the criterion-identifier reconciliation that follows, or the envelope-level fields.

## Resolved decisions
Missing and unexpected keys are reported as separate lists rather than a single set-mismatch phrase, because they call for opposite corrections and conflating them is exactly what made the observed message unactionable. The criterion is identified by its position in the array, and by its `id` when one is present, so an author with eight criteria can find the one at fault.

Value errors name the criterion, the field and the offending value rather than asserting the whole payload is malformed. A status of `passed` instead of `pass` should say so.

The diagnostics are asserted by tests on the message text, because the failure mode here was a message that a competent reader could not act on, and only a test that reads the message can pin that.

## Concrete locations
Edit the criterion loop in `parse_verdict()` in `src/ortus/core/verdict.py` around lines 134-142: the shape check at line 135 raising `each criterion needs id, status, and evidence`, and the value check at line 137 raising `criterion values are malformed`. `VerdictError` is raised and consumed by the verification path in `src/ortus/commands/grind.py`, which surfaces the text to the operator and into the correction feedback, so no plumbing changes. Cover in `tests/test_verdict.py`.

## Compatibility constraints
A payload that is genuinely missing a key must still be rejected, with a message naming the missing key. `VerdictError` stays the exception type and the failure stays fatal to that verdict, so the correction routing is unchanged. Existing tests that assert a rejection occurs must keep passing; only tests asserting exact message text may need updating. The message is embedded in operator output and in the correction prompt, so it must stay a single line and free of characters that would break either.

## Ordered steps
1. Compute the missing and unexpected key sets for each criterion instead of a single equality test.
2. Raise a message naming the criterion position, its id when present, and the two key sets separately.
3. Replace the value-error message with one naming the criterion, the field and the offending value.
4. Add tests for a missing key, an extra key, both at once, and a bad status value, asserting the message identifies each correctly.
5. Confirm the correction feedback path carries the new text unchanged.

## Dependencies
No issue dependency. Related to the verdict contract text in the verifier prompt in `src/ortus/commands/grind.py`, which already states the key set exactly; the prompt is correct and the diagnosis is what fails, so no prompt change is required by this issue.

## Edge cases
A criterion that is not an object at all must be reported as such rather than as a key problem. A criterion with no `id` must still be identifiable by position. A payload with many malformed criteria must produce a message bounded in length rather than enumerating hundreds. A key differing only by case or surrounding whitespace must be reported as unexpected rather than silently accepted.

## Plan-gap guidance
If the correction feedback path turns out to truncate or rewrite the message before the next attempt sees it, record PLAN-GAP naming that path, since a precise message that never reaches the author fixes nothing.
acceptance_criteria:
## Observable criteria
- AC-1: A criterion carrying an extra key is rejected with a message naming that key as unexpected and reporting no missing keys.
- AC-2: A criterion missing a required key is rejected with a message naming the missing key.
- AC-3: The message identifies which criterion is at fault by position, and by id when one is present.
- AC-4: A criterion with an invalid status value is rejected with a message naming the field and the offending value.

## Criterion checks
- AC-1: Run `uv run pytest tests/test_verdict.py -k criterion_extra_key_is_named -q`.
- AC-2: Run `uv run pytest tests/test_verdict.py -k criterion_missing_key_is_named -q`.
- AC-3: Run `uv run pytest tests/test_verdict.py -k criterion_fault_is_located -q`.
- AC-4: Run `uv run pytest tests/test_verdict.py -k criterion_bad_status_is_named -q`.

## Targeted tests
Run `uv run pytest tests/test_verdict.py --test-timeout=30 --enforce-duration-budget -q`.
notes:
Observed 2026-08-08 in a downstream repository using this loop. The rejected payload carried eight criteria, every one with keys evidence, id, status and verdict — all three required keys present, one unexpected key named verdict. The run reported "each criterion needs id, status, and evidence", which was false of that payload.

Cost: the initial verification plus correction attempts 1/2 and 2/2 all failed identically, roughly 85 minutes of model time, zero issues closed, candidate left uncommitted. A correction loop cannot converge when the diagnosis describes a condition that does not hold.

Current code, src/ortus/core/verdict.py:135 — if not isinstance(item, dict) or set(item) != {"id", "status", "evidence"}. Exact set equality, so extra keys and missing keys produce the same missing-field wording. Line 141 raises "criterion values are malformed" with no criterion, field or value named.

title: A missing textual breaks every ortus verb, because cli.py imports the dashboard eagerly
description:
## Objective
Stop one command optional-heavy dependency from taking down the whole CLI: a missing `textual` must break `ortus dashboard` only, with a clear message, while every other verb keeps working.

## Behavioral context
`src/ortus/cli.py:8` imports `dashboard` at module scope, and `src/ortus/commands/dashboard.py` imports `textual.app` at module scope. Registration therefore drags a terminal UI framework into every invocation of every verb.

Observed 2026-08-08, twice, on the machine that develops this project. `ortus grind` aborted before doing anything:

    File "$HOME/code/ortus/src/ortus/cli.py", line 8, in <module>
        from ortus.commands.dashboard import dashboard
    File "$HOME/code/ortus/src/ortus/commands/dashboard.py", line 78, in <module>
        from textual.app import App, ComposeResult
    ModuleNotFoundError: No module named textual

The dependency is correctly declared in `pyproject.toml`, so this is not a missing declaration. It is that any environment installed before that declaration — a `uv tool` install, a container image, a colleague checkout — is now a broken CLI rather than a CLI with one unavailable command. The operator could not run `init`, `check`, `plan`, `human` or `grind` either, none of which need textual. The failure surfaces as a traceback with no guidance.

Every verb also pays the framework import cost at startup, on every invocation, for a command almost never run.

After this change a stale environment loses only `ortus dashboard`, and loses it with a sentence telling the operator how to fix it.
design:
## Readiness schema
v1

## Scope
Defer the textual import to the point of use, and turn its absence into an actionable error on the dashboard verb alone.

## Non-goals
Do not remove textual from the dependencies; it is a real requirement of a real command and stays declared. Do not make the dashboard optional in any packaging sense, and do not add an extras group. Do not change the dashboard behaviour when textual is present. Do not restructure verb registration for the other verbs.

## Resolved decisions
The import moves inside the callback rather than the module, because the callback is the first point that genuinely needs a running application. Registration only needs the function object and its typer signature, neither of which requires the framework.

The absence is reported as a message naming the install command, not as a traceback. An operator whose environment predates the dependency needs one sentence, not a stack; the traceback observed here told a competent user nothing about what to do.

A regression test asserts the property directly — that the CLI imports and every other verb runs with textual absent — rather than asserting where the import statement sits, because the statement can move back without the test noticing.

## Concrete locations
Move the module-scope textual imports in `src/ortus/commands/dashboard.py` (currently around line 78, `from textual.app import App, ComposeResult` plus the sibling `textual.binding`, `textual.containers` and `textual.widgets` imports) into the `dashboard()` callback and the application class construction. `src/ortus/cli.py:8` keeps importing the callback. Cover in `tests/test_dashboard.py` and `tests/test_cli_verbs.py`.

## Compatibility constraints
`ortus --help` must still list `dashboard` with its current description and in its current position, since registration is unchanged. `ortus dashboard --help` must still work with textual absent, because argument parsing does not need the framework. Type annotations referencing textual classes must not be evaluated at import time. The dashboard must behave identically when textual is present. Every other verb must import and run with textual uninstalled.

## Ordered steps
1. Move the textual imports out of module scope into the callback and the application construction.
2. Ensure no module-scope annotation or base class forces evaluation of a textual symbol at import time.
3. Raise a clear operator-facing error naming the install command when the import fails.
4. Add a test that the CLI imports and a non-dashboard verb runs with textual absent.
5. Add a test that `ortus dashboard` with textual absent exits with the actionable message rather than a traceback.
6. Confirm `ortus --help` still lists every verb in its current order.

## Edge cases
A partially installed textual that imports but lacks a submodule must be reported the same way as an absent one. `ortus dashboard --help` must succeed without textual. A test that stubs textual out must not leak the stub into other tests. The published entry point and `python -m ortus` must behave identically, since both reach the same module.

## Dependencies
No issue dependency. Related to the dashboard epic, which introduced the verb; this hardens it rather than changing it.

## Plan-gap guidance
If some textual symbol genuinely cannot be deferred — a base class the application must inherit at definition time — record PLAN-GAP naming the symbol and why, rather than leaving the eager import in place.
acceptance_criteria:
## Observable criteria
- AC-1: With textual absent, the CLI imports and a non-dashboard verb runs successfully.
- AC-2: With textual absent, `ortus dashboard` exits with a message naming the install command rather than a traceback.
- AC-3: `ortus --help` still lists every verb, including dashboard, in its current order.
- AC-4: With textual present, the dashboard behaves exactly as before.

## Criterion checks
- AC-1: Run `uv run pytest tests/test_dashboard.py -k cli_imports_without_textual -q`.
- AC-2: Run `uv run pytest tests/test_dashboard.py -k dashboard_reports_missing_textual -q`.
- AC-3: Run `uv run pytest tests/test_cli_verbs.py -q`.
- AC-4: Run `uv run pytest tests/test_dashboard.py -q`.

## Targeted tests
Run `uv run pytest tests/test_dashboard.py tests/test_cli_verbs.py --test-timeout=30 --enforce-duration-budget -q`.

Observed 2026-08-08 on the development host: `ortus grind` aborted with ModuleNotFoundError raised from src/ortus/commands/dashboard.py line 78, reached via src/ortus/cli.py line 8. textual IS declared in pyproject.toml; the broken environment was a uv tool install created before that declaration, at $HOME/.local/share/uv/tools/ortus. The project .venv had textual and worked, so the same source tree was simultaneously working and broken depending on which interpreter invoked it.

title: Ordinary bd metadata edits abort a grind: hash the issue contract, not the whole packet
description:
## Objective
Make `implementation worker changed the immutable issue packet; candidate rejected` reachable only by a genuine edit to what the issue asks for, and stop one such edit from ending an entire session.

## Behavioral context
The guard binds a verdict to the issue packet so a verdict cannot be judged against a spec that moved. That intent is right. Its implementation is a denylist: `VOLATILE_PACKET_FIELDS` exempts seven fields and hashes everything else, so `labels`, `priority`, `dependents`, `dependencies`, `notes`, `estimated_minutes` and every field bd adds in future are all load-bearing.

The result is that routine tracker work is fatal to a running grind. Observed twice on 2026-08-08. First, `bd dep add <other> <claimed>` ended a session: the claimed issue was not even an argument to that command, because adding a dependency writes a `dependents` entry onto the other side. Second, and worse, an implementation worker correctly concluded a criterion was unmeetable, followed this repo escalation convention by adding the `human` label, and that label write ended the session at 18:07:52 with three issues still queued. The harness punished a worker for using the harness own escalation path.

The blast radius compounds the trigger. The rejection is a bare `break` out of the iteration loop, so one drifted packet stops all remaining work rather than that one issue. And the message names a culprit the code cannot identify: grind compares two hashes and cannot know who wrote the change, yet it reports the worker. Diagnosing the first incident required a hand-written script to discover the changed field was `dependents`.

After this change, `bd update --priority`, `bd label add/remove`, `bd dep add/remove`, and note edits are all safe against a claimed issue; a real spec edit is still caught; a caught issue no longer stops the queue; and the message names the fields that changed.
design:
## Readiness schema
v1

## Scope
Replace the packet-hash denylist with an allowlist of contract fields, make the rejection non-fatal to the outer loop, and report the changed fields instead of naming a culprit.

## Non-goals
Do not remove the guard: a mid-flight edit to what the issue asks for must still reject, because a verdict judged against a moved spec is worthless. Do not change candidate hashing, the diff capture, the verdict schema, or the finalization gate. Do not alter the lifecycle-state check, which is a separate and correct guard on status.

## Resolved decisions
The hashed set becomes an allowlist of the fields that define the contract: `title`, `description`, `design`, `acceptance_criteria`, `issue_type`. Everything else is metadata about scheduling and bookkeeping and cannot change what a worker must build or how a verifier judges it. A denylist fails open on every field bd adds; an allowlist fails closed, which is the correct direction for a guard whose false positives cost a session.

`notes` is deliberately excluded despite being prose. It is where operators and workers record evidence and measurements during a run, and hashing it makes recording evidence fatal. Its content is advisory: the criteria a verifier runs live in `acceptance_criteria`, which is hashed.

`dependents` deserves explicit mention because it is the sharpest edge: it changes when a completely different issue is edited, so an issue can be poisoned without anyone touching it. No allowlist containing it could be defended.

The rejection stops being fatal to the loop. The issue keeps its preserved candidate and its rejected phase, and the loop continues to the next ready issue, matching how a rejected verdict is already handled. One bad packet is an issue-level event, not a session-level one.

The message stops asserting an author. It reports which fields changed, with a short before and after for each, because that is all the code actually knows and it is what an operator needs.

## Concrete locations
Edit `VOLATILE_PACKET_FIELDS` and `authoritative_packet()` in `src/ortus/core/transaction.py` around lines 48-75, inverting the filter; `issue_packet_hash()` below them consumes it unchanged. In `src/ortus/commands/grind.py`, the implementation-phase guard around line 3027 sets the reason and the `break` around line 3069 ends the loop; the verification-phase equivalents are around lines 1109 and 1183. Add a field-diff helper next to `authoritative_packet()` and use it to build the message at every site. Cover in `tests/test_transaction.py` and `tests/test_grind_state_delta.py`.

## Compatibility constraints
A genuine edit to `description`, `design`, `acceptance_criteria`, `title` or `issue_type` on a claimed issue must still reject, and the existing tests asserting that must still pass. Journals written before this change store a hash computed under the old rule; a resumed transaction whose stored hash was computed differently must be handled by the existing handoff adoption path rather than by crashing. The status check that catches lifecycle changes is untouched. The verification-phase and implementation-phase guards must use the same hashed set, or a packet could pass one and fail the other.

## Ordered steps
1. Invert `authoritative_packet()` to an allowlist of the contract fields, keeping the function signature.
2. Update the module comment to state why an allowlist and why `notes` and `dependents` are out.
3. Add a helper that returns the changed contract fields with truncated before and after values.
4. Use that helper in the implementation-phase and both verification-phase messages, and remove the worker attribution.
5. Replace the loop-ending `break` with continuation to the next ready issue, leaving the journal phase and preserved candidate as they are.
6. Add tests: a label change, a priority change, a dependency edge added from another issue, and a notes edit each leave the hash unchanged; a description edit still changes it.
7. Add a test that a rejected packet does not stop the outer loop.

## Dependencies
No issue dependency. Related to the escalation convention in `src/ortus/prompts/grind-prompt.md`, which tells a blocked worker to signal for a human; that path currently mutates a hashed field, and this change is what makes it safe.

## Edge cases
An issue whose contract field is absent versus empty must hash consistently, so the allowlist must not make a missing key and an empty string differ. A field added to the contract set later must invalidate stored hashes only through the adoption path, never by crashing a resume. A worker that changes both a contract field and a label must still reject, and the message must name only the contract field. The correction route re-verifies after a worker edits code, not the packet, so its behaviour must be unchanged.

## Plan-gap guidance
If any current test depends on a non-contract field being hashed, record PLAN-GAP naming the test and the field rather than widening the allowlist to keep it passing.
acceptance_criteria:
## Observable criteria
- AC-1: Adding or removing a label on a claimed issue leaves its packet hash unchanged.
- AC-2: Changing priority, adding a dependency edge from another issue, and editing notes each leave the packet hash unchanged.
- AC-3: Editing description, design, acceptance criteria, title or issue type still changes the hash and still rejects the candidate.
- AC-4: A rejected packet does not end the outer loop; the run continues to the next ready issue.
- AC-5: The rejection message names the changed contract fields with before and after values and does not attribute the change to any agent.

## Criterion checks
- AC-1: Run `uv run pytest tests/test_transaction.py -k packet_hash_ignores_labels -q`.
- AC-2: Run `uv run pytest tests/test_transaction.py -k packet_hash_ignores_scheduling_metadata -q`.
- AC-3: Run `uv run pytest tests/test_transaction.py -k packet_hash_tracks_contract_fields -q`.
- AC-4: Run `uv run pytest tests/test_grind_state_delta.py -k packet_drift_does_not_end_the_loop -q`.
- AC-5: Run `uv run pytest tests/test_grind_state_delta.py -k packet_drift_message_names_fields -q`.

## Targeted tests
Run `uv run pytest tests/test_transaction.py tests/test_grind_state_delta.py --test-timeout=180 -q`.
notes:
Two incidents on 2026-08-08. 14:10:20 — `bd dep add ortus-j3xw ortus-kwfm` wrote a `dependents` entry onto the claimed issue ortus-kwfm and ended the session; the claimed issue was not an argument to the command. 18:07:48 — the ortus-apmf implementation worker measured its criterion as unmeetable (6.9% against a 25% threshold), followed the repo escalation convention by adding the `human` label, and that write ended the session with three issues still queued.

Currently hashed and therefore fatal: labels, priority, dependents, dependencies, notes, estimated_minutes, owner, created_by, created_at, plus the contract fields. Currently exempt: assignee, close_reason, closed_at, comments, started_at, status, updated_at.

Diagnosing the first incident took a hand-written script because the message names no field and asserts the worker did it; grind compares two SHA-256 values and cannot know the author.

title: A resumed worker can disown its own issue's inherited candidate
description:
## Objective
Stop a worker resuming an issue from declaring that same issue prior candidate unrelated, which abandons work the resume exists to carry forward.

## Behavioral context
Observed 2026-08-08 in a downstream repository. A grind resumed an issue from corrections-exhausted with seven inherited paths, and the implementation worker declared all seven unrelated:

    resuming <issue> from corrections-exhausted with 7 inherited path(s)
    7 inherited path(s) declared unrelated; left untouched

Those seven were the issue own subject matter, the prior attempt at the same work. The journal then recorded five candidate paths of fresh work while seven paths of earlier work sat disowned in the worktree. Had the run finalized, it would have committed the five and silently abandoned the seven.

`_absorb_unrelated_declaration` already refuses declarations outside the inherited set, so work this attempt produced cannot be disowned. It does not check the other direction: whether the inherited work came from the issue now being worked. Disowning is meant for foreign leftovers, such as a stranded doc from an unrelated issue, not for the resumed issue own candidate.

After this change a declaration naming inherited work that belongs to the claimed issue is refused and logged, the paths stay in the candidate, and the run continues.
design:
## Readiness schema
v1

## Scope
Refuse an unrelated declaration for inherited paths whose journal issue matches the claimed issue, log the refusal, and keep those paths in the candidate.

## Non-goals
Do not remove the disown feature: inheriting a genuinely foreign path is real and was exercised correctly twice in this repo on the same day. Do not change what happens to paths from a different or unknown issue. Do not change the candidate hashing, the verdict contract, or the finalization gate.

## Resolved decisions
The refusal is non-fatal. A worker that misjudges ownership must not be able to end the run, because a hard abort converts a recoverable misjudgement into a stop, which is the failure mode that cost most of 2026-08-07 and 2026-08-08. Grind overrides the declaration, records that it did, and proceeds, so the verifier sees the full candidate and can judge it. The check keys on the journal issue id rather than on path shape, because only the journal knows which issue produced an inherited path; guessing from directory names would misclassify a repo whose issues share a subsystem.

## Concrete locations
Edit `_absorb_unrelated_declaration()` in `src/ortus/commands/grind.py` around line 410, which currently computes `honored = declared & set(journal.handoff_paths)` and honors everything in the inherited set. The journal carries the owning issue in `CandidateJournal.issue_id` in `src/ortus/core/transaction.py`, and `with_unrelated()` at line 343 accumulates the declarations. Cover in `tests/test_grind_recovery.py`, which already exercises the handoff and disown paths.

## Compatibility constraints
A declaration naming a path from a different issue, or from no journal at all, must keep working exactly as it does today: honored, left untouched, never committed. Existing journals that predate this change carry no extra field and must load without migration. Both backends resume through the same path, so the behavior must not depend on which one produced the candidate. The refusal must not consume a correction attempt.

## Ordered steps
1. Establish which issue each inherited path belongs to, using the journal that produced the handoff.
2. Partition the declaration into foreign paths, which stay honored, and paths belonging to the claimed issue, which are refused.
3. Log refusals in the same shape as the existing out-of-handoff refusal, naming the paths and the issue.
4. Leave refused paths in the candidate so the verifier judges them.
5. Add tests for a foreign declaration still honored, a same-issue declaration refused, and a mixed declaration partitioned correctly.

## Dependencies
No issue dependency. Introduced with the handoff work in ortus-pzfd.6. Blocks the companion issue about the verification baseline: fixing that one alone would let a run finalize while silently abandoning same-issue work, which is a worse outcome than the current rejection.

## Edge cases
A declaration naming a path that appears in more than one prior journal must resolve to the issue that actually handed it off. A resume whose journal has no issue id must fall back to honoring the declaration rather than refusing everything. An empty declaration file stays a no-op. A worker that declares the same path on successive attempts must not accumulate duplicate log lines or duplicate journal entries.

## Plan-gap guidance
If the journal cannot attribute an inherited path to an issue at all, record PLAN-GAP naming the path and the journal fields available, and route to planning rather than guessing ownership from the path string.
acceptance_criteria:
## Observable criteria
- AC-1: A declaration naming inherited work that belongs to the claimed issue is refused, and those paths remain in the candidate.
- AC-2: A declaration naming inherited work from a different issue is still honored and left untouched.
- AC-3: A mixed declaration honors only the foreign paths and refuses the rest.
- AC-4: A refusal is logged naming the paths, and neither ends the run nor consumes a correction attempt.

## Criterion checks
- AC-1: Run `uv run pytest tests/test_grind_recovery.py -k disown_same_issue_refused -q`.
- AC-2: Run `uv run pytest tests/test_grind_recovery.py -k disown_foreign_issue_honored -q`.
- AC-3: Run `uv run pytest tests/test_grind_recovery.py -k disown_mixed_declaration -q`.
- AC-4: Run `uv run pytest tests/test_grind_recovery.py -k disown_refusal_is_not_fatal -q`.

## Targeted tests
Run `uv run pytest tests/test_grind_recovery.py -q --test-timeout=180`.
notes: Evidence from a downstream repository, 2026-08-08: journal recorded 5 candidate paths while 7 inherited paths of the same issue subject matter sat disowned and dirty. The disown feature itself is sound and was exercised correctly twice in this repo the same evening, where a stranded README from a different issue was inherited and declined by two consecutive workers.

title: Read-only verifier cannot start its inner sandbox over the repo git directory
description:
## Objective
Restore the read-only verification posture: a fresh verifier currently cannot execute a single command, so every acceptance criterion comes back unrun rather than judged.

## Behavioral context
Verification of ortus-q3lh was rejected twice with no check executed. Every Bash invocation inside the read-only session — including `true` and `sha256sum` — aborts before the command runs with:

    bwrap: Can't create file at $HOME/code/ortus/.git/config.lock: Read-only file system

The agent CLI nests its own bwrap sandbox inside the ortus `_readonly_wrapper` posture, and that inner sandbox binds placeholders over the git config files an agent must not rewrite (`<git-dir>/config.lock`, `config.worktree`, and one `config.worktree` per registered worktree). Those paths usually do not exist, so bwrap must create them, which `--ro-bind / /` refuses. The inner sandbox aborts before exec, so nothing runs.

This is the same failure family as ortus-dyio (`<repo>/.claude` unwritable) and it has the same shape of fix: a writable layer over the directory the inner sandbox needs mountpoints in, with the real contents re-bound read-only on top so the candidate and its git metadata stay unwritable.

Also note `preflight_readonly` reports a clean posture here: `_preflight_targets` in src/ortus/core/claude.py does not probe the repo's git directory, so the guard has the same blind spot its first two versions had.

## Why this is a separate issue
Discovered while implementing ortus-q3lh, whose scope is verification flag parity and the ambient-git-identity fixture only. A fresh verifier flagged the sandbox change as a scope deviation, so it was removed from that candidate and is carried here. A working, tested implementation exists — see notes for the full patch.
notes:
Implementation removed from the ortus-q3lh candidate for scope, preserved verbatim below. It adds `_repo_git_dir` (follows a linked worktree `gitdir:` pointer), `_writable_git_dirs`, `_writable_tree_mounts`, and `_repo_git_dir_tmpfs` to src/ortus/core/claude.py; mounts the git dir last in `_readonly_wrapper` for the same ordering reason as the agent-dir tmpfs; extends `_preflight_targets` to probe it; and adds four tests, one of which asserts by executing a nested bwrap that binds a nonexistent config placeholder.

```diff
diff --git a/src/ortus/core/claude.py b/src/ortus/core/claude.py
index 0729938..e82e332 100644
--- a/src/ortus/core/claude.py
+++ b/src/ortus/core/claude.py
@@ -263,17 +263,21 @@ def _preflight_targets(home: Path, repo: Path) -> list[Path]:
     Probing more than that would fail a healthy posture; probing less is how
     this guard grew a blind spot — its first version covered only $HOME and
     reported a clean posture to a verifier that could not run a single command
-    because `<repo>/.claude` was unwritable (ortus-dyio).
+    because `<repo>/.claude` was unwritable (ortus-dyio), and its second missed
+    the repo's git directory the same way (ortus-q3lh).
     """
 
     targets = [home / relative for relative in _AGENT_SCRATCH_DIRS]
     targets = [target for target in targets if target.is_dir()]
     if platform.system() == "Linux":
         # Only the Linux posture nests a bwrap sandbox that materialises
-        # bind-mount placeholders under the repo's .claude/. Seatbelt denies
-        # writes there deliberately and the CLI does not need them, so probing
-        # it on macOS would report every healthy posture as blocked.
-        targets.append(repo.resolve() / ".claude")
+        # bind-mount placeholders under the repo's .claude/ and git directory.
+        # Seatbelt denies writes there deliberately and the CLI does not need
+        # them, so probing it on macOS would report every healthy posture as
+        # blocked.
+        resolved = repo.resolve()
+        targets.append(resolved / ".claude")

+def _repo_git_dir(repo: Path) -> Path | None:
+    """The git directory backing `repo`, or None when it has none.
+
+    A linked worktree carries a `gitdir: <path>` pointer file instead of a
+    directory, and its metadata lives under the main repo's `.git/worktrees/`,
+    so the pointer has to be followed to find the directory that needs mounting.
+    """
+
+    git_path = repo / ".git"
+    if git_path.is_dir():
+        return git_path

+        pointer = git_path.read_text(encoding="utf-8", errors="replace").strip()
+        prefix = "gitdir:"
+        if pointer.startswith(prefix):
+            target = Path(pointer[len(prefix) :].strip())
+            if not target.is_absolute():
+                target = (repo / target).resolve()

+def _writable_git_dirs(repo: Path) -> list[Path]:
+    """Git-metadata directories the agent CLI's inner sandbox writes into.
+
+    The inner sandbox binds over the git config an agent must not be able to
+    rewrite: `<git-dir>/config`, `config.lock`, `config.worktree`, and one
+    `config.worktree` per registered worktree. Only `config` normally exists —
+    a lock file is transient by definition and `config.worktree` appears only
+    under `extensions.worktreeConfig` — so the inner sandbox creates the rest as
+    placeholders, which `--ro-bind / /` refuses:
+
+        bwrap: Can't create file at <git-dir>/worktrees/<name>/config.worktree:
+        Read-only file system
+
+    That aborts the inner sandbox before it runs anything, so every criterion
+    comes back unrun rather than judged (ortus-q3lh). The directories returned
+    here are the ones made writable; the outermost is listed first.
+    """
+
+    git_dir = _repo_git_dir(repo)
+    if git_dir is None:
+        return []
+    dirs = [git_dir]
+    worktrees = git_dir / "worktrees"
+    if worktrees.is_dir():

+        # one level inside every worktree, so both levels have to be writable.
+        dirs.append(worktrees)
+        dirs.extend(sorted(entry for entry in worktrees.iterdir() if entry.is_dir()))

+def _writable_tree_mounts(
+    directory: Path, nested: frozenset[Path], flag: str
+) -> list[str]:
+    """Mount `directory` writable while re-exposing the real entries under it.
+
+    `flag` is `--tmpfs` for the outermost directory and `--dir` for the ones
+    nested inside it, which bwrap can create because their parent is by then a
+    tmpfs. Entries in `nested` recurse; every other entry is re-bound read-only
+    so the git directory still reads exactly as it does on disk, and the
+    writable layer is discarded with the sandbox.
+
+    The re-binds are `--ro-bind-try` because this list is built from a directory
+    that git writes to: an `index.lock` or `config.lock` present while the argv
+    is assembled and gone by the time bwrap runs would otherwise be a missing
+    bind source, which is fatal. A dangling symlink is skipped the same way.
+    """
+
+    args = [flag, str(directory)]
+    for entry in sorted(directory.iterdir()):
+        if entry in nested:
+            args.extend(_writable_tree_mounts(entry, nested, "--dir"))
+        else:
+            args.extend(["--ro-bind-try", str(entry), str(entry)])
+    return args

+
+def _repo_git_dir_tmpfs(repo: Path) -> list[str]:
+    """Make the repo's git directory writable without changing what it holds.
+
+    Same shape as `_repo_agent_dir_tmpfs` and for the same reason: the set of
+    paths the inner sandbox protects is owned by the CLI, not by ortus, so a
+    writable layer beats pre-creating the placeholders it happens to want today.
+    Unlike `.claude/`, the contents here are load-bearing, so every real entry is
+    re-bound read-only on top — a verifier can no more commit, rewrite a ref, or
+    edit git config than before, and the candidate itself is untouched.
+    """

+    dirs = _writable_git_dirs(repo)
+    if not dirs:
+        return []
+    return _writable_tree_mounts(dirs[0], frozenset(dirs[1:]), "--tmpfs")

     """Escape a path for a Seatbelt string literal."""
```
