comments.text:
Implemented and pushed (7607137).

_repo_source_readonly() binds the repo writable, then re-binds every top-level entry that is not tool state read-only (.git, .gitconfig, .claude, .codex, .beads, .ortus stay writable). bwrap applies mounts in order, so the read-only binds win. --ro-bind / / is kept for everything outside the repo, so containment is unchanged.

Validated by executing the posture, not by asserting on argv — the argv has been right while the posture was wrong before:
  src/, tests/, README.md, /etc     -> unwritable
  .git/config.lock                  -> creatable (layer 4)
  .gitconfig                        -> creatable (layer 5)
  .claude/hooks                     -> creatable (layer 2)
  .git/worktrees/x/config.worktree  -> creatable (layer 3)
  settings.json                     -> readable
  git status, preflight_readonly    -> succeed
512 passed serial under the CI flags; 511 parallel.

Two behaviour changes recorded deliberately:
- Tool state is a real bind, not a discarded tmpfs. .git and .claude writes persist. A lock file the sandbox cannot see is a lock file git cannot take. Candidate mutation is still caught by the post-verdict hashes in _verify_candidate, and a verifier that commits is caught by the transaction's commit check.
- A repo with no .claude/ was previously unverifiable outright, because bwrap cannot mount a tmpfs on a missing directory under a read-only root. That condition no longer exists.

Not yet proven: an unattended grind closing an issue end to end. That is the next run.

title: Verification sessions intermittently cannot execute any command (EROFS on session-env)
description:
## Objective
Restore the ability of a verification phase to execute commands, and make ortus fail fast and legibly when it cannot, instead of recording a FAIL whose every criterion is BLOCKED.

## Behavioral context
On 2026-08-07 and 2026-08-08 multiple verification sessions were unable to run a single command. Every Bash invocation aborted at harness level with `EROFS: read-only file system, mkdir $HOME/.claude/session-env/<uuid>`, including bare `echo ok` and `pwd` probes recorded by the ortus-apmf verifier. No pytest, git, rg or sha256sum could run, so verifiers fell back to static reading and returned every criterion as BLOCKED rather than judged. Two issues died this way, ortus-6ur4 and ortus-apmf, and a third repository (a downstream repository) hit the same failure earlier, where the verifier invented an out-of-packet criterion id to report the blockage and tripped the verdict id check.

The failure is intermittent, not a clean regression. Verifiers executed commands successfully at 20:03, 20:56 and 22:27 UTC (the last ran `uv run pytest tests/test_grind_prompt_content.py -k verifier_states_criterion_ids -q` and reported 1 passed) and failed at approximately 21:05, 00:41, 02:18 and 02:29 UTC. Implementation phases in the same runs executed long test suites without trouble. The host filesystem is healthy: `$HOME/.claude/session-env` is owner-writable with 526 entries, the newest created during the affected window by a non-verification session, and the disk is 11 percent used with 852 GB free.

After this change a verification phase can execute commands again, and any future occurrence stops the run immediately with a message naming the probe that failed rather than producing a verdict that looks like a code judgement but is not.

## Resolved: the abort ordering is a requirement, and structure alone is not evidence

Verification of the candidate confirmed by reading that the preflight runs before `journal.begin_verification()` and before any worker dispatch, so a blocked verification cannot consume a correction attempt or route a plan gap. That confirmation was static: the verifying session could not execute a command, so nothing was demonstrated by running it. Two decisions the packet had left open are now settled.

First, that ordering is a requirement of this issue, not an incidental property of where the call currently sits. The no-budget guarantee in AC-3 is produced entirely by call order — no counter, flag, or rollback backs it up — so a later refactor that moves the preflight after the journal mutation or after the dispatch silently removes the guarantee while every other test still passes. The order is therefore stated explicitly in the design and named in AC-3.

Second, structural placement is necessary but not sufficient evidence for AC-3. A verification session that cannot execute commands must report AC-3 as BLOCKED; it must not report it satisfied by construction on the strength of reading the source. The behavioral test has to be executed and pass.
design:
## Readiness schema
v1

## Scope
Diagnose why a verification session loses the ability to execute commands, fix the cause, and add a preflight probe that aborts the verification phase with an explicit error when the sandbox cannot run a trivial command.

## Non-goals
Do not weaken the read-only guarantees of the verification phase to work around the symptom: a verifier that can mutate the candidate defeats the transaction. Do not change verdict schema or criterion-id validation, which ortus-wz3v already handled. Do not silence or auto-retry a blocked verification, because a verdict produced without executing anything must never be recorded as a judgement of the code.

## Resolved decisions
The preflight guard ships regardless of what the diagnosis finds, because it is valuable independently: it converts a confusing FAIL-with-everything-BLOCKED into an unambiguous environment error, and it costs one trivial subprocess per verification. A blocked verification aborts the run rather than consuming a correction attempt or routing a plan gap, since neither a correction nor a planning pass can fix a sandbox that cannot execute commands, and both were observed wasting attempts on exactly that. The candidate is left uncommitted and the issue left claimable, matching existing failure handling.

## Concrete locations
Add the preflight probe in `_verify_candidate()` in `src/ortus/commands/grind.py`, which composes and runs the verification subprocess, before the verifier prompt is dispatched. The sandbox configuration that governs the verification session is the `sandbox` block in the repository `.claude/settings.json` and its emitted counterpart `src/ortus/templates/.claude/settings.json.jinja`. Consider surfacing the same probe through `check_sandbox()` in `src/ortus/commands/check.py` so the condition is detectable before a run rather than mid-run. Cover in `tests/test_grind.py` and `tests/test_check.py`.

## Compatibility constraints
The probe must not require network, a bd workspace, or a writable repository, so it works in the most restricted sandbox ortus supports. It must run on Linux, WSL2 and macOS, whose sandbox mechanisms differ (bubblewrap versus Seatbelt). A healthy verification session must see no behavior change beyond one extra trivial subprocess. Existing log line formats stay intact so tail parsing is unaffected.

## Ordered steps
1. Reproduce by running a verification-profile session directly and capturing whether `echo ok` succeeds, recording the Claude Code version, the resolved sandbox settings, and the session-env path in use.
2. Determine what differs between sessions that can execute commands and sessions that cannot, given both classes were observed on the same host within hours.
3. Fix the cause once identified, in the sandbox configuration or in how the verification session is launched, without granting the verifier write access to the candidate.
4. Add a preflight probe to the verification phase that runs a trivial command and, on failure, aborts the run with a message naming the probe, its error, and the session-env path.
5. Ensure a blocked verification does not consume a correction attempt or route a plan gap.
6. Add tests for the abort path and for a healthy session being unaffected.

## Dependencies
No issue dependency. Related to ortus-wz3v, whose degraded-fail handling is why the blocked verdicts parsed and persisted reports instead of hard-aborting. Related to ortus-6ur4 and ortus-apmf, both of which failed only for this reason and whose candidates were verified or preserved by hand. Callers affected are the implementation, correction and verification phases in `src/ortus/commands/grind.py`.

## Edge cases
The probe must distinguish a sandbox that cannot execute anything from a command that legitimately exits nonzero, so it must assert on the harness-level error rather than the exit status. A session that can run some commands but not others must still be caught, so the probe should run at the point of use rather than only at startup. The abort must not leave the issue claimed and unrecoverable, and must not commit or push. Because the failure is intermittent, a single successful reproduction attempt does not prove the fix; the diagnosis step must establish a reliable trigger before the fix is judged.

## Plan-gap guidance
If the cause turns out to be outside ortus, in Claude Code or in the host sandbox, record PLAN-GAP with the version, the exact configuration, and the reproduction, then ship the preflight guard alone and route the underlying fix to planning. Do not disable the sandbox or grant the verifier write access in order to make the symptom disappear.

## Resolved decisions (ordering invariant)

The abort-spends-nothing property is a consequence of call order alone, so the order is the thing to protect and to state. In `_verify_candidate()` (`src/ortus/commands/grind.py:440`) the `preflight_readonly` call and its `ReadOnlyExecutionBlocked` handler (grind.py:471-488) must remain the first work the function does, ahead of:

- `journal.begin_verification()` (grind.py:493) and the `store.save(journal)` that follows it — `CandidateJournal.begin_verification` (`src/ortus/core/transaction.py:241`) advances the attempt counter, and any later `begin_correction` (transaction.py:268) or `route_plan_gap` (transaction.py:297) is reachable only from a parsed verdict;
- the CodeGraph handshake and `configure_codegraph` calls (grind.py:495-516);
- the verifier dispatch `runner.run(..., readonly=True)` (grind.py:528).

Nothing that mutates the journal, spends an attempt, writes a bd comment, or launches a worker may be inserted ahead of the preflight. The handler's own actions are the full permitted set: `bd.update_status(issue_id, "open")`, one `HALT` log line, `output.error`, `typer.Exit(1)`. This holds for both the initial verification and every bounded correction attempt, because both re-enter the same `_verify_candidate()`.

The guarantee is not conditional on the runner. `ClaudeRunner.preflight_readonly` (`src/ortus/core/claude.py:154`) probes; `CodexRunner.preflight_readonly` (`src/ortus/core/agent.py:135`) is a deliberate no-op because the Codex verifier is unwrapped; the `getattr(runner, "preflight_readonly", None)` dispatch at grind.py:476 means a runner without the hook skips the probe entirely and proceeds — which is correct only because a runner that never blocks has nothing to abort for.

## Resolved decisions (evidence standard for AC-3)

Reading the source is not sufficient evidence that the abort spends no budget. AC-3 requires the behavioral test to have been executed and passed in the verifying session, plus a source check that the ordering above still holds. A verification session that cannot execute commands reports AC-3 as BLOCKED. "Correct by construction" is not a verdict this criterion accepts, because the construction is exactly what a refactor can quietly change.

The behavioral coverage already exists and is the artifact AC-3 points at: `_blocked_verifier_grind` (`tests/test_grind.py:681`) drives a whole `ortus grind` with a runner whose `preflight_readonly` raises `ReadOnlyExecutionBlocked`, and `test_blocked_verification_spends_no_budget` (tests/test_grind.py:751) asserts `journal.corrections == 0`, `journal.plan_gap_routed is False`, `journal.verifier_refs == ()`, exactly one worker prompt, no `ORTUS_VERDICT` and no correction-escalation comment on the issue, and an unchanged git HEAD. The fixture runner's `run()` also asserts `not readonly`, so a verifier dispatched after a failed probe fails the test rather than passing silently.
acceptance_criteria:
## Observable criteria
- AC-1: A verification session can execute a trivial command on this host.
- AC-2: A verification phase whose sandbox cannot execute commands aborts the run with a message naming the failing probe and its error.
- AC-3: A blocked verification consumes no correction attempt and routes no plan gap, and the preflight still precedes every journal mutation, every bd write, and every worker dispatch in `_verify_candidate()`.
- AC-4: A healthy verification session behaves exactly as before apart from the added probe.
- AC-5: The diagnosis is recorded on the issue, including what differed between sessions that could and could not execute commands.

## Criterion checks
- AC-1: Run `uv run pytest tests/test_grind.py -k verification_can_execute -q`.
- AC-2: Run `uv run pytest tests/test_grind.py -k verification_preflight_aborts -q`.
- AC-3: Run `uv run pytest tests/test_grind.py -k blocked_verification_spends_no_budget -q` — it must be executed, not read; then read `src/ortus/commands/grind.py` and confirm the `preflight_readonly` call (grind.py:476) still precedes `journal.begin_verification()` (grind.py:493), the CodeGraph handshake, and `runner.run(..., readonly=True)` (grind.py:528). Both halves are required. A session that cannot execute commands reports this criterion as BLOCKED; source placement alone never satisfies it.
- AC-4: Run `uv run pytest tests/test_grind.py tests/test_check.py -q`.
- AC-5: Inspect `bd show` on this issue and confirm a comment records the reproduction, the differing factor, and the resolution.

## Targeted tests
Run `uv run pytest tests/test_grind.py tests/test_check.py --test-timeout=180 -q`.
notes: Evidence. Failing sessions: a downstream repository approx 21:05 UTC 2026-08-07 (uuid 5425724a, verifier invented AC-TESTS and tripped the verdict id check); ortus-6ur4 00:41 UTC 2026-08-08 (uuids 45c93e5a and c730bcf6, all criteria BLOCKED); ortus-apmf 02:18 and 02:29 UTC (uuid 56a35423, log records ATTEMPTED and FAILED for both `echo ok` and `pwd`, and states DECISIVE: the verification sandbox cannot execute any command). Working sessions on the same host: ortus-pzfd.5 verifiers at 20:03 and 20:56 UTC ran the six-module suite to completion (44 passed in 804s); ortus-wz3v verifier at 22:27 UTC ran `uv run pytest tests/test_grind_prompt_content.py -k verifier_states_criterion_ids -q` and reported 1 passed. Implementation phases were unaffected throughout. Host state during the window: $HOME/.claude/session-env owner-writable, 526 entries, newest created 17:41 local by a non-verification session; disk 11 percent used, 852 GB free. One untested correlation worth checking first: the repository .claude/settings.json sandbox.network.allowedDomains list was edited at approximately 00:05-00:15 UTC, between the last working ortus verifier (22:27) and the first failing one (00:41) — but the a downstream repository failure at 21:05 predates that edit, so it cannot be the sole cause.

comments.text:
Root cause found and partially fixed in 0fff74c.

CAUSE: _readonly_wrapper (src/ortus/core/claude.py) mounts `--ro-bind / /`, which makes $HOME read-only. The verification phase is the only caller passing readonly=True (grind.py:516), so only verifiers were affected. The agent CLI writes ~/.claude/session-env/<uuid> before it can start a shell, hence EROFS on every Bash call including 'echo ok' and 'pwd'. Introduced by 2cc1e5c (ortus-pzfd.4), which added the read-only verifier.

Reproduced directly:
  bwrap --ro-bind / / --dev-bind /dev /dev --proc /proc --tmpfs /tmp -- mkdir -p ~/.claude/session-env/probe
  -> mkdir: cannot create directory: Read-only file system

Intermittency explained: verifiers that appeared to work (20:03, 20:56, 22:27 UTC) ran before the installed ortus picked up the read-only wrapper, or under an agent build that had not yet needed a fresh session-env dir. Implementation phases were never affected because they do not pass readonly=True.

FIXED SO FAR: each agent scratch dir under ~/.claude (session-env, shell-snapshots, sessions, projects, file-history, paste-cache) now gets an empty tmpfs inside the sandbox. Absent dirs are skipped because a read-only root means bwrap cannot create a missing mountpoint. --ro-bind / / is untouched, so the candidate stays read-only.

title: Prime a bd workspace template once per session instead of bd init per test
description:
## Objective
Replace per-test `bd init` and per-test issue seeding with a session-scoped template workspace that tests copy, so the grind-family suite stops paying database setup cost on every single test.

## Behavioral context
Measured on 2026-08-07: every bd invocation costs roughly one second because each one is a fresh Go process opening a Dolt database. `bd init` is 1621 ms, `bd create` 1196 ms, `bd list --json` 1013 ms, `bd show` 817 ms, `bd ready --json` 730 ms. Git doing comparable filesystem work is 2 to 3 ms. Eighteen test files call `bd init` at test scope, and the `seeded_3_issues` fixture adds three `bd create` calls on top, so its setup alone is about 5.2 seconds before a single assertion runs. The CI duration report shows the result: roughly twenty grind-family tests clustered between 6.8 and 8.4 seconds, a flat floor that is fixed setup rather than work. After this change a test acquires its workspace by copying a prepared template, measured at 20 ms against 1621 ms, and the copy is fully functional: `bd list` and `bd create` both succeed inside it and mint new ids.
design:
## Readiness schema
v1

## Scope
Add session-scoped template workspaces to the shared test harness, one bare and one pre-seeded, and migrate the fixtures that run `bd init` at test scope to copy a template instead.

## Non-goals
Do not attempt to make bd itself faster; the per-invocation cost is a fresh process opening Dolt and belongs upstream. This issue removes calls rather than speeding them up. Do not change what any test asserts, do not alter the marker taxonomy or the duration budget, and do not touch tests that legitimately exercise `bd init` itself. Do not introduce parallelism as part of this work: pytest-xdist is already available and is a separate lever, and mixing the two would make this issue unmeasurable.

## Resolved decisions
Templates are copied rather than shared, because grind tests mutate issue state and a shared workspace would couple them; the copy measured 20 ms, so isolation is effectively free. Seeded variants bake their issues into the template rather than creating them after the copy, since three `bd create` calls cost about 3.6 seconds and copying them costs nothing extra. Templates are session-scoped so the 1621 ms init is paid once per run. Fixtures that assert on a specific bd prefix keep their own init and are out of scope.

No fixed percentage is required. Measured on this host: before 598.34 s, after 556.93 s, a 6.9 percent reduction. That is the arithmetic ceiling here, not a shortfall: this issue removes about 2.8 s of setup per test, while the tests in the measured command each run 17 to 44 s because of grind own in-loop bd traffic, which this issue must not touch. The same 2.8 s is roughly 35 percent on the CI hosts where grind-family tests sit at 6.8 to 8.4 s. A percentage threshold is therefore a property of the host, not of the work, and the criterion records the numbers instead of gating on them.

The measurement is taken serially and by this issue itself. `pytest-xdist` is now a dev dependency but is deliberately absent from `addopts`, so the default run is still single-process. A worker that measures under `-n auto` would report a speedup it did not cause. The before and after figures must therefore both be taken in the same serial run of the same command, recorded by this issue, rather than compared against any older number.

## Concrete locations
Cited by symbol, since line numbers drift. In `tests/conftest.py`, the `seeded_3_issues()` fixture currently runs `bd init` plus three `bd create` calls. The per-test workspace builders that follow the same pattern are `_seed_repo()` in `tests/test_grind_state_delta.py`, `_seed_repo()` in `tests/test_grind_worker_timeout.py`, the three inline `bd init` call sites in `tests/test_grind.py`, and the equivalent in `tests/test_grind_orphan_policy.py`. Record the pattern in `docs/testing.md` next to the phase-aware command table. Add the fixture assertions to `tests/test_test_policy.py`.

## Compatibility constraints
Copied workspaces must work from a different absolute path than the template, on macos as well as linux. Tests keep their current isolation: no test may observe issues created by another. The bd binary must be able to read a workspace it did not create in place. Any fixture asserting on a specific issue prefix, or on `bd init` behaviour itself, keeps its current setup. The suite must still collect and pass identically under `-n auto`, since workers use it even though this measurement does not.

## Ordered steps
1. Record a fresh serial baseline for the measurement command below, before changing anything, and post it as a comment on this issue.
2. Add a session-scoped fixture that runs `bd init` once into a template directory and yields its path.
3. Add a seeded variant that bakes the grind fixtures issues into the template before any test copies it.
4. Add a function-scoped fixture that copies a requested template into `tmp_path`, preserving symlinks.
5. Migrate `seeded_3_issues` and the per-file workspace builders to consume the copy fixture.
6. Re-run the same command serially, post the after figure, and confirm no test performs `bd init` at test scope except those explicitly exercising it.
7. Document the copy-a-template pattern in the testing guide.

## Dependencies
No issue dependency. Related to the parallel-sweep work, which is a different lever on the same cost and must not be conflated with this one. Consumers are every grind-family test module.

## Edge cases
A template must not be mutated by any test, so the copy direction needs enforcing rather than assuming. A workspace carrying absolute paths in its own config would break when copied and must be detected rather than silently pointing at the template. `bd init` also creates an incidental git repository whose branch is normalized today, so the template must carry the normalized branch or the normalization must move to the copy step. Tests running under xdist must not share a copy destination. If a copied workspace is unusable on any platform, the fixture must fail loudly rather than falling back to a per-test init that hides the regression.

## Plan-gap guidance
If copied Dolt workspaces prove unreliable on any supported platform, record PLAN-GAP with the platform, the bd version, and the observed failure, and route to planning. Do not paper over it with a per-test init fallback, because that silently restores the cost this issue exists to remove.
acceptance_criteria:
## Observable criteria
- AC-1: A session-scoped template fixture exists and runs bd init exactly once per test session.
- AC-2: Grind-family fixtures obtain their workspace by copying a template rather than running bd init at test scope.
- AC-3: A copied workspace is fully functional: listing works and creating an issue returns a new identifier.
- AC-4: A before and after wall clock for the same serial command are both recorded as comments, together with the per-test setup cost removed and the resulting ceiling on the measuring host.
- AC-5: The testing guide documents the copy-a-template pattern for new tests.

## Criterion checks
- AC-1: Run `uv run pytest tests/test_test_policy.py -k template_workspace_initialized_once -q`.
- AC-2: Run `rg -n "\"init\"" tests/test_grind.py tests/test_grind_state_delta.py tests/test_grind_worker_timeout.py tests/test_grind_orphan_policy.py tests/conftest.py` and confirm only fixtures that explicitly exercise bd init remain.
- AC-3: Run `uv run pytest tests/test_test_policy.py -k copied_workspace_is_usable -q`.
- AC-4: Inspect `bd comments ortus-apmf` and confirm both figures, the per-test setup saving, and the host ceiling are recorded; the reduction is reported, not thresholded.
- AC-5: Run `uv run pytest tests/test_test_policy.py -k testing_guide_documents_template_pattern -q`.

## Targeted tests
Run `uv run pytest tests/test_test_policy.py tests/test_grind_state_delta.py tests/test_grind_corrections.py --test-timeout=180 -q`.
notes:
Per-invocation bd cost measured 2026-08-07: bd init 1621-1750 ms, bd create 1196 ms, bd list --json 1013 ms, bd show 817 ms, bd ready --json 730 ms; git init 3 ms, git status 2 ms. Template validation: workspace is 0.4 MB across 102 entries, shutil.copytree measured 20-21 ms across three runs, and inside a copy bd list and bd create both returned rc=0 with a fresh id.

Deliberately NO stored wall-clock baseline. The 2026-08-07 figure (865 s, 46 tests) is void: the suite has since gained tests/test_core_runstate.py and tests/test_dashboard.py, and pytest-xdist landed as a dev dependency (pyproject.toml, kept out of addopts on purpose). AC-4 therefore requires the worker to measure before and after itself, serially, in the same session. Cited line numbers were removed after three of five drifted within a day; locations are given by symbol instead.

This issue removes bd calls. Parallelism is the other lever on the same cost and is tracked separately; do not combine them.

`uv run pytest tests/test_grind.py tests/test_grind_state_delta.py tests/test_grind_corrections.py -q --durations=20`
- before: 38 passed in 595.34s (shell wall 9m01s)
- after:  38 passed in 521.18s (shell wall 7m54s) -> 12.5% faster

AC-4 (>=25%) is NOT met on this host, and cannot be met within this issue's scope here. Per-test fixed setup was one bd init (~1.5s) plus per-test bd create(s) (~1.2s each) = ~2.6s, against tests that spend 16-43s inside grind's own in-loop bd traffic; eliminating setup entirely caps the reduction near 17% on this host. The same ~2.6s removal is ~35% on the CI hosts the notes measured (grind-family tests at 6.8-8.4s), so the criterion is host-dependent rather than unmet by the implementation. Flagging for the verifier instead of restating the criterion.

Design note found against repository reality: `bd init` writes an ABSOLUTE `core.hooksPath` into .git/config, so a plain copy would run - and let git write through - the template's own hooks. The copy helper repoints it at the copy and fails loudly on any other absolute reference to the template (the documented "workspace carrying absolute paths" edge case).

Other criteria: AC-1, AC-2, AC-3, AC-5 met. Suites run green: the three AC-4 modules (38 passed), worker_timeout + orphan_policy + finalization + e2e_smoke + test_test_policy (37 passed), and `-m fast --test-timeout=30 --enforce-duration-budget` (333 passed).

title: Restore the comprehensive CI gate to green
description:
## Objective
Make the comprehensive hermetic pytest gate pass again on every matrix job, so main stops landing commits on top of a red build.

## Behavioral context
The gate has failed on every push since 2026-08-07T16:45Z, across all six matrix jobs (ubuntu and macos, Python 3.10, 3.11, 3.12), including beads-sync commits that change no code. Run 31223899753 reports 12 failed, 482 passed. The grind loop never noticed because workers run targeted subsets and the not-slow marker, while CI runs the fast-or-integration set with a duration budget on a bare runner. After this change the same gate command passes locally under CI-like conditions and the workflow returns to green.

## Behavioral context addendum
Three independent defects are bundled deliberately: each one alone still leaves the gate red, and a single gate run verifies all three, so splitting them would triple a ten-minute verification for no isolation benefit.

## Resolved plan gap (routing pass, 2026-08-08)
Verification raised the seven over-budget parametrizations as an unresolved deviation: the candidate marks them `slow` rather than optimizing them, and `tests/conftest.py:99` shows the marker exempts a test from the budget rather than satisfying it. That branch is now decided, not left to a worker: the fallback the design already authorized is taken, and AC-2 is reworded so it states the accepted outcome instead of an outcome the fallback can never produce. The marker is the sanctioned waiver — `pyproject.toml:93` documents `slow` as "tests allowed to exceed the 5s per-test hermetic budget" — and `tests/test_grind.py:29` sets a module-level `pytestmark = pytest.mark.integration`, so `-m "fast or integration"` keeps all seven cases inside the gate. The waiver removes the duration signal for this one test, not its coverage. No worker is authorized to reopen this by deleting cases, weakening assertions, or lowering `_HERMETIC_TEST_BUDGET_SECONDS`.
design:
## Readiness schema
v1

## Scope
Fix the three defect classes that fail the gate: missing git identity in two test fixtures, seven over-budget parametrizations of one test, and headless parsing of the CLI help output.

## Non-goals
No change to the CI workflow matrix, the marker taxonomy, or the duration budget itself: the budget is correct and the tests must meet it or take the documented `slow` waiver. No change to the finalization code that pzfd.4 and pzfd.5 shipped; the finalization failures are a fixture gap, not a product defect. Preventing recurrence is tracked separately. Sandbox and network-allowlist configuration is out of scope: the candidate's `.claude/settings.json` hunk (wildcard `*.blob.core.windows.net` and two Actions hosts) is a durable permission grant unrelated to any of the three defects and must not land under this issue.

## Resolved decisions
The seven over-budget cases are all parametrizations of one test. The original preference was to optimize the shared fixture rather than mark it slow, with the slow marker named as the accepted fallback if optimization could not bring the shared setup under five seconds. That fallback is now the resolved decision, taken on measurement rather than convenience: the profile recorded at `tests/test_grind.py:463-474` puts the shared setup at 3.4s (bd init 1.3s, branch plus bd create 1.1s, git baseline commit 1.0s), and only the bd init and create pair is shareable across cases because each case mutates its own repo. Subtracting the shareable 2.4s from the CI-measured 5.14s to 8.07s still leaves the slowest case near 7s, so no fixture-level optimization reaches the budget; the remaining cost is grind's own subprocess traffic, which is the behavior this test exists to pin. The CI figures are authoritative for the budget judgement; the 17-26s per-case figure in that comment is a developer-machine measurement used only to derive the setup-to-total ratio, and the two must not be conflated. `@pytest.mark.slow` therefore stays on `test_verifier_report_and_mutation_isolation`, scoped to that one test rather than the module. This is a waiver of the duration signal, not of coverage: `pyproject.toml:93` documents the marker as exactly this, `tests/conftest.py:88-105` skips the budget check for slow-marked items, and `tests/test_grind.py:29` keeps the module `integration` so `-m "fast or integration"` still selects all seven cases in the gate. Established precedent for slow-marked integration modules already exists at `tests/test_grind_finalization.py:38`, `tests/test_plan.py:23`, and `tests/test_grind_orphan_policy.py:35`. Git identity is set in the fixtures that lack it rather than globally in the workflow, so the tests stay hermetic and self-describing on any machine.

## Concrete locations
Add git identity to `_seed_repo()` in `tests/test_grind_state_delta.py` at line 52 and to the repo fixture in `tests/test_grind_corrections.py`, mirroring the existing `git config user.email` calls already present at `tests/test_grind.py` line 498 and `tests/test_grind_recovery.py` line 96. Apply the resolved slow waiver plus its profiling rationale directly above `test_verifier_report_and_mutation_isolation()` in `tests/test_grind.py`. The budget gate that honours the marker is `pytest_runtest_makereport` in `tests/conftest.py` lines 88 to 105, with `_HERMETIC_TEST_BUDGET_SECONDS` at line 25; the marker's documented meaning is `pyproject.toml` line 93. Fix headless help parsing for `test_help_keeps_existing_verb_order_with_new_verbs_appended()` and the parametrization source at `tests/test_cli_verbs.py` line 67. The gate command itself is `.github/workflows/test.yml` lines 81 to 86.

## Compatibility constraints
The gate command and its flags stay exactly as the workflow spells them, so a local pass predicts a CI pass. Tests must pass both with and without an ambient global git identity, since developer machines have one and runners do not. No test may be deleted or its assertion weakened to reach green, and the slow waiver may not be used to drop a case from collection. Behavior must hold on ubuntu and macos across Python 3.10 through 3.12. The waiver must stay scoped to the one parametrized test, not applied at module level, so the rest of `tests/test_grind.py` keeps its duration signal.

## Ordered steps
1. Reproduce headlessly with `GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL=/dev/null` so the missing-identity failures appear locally.
2. Add git identity configuration to the two fixtures that lack it and confirm the four finalization assertions pass.
3. Keep the resolved slow waiver on the seven parametrizations with its measured rationale beside it, and confirm by collect-only that all seven remain selected by the gate's marker expression.
4. Make the help-output verb parsing robust without a TTY so the parsed list is non-empty and the empty-parameter-set skip disappears.
5. Run the exact workflow gate command locally and confirm zero failures.

## Dependencies

title: Add an issue-authoring contract section to the bundled AGENTS.md template
description:
## Objective
Make the readiness contract part of the always-loaded agent instructions that ortus init renders into a new repo.

## Behavioral context
The bundled AGENTS.md template documents bd usage and the ortus grind orchestrator but never mentions that non-epic issues must satisfy readiness schema v1, so an agent following it faithfully still produces unworkable issues. After this change the rendered AGENTS.md states the contract next to the bd guidance and names the command that prints the full text.
design:
## Readiness schema
v1

## Scope
Add a short issue-authoring contract subsection to the bundled template, anchored to the existing bd section, naming the required fields and pointing at the printer command for full detail.

## Non-goals
Do not paste the full generated contract into the template: the rendered file is loaded in full every session and a stale copy would drift from readiness.py between ortus upgrades. Do not touch the legacy copier template under `template/`, which is already slated for deletion by ortus-sod1.2.

## Concrete locations
Edit `src/ortus/templates/AGENTS.md.jinja` under the `## Issue tracking with bd` heading at line 8, above the `## Orchestrator (ortus grind)` section at line 21. Rendering flows through `render_all()` and the `BUNDLED_TEMPLATES` entry for AGENTS.md in `src/ortus/core/init_render.py`. Cover in `tests/test_init_render.py` and `tests/test_instruction_files_per_backend.py`.

## Resolved decisions
The template carries a condensed contract plus the printer command rather than the full spec, so the always-on context cost stays small and the authoritative text stays generated. The section sits with the bd guidance rather than the orchestrator section because the failure happens at authoring time, not at grind time.

## Compatibility constraints
The template must render for both the claude and codex backends and under every project type in the render matrix, with StrictUndefined still satisfied. CLAUDE.md stays a pointer to AGENTS.md and gains no copy of the contract. Existing repos need a re-render to pick this up, which is why the bd memory leaf covers retrofit.

## Ordered steps
1. Draft the contract subsection naming the description, design, and acceptance fields and the epic exemption.
2. Insert it into the bundled template under the bd section, keeping jinja variables valid under StrictUndefined.
3. Reference the printer command as the source of the full contract.
4. Extend the render tests to assert the section is present for both backends.

## Dependencies
Blocked by the ortus spec verb leaf, whose command name the section cites. Related to the bd memory leaf, which carries the same pointer for repos that will not re-render.

## Edge cases
A repo initialized with --force re-renders AGENTS.md and must not duplicate the section. Codex reads AGENTS.md and not CLAUDE.md, so nothing load-bearing may land only in CLAUDE.md. Literal braces or jinja-like syntax in the example text must not break rendering.

## Plan-gap guidance
If the condensed section cannot state the contract without effectively restating the whole generated spec, record PLAN-GAP with the minimum wording tried and route to planning rather than embedding the full generated text.

## Criterion checks
- AC-1: Run `uv run pytest tests/test_init_render.py -k authoring_contract -q`.
- AC-2: Run `uv run pytest tests/test_instruction_files_per_backend.py -q`.
- AC-3: Run `uv run pytest tests/test_init_render.py -q`.

## Targeted tests
Run `uv run pytest tests/test_init_render.py tests/test_instruction_files_per_backend.py --test-timeout=30 --enforce-duration-budget`.

title: Let Codex grind resume owned dirty candidates after timeout
description: Objective: remove the generic clean-checkout veto from Codex grind while preserving operator edits. Behavioral context: a verifier timeout currently leaves valid candidate edits, reverts the claim, and the next preflight mislabels those edits as unowned, halting the queue.
design: Scope: add a persistent per-repository Codex transaction baseline/journal and use it in commands/grind.py plus core/git.py. Non-goals: full structured verifier verdict work remains in the existing transaction feature. Concrete locations: src/ortus/commands/grind.py::_checkpoint_codex_preflight and grind(); src/ortus/core/git.py::GitClient; a focused transaction module; tests/test_core_git.py and timeout regressions. Resolved decisions: pre-existing dirty paths are a preserved baseline, not a startup error; only newly transaction-owned paths may be committed; a timed-out claimed issue keeps durable ownership evidence and resumes deterministically. Compatibility constraints: Claude behavior remains unchanged; no Windows paths; existing clean Codex flow remains unchanged. Ordered steps: 1. Record baseline HEAD and dirty paths before claim. 2. Persist claimed issue and candidate paths around worker execution. 3. On timeout or restart, recognize matching state and resume instead of generic halt. 4. Commit only owned paths and retain baseline dirty paths. Dependencies: builds on readiness issue ortus-pzfd.3. Edge cases: untracked baseline files, staged baseline paths, worker changes a baseline path, HEAD mismatch, extra paths after timeout, missing/corrupt journal. Plan gap guidance: halt only when identity cannot be proven without absorbing unrelated work.
acceptance_criteria: Observable criteria: AC-1 Codex grind starts with a dirty checkout and preserves those baseline paths. AC-2 Timeout-after-edit retains issue ownership and restart does not emit the generic unowned-worktree halt. AC-3 successful close commits only transaction-owned paths. AC-4 mismatched HEAD or paths produces a precise safety diagnostic. Criterion checks: AC-1 through focused dirty-baseline integration test; AC-2 through timeout/restart integration test; AC-3 through commit path assertions; AC-4 through journal mismatch tests. Targeted tests: uv run pytest tests/test_core_git.py tests/test_grind_worker_timeout.py. Tests covering the changed surface must pass; CI catches regressions elsewhere.
close_reason: Codex grind now accepts dirty baselines and deterministically resumes timeout-owned candidates without absorbing operator paths

title: Automatically checkpoint tracker-only startup changes
description: Codex Grind currently checks for a clean worktree only after its startup bd queries. Beads may auto-export and stage .beads/issues.jsonl during those queries, causing Grind to reject a repository that was clean when the command began. Add tracker-aware preflight that distinguishes generated Beads exports from source/operator changes and creates a separate housekeeping commit before selecting an issue.
design: After startup snapshot and orphan reconciliation, inspect Git porcelain state including staged, unstaged, and untracked paths. When every dirty path is an explicitly allowlisted generated tracker export, stage only those paths, create a 'chore: sync beads state' commit, and apply normal integration-branch push discipline. Never use git add -A. If any non-tracker path is dirty, retain the safety halt and report the exact paths; mixed tracker/source state must not create a partial housekeeping commit. The preflight must be idempotent when no changes exist or when tracker content is already committed. Keep this initial fix separate from the later transaction journal that owns timeout candidates.
acceptance_criteria: A Codex grind whose startup bd operations stage only generated tracker exports automatically creates and pushes one housekeeping commit, then proceeds to issue selection. A clean tree creates no housekeeping commit. Untracked, unstaged, or staged source changes still halt with exact path diagnostics. Mixed tracker and source changes do not commit either category. The housekeeping operation stages only allowlisted tracker paths and never uses git add -A. Tests reproduce the current staged .beads/issues.jsonl case, mixed dirt, commit failure, and idempotent restart. Tests covering the changed surface must pass; CI catches regressions elsewhere.
close_reason: Tracker-only startup state now receives a separate automatic housekeeping commit and push

title: Prevent oversized Claude /goal conditions and retry loops
description: Claude grind currently injects the complete bd issue packet and worker procedure into the /goal condition. Thorough issues can exceed Claude Code's 4,000-character goal-condition limit. Claude then returns a synthetic success with zero turns, and grind misclassifies the unchanged in-progress issue as an orphan claim and retries indefinitely.
design: Keep the complete implementation packet in bd. For harness-selected Claude work, build a compact /goal condition containing the exact claimed issue ID, the terminal condition, and an instruction to load the authoritative packet with bd show. Codex continues receiving the complete plain worker prompt. Add a defensive transcript/result classifier so a zero-turn goal rejection is treated as a worker failure and does not enter the orphan-retry path.

The prompt names only the harness-selected issue and directs the worker to retrieve its full bd packet without selecting other work. Codex retains the complete injected issue packet. A synthetic zero-turn Claude result reporting an invalid or oversized goal condition terminates with an actionable error and restores the claim instead of retrying. Tests cover a bd issue larger than 4,000 characters, backend-specific prompt composition, and rejection-loop prevention. Tests covering the changed surface must pass; shared core changes require the full local suite.
close_reason: Bounded Claude goal conditions now load thorough packets from bd, and zero-turn goal rejection halts after restoring the claim

title: Codex backend: 'codex exec' does not honor /goal — agent shells into goal.sh, recursion/deadlock (Q1 FAILS)
description:
Live probe (scripts/codex-m2-acceptance.sh --probe, 2026-07-19) disproves the core PRD assumption that 'codex exec "/goal <cond>"' runs a self-terminating goal loop like 'claude -p "/goal <cond>"'. It does NOT.

WHAT HAPPENS: codex treats the '/goal <condition>' string as an ordinary prompt (there is no native /goal in 'codex exec' — the /goal command suite is an INTERACTIVE TUI slash-command only). Reading the project's AGENTS.md + goal-prompt framing that goal.sh is 'the orchestrator', the codex agent's plan is to RUN ./ortus/goal.sh, which spawns another codex, which shells into goal.sh again -> recursion -> deadlock on .beads/ralph.flock (the single-loop lock).

EVIDENCE (codex's own --json event stream, probe.jsonl):
- agent_message: 'drive the ready queue through the required Goal orchestrator.'
- command_execution: /bin/bash -lc ./ortus/goal.sh
- agent_message (verbatim): 'The worker recursively invoked a second Goal loop and deadlocked on the repository single-loop lock.'
- retried: ./ortus/goal.sh -c '...you are already the worker... do not invoke ./ortus/goal.sh...' (still shelling into the orchestrator)
- exit 124 (180s timeout)

This is exactly the earlier 'spinning' the operator saw in the full acceptance run (a new goal.sh + log every ~13s).

NOT a creds issue: the auth bridge (copy ~/.codex/auth.json into the project .codex/) works — codex authenticated and ran. Separately, codex warns it refuses to create PATH aliases when CODEX_HOME is under /tmp (cosmetic).
design:
TWO root causes, both must be fixed:
1. Strip the /goal prefix for codex. The codex goal-role prompt (backend.sh _backend_argv_codex) currently passes the SAME '/goal <condition>' string as claude. For codex it must pass the condition as a plain worker directive WITHOUT '/goal' — there is no native goal loop to trigger, and the literal '/goal' adds nothing but confusion.
2. Reframe the prompt/AGENTS for codex so the agent is the WORKER, not a launcher. It must be told explicitly: you ARE the autonomous worker; drive the bd ready queue directly (claim/implement/verify/commit/close); do NOT invoke ./ortus/goal.sh or ortus/ralph.sh. The claude goal-prompt/AGENTS 'run the orchestrator' framing is Claude-only.

Then either (a) let codex's own turn loop run to evidence-based completion against the condition, or (b) drive a shell-side per-task loop (revive the ralph one-task-per-invocation shape) if codex won't self-continue across the whole queue. Determine which in the redo probe.
acceptance_criteria: CONDITIONS: (1) a single codex invocation drives the tiny-3-task queue: its --json event stream shows it claiming/closing bd issues DIRECTLY (bd close command_execution items), NOT a './ortus/goal.sh' command; (2) no recursion — grep the event stream and logs/ for './ortus/goal.sh' returns nothing; (3) it terminates on its own (or the shell loop terminates) with bd ready == [] and all 3 closed. TESTING: re-run scripts/codex-m2-acceptance.sh --probe after the prompt/argv fix; assert the histogram shows bd-work command_executions and zero goal.sh invocations; then run the full acceptance and confirm queue-zero without spinning.

title: grind drifts onto a feature branch and strands all work there (closed issues never reach main/prod)
description: CRITICAL: on a real prdpad run, grind's local checkout ended up on a feature branch (prdpad-01v-clerk-dark) and committed ~12 iterations of work there, pushing THAT branch to origin while origin/main stayed stale. Deploys come from main, so a dozen 'closed' bd issues (UI fixes, a refresh-durability data fix, two epics) were never deployed and the operator kept seeing them as still-broken. main was cleanly fast-forwardable to the branch tip (no divergence), confirming the work was simply stranded, not conflicting. Likely cause: a worker ran 'git checkout -b <branch>' (or similar) and grind never returned to / merged into main; subsequent iterations inherited the wrong branch. The session-close protocol says 'merged to main locally' but that did not happen here.
design: Make grind branch-disciplined and fail-loud: (1) the orchestrator should pin/verify the working branch (main, or a known integration branch) at the start of EACH iteration and refuse to proceed / re-checkout if a worker left it on a stray branch; (2) after a worker closes an issue, ensure its commit is on main (merge/ff) and PUSHED to origin/main, not to an ad-hoc branch; (3) detect the 'local ahead of origin/main on a non-main branch' condition and surface it loudly rather than silently continuing; (4) consider forbidding workers from creating/switching branches at all. Net: a closed issue must always be on origin/main (deployable), or the loop halts with a clear error.
acceptance_criteria: DONE WHEN: grind keeps the working branch on main (or re-asserts it each iteration), every closed issue's commit lands on origin/main, and a stray-branch / main-behind condition is detected and surfaced instead of silently stranding work.
notes: FORENSICS (from prdpad run grind-20260530-120841.log): the branch was created 2026-05-30 ~12:29 by the prdpad-01v worker, which at its commit step ran exactly: 'git checkout -b prdpad-01v-clerk-dark 2>/dev/null; git add -A && git commit -q -m "..."'. It branched from main (6b1a369) and committed the 01v fix to the new branch instead of main. No narrated reason — looks like a generic feature-branch-per-change commit habit, not intentional. Because grind never re-asserts the working branch between iterations, every later worker inherited prdpad-01v-clerk-dark and kept committing+pushing there, orphaning origin/main at 6b1a369 (82 commits stranded). Reinforces the fix: re-pin the working branch to main at the START of each iteration (or forbid workers from running git checkout/switch -b), so a single worker's stray branch can't silently capture the whole run.
close_reason: grind branch discipline: re-assert integration branch each iteration (startup/pre-iter/post-close), HALT loudly on stray-branch-with-commits or detached HEAD, push integration branch so every close lands on origin; workers told not to switch branches

title: release.yml: pyproject.toml has hardcoded version=0.1.0; every tag builds 0.1.0 wheel and PyPI rejects 'file already exists'
description:
**Repro:** `git tag v0.1.2 && git push origin v0.1.2` → release workflow runs → `publish-pypi` job fails with:

```
ERROR  HTTPError: 400 Bad Request from https://upload.pypi.org/legacy/
       400 File already exists ('ortus-0.1.0-py3-none-any.whl', ...)
```

**Root cause:** `pyproject.toml:7` has `version = "0.1.0"` hardcoded. The build step reads it verbatim, so:

- Tagging `v0.1.1` → builds `ortus-0.1.1`? No — built `ortus-0.1.0` UNLESS someone manually edited pyproject.toml between v0.1.0 and v0.1.1 (history shows 0.1.0.dev0 ↔ 0.1.0 churn).
- Tagging `v0.1.2` → builds `ortus-0.1.0` again → PyPI rejects because that filename was already uploaded.

The git tag is purely cosmetic from the build's perspective; it doesn't propagate into the artifact name or PyPI metadata.

**Blast radius:** **every future PyPI release is blocked** until this is fixed. The only path to ship a new version today is (a) manually bump `pyproject.toml`, commit, tag, push (operator discipline that's easy to forget), or (b) wire up dynamic versioning so the tag IS the version.

**Workflow run (for the report):** https://github.com/who/ortus/actions/runs/26002863880
acceptance_criteria:
**Approach: dynamic versioning from the git tag.** Choose one of:

**Option A — `hatch-vcs`** (recommended if pyproject.toml already uses hatchling as the build backend; the prior PyPI bug noted hatchling was wired up). Add:

```toml
[build-system]
requires = ["hatchling", "hatch-vcs"]
build-backend = "hatchling.build"

[project]
dynamic = ["version"]

[tool.hatch.version]
source = "vcs"
```

And remove the static `version = "0.1.0"` line. Verify with `uv build` locally on a tagged commit: the produced `dist/*.whl` should have the tag's version (sans the leading `v`).

**Option B — `setuptools_scm`** (only if pyproject uses setuptools as build backend). Different config but same idea.

**Option C — manual bump-before-tag** (the operator's-discipline path). NOT recommended — easy to forget, exactly the kind of foot-gun the build system should remove. Document it only if (A) and (B) are blocked.

**Verify after the fix:**

1. `uv build` locally on an untagged commit → version like `0.1.2.dev3+g<sha>` (dev marker)
2. `git tag v0.1.3 && uv build` → version exactly `0.1.3`
3. Push the tag; observe `publish-pypi` succeeds and `ortus 0.1.3` appears at https://pypi.org/project/ortus/

**Tests:**

- Add a smoke test that runs `uv build` and asserts the produced wheel's version matches the current git description. Targeted test per ortus-4ni7.
- Verify `tests/test_install_sh.py` still passes (it references the installed package version somewhere).

**Out of scope:**
- Re-publishing the orphaned v0.1.0 / v0.1.1 / v0.1.2 tags (those go forward only).
- Backfilling intermediate PyPI versions.
- The `ortus-tper` trusted-publisher setup (separate, was a prerequisite).

Standard close: commit on main; `git push`; then verify with the next tag (v0.1.3+). Commit message must not contain the protected term.
close_reason: Switched pyproject.toml to hatch-vcs dynamic versioning so each git tag produces a uniquely-versioned wheel; added uv-build smoke test as regression guard

title: ortus init: bd-init phase hangs ~55s+ on fresh dir; bare 'bd init' completes in 1s
description:
**Operator-confirmed mechanism (corrected from initial pipe-deadlock theory):** the bd init step hangs because **bd asks two interactive yes/no questions** that the operator can't see and can't answer.

When the operator ran ortus init from a TTY (visible output below for diagnostic purposes — does not happen normally because `capture_output=True` swallows it), bd's actual prompts surfaced:

```
[ortus init] target: /home/[REDACTED]/code/foo
[ortus init] creating .beads/ workspace (prefix=foo)
  ✓ Initialized git repository
  Repository ID: bfe6a13c
  Clone ID: 41f1c948825ca56e
Contributing to someone else's repo? [y/N]:

▶ Auto-export keeps .beads/issues.jsonl up to date after every write command.
  This is useful for viewers (bv) and git-based sync workflows.

Enable auto-export? [Y/n]:
  ✓ Auto-export enabled → .beads/issues.jsonl
  ...
```

Two prompts. Each one waits on stdin.

**Why the auto-detection in `bd --non-interactive` doesn't save us:** bd's help says "Skip all interactive prompts (auto-detected in CI or non-TTY environments)". The detection presumably checks whether **stdin** is a TTY. But under Python's `subprocess.run(args, capture_output=True)`, only stdout/stderr get redirected to pipes — **stdin is inherited from the parent ortus process**. If the operator runs `ortus init` from a terminal, stdin IS a TTY, and bd happily prompts on it. ortus has captured stdout, so the prompt is invisible. bd waits forever on stdin that the operator doesn't know to type to.

**Code site:** `src/ortus/commands/init.py:30`:

```python
subprocess.run(args, cwd=str(repo), check=True, capture_output=True)
```

**bd flags relevant to the fix:**

```
--non-interactive      Skip all interactive prompts (auto-detected in CI or non-TTY environments)
--role string          Set beads role without prompting: "maintainer" or "contributor"
--agents-profile       AGENTS.md profile (so the AGENTS.md generation step doesn't prompt either)
```

**Blast radius:** every brand-new operator who runs `ortus init <fresh-dir>`. P0.
acceptance_criteria:
**Status: re-opened.** Part 2 of the original AC (drop `capture_output=True`) already shipped in commit 6cc5843. Part 1 (add `--non-interactive` to the bd argv) was never applied — confirmed by `grep -n 'non-interactive' src/ortus/commands/init.py` returning empty.

**Only Part 1 remains — add `--non-interactive` and any required co-flags to the bd init subprocess.**

In `src/ortus/commands/init.py` (around line 30, the `_bd_init` helper), update the bd argv from:

```python
args = ["bd", "init", "--prefix", prefix]
```

to:

```python
args = ["bd", "init", "--non-interactive", "--prefix", prefix]
```

Optionally also pass `--role maintainer` and `--agents-profile minimal` if the resulting defaults don't already match what ortus init users want (check bd's auto-defaults first; only override if needed).

**Why this is necessary even though Part 2 shipped:** Part 2 made bd's prompts visible to the operator (good — they can answer). But the project principle (bd memory `ortus-design-principle-cli-verbs-default-to-non`) is that ortus verbs default to non-interactive — they should never prompt. With Part 1 applied, `ortus init` runs headlessly: works in scripts, CI, and `ortus grind` without operator input. If a future operator genuinely wants the interactive bd flow, that's a separate `ortus init --interactive` mode (out of scope for this issue).

**Verify after the change:**

1. `rm -rf /tmp/btt3-verify && uv run --project . ortus init /tmp/btt3-verify </dev/null` — should complete cleanly in seconds with NO prompts blocking on stdin.
2. Manual run in a TTY: `rm -rf /tmp/btt3-tty && ortus init /tmp/btt3-tty` — should also complete without any "[y/N]" prompts appearing.

**Tests:**

- Add or extend a test in `tests/test_init.py` that runs `ortus init <tmpdir>` with `stdin=/dev/null` (or similar non-TTY stdin) and asserts it completes in under 10s with exit 0. This catches any future regression where bd starts expecting interactive input again.
- Per ortus-4ni7: targeted tests only (`uv run pytest tests/test_init.py`); skip the full suite.

**Out of scope:**
- `ortus init --interactive` mode (separate issue if wanted).
- Any other progress / output behavior (covered by ortus-s60a).

Standard close: commit on main; `git push`. Commit message must not contain the protected term.
close_reason: Added --non-interactive to bd init subprocess; bd now uses sensible defaults (role=maintainer, auto-export=enabled) instead of blocking on hidden stdin prompts. Verified end-to-end: ortus init <fresh-dir> </dev/null completes in 1.26s. Tests assert argv + end-to-end completion <10s with closed stdin.

title: Drop Windows from supported platforms; scope NFR-008 down to Linux + macOS
description:
**Operator decision 2026-05-17**: drop Windows from the supported-platforms list for ortus. CI matrix shrinks to Linux + macOS. All currently-open Windows-specific bd issues close as "out of scope; reopen if/when a real Windows user surfaces with a concrete use case."

**Why now:**

- **5+ reactive CI iterations on Windows-only failures** with no convergence: each fix exposes the next Windows-specific layer (PowerShell shell defaults → fcntl POSIX-only → utf-8 encoding → fake-claude shim → command-line-length limits → ortus init exit-1 → grind stream-leak → ...). Cost is roughly 1-2 iteration cycles per push when Windows is in the matrix.
- **No actual Windows users yet.** PRD NFR-008's cross-platform promise was operator aspiration, not user-driven. There's no person on the other end waiting for ortus on Windows native.
- **Linux + macOS cover the modern dev demographic** (~90%). The "I'm on Windows native, no WSL2" cohort is real but small; they can use WSL2 if they want ortus (or migrate to Mac/Linux for ortus-related work specifically).
- **The codebase has dense POSIX-bias** that wasn't caught during dev because there's no Windows dev environment. Fixing this properly requires either (a) one operator with a Windows env doing a sustained audit-and-fix pass, or (b) accepting weeks of CI-iteration overhead. Neither is on the operator's roadmap.
- **Decision is reversible.** Re-adding Windows is a matrix-edit + bug-bash. If a real Windows user shows up later with a concrete need, the support can be added back driven by their actual use case.
- **PR #11 is blocked on Windows-only failures** while Linux + macOS are stable. Dropping Windows unblocks the merge of a substantial body of work (Phase 1-4 of PRD-ortus-global-cli, plus the architectural pivot, plus 6+ bug fixes).

**Bigger principle:** the ortus project's whole reason for existing is to help the operator (currently solo). Promising Windows support that requires unmaintained-by-anyone deferred work is worse than honest scope-down. "Linux + macOS, fully tested, validated" beats "Linux + macOS + Windows, but Windows is theoretically broken."
design:
**Five concrete changes, all in one commit:**

**1. Remove Windows from the CI matrix.** Edit `.github/workflows/test.yml`:

```yaml
# Before:
matrix:
  os: [ubuntu-latest, macos-latest, windows-latest]
  python-version: ['3.10', '3.11', '3.12']
  include:
    - os: windows-latest
      continue-on-error: true

# After:
matrix:
  os: [ubuntu-latest, macos-latest]
  python-version: ['3.10', '3.11', '3.12']
# (remove the include: block entirely; Windows is gone)
```

Also: any Windows-conditional install step can be removed (e.g., the `Install bd (beads) — Windows` step using pwsh). Cleanup pass.

**2. Update PRD-ortus-global-cli.md NFR-008.** Edit `prd/PRD-ortus-global-cli.md`:

Find: `**[P1] NFR-008** — The package shall be cross-platform: Linux, macOS, Windows. CI tests on all three.`

Replace with:
```
**[P1] NFR-008** — The package shall be cross-platform: Linux + macOS. CI tests on both. Windows is NOT supported (decision 2026-05-17; see bd issue ortus-XXX). Windows users should use WSL2 to access a Linux environment for ortus.
```

Add a `Revision` line at top of the PRD metadata noting the 2026-05-17 scope-down.

**3. Close the open Windows-specific bd issues as "out of scope."** Identify and close:

```bash
# Find any still-open Windows-related bd issues
bd list --status=open --label=windows 2>&1

# Expected (as of 2026-05-17): ortus-rlob, possibly others that linked to windows
# Close each with:
bd close <id> --force --reason="Windows support dropped 2026-05-17 (see this issue's ID). Out of scope going forward; reopen if/when a real Windows user surfaces with a concrete use case driving the requirement."
```

Also note this issue's ID in each closure reason so the cross-reference is traceable.

**4. Update README.md** to mention Windows is not supported:

Add a "Supported platforms" subsection in the install section:

```markdown
### Supported platforms

- Linux (Ubuntu 22.04+, similar distros)
- macOS (latest two major versions)
- **Windows is not supported.** Windows users should run ortus inside WSL2 (Windows Subsystem for Linux), where ortus runs as a normal Linux process.
```

**5. Update AGENTS.md (or equivalent)** with one line noting the decision so AI agents working on the codebase don't accidentally try to add Windows-compat code:

```markdown
## Supported platforms
Linux + macOS only. Windows was dropped 2026-05-17 (see bd issue ortus-XXX). Do not add Windows-specific code paths without explicit operator direction.
```

**Acceptance (local-verify per ortus-ctun protocol):**

(1) `.github/workflows/test.yml` matrix has only `ubuntu-latest` and `macos-latest`; no `windows-latest`; no `continue-on-error: true` Windows include; no Windows-specific install steps.

(2) `python -c 'import yaml; yaml.safe_load(open(".github/workflows/test.yml"))'` exits 0 (YAML still parses).

(3) `grep -E 'NFR-008|Windows' prd/PRD-ortus-global-cli.md` shows the updated NFR-008 with the Linux+macOS-only scope and the Windows-dropped note.

(4) `bd list --status=open --label=windows` returns empty (or only contains issues that should NOT be closed — verify on a per-issue basis; default is "close them all").

(5) `grep -iE 'windows|WSL2' README.md` returns at least one match in the install section.

(6) `grep -iE 'windows|supported platforms' AGENTS.md` returns at least one match.

(7) The change is committed and pushed.

EXPLICITLY NOT REQUIRED FOR CLOSE:
- CI passing. Operator observes CI separately after the push; should be 6/6 green (was 6/9 before; Windows cells gone now means 6/6 total).
- Reaching out to potential Windows users — there aren't any to reach.

**Don't wait for CI.** Close on local-verify + push. Operator observes the next CI run; it should be unambiguous green for the first time.
acceptance_criteria:
TESTABLE CONDITIONS (locally verifiable; do NOT wait for CI):

(1) `.github/workflows/test.yml`'s matrix contains only `ubuntu-latest` and `macos-latest`. No `windows-latest`. No `include:` block for Windows. Verifiable via `grep -E 'windows-latest|continue-on-error' .github/workflows/test.yml` returning zero matches.

(2) Any Windows-specific steps in test.yml (e.g., `Install bd (beads) — Windows`) are removed. Verifiable via `grep -iE 'windows' .github/workflows/test.yml` returning only documentation-style matches (e.g., none, or only the matrix listing).

(3) `python -c 'import yaml; yaml.safe_load(open(".github/workflows/test.yml"))'` exits 0.

(4) `prd/PRD-ortus-global-cli.md` NFR-008 reflects Linux + macOS scope explicitly, with a note that Windows is dropped. Verifiable via `grep -E 'NFR-008' prd/PRD-ortus-global-cli.md` returning the updated text.

(5) All currently-open Windows-labeled bd issues are closed with a reason referencing this issue's ID. Verifiable via `bd list --status=open --label=windows` returning empty.

(6) README.md has a "Supported platforms" section mentioning Linux + macOS and WSL2 for Windows users. Verifiable via `grep -iE 'supported platforms|WSL2' README.md` returning matches.

(7) AGENTS.md (or equivalent) has a one-line note about Windows being dropped. Verifiable via `grep -iE 'windows.*not supported|dropped' AGENTS.md` returning a match.

(8) Branch in sync.

TESTING INSTRUCTIONS:

(a) `cat .github/workflows/test.yml | grep -A2 'matrix:'` shows only ubuntu + macos.

(b) `python -c 'import yaml; yaml.safe_load(open(".github/workflows/test.yml"))'` exits 0.

(c) `grep -A3 'NFR-008' prd/PRD-ortus-global-cli.md` shows the updated scope.

(d) `bd list --status=open --label=windows` returns empty.

(e) `grep -iE 'WSL2|supported platforms' README.md` returns matches.

(f) `git status -sb | head -1` shows no unpushed commits.
notes: Operator decision 2026-05-17 after 5+ Windows-only CI iterations without convergence. Predecessor open Windows bugs (close as part of this task): ortus-rlob (umbrella), and any others surfacing from 'bd list --status=open --label=windows'. The decision is fully reversible — re-adding Windows is a matrix edit + bug bash, driven by a real user's needs if/when that happens. For the next 'observe CI' step after this lands: expect 6/6 green for the first time in this iteration cycle.
close_reason: Dropped Windows from CI matrix (.github/workflows/test.yml), updated PRD NFR-008, README.md Supported platforms section, and AGENTS.md to scope to Linux + macOS only; WSL2 recommended for Windows users.

title: CI: 'Install editable + dev deps' fails on Linux+macOS — PEP 668 externally-managed Python
description:
**TL;DR**: After ortus-ctun's bd-install fix landed, the NEXT install step ("Install editable + dev deps") now fails on all 6 Linux+macOS matrix cells. Different root cause than ortus-ctun: this is the PEP 668 "externally-managed-environment" block. The workflow uses `uv pip install --system -e '.[dev]'`, which tries to install into the OS-managed system Python; modern Ubuntu (24.04 on the runner) and macOS-latest (Python 3.14 via Homebrew) both refuse.

**Run**: https://github.com/who/ortus/actions/runs/25981396072

**Linux error** (ubuntu-latest, all 3 Python versions):
```
##[group]Run uv pip install --system -e '.[dev]'
##[endgroup]
error: The interpreter at /usr is externally managed, and indicates the following:
##[error]Process completed with exit code 2.
```

**macOS error** (macos-latest, all 3 Python versions):
```
error: The interpreter at /opt/homebrew/opt/python@3.14/Frameworks/Python.framework/Versions/3.14 is externally managed, and indicates the following:
  will permanently disable this error.
  If you disable this error, we STRONGLY recommend that you additionally
##[error]Process completed with exit code 2.
```

Note the macOS path: `python@3.14` — meaning `--system` resolved to the brew-installed Python 3.14 instead of the uv-installed 3.12 from the matrix. `--system` doesn't respect uv's just-installed Python; it uses whatever the OS default is.

**Scope**:
- 6 of 9 matrix cells fail at this step (3 Linux × 1 step, 3 macOS × 1 step)
- 3 Windows cells fail in a *different* step ("Run pytest with coverage" — PowerShell ParserError); separate bug, filing recommended
- All test execution is gated on this; nothing past it has run since CI was set up

**Why PEP 668 matters here**: Python packaging community decided in 2022 that distros should mark their system Python as off-limits to pip/uv direct installs, to prevent users from breaking system tools (apt-installed Python packages, etc.). Modern distros (Ubuntu 23.04+, Debian 12+) enforce this. macOS Homebrew Python enforces it too. The `--system` flag tells uv to bypass venv logic and install into system Python — the exact thing the PEP 668 marker is designed to block.

The intent of the original CI line (`uv pip install --system`) was probably "skip venv setup, install into the default Python." That worked on old runners; doesn't work on modern ones.

**Related**: ortus-ctun (just-closed predecessor in this CI iteration cycle) — same broad class (CI install step blocks all 9 matrix cells), different specific cause.
design:
**Three fix options, ranked:**

**Fix A (preferred): use `uv venv` + drop --system**

The modern uv pattern for CI is to create a per-job venv. uv auto-detects the venv from `.venv/` in cwd or via `$VIRTUAL_ENV`; no manual activation needed for subsequent `uv pip install` or `uv run`.

```yaml
- name: Install editable + dev deps
  run: |
    uv venv --python ${{ matrix.python-version }}
    uv pip install -e '.[dev]'

- name: Run pytest with coverage
  run: uv run pytest ...   # or: source .venv/bin/activate && pytest ...
```

The `--python ${{ matrix.python-version }}` ensures the venv uses the version the matrix asked for (not whatever the OS default is — fixes the macOS-uses-3.14-instead-of-3.12 surprise).

Subsequent uv invocations in the same job auto-pick up `.venv/` since uv's path resolution checks cwd. `uv run` is also venv-aware.

**Fix B: use `uv sync` (modern uv-native)**

If we add a `uv.lock` file to the repo (one-time `uv lock` to generate, then check in), the install becomes one command:

```yaml
- name: Install editable + dev deps
  run: uv sync --all-extras --python ${{ matrix.python-version }}
```

uv sync handles venv creation, dependency resolution from the lock file, editable install of the project itself, all in one. This is the most idiomatic 2026 uv pattern but requires committing a lock file (which has its own ongoing maintenance: must regenerate on dependency changes).

**Fix C (NOT recommended): `--break-system-packages` override**

```yaml
- name: Install editable + dev deps
  run: uv pip install --system --break-system-packages -e '.[dev]'
```

Tells uv to ignore the PEP 668 marker. Technically works. Wrong policy direction — defeats the point of the marker. Also still has the wrong-Python-version issue on macOS. **Avoid.**

**Recommended: Fix A.** Smallest diff, no lock-file machinery, idiomatic. Lock-file approach (Fix B) can be a separate follow-up if and when the project wants reproducible installs.

**Coordinating with the pytest run step:**

The current "Run pytest with coverage" step probably does something like `pytest ...` (calling bare pytest, assuming it's on PATH). After Fix A, pytest will be in the venv at `.venv/bin/pytest`. Use `uv run pytest ...` to invoke through the venv (uv resolves to the right binary automatically), or explicitly activate the venv first.

**Acceptance per local-verify pattern (per ortus-ctun's iteration protocol):**

Operator can't easily replicate GitHub's Ubuntu 24.04 runner locally. Instead, verify the YAML pattern matches the recommended Fix A shape, plus a smoke check that the new commands run without obvious syntax errors:

```bash
# 1. Workflow uses uv venv + uv pip install -e (no --system)
grep -E 'uv venv|uv pip install -e' .github/workflows/test.yml
grep -E 'uv pip install --system' .github/workflows/test.yml
# First: matches; second: NO matches (the bad pattern is gone)

# 2. Workflow YAML still parses
python -c 'import yaml; yaml.safe_load(open(".github/workflows/test.yml"))'

# 3. Optional: replicate locally in a clean env
rm -rf /tmp/uv-venv-test && mkdir -p /tmp/uv-venv-test && cd /tmp/uv-venv-test
uv venv --python 3.12
cd $HOME/code/ortus && VIRTUAL_ENV=/tmp/uv-venv-test/.venv uv pip install -e '.[dev]'
# Should succeed without PEP 668 error.
```

Per ortus-ctun's protocol: close on local-checks-pass + push. Operator observes the next CI run separately; if it fails for a NEW reason, reopen with the new failure data.
