title: grind: re-cutting a resumed journal's branch keeps its stale fork point, rejecting every retry
description:
## Objective

A claim that cuts a fresh branch for a resumed journal resets the journal's base to the new cut point, so the integration-moved guard judges against the branch that exists rather than a fork point that no longer does — and a retry loop that can never succeed becomes impossible.

## Behavioral context

Before. Observed 2026-08-12 07:08: ortus-f26b's journal survived an operator adjudication that deleted its branch (base_head recorded at the old fork point b9dd6bc). The morning claim correctly cut a fresh ortus/ortus-f26b at the current head 64eb84b — but the ortus-4fxr fix preserves a branch-scoped journal's base_head unconditionally, so the guard compared main (64eb84b) against the stale base (b9dd6bc) and rejected before any worker spawned. The exit advice ("run ortus grind again; it resumes at verification") loops into the identical rejection forever. Two contributing defects: base_head is not refreshed when the branch is newly cut or reused at the integration head, and an empty-candidate journal (this one recorded zero candidate paths) is resumed at all when there is nothing to verify.

After. _prepare_issue_branch reports whether it resumed an existing branch or established one at the integration head; in the latter case the claim resets base_head to the cut point alongside the existing branch_head update. A journal whose candidate is empty and whose branch is gone re-implements instead of resuming into a guard trap. The invariant, stated once: base_head equals the branch's fork point, always — preserved when the branch persists, refreshed when the branch is (re)established.
design:
## Readiness schema

v1

## Scope

Return the branch-establishment mode from `_prepare_issue_branch`, refresh `base_head` (with `branch_head`) when the branch was created or reused at the integration head, and treat a resumed journal with no candidate paths and no surviving branch as a fresh implementation rather than a resume.

## Non-goals

Do not weaken the integration-moved guard — with a truthful fork point it judges correctly, and a genuinely advanced main SHOULD reject a surviving parked branch until merge-forward exists (ortus-u4zv.2). Do not change the 4fxr preservation for branches that still exist with their commits.

## Concrete locations

- `src/ortus/commands/grind.py` — `_prepare_issue_branch()` (returns mode), the claim-path `with_branch` call site (base refresh), and the startup resume-eligibility check for empty-candidate journals.
- `src/ortus/core/transaction.py` — `CandidateJournal.with_branch()` or a `replace` at the call site for the base refresh.
- `tests/test_grind.py`, `tests/test_grind_recovery.py` — regressions.

## Resolved decisions

1. One invariant owns this file's arithmetic: base_head == the branch's fork point. Establishment refreshes it; survival preserves it; nothing else touches it.
2. `_prepare_issue_branch` returns an explicit mode (resumed / established) rather than callers re-deriving it from ref comparisons that race.
3. An empty-candidate journal with no surviving branch is not a resume — there is nothing to verify and nothing to keep; the claim starts a fresh implementation on its fresh branch.
4. The stale journal that triggered this is deleted as part of landing (its candidate was empty; nothing is lost).

## Compatibility constraints

The 4fxr regressions (candidate survives resume, fork-point preserved for surviving branches) must keep passing unchanged. Legacy non-branch journals untouched.

## Ordered steps

1. Return the mode from `_prepare_issue_branch`; refresh base_head at the claim when established.
2. Gate resume-to-verification on a non-empty candidate or surviving branch.
3. Regressions: stale-base journal with deleted branch → claim succeeds, base refreshed, no guard rejection; 4fxr tests unchanged.
4. Full gate with codegraph masked; clean up the live stale state.

## Dependencies

None open on these lines. Human-landed: claim path.

## Edge cases

A journal whose branch survives at exactly the integration head (reuse path) also refreshes — tip==head==fork means refresh and preserve agree. A journal with a candidate but a deleted branch keeps today's conservative report path. Operator deletions of branches out from under journals are now survivable, which is the actual lesson.

## Plan-gap guidance

Stop and report rather than improvising if refreshing the base would mask a genuine integration advance for a surviving branch, or if the 4fxr regressions conflict. Never let two sources of truth exist for the fork point.
acceptance_criteria:
## Observable criteria

- AC-1: A branch-scoped journal whose branch was deleted claims successfully on a fresh branch with base_head refreshed to the new cut point.
- AC-2: A surviving branch with commits still preserves its recorded base (4fxr behavior unchanged).
- AC-3: An empty-candidate journal with no surviving branch re-implements instead of resuming.
- AC-4: The full gate passes.

## Criterion checks

- AC-1: `uv run pytest tests/test_grind.py -k stale_base_refreshes_on_fresh_cut -q`
- AC-2: `uv run pytest tests/test_grind_recovery.py -k resume_preserves_fork_point_base -q`
- AC-3: `uv run pytest tests/test_grind_recovery.py -k empty_candidate_reimplements -q`
- AC-4: `uv run pytest -m "fast or integration" -n auto --test-timeout=180 -q`

## Targeted tests

`uv run pytest tests/test_grind.py tests/test_grind_recovery.py -m "fast or integration" -n auto --test-timeout=180 -q`

Six guards green together: the two new ti4i regressions (stale base refreshes on fresh cut; empty candidate re-implements) plus the 4fxr and mfyu suites unchanged. Live trap state cleared: f26b's stale journal and branch removed, claim reverted — it re-runs fresh on the next grind.

title: grind: resume clobbers a branch-scoped journal's base and erases its committed candidate
description:
## Objective

Resuming a branch-scoped transaction preserves what the keystone recorded — the fork-point base and the committed candidate — instead of overwriting the base with the branch tip and re-diffing the worktree into an empty candidate.

## Behavioral context

Before. Observed 2026-08-11 23:19: resuming ortus-k46v.2 from verification-rejected, with its candidate committed as 47fc66d on its branch, the startup handoff (a) recorded base_head=current_head while the tree sat on the issue branch — poisoning the base with the worker's own commit — and (b) recomputed the candidate as worktree-vs-HEAD, got an empty diff (the work is committed), logged "the candidate changed" and refreshed the journal to zero candidate paths ("resuming ... with 0 inherited path(s)"). The integration-moved guard then correctly compared main (2a37337) against the poisoned base (47fc66d) and falsely rejected: "the integration branch main moved during implementation." The transaction is unresumable until repaired. Both defects are pre-keystone assumptions (tree always on main; candidate always dirty) that commit B updated everywhere except this resume path — capture, the blocker and both verifier guards already share the range-aware _candidate_view lens; the resume never joined them.

After. The resume computes candidate and diff base through _candidate_view exactly like every other integrity site, and the handoff preserves journal.base_head whenever the journal names an issue branch. A verification-rejected branch transaction resumes with its committed candidate intact and re-verifies.
design:
## Readiness schema

v1

## Scope

Route the startup resume's candidate recomputation through `_candidate_view`, diff with its base, and preserve `journal.base_head` in the handoff for branch-scoped journals. Repair tonight's poisoned journal by hand as part of landing.

## Non-goals

Do not change non-branch (legacy) resume behavior — worktree semantics stay for journals without an issue branch. Do not touch the integration-moved guard: with a truthful base it judges correctly, and a legitimately advanced integration branch SHOULD reject until rebase-on-resume exists (ortus-u4zv.2 territory).

## Concrete locations

- `src/ortus/commands/grind.py` — `_prepare_handoff()`: the candidate recomputation (`candidate_diff(repo, candidate)` without a base) and the `with_handoff(..., base_head=current_head, ...)` call.
- `src/ortus/commands/grind.py` — `_candidate_view()`, the shared lens; consumed, not modified.
- `tests/test_grind_recovery.py` — the resume coverage.

## Resolved decisions

1. One lens everywhere: the resume uses `_candidate_view` verbatim, so the five integrity sites cannot disagree about what a candidate is.
2. The handoff's base is `journal.base_head` when `journal.issue_branch` is set — the keystone recorded the fork point at claim and nothing since has better information; `current_head` remains correct for legacy journals where the tree provably sits on the integration branch.
3. Tonight's poisoned journal is repaired in place (base restored to the fork point, phase restored to verification-rejected); the fixed resume recomputes the candidate itself.

## Compatibility constraints

Legacy journals resume byte-identically. The `_SEALED_PHASES` changed-candidate note still fires for genuine drift, now measured range-aware. No schema change.

## Ordered steps

1. Compute `(candidate, diff_base)` via `_candidate_view` in `_prepare_handoff` when the repo is git-backed; diff with that base.
2. Preserve `journal.base_head` in the `with_handoff` call for branch-scoped journals.
3. Add a regression: a verification-rejected journal with a committed branch candidate resumes with paths and hash intact and base unchanged.
4. Run the full gate with `codegraph` masked from `PATH`.

## Dependencies

None open in these lines. Human-landed: scheduler resume path.

## Edge cases

A branch journal whose worker also left uncommitted edits resumes with the union, exactly as capture recorded it. A branch deleted between runs degrades to the legacy path with a note (view returns worktree-only). A journal already poisoned by tonight's defect is corrected by the hand repair, not by code.

## Plan-gap guidance

Stop and report rather than improvising if `_candidate_view` cannot serve the handoff without signature changes, or if any test depends on the clobbered-base behavior. Never let resume rewrite `base_head` for a journal that names its branch.

title: grind: errors and the exit line name the issue, state the truth, and say the next action
description:
## Objective

Every error grind prints and the line it exits on answer the operator's three questions — what happened, to which issue, and what do I do now — and never state something false about the work's safety.

## Behavioral context

Before. The 2026-08-11 22:30 run ended with: "error: grind: verifier rejected candidate: expected exactly one verdict envelope; found 0" twice (once with "; candidate left uncommitted" appended), then "done; closed 6 this session". The failing issue is never named — the operator must infer ortus-k46v.2 from context. "Candidate left uncommitted" is false under branch-scoped candidates: the worker's commit sat safely on ortus/ortus-k46v.2, which is the exact durability the keystone bought. And the correct next action — run ortus grind again; it resumes that issue directly at verification — appears nowhere. The operator's verbatim verdict on readability and actionability was unprintable. ortus-kawu (landed) narrates milestones but passes errors through verbatim; ortus-hsm2 covers only readiness warnings; this leaf is the remaining surface.

After. The same ending reads:

    verification of "refresh the Python lock" (ortus-k46v.2) failed: the verifier emitted no verdict.
    Its work is safe — committed on ortus/ortus-k46v.2 — and the claim is kept.
    Next: run `ortus grind` again; it resumes this issue at verification with a fresh verifier.
    done — 6 landed this session, 1 awaiting retry, 10 open.

Every error path names its issue by title and id, describes candidate state truthfully from the journal (committed on its branch, uncommitted in the tree, or none), and states the concrete next action. The exit line accounts for unfinished work instead of burying it in a status-count tuple.
design:
## Readiness schema

v1

## Scope

Route grind's error and exit reporting through issue-aware, truth-checked rendering: rejection/halt/blocker messages carry the issue title and id, candidate-state phrasing derives from the journal (branch-committed versus worktree-only versus none), each terminal error appends its next action, the duplicated rejected-then-summary double print collapses to one message, and the exit line states landed / awaiting-retry / open in words.

## Non-goals

Do not change any failure semantics, phases, or recovery behavior — only what is printed. Do not touch the log's machine record. Do not restyle readiness warnings (ortus-hsm2) or healthy-path narration (landed ortus-kawu).

## Concrete locations

- `src/ortus/commands/grind.py` — the verification-rejection reporting (the "verifier rejected candidate"/halt double print and its "candidate left uncommitted" suffix), `_finalize_candidate`'s blocker `output.error` call sites, the orphan/incomplete preservation messages, and the end-of-run "done; closed N" line.
- `src/ortus/core/transaction.py` — `CandidateJournal.issue_branch`/`branch_head`, the source of truthful candidate-state phrasing; read only.
- `tests/test_grind.py`, `tests/test_grind_finalization.py` — console assertions for each terminal path.

## Resolved decisions

1. One error narrative per failure, not two: the rejection line and the halt line merge into a single message with title, id, cause, safety statement, and next action.
2. Candidate-state phrasing is computed, never templated: branch tip ahead of base means "committed on <branch>"; dirty candidate paths mean "uncommitted edits preserved in the tree"; both mean both; neither means "no changes were made". The pre-keystone "candidate left uncommitted" string is removed everywhere.
3. Next-action text is per failure class: verdict-less or failed verification → re-run to retry verification; corrections exhausted or plan gap → see the issue's newest comment, decide, relabel; finalization blocker → the blocker's own remedy line; halt on branch state → the named manual step. The class-to-action table lives beside the messages so new failure classes must pick one.
4. The exit line speaks operator: "N landed, M awaiting retry, K open" with "awaiting retry" derived from claimed-issues-with-journals, and it prints the next action when M > 0.

## Compatibility constraints

Log lines keep their exact current text — the dashboard, tail and tests parse them. Only `output.error`/console rendering changes. Exit codes unchanged.

## Ordered steps

1. Add the candidate-state phrasing helper from the journal and the failure-class → next-action table.
2. Merge and rewrite the terminal error call sites through them.
3. Rewrite the exit line with the landed/awaiting/open accounting and conditional next action.
4. Update console assertions; add one test per failure class asserting title, truth, and action are present.
5. Run `uv run pytest tests/test_grind.py tests/test_grind_finalization.py tests/regression/test_grind_no_stream_leak.py -m "fast or integration" -n auto --test-timeout=180 -q`.

## Dependencies

None open; complements landed ortus-kawu and open ortus-hsm2 without file overlap on hsm2's readiness surface (both touch grind.py — serialize by claiming order; if hsm2 is open when this is claimed, the scheduler's one-at-a-time flow already prevents same-file concurrency within a run).

## Edge cases

A failure before any journal exists states "no changes were made" rather than guessing. A rejection whose issue title cannot be read from bd degrades to the id alone, never crashes the error path. Titles pass through `_console_safe`. The no-stream-leak guard still holds — narrative errors carry no transcript content.

## Plan-gap guidance

Stop and report rather than improvising if any consumer parses the console error strings (none is known; the log is the parse surface), or if a failure class has no safe next action to name — that is a missing recovery design, not a wording problem. Never soften a failure into reassurance the journal cannot back.

description:
## Objective

Finalization generates the tracker exports it commits by invoking `bd export` explicitly, instead of sweeping whatever ambient JSONL the tracker last wrote — making Ortus compatible with bd ≥1.1 (which no longer writes `.beads/issues.jsonl` as a side effect) and making export timing deterministic for the first time.

## Behavioral context

Before. Ortus assumes the tracker maintains `.beads/issues.jsonl` ambiently: finalization stages `dirty & _TRACKER_EXPORT_PATHS` into the issue's commit, the export carve-out excludes those paths from candidates, and the repo tracks the JSONL as the reviewable record. bd 1.0.4 was the last release to behave this way. The `ortus-k46v.1` validation worker proved (probe workspace, reproduced twice) that under 1.1.0+ the file is never written — not at init, not at close — so the fold model commits nothing and the tracked export rots. Every ambient-timing race this repo hit on 2026-08-11 (the finalization checkout race fixed by ref-first fast-forward; the claim-path race filed as ortus-mfyu) traces to the same root: export timing Ortus does not control.

After. At the moment finalization needs the exports — before staging or folding — it runs `bd export` to regenerate `.beads/issues.jsonl` from the database, deterministically, then stages the result exactly as today. The interactions log's ≥1.1 equivalent (`bd audit`, append-only JSONL) is resolved during implementation and handled the same way or consciously retired. With this landed, the bd-toolchain pin leaf (`ortus-k46v.1`) unblocks: its fixture work (bd ≥1.1's init scaffolding: `.agents/`, `.claude/`, `.codex/`, gate lockfile) is the remaining scope there.
design:
## Readiness schema

v1

## Scope

Replace ambient-export trust with an explicit `bd export` invocation at finalization's staging moment, behind a version-tolerant seam (1.0.x, which still writes ambiently, must keep working unchanged). Resolve the interactions-log equivalent under ≥1.1. Keep the carve-out and the committed-JSONL model exactly as they are.

## Non-goals

Do not bump the bd pin — that is `ortus-k46v.1`, which this leaf unblocks. Do not change what is committed, the carve-out set, the finalization sequence, or the fold-into-worker-commit mechanics. Do not adopt bd's dolt-remote sync as a replacement for committed JSONL; retiring the committed-export model is a separate design question this leaf deliberately does not open.

## Concrete locations

- `src/ortus/core/bd.py` — `BdClient` gains `export_issues()` invoking `bd export` with output routed to `.beads/issues.jsonl`; capability-probed so 1.0.x (no such need) skips it.
- `src/ortus/commands/grind.py` — `_finalize_candidate()`'s commit step, immediately before `stage` is computed: regenerate exports, then proceed unchanged. The startup tracker-housekeeping path gets the same treatment.
- `src/ortus/core/git.py` — `_TRACKER_EXPORT_PATHS`; read for the target set, unchanged.
- `tests/test_grind_finalization.py`, `tests/test_core_bd.py` — coverage under a fake bd for both the exporting and ambient regimes.

## Resolved decisions

1. Ortus owns export timing: the export runs at the exact moments its output is consumed (finalization staging; startup housekeeping), never on a timer or hook. This closes the ambient-timing race class permanently rather than accommodating it.
2. Version tolerance by behavior, not version parsing: after `bd export` support is probed once per run (`bd export --help` exit status), the exporting path is used; otherwise today's ambient path stands. 1.0.4 keeps byte-identical behavior.
3. `bd export` output is written atomically (temp file, rename) so a crash mid-export cannot commit a truncated record.
4. The interactions log: if `bd audit`'s file is append-only and ambient under ≥1.1, it stays swept as today; if it too went silent, it joins the explicit export or is dropped from `_TRACKER_EXPORT_PATHS` with the README's tracker-state description updated — resolved during implementation with a probe, recorded in the completion comment.
5. Export failure at finalization is a blocker, not a silent skip: committing an issue while knowingly omitting its tracker record is the rot this leaf exists to prevent.

## Compatibility constraints

Under bd 1.0.4 the full gate is byte-identical. The export carve-out, candidate capture, verifier hashing and the fold mechanics are untouched — the only change is who writes the file and when. `bd export`'s output format must be verified compatible with the currently tracked JSONL shape (same per-line objects) before adoption; a format break is a plan gap.

## Ordered steps

1. Add the capability probe and `export_issues()` with atomic write.
2. Invoke it at finalization staging and startup housekeeping when supported.
3. Resolve the interactions-log question with a probe; implement per decision 4.
4. Add tests for both regimes and the failure blocker.
5. Run the full gate under the machine bd (1.0.4-era) and under a downloaded ≥1.1 binary with rebuilt templates — the validation discipline `ortus-k46v.1` established.

## Dependencies

Blocks `ortus-k46v.1` (the pin bump), which currently carries the human escalation this leaf answers. Human-landed: it modifies finalization.

## Edge cases

A repository whose `.beads/issues.jsonl` is absent (fresh ≥1.1 init) gains the file on first finalization — expected, and the gitignore negation pattern must admit it. `bd export` on an empty database writes an empty file, staged only if changed. Concurrent bd writes during export are the tracker's problem (single-writer lock); a locked-out export retries once then blocks. The fold path (`amend_paths`) sees the regenerated file exactly as it sees ambient churn today.

## Plan-gap guidance

Stop and report rather than improvising if `bd export`'s format diverges from the tracked shape, if the interactions equivalent cannot be determined by probe, or if export latency at finalization is pathological on a large database. Never commit with a knowingly stale or failed export, and never open the retire-committed-JSONL design inside this leaf.
acceptance_criteria:

- AC-2: Under bd 1.0.4 behavior, finalization output is byte-identical to today.
- AC-3: The export write is atomic.
- AC-4: An export failure at finalization is a blocker, and the issue is not committed with a stale record.
- AC-5: The interactions-log disposition under ≥1.1 is implemented per a recorded probe result.
- AC-6: The full gate passes under both regimes.

## Criterion checks

- AC-1: `uv run pytest tests/test_grind_finalization.py -k exporting_bd_regenerates_before_staging -q`
- AC-2: `uv run pytest tests/test_grind_finalization.py -k ambient_bd_behavior_unchanged -q`
- AC-3: `uv run pytest tests/test_core_bd.py -k export_write_is_atomic -q`
- AC-4: `uv run pytest tests/test_grind_finalization.py -k export_failure_blocks_finalization -q`
- AC-5: `uv run pytest tests/test_core_bd.py -k interactions_disposition_matches_probe -q`
- AC-6: `uv run pytest -m "fast or integration" -n auto --test-timeout=180 -q` under the machine bd, and the bd-sensitive suites under a downloaded ≥1.1 binary per the k46v.1 method

## Targeted tests

`uv run pytest tests/test_grind_finalization.py tests/test_core_bd.py -m "fast or integration" -n auto --test-timeout=180 -q`

Machine-bd full gate 1030 passed (single failure: tests/test_dashboard.py workspace-count test, untouched by this change, green in isolation — load flake); bd-1.2.1 regime: tests/test_core_bd.py + tests/test_grind_finalization.py 82/82 with rebuilt templates per the k46v.1 method. ACs: AC-1 exporting_bd_regenerates_before_staging, AC-2 ambient_bd_behavior_unchanged, AC-3 export_write_is_atomic, AC-4 export_failure_blocks_finalization, AC-5 interactions_disposition_matches_probe (probe recorded: bd 1.2.1 bd audit = optional append-only git-versioned sidecar, stays in _TRACKER_EXPORT_PATHS; issues.jsonl alone gains the explicit producer), AC-6 both regimes green. Probe notes: bd 1.0.3 (machine) already carries bd export with record-equal output, so the exporting path engages there too — deterministic timing everywhere, ambient path retained for bds without the command. This unblocks ortus-k46v.1.

title: grind: claiming across a stranded issue branch races diverged tracker exports and strands its own new branch
description:
## Objective

Claiming an issue must succeed regardless of which branch the previous iteration stranded the tree on and regardless of divergent tracker-export state — and when it cannot, it must clean up the branch it just created and report git's own reason.

## Behavioral context

Before. Observed 2026-08-11, run `grind-20260811-181354`: iteration 1 ended with `ortus-k46v.1` plan-gapped to `human` (correctly excluded from snapshots), leaving the tree on `ortus/ortus-k46v.1` — held there by the pre-iter guard's `allowed_branch` tolerance, which applies whenever a journal names the branch, even though the loop was about to claim a *different* issue. Iteration 2 claimed `ortus-u4zv.1`, created its branch at the integration head, and `git checkout` refused: the tracker exports were staged-modified against a branch whose export content diverged from main (an intake commit plus normal churn), and switching would overwrite them. The run halted with `could not check out ortus/ortus-u4zv.1` — no reason from git (the checkout helper returns a bare bool, the exact opacity ortus-pgqg fixed for commits), and the just-created branch was left behind, which the reuse guard would later refuse once main moved. This is the same dirty-exports checkout race the finalization step already fixed by fast-forwarding the ref before switching; the claim path missed it.

After. An iteration that claims a different issue than the journal's reasserts the integration branch first, carrying divergent tracker exports across the switch (they are bd-generated, regenerable, and already carved out of every candidate — the worktree's copy is the freshest and wins). A claim whose checkout still fails deletes the branch it created in that same claim, reverts the claim, and reports git's stderr. The `allowed_branch` tolerance narrows to the case it was built for: the journal's own issue being resumed or replayed.
design:
## Readiness schema

v1

## Scope

Make the claim path branch-safe: reassert the integration branch before claiming when the tree sits on a prior issue's branch, add an exports-preserving switch for tracker-export divergence, carry git's reason out of failed checkouts, delete a claim-created branch on claim failure, and narrow the pre-iter guard's `allowed_branch` to resume/replay of the journal's own issue.

## Non-goals

Do not change selection, the branch-cut rules (cut at integration head, reuse only at head, never reset), finalization, or the export carve-out. Do not carry non-export dirty files across switches — foreign source edits keep today's handling. Do not touch the human-label exclusion that correctly hid the plan-gapped issue.

## Concrete locations

- `src/ortus/commands/grind.py` — the claim-path branch cut and its failure handling; the pre-iter `_enforce_branch_discipline(..., allowed_branch=...)` call, whose tolerance must check that the claimed issue equals the journal's issue.
- `src/ortus/core/git.py` — `checkout()` at its bare-bool return (gains a reason-carrying variant per the `CommitResult` pattern), and a new exports-preserving switch helper: snapshot the worktree's tracker-export bytes, switch hook-free, restore the snapshot.
- `src/ortus/core/git.py` — `_TRACKER_EXPORT_PATHS` consumers in `grind.py`, the definition of which files the helper may carry.
- `tests/test_grind.py`, `tests/test_core_git.py` — flow and helper coverage.

## Resolved decisions

1. Exports may be carried across a switch because they are tracker-generated, regenerable from the database, and excluded from every candidate; the worktree copy is the newest export and wins. No other file class gets this treatment.
2. Reassert-before-claim happens whenever the journal's issue is not the one being claimed, before the new branch is cut — the tolerance that held the tree on the old branch exists solely for finalization replay and same-issue resume.
3. A claim that created a branch and then failed deletes that branch before reverting the claim; a claim that *reused* an existing branch never deletes it. The observed stale-branch trap (`ortus/ortus-u4zv.1` left at a head main would outgrow) must be impossible.
4. Failed checkouts report git's stderr, bounded, in the blocker text — the ortus-pgqg rule applied to the remaining bare-bool git write.

## Compatibility constraints

The keystone's crash-recovery predicates (finalization replay on the journal's own branch) keep their tolerance. Reused-branch and invalid-ref claim failures keep their current messages plus git's reason. No journal schema change. Full gate green under both machine bd and the CI-pinned bd.

## Ordered steps

1. Add the reason-carrying checkout and the exports-preserving switch to the git client.
2. Narrow the pre-iter `allowed_branch` to journal-issue-equals-claim; reassert integration (exports-preserving) otherwise.
3. Route the claim's branch cut through the exports-preserving switch; on failure, delete a claim-created branch, revert the claim, and report the carried reason.
4. Add regression tests reproducing the observed sequence: plan-gapped issue leaves tree on its branch with diverged staged exports → next claim succeeds on a fresh branch.
5. Run the full gate with `codegraph` masked from `PATH`.

## Dependencies

None open; touches the claim path (scheduler loop) — human-landed per the self-modification rule. The workspace-isolation leaf (`ortus-u4zv.2`) will obsolete most of this by keeping the primary checkout on the integration branch permanently; this fix is what makes the pipeline safe *until* that lands, and its regression tests survive as guards.

## Edge cases

Exports staged versus unstaged must both carry. A prior branch with worker commits (not just intake commits) reasserts identically — the branch keeps the commits; only the checkout moves. A journal whose issue was closed between iterations reasserts without tolerance. Claim failure after branch creation but before checkout still deletes the branch. The exports snapshot must be byte-faithful (no encoding pass).

## Plan-gap guidance

Stop and report rather than improvising if any non-export file class appears to need carrying (that is the workspace-isolation problem, not this fix), or if narrowing the tolerance breaks a finalization-replay test. Never force-checkout, never delete a reused branch, and never resolve export divergence by discarding the worktree copy.
acceptance_criteria:
## Observable criteria

- AC-1: A claim following a plan-gapped issue that left the tree on its branch with diverged staged tracker exports succeeds on a fresh branch.
- AC-2: The worktree's tracker-export bytes survive the switch byte-identically.
- AC-3: A claim whose checkout fails deletes the branch it created in that claim and reverts the claim.
- AC-4: A claim that reused an existing branch never deletes it on failure.
- AC-5: Failed checkout blockers carry git's own reason.
- AC-6: The pre-iter tolerance holds the tree on an issue branch only when the journal's issue is the one being resumed.
- AC-7: Finalization crash-replay on the journal's own branch keeps its existing tolerance and tests.

## Criterion checks

- AC-1: `uv run pytest tests/test_grind.py -k claim_after_plan_gap_with_diverged_exports -q`
- AC-2: `uv run pytest tests/test_core_git.py -k exports_survive_switch_byte_identically -q`
- AC-3: `uv run pytest tests/test_grind.py -k failed_claim_deletes_its_own_branch -q`
- AC-4: `uv run pytest tests/test_grind.py -k failed_claim_keeps_a_reused_branch -q`
- AC-5: `uv run pytest tests/test_grind.py -k checkout_blocker_carries_git_reason -q`
- AC-6: `uv run pytest tests/test_grind.py -k tolerance_only_for_the_journals_own_issue -q`
- AC-7: `uv run pytest tests/test_grind_finalization.py -m fast -n auto --test-timeout=30 -q`

## Targeted tests

`uv run pytest tests/test_grind.py tests/test_core_git.py tests/test_grind_finalization.py -m "fast or integration" -n auto --test-timeout=180 -q`
close_reason: Landed by hand as 48bb9f3. Full gate: 892 passed, 0 failed, codegraph masked. All seven AC selectors pass; the strand is pinned as pure git state in _stranded_claim_repo. Bonus defect found and fixed by the faithful fixture: same-issue crash-resume with worker commits was refused by the at-head-only reuse guard; resume-by-checkout now honors the keystone's promise. The claim-path portion is interim by design — ortus-u4zv.2 (workspace isolation) retires the shared-tree hazard class; these regression tests survive as guards.

title: hooks: refuse git-mutating commands in interactive sessions while a grind run holds the flock
description:
## Objective

An interactive session that tries to `git commit`, `push`, `checkout`, `switch` or `reset` while a grind run is in flight gets a polite refusal naming the run and the claimed issue, instead of silently landing changes inside a live candidate — a project-level Claude Code hook, active until workspace isolation makes the shared tree a non-issue.

## Behavioral context

Before. The operator keeps an interactive Claude session open as the intake mechanism while grind runs, by design — tracker writes are carved out and safe. But git writes are not: the shared checkout sits on the worker's issue branch mid-run, so an interactive commit lands inside the candidate range. On 2026-08-11 an intake session committed tracker churn onto a live issue branch exactly this way; the safeguard today is session discipline and a tracker memory, which is etiquette where there should be structure.

After. The project's Claude settings carry a `PreToolUse` hook on Bash: when the proposed command mutates git state (`commit`, `push`, `checkout`, `switch`, `reset`, `rebase`, `merge`) and the grind flock is held, the hook blocks the call with a message naming the in-flight run and the claimed issue, and pointing at the safe alternatives (bd intake is always fine; retry after the run). Worker sessions are exempt via an environment marker the harness sets, so the pipeline's own commits are untouched. Read-only git commands pass through untouched at all times.
design:
## Readiness schema

v1

## Scope

A hook script that detects git-mutating Bash commands and probes the grind flock, wired as a `PreToolUse` hook in the project's Claude settings and in the `ortus init` template; an `ORTUS_WORKER=1` marker in the worker spawn environment that exempts pipeline sessions; tests for the script's decision table.

## Non-goals

Do not intercept anything except Bash tool calls in Claude sessions — the harness's own subprocess git calls never pass through hooks and need no exemption. Do not block bd commands, read-only git, or anything when no run is in flight. Do not build the workspace-isolation clone model; this guard is the interim protection that leaf retires. Do not enforce via git hooks — `core.hooksPath` belongs to bd.

## Concrete locations

- `scripts/grind_commit_guard.py` (new) — the hook: reads the tool input JSON on stdin, matches git-mutating commands, probes the flock non-blockingly, exits 2 with the refusal message when blocked.
- `.claude/settings.json` — the `hooks.PreToolUse` wiring for the live repo; note the operator may need to apply this file's edit themselves if session permissions deny writing it — the completion comment must carry the exact snippet in that case.
- `template/.claude/settings.json` / `template/.claude/settings.json.jinja` — the same wiring for repositories `ortus init` creates.
- `src/ortus/core/claude.py` — the worker spawn environment, which gains `ORTUS_WORKER=1`.
- `src/ortus/commands/unlock.py` — documents the flock's semantics this probe relies on (a held flock always means a live process); read, not modified.
- `tests/test_grind_commit_guard.py` (new) — the decision table.

## Resolved decisions

1. The trigger is the flock, not a state file: the grind flock cannot go stale (kernel advisory lock; held implies a live process, per `ortus unlock`'s own contract), so the guard can never wedge intake after a crash.
2. Command matching is conservative and word-based: `git` followed by a mutating subcommand anywhere in the command string blocks; `git status/log/diff/show/branch --list` and non-git commands never match. False negatives are acceptable (the pipeline's own guards remain the backstop); false positives on read-only work are not.
3. Worker exemption is an environment marker (`ORTUS_WORKER=1`) set at spawn, checked first by the script. The harness's direct git calls bypass hooks inherently.
4. The refusal is instructive: it names the claimed issue (`bd list --status=in_progress`, best-effort), states that bd intake remains safe, and says when to retry. A guard that just says "no" teaches nothing.
5. Exit code 2 (blocking) with the message on stderr, per the Claude Code hooks contract; a hook that itself fails (missing python, unreadable input) exits 0 — the guard must degrade open, never brick every Bash call.
6. This guard is explicitly interim: the workspace-isolation leaf's completion criteria include removing the block-on-flock behavior or narrowing it to pushes of the integration branch. Recorded here so it is retired deliberately, not discovered as mystery friction.

## Compatibility constraints

No Ortus runtime behavior changes; grind never reads the hook. Sessions in repositories without the hook are unaffected. The template change must keep `ortus init --force`'s re-render semantics. The worker env marker must not disturb `extra_env` handling for either backend.

## Ordered steps

1. Write the guard script with the decision table (worker marker → allow; no flock held → allow; read-only → allow; mutating + flock held → block with message).
2. Add `ORTUS_WORKER=1` to the worker spawn environment.
3. Wire the hook in the live repo's settings (or emit the exact snippet in the completion comment if the file is write-denied to the worker) and in both template variants.
4. Add `tests/test_grind_commit_guard.py` covering the decision table, the degrade-open path, and the marker exemption.
5. Run `uv run pytest tests/test_grind_commit_guard.py tests/test_core_claude.py -m fast -n auto --test-timeout=30 -q`.

## Dependencies

None in the graph; independent of the workspace-isolation leaf it will eventually be retired by (that leaf names the retirement). No open leaf touches these files.

## Edge cases

Compound commands (`cd x && git commit`) must match. `git commit` inside a quoted string an unrelated tool prints must not be executed anyway — matching on the command string errs toward blocking, acceptable per decision 2's asymmetry only when the flock is held. A hook invoked while bd is unreachable still blocks but with a generic message (issue lookup is best-effort). Two grinds are impossible under the flock, so "which run" is unambiguous. Windows/macOS template consumers get the same script via `uv run python`.

## Plan-gap guidance

Stop and report rather than improvising if the Claude hooks contract cannot express per-tool blocking with a message, if `extra_env` cannot carry the marker to both backends, or if the live settings file cannot be written and the snippet-in-comment fallback is deemed insufficient. Never let the guard fail closed on its own errors, and never block bd commands.
acceptance_criteria:
## Observable criteria

- AC-1: With a run in flight, a Bash `git commit` from a non-worker session is blocked with a message naming the claimed issue.
- AC-2: `git push`, `checkout`, `switch`, `reset`, `rebase` and `merge` block under the same condition; `status`, `log`, `diff` and non-git commands never block.
- AC-3: With no run in flight, nothing blocks.
- AC-4: A session with `ORTUS_WORKER=1` is never blocked.
- AC-5: The guard degrades open when its own execution fails.
- AC-6: The `ortus init` template wires the hook for new repositories.
- AC-7: The worker spawn environment carries the marker for both backends.

## Criterion checks

- AC-1: `uv run pytest tests/test_grind_commit_guard.py -k blocks_commit_and_names_the_claimed_issue -q`
- AC-2: `uv run pytest tests/test_grind_commit_guard.py -k decision_table_mutating_vs_readonly -q`
- AC-3: `uv run pytest tests/test_grind_commit_guard.py -k idle_flock_never_blocks -q`
- AC-4: `uv run pytest tests/test_grind_commit_guard.py -k worker_marker_exempts -q`
- AC-5: `uv run pytest tests/test_grind_commit_guard.py -k guard_degrades_open_on_own_failure -q`

`uv run pytest tests/test_grind_commit_guard.py tests/test_core_claude.py -m fast -n auto --test-timeout=30 -q`

Guard at scripts/grind_commit_guard.py wired as PreToolUse/Bash in the live .claude/settings.json (the file was writable after all — no operator snippet needed) and in the init template, which also ships a byte-identical copy of the script (parity pinned by test). Interactive sessions are never grind descendants, so protection is unchanged.

title: Epic: graceful concurrent intake — the operator's session can never foul a run
description: The operator keeps an interactive Claude session open as the intake mechanism while grind runs. Tracker writes are already safe by design (the export carve-out); git writes and file edits are not, because workers share the operator's checkout — on 2026-08-11 an intake session committed onto a live issue branch. Two leaves, one interim and one structural: a PreToolUse guard that politely refuses git-mutating commands in non-worker sessions while the grind flock is held, and workspace isolation that moves each worker into a disposable shared clone so the primary checkout never leaves the integration branch again. The guard is explicitly retired (or narrowed) by the isolation leaf.

title: ci: pin the bd toolchain to the latest tagged release, validated under that binary
description:
## Objective

Move the pinned bd (beads) toolchain to the latest tagged release — v1.2.1 as of 2026-08-11 — with the suite validated under that exact binary before the pin lands, so the version the checks run against is the version the pipeline actually meets.

## Behavioral context

Before. CI pins bd 1.0.4 in two workflow jobs while the development machine runs 1.0.3, and that exact skew produced a live escape on 2026-08-11: beads 1.0.4 introduced a `post-checkout` git hook absent in 1.0.3, the keystone's claim-time checkout fired it only on the runners, and every CI leg went red against a locally-green gate. The remedy that worked — download CI's exact binary, rebuild the test templates with it, reproduce red locally, fix, re-verify under both versions — is recorded in tracker memory (`environment-escape-caught-by-ci-2026-08-11`) and is the validation discipline this leaf packages.

After. The workflow pins the latest tagged bd in both jobs, the sensitive suites are green under that binary via a local PATH override before the pin is pushed, and the packet's completion comment tells the operator the one thing a worker cannot do: upgrade the machine-local bd to the same tag so the skew cannot re-open.
design:
## Readiness schema

v1

## Scope

Bump the `BD_VERSION` pin in both workflow jobs to the latest tagged beads release, after validating the bd-sensitive test suites under that exact binary downloaded to a scratch directory and placed first on `PATH`. Record the operator's local-upgrade step in the completion comment.

## Non-goals

Do not change how bd is installed in CI, the hook-free branch-plumbing policy in `GitClient._run`, or any Ortus behavior to accommodate the new bd — a behavioral incompatibility is a finding to report, not something to patch around inside an upgrade leaf. Do not upgrade the operator's machine; a worker cannot and must not install system binaries. Do not bump other dependencies; they have their own leaves.

## Concrete locations

- `.github/workflows/test.yml` — the `BD_VERSION="1.0.4"` pin in the `Install bd (beads)` step of the `test` job, and the second pinned download in the `release-smoke` job.
- `src/ortus/core/git.py` — `GitClient._run()` and its `hooks=False` plumbing policy, the surface a bd hook change is most likely to probe; read, not modified.
- `tests/test_grind.py`, `tests/test_grind_finalization.py`, `tests/test_grind_corrections.py` — the suites that exercise claim, verification and finalization against real bd workspaces.

## Resolved decisions

1. Validate under the exact pinned binary before the pin lands: download the tagged release asset into a scratch directory, place it first on `PATH`, and run the bd-sensitive suites in a fresh pytest process so the session-built test templates are constructed by the new bd — templates carry the new version's hooks and export timing, which is where 1.0.4's breakage lived.
2. Pin to the latest tag at implementation time, not the tag named here — check `gh api repos/gastownhall/beads/releases/latest` first; v1.2.1 is the floor this packet was written against.
3. Both jobs move in one commit. Two jobs on different bd versions is the same skew class inside one workflow.
4. A behavior change that fails a suite under the new bd stops the leaf as a plan gap carrying the failing test names and the version diff — exactly the evidence the 2026-08-11 escape needed after the fact.
5. The operator's local upgrade is completion-comment guidance, not a code change: the skew closes only when the machine and CI agree, and only the operator can move the machine.

## Compatibility constraints

The install steps' shape (curl, tar, `bd --version` echo) is unchanged — only the version string moves. The suite must pass under the machine bd (1.0.3) and the pinned bd in the same working tree, since the two coexist until the operator upgrades. No Ortus source changes.

## Ordered steps

1. Resolve the latest tagged release and download its Linux binary to a scratch directory.
2. Run `uv run pytest tests/test_grind.py tests/test_grind_finalization.py tests/test_grind_corrections.py -m "fast or integration" -q --test-timeout=180` with the new bd first on `PATH` and codegraph masked; a fresh process so templates rebuild under it.
3. Update `BD_VERSION` in both workflow jobs to the resolved tag.
4. Run the same suites under the machine bd unchanged, confirming both versions coexist green.
5. Write the completion comment naming the tag and the operator's local-upgrade command.

## Dependencies

None in the graph. The Actions-bump leaf depends on this one: both edit `.github/workflows/test.yml`, and no two open leaves may touch one file (PRD NFR-3).

## Edge cases

A release published mid-implementation is fine — pin what was validated, not what is newest at push time. A tag whose asset naming changed breaks the install step and is a plan gap, not a workaround. A new bd whose hooks change behavior again must surface in step 2, because the templates were rebuilt under it; if it only reproduces under CI's slower runners, the escape record's method — reproduce with the exact binary and fixture rebuild — is the named fallback. macOS assets are not validated locally; the matrix covers them.

## Plan-gap guidance

Stop and report rather than improvising if any suite fails under the new bd, if the release layout no longer matches the install step, or if the new bd requires a behavioral accommodation in Ortus — each of those is its own issue with this leaf's evidence attached. Never bump the pin without the step-2 validation run, and never patch Ortus inside this leaf.

- AC-4: No Ortus source file changed.

- AC-2: `uv run pytest tests/test_grind.py tests/test_grind_finalization.py tests/test_grind_corrections.py -m "fast or integration" -q --test-timeout=180` run with the downloaded pinned bd first on PATH, exit 0

title: checks: the red–green proof — proves-new criteria must fail on the merge base
description:
## Objective

The red–green proof: criteria tagged `proves-new` must fail on the merge base and pass on the branch, so a test that also passes without the change — a test that proves nothing — is rejected mechanically instead of trusted.

## Behavioral context

Before. The AC runner executes criteria against the branch tree only. A worker verifying its own work could satisfy a criterion with a vacuous test — one that passes with or without the change — and nothing mechanical would notice; catching that was the reviewer's job, at the cost of a full orientation per candidate.

After. A criterion may carry a kind: `proves-new` runs on both the merge base and the branch, and passes overall only when it fails on the base and passes on the branch; `guards-existing` must pass on both; an untagged criterion runs on the branch only, exactly as before, so every existing packet keeps its meaning. The largest class of reviewer judgment becomes an inequality between two exit codes. Phase L1 of `prd/PRD-lean-pipeline.md`.
design:
## Readiness schema

v1

## Scope

Extend the AC runner with criterion kinds: parse an optional kind tag from the Observable criteria line, run `proves-new` and `guards-existing` criteria against a second shared clone checked out at the merge base, and fold the two verdicts into one per-criterion result. Extend readiness validation to accept (not require) the tags.

## Non-goals

Do not require kinds — untagged criteria keep branch-only behavior, and no existing packet becomes invalid. Do not wire anything into grind; the wiring leaf consumes this. Do not attempt to detect vacuous tests for untagged criteria by heuristic. Do not change the readiness schema version; the tag is an addition v1 tolerates, and schema v2 is a Phase L3 question.

## Concrete locations

- `src/ortus/core/checks.py` — the runner this extends: kind parsing, the merge-base extraction, the combined verdict.
- `src/ortus/core/readiness.py` — the Observable-criteria validation that must accept a trailing kind tag on an `AC-N` line without breaking any current packet.
- `src/ortus/core/git.py` — the merge-base query beside the existing helpers, if not already added by the keystone.
- `tests/test_core_checks.py` — extended suite.

## Resolved decisions

1. The tag lives on the criterion line in the packet (for example `AC-3 (proves-new): ...`), not in a parallel structure — one source of truth per criterion, hashed with the rest of the field at claim.
2. `proves-new` passes only as fail-on-base AND pass-on-branch. Pass-on-both is reported as `vacuous` — a distinct verdict, because "your test proves nothing" is more actionable than "failed".
3. `guards-existing` passes only as pass-on-both; fail-on-base is reported as `broken-base`, which usually indicts the criterion or the base, not the change.
4. Both trees are disposable shared clones with prepared environments, exactly as the sibling leaf builds them — never archives, which cannot build here (the sibling leaf carries the measured evidence). The base clone is made once per run (`git clone --shared --no-checkout`, then checkout of the merge base) and shared across criteria.
5. A `proves-new` command that times out on the base is a timeout, never treated as the required failure — a wedged command is not evidence.

## Compatibility constraints

Untagged criteria behave byte-identically to the pre-kind runner, so the sibling leaf's tests keep passing unchanged. Readiness validation accepts tagged and untagged lines; every packet currently in the tracker validates exactly as before. The result record gains fields; no existing field changes meaning.

## Ordered steps

1. Accept the optional kind tag in readiness's criterion grammar, shared with the runner.
2. Add the merge-base clone to the runner, once per run.
3. Run tagged criteria on both trees and fold verdicts: `vacuous`, `broken-base`, pass, fail, timeout.
4. Extend the tracker-comment rendering to state both exit codes for tagged criteria.
5. Extend `tests/test_core_checks.py` per Targeted tests.
6. Run `uv run pytest -m "fast or integration" -q`.

## Dependencies

Depends on the AC-runner leaf, which owns the module and the single-tree executor. Consumers: the wiring leaf.

## Edge cases

A `proves-new` criterion whose test file does not exist on the merge base fails there by collection error — that counts as the required failure, and the record says why. A tagged criterion in a packet claimed before this leaf lands validates and runs correctly, because the tag is data, not schema. A merge base identical to the branch head (empty change) makes every `proves-new` criterion vacuous by construction and the run says so. Two criteria sharing one command run it twice with independent verdicts.

## Plan-gap guidance

Stop and report rather than improvising if the readiness grammar cannot accept the tag without invalidating an existing packet, or if the merge base cannot be established for the ref pair the caller supplies. Never infer a kind for an untagged criterion, and never let a vacuous verdict be rendered as a pass.
acceptance_criteria:

- AC-1: A `proves-new` criterion passing on both trees is reported as vacuous, not as a pass.
- AC-2: A `proves-new` criterion failing on the base and passing on the branch passes.
- AC-3: A `guards-existing` criterion failing on the base is reported as broken-base.
- AC-4: An untagged criterion behaves exactly as before this leaf.
- AC-5: Readiness accepts tagged and untagged criterion lines, and every pre-existing packet still validates.
- AC-6: A timeout on either tree is reported as a timeout, never as the required base failure.
- AC-7: The rendering states both exit codes for tagged criteria.

## Criterion checks

- AC-1: `uv run pytest tests/test_core_checks.py -k passes_on_both_trees_is_vacuous -q`
- AC-2: `uv run pytest tests/test_core_checks.py -k red_on_base_green_on_branch_passes -q`

## Targeted tests

`uv run pytest tests/test_core_checks.py tests/test_readiness.py -m fast -n auto --test-timeout=30 -q`

title: grind: wire the machine pipeline; verifier agent behind a default-off flag; corrections in-context
description:
## Objective

Wire the machine-verification pipeline into grind: the AC runner with the red–green proof replaces the verifier agent as the default judgment, the worker's claims are diffed against actual results, and corrections return to the worker's own session — the agent reviewer becomes a default-off pipeline step, one flag from returning.

## Behavioral context

Before. After the keystone, verification is still an agent: a fresh context re-orients, runs checks in the author's environment, and narrates a verdict; a rejection spawns a correction task in another fresh context that has never seen its own previous attempt — the mechanism that once produced byte-identical candidates across two rounds.

After. When a worker session ends, the harness runs the pipeline: AC runner against a clean extraction of the branch, red–green proof for tagged criteria, then a comparison of the worker's completion-report claims against the actual results — any disagreement fails the run outright, so the worker's word is never load-bearing. Failures return to the same worker session, bounded as today; at the bound the branch parks committed and the issue routes to a human. The verifier agent is a configuration-selected step, off by default, so reinstating it — globally or per risk tier — is one flag, per the escape-rate reversal threshold in `prd/PRD-lean-pipeline.md`. Phase L1; landed by a human because it replaces the verification path that would otherwise judge it.
design:
## Readiness schema

v1

## Scope

Replace the verification phase's default implementation with the machine pipeline (AC runner + red–green + claim diff), record its results as the verification comment, route failures back to the same worker session with bounded retries, park at the bound, and demote the agent verifier to a default-off configured step. Hash the acceptance_criteria field at claim and judge against the hash.

## Non-goals

Do not delete the verifier's code, the correction-task machinery, attribution, or the mutation guard — deletion is the strictly-after leaf, once this one has held. Do not change the gate leaves (`ortus-kdqt`, `ortus-6a0a.1`), which slot after this pipeline unchanged. Do not implement risk tiers beyond the single reviewer flag; tiering is Phase L3. Do not change selection, readiness validation, or the keystone's finalization sequence.

## Concrete locations

- `src/ortus/commands/grind.py` — the verification phase around `_verifier_prompt()` at line 1034 and the verdict handling at line 1519; `_correction_task()` at line 1554, whose fresh-context spawn is replaced by same-session return.
- `src/ortus/core/checks.py` — the runner and proof this leaf consumes.
- `src/ortus/core/lifecycle.py` — `VERIFIED_PASS` at line 117 and `VERIFIED_FAIL` at line 119, which keep their meaning; any phase vocabulary change regenerates the README state-graph block.
- `src/ortus/core/config.py` — `load_config()` at line 142: the reviewer flag, default off, resolved with the standard layering.
- `src/ortus/prompts/grind-prompt.md` — the completion report gains the claims-per-criterion block the claim diff reads.

## Resolved decisions

1. The machine pipeline is the default and the agent reviewer is a step behind a flag — review becomes policy, not architecture, and the escape-rate threshold acts by configuration.
2. Claims disagreeing with results fail the run outright. Lying must be strictly worse for the worker than silence; a missing report is merely a failed claim diff, not a crash.
3. Corrections resume the worker's session with the exact failing command and output. The retry budget is unchanged from today's correction budget; the byte-identical-resubmission pathology is removed by context, not by more budget.
4. At the bound, the branch parks committed and the issue routes to a human with the pipeline record attached — a parked branch plus a diagnosis, never an abandoned dirty tree.
5. The acceptance_criteria hash is taken at claim and rechecked before judgment; a packet edited mid-run is a blocker, not a re-read.
6. The verification comment is the runner's rendering — commands, verdicts, exit codes — keeping the durable record the tracker already expects, minus the agent that used to type it.

## Compatibility constraints

`VERIFIED_PASS` and `VERIFIED_FAIL` keep their names and meanings; if the journal needs a new phase for the claim-diff failure, `lifecycle.py` is updated and the README state-graph regenerated, never hand-edited. With the reviewer flag on, the agent verifier runs exactly as it does today, after the machine pipeline. The gate leaves compose unchanged. Existing correction-budget semantics (count, exhaustion behavior) are preserved; only the context that receives the correction changes.

## Ordered steps

1. Add the reviewer flag and the acceptance-hash-at-claim.
2. Emit and parse the claims-per-criterion completion block.
3. Run the machine pipeline at the verification boundary; write its rendering as the verification comment.
4. Route failures to the same session with bounded retries; park at the bound with the record attached.
5. Put the agent verifier behind the flag, off by default.
6. Regenerate the README state-graph if the phase vocabulary changed.
7. Run `uv run pytest -m "fast or integration" -n auto -q` with `codegraph` masked from `PATH`.

## Dependencies

Depends on the keystone (workers commit on branches; there is no ref to verify without it), the AC-runner leaf, and the red–green leaf. Consumers: the deletion leaf, strictly after; the gate leaves compose after the pipeline.

## Edge cases

A worker emitting no completion block fails the claim diff with a message naming the block, not a crash. A session that cannot be resumed (backend restart) falls back to a fresh correction context carrying the pipeline record — degraded, logged, never silent. A packet with zero tagged criteria still runs the AC runner and claim diff. A pipeline in which every criterion passes but the claim diff disagrees fails with the disagreement stated per criterion. Reviewer flag on plus machine pipeline red short-circuits before spending the reviewer's tokens.

## Plan-gap guidance

Stop and report rather than improvising if same-session correction cannot be expressed with the backend's resume semantics, or if the claims block cannot be parsed with the tolerance the completion contract requires elsewhere. Never let a claim stand in for a result, never spend reviewer tokens on a machine-red candidate, and never park without the pipeline record attached.

title: checks: a deterministic AC runner executes criterion commands in a disposable shared clone
description:
## Objective

A deterministic AC runner: a new module that executes a packet's Criterion checks as subprocesses in a disposable shared clone of a branch tree and records every command, exit code, and output — the machine that replaces the verifier's mechanical half at zero model tokens.

## Behavioral context

Before. The packet's Criterion checks are exact backticked commands, but only an agent reads and runs them: the verifier re-orients in the repository, re-derives what to check, runs the commands, and narrates the results — a full model orientation spent re-establishing facts a subprocess could establish directly. Review also runs in the author's environment against mutable state, which is how a candidate once nearly landed two tests that fail on a clean checkout.

After. A module takes an issue's acceptance criteria and a git ref, materializes the ref as a disposable shared clone — an ordinary directory that removal deletes, not a worktree — prepares its environment with the repository's sync convention, runs each criterion's command there, and returns a structured result per `AC-N`: command, exit code, bounded output. Callers can render that as a durable tracker comment. Nothing calls it in the live pipeline yet — wiring is a separate, human-landed leaf. Phase L1 of `prd/PRD-lean-pipeline.md`.

Why not `git archive`, corrected 2026-08-11 after external review: this repository's version derives from vcs metadata (`dynamic = ["version"]` with hatch-vcs), so an archive tree cannot build and zero criteria can execute — measured both ways: `uv run pytest tests/test_core_git.py` in an archive extraction dies at the build with the setuptools-scm hint, while the same suite in a shared clone passes 17 tests in 0.74s with a 204K `.git`. The failure generalizes to any downstream repository whose build reads git metadata.
design:
## Readiness schema

v1

## Scope

A new module `src/ortus/core/checks.py`: parse Criterion checks from an acceptance_criteria field, materialize a ref as a disposable shared clone, prepare its environment, execute each command with a per-command timeout, and return structured per-criterion results plus a rendering suitable for a tracker comment. Library only; no scheduler wiring.

## Non-goals

Do not wire the runner into grind, verification, or finalization — that is the human-landed wiring leaf. Do not implement criterion kinds or the red–green proof — that is the sibling leaf. Do not judge anything a command's exit code does not state: no model calls, no heuristics about flaky output. Do not modify the readiness validator, the bd client, or any prompt.

## Concrete locations

- `src/ortus/core/checks.py` — new module: the parser, the clone materialization, the environment preparation, the executor, the result types.
- `src/ortus/core/readiness.py` — the existing Criterion-checks parsing it must agree with: readiness validates that every `AC-N` has exactly one backticked command, so the runner reuses that extraction rather than re-implementing it; import or lift the helper, do not duplicate the grammar.
- `src/ortus/core/git.py` — `GitClient` at line 111; shared-clone materialization (clone, checkout ref, remove) is a new method beside `checkout()` and `head_oid()`, taking a ref and a target directory.
- `tests/test_core_checks.py` — new suite.

## Resolved decisions

1. `git clone --shared` into a scratch directory — never `git worktree` (cleanup is unrecoverable under the sandbox, codified in ortus-z7ib), and never `git archive`: an archive strips the vcs metadata this repository's build derives its version from, so the tree cannot build and no criterion can run. Measured both ways on 2026-08-11 — archive: build failure before any test; shared clone: 17 tests in 0.74s, `.git` at 204K. A shared clone is an ordinary directory that `rm -rf` removes, and its objects are shared with the source repository, so it stays cheap.
2. The hermeticity trade is accepted and named. An archive tree with no `.git` could never let a criterion accidentally consult repository state; a clone can. A hermetic tree where nothing runs is worth less than a slightly leakier one where the checks execute. The clone lives outside the repository, so accidental writes stay out of the source tree.
3. The runner prepares the clone's environment before the first criterion: a configurable sync command, defaulting to `uv sync --all-extras` where uv manages the project. Discovered in verification: a fresh clone has no venv, and `uv run` alone installs the project but not the test extras, so `pytest` fails to spawn. A sync failure is reported as an environment failure, distinct from any criterion's verdict.
4. One clone per verification, shared by all commands, removed after the run. The documented `--shared` caveat — objects can vanish if the source repository prunes mid-run — is tolerated because verification clones live minutes; a gc mid-verification is an operator action the resulting failure report would name.
5. Per-command timeout, configurable, generous by default. A wedged check is reported as timed out, distinct from failed — the ortus-xjdf lesson applied mechanically.
6. Output is captured to a file and bounded on read, never piped through a filter — the pipeline-through-tail pathology is documented and must not be rebuilt here.
7. Results are data first, rendering second: a list of per-criterion records (id, command, exit code, duration, bounded output, verdict pass/fail/timeout), with a separate function producing the tracker-comment text.
8. A criterion whose command cannot be parsed is a structural failure of the packet, reported as such — the runner never guesses a command.

## Compatibility constraints

Pure addition: no existing module changes behavior. The command grammar is exactly what readiness v1 validates, so any packet that passes readiness is runnable. The git client gains a method; nothing loses one. Subprocess use follows the repository's sandbox conventions (`UV_CACHE_DIR` respected, no writes outside the clone and scratch directories).

## Ordered steps

1. Add shared-clone materialization (clone, checkout ref, remove) to the git client.
2. Add the criterion parser to `checks.py`, reusing the readiness grammar.
3. Add environment preparation with the configurable sync command and its `uv sync --all-extras` default.
4. Add the executor: per-command subprocess, timeout, file-captured bounded output.
5. Add the result types and the tracker-comment renderer.
6. Add `tests/test_core_checks.py` per Targeted tests.
7. Run `uv run pytest -m "fast or integration" -q`.

## Dependencies

Depends on the keystone (`ortus-rcdf.1`), which also modifies `src/ortus/core/git.py` — NFR-3 serialization — and whose branches are what the runner will be pointed at. Consumers: the red–green leaf extends it; the wiring leaf calls it.

## Edge cases

A command that exits non-zero with useful output keeps the output in the record. A command that times out is killed with its process group so parallel test workers cannot hold the pipe open. An empty acceptance_criteria field yields an empty run, reported as such rather than as success. A criterion command containing shell metacharacters runs exactly as written, as readiness validated it. Non-ASCII output survives capture. A clone target that already exists is refused rather than overwritten. A repository not managed by uv skips the default sync, and the configured command decides. A sync failure fails the run as an environment failure before any criterion is attempted, naming the command that failed.

## Plan-gap guidance

Stop and report rather than improvising if the readiness grammar cannot be reused without refactoring the validator, or if the repository's environment cannot be prepared by a single configurable command. Never fall back to running commands in the live working tree, never use `git archive` for a tree that must build, and never summarize output with a model.

title: grind: the worker commits on its issue branch and the harness merges on green
description:
## Objective

The worker commits its change on `ortus/<issue-id>` with its own commit message, and the harness cuts the branch at claim, merges it on verification, closes the issue and pushes — one keystone change that makes the candidate a commit and retires the compose pass.

## Behavioral context

Before. A worker leaves uncommitted candidate edits in the shared tree; finalization infers what belongs to the issue, stages those paths, composes a commit message with a separate model pass, and commits directly onto the integration branch. Work that never reaches finalization dies as dirty paths the next worker inherits — three issues were stranded that way over 2026-08-09 and 2026-08-10 — and every correction or verification pass re-derives, from nothing, context the implementer held minutes earlier.

After. The harness creates `ortus/<issue-id>` at the integration head when it claims the issue and hands the worker that branch. The worker implements and commits there, writing the commit message at commit time under the existing subject rules. Finalization validates the message deterministically (amending via the existing deterministic assembly when invalid), merges the branch into the integration branch by fast-forward, closes, and pushes. The verifier survives this phase as an interim shim: it reads the `merge-base..head` range instead of the worktree diff, so verification is never absent between phases. Blocked or interrupted work now parks as a committed branch instead of dirty paths. The journal records the branch and its head; resume is a checkout. Phase L0 of `prd/PRD-lean-pipeline.md`; landed by a human because it replaces the mechanism that would otherwise ship it.
design:
## Readiness schema

v1

## Scope

Cut `ortus/<issue-id>` at claim and hand the worker the branch. Amend the worker contract to permit `git commit` on that branch only. Point verification at the branch commit range. Replace finalization's stage-and-commit with validate-message, merge, close, push. Record branch and head in the journal and resume by checkout.

## Non-goals

Do not build the AC runner, the red–green proof, or the claim diff — machine verification is Phase L1, and the agent verifier remains in place here. Do not delete attribution, disowning or the mutation guard; they still have callers until L1 removes their reasons to exist. Do not add merge handling beyond fast-forward: with one issue in flight the integration head does not move mid-issue, and anything that cannot fast-forward is a blocker to report. Do not change the gate, selection, readiness, or the correction flow.

## Concrete locations

- `src/ortus/commands/grind.py` — `_finalize_candidate()` at line 2170, whose commit step stages paths and commits; the claim path where the branch must be cut; `_verifier_prompt()` at line 1034, whose diff source becomes the branch range.
- `src/ortus/core/git.py` — `GitClient` at line 111: `checkout()` at 284, `head_oid()` at 230, `push()` at 288; branch creation, merge-base and fast-forward are new methods beside them.
- `src/ortus/core/compose.py` — `validate_message()` and `shortened()`, which survive as the deterministic validation applied to the worker's own message; `compose_commit_message()` and its prompt are retired from the finalization path.
- `src/ortus/core/transaction.py` — `CandidateJournal` and `with_finalization()` at line 517; branch name and head fields, defaulted so older journals load.
- `src/ortus/core/grind_loop.py` — `BranchDisposition` at line 347, which must learn that a run legitimately sits on an issue branch between claim and merge.
- `src/ortus/prompts/grind-prompt.md` and `src/ortus/prompts/conditions/work-issue.txt` — the flat prohibition on `git commit` narrows to: commit on your own branch only; closing, pushing, and touching the integration branch stay forbidden.
- `src/ortus/core/lifecycle.py` — `FINALIZATION_STEPS` at line 147; any phase vocabulary change regenerates the README state-graph block.

## Resolved decisions

1. One keystone change, not two phases. The superseded PRD split branch-scoped finalization from worker commits to preserve the verification contract across the migration; that contract is being retired, so the split bought nothing but an intermediate state.
2. The worker writes the commit message at commit time, like any author. Finalization validates with the existing deterministic rules — an over-long subject is shortened, a wrong message is replaced by the deterministic assembly via amend on the branch before merge. The compose model pass and its prompt are retired.
3. The verifier shim reads `merge-base..head`. Cheap, throwaway by design, and it keeps NFR-1: verification exists in some form at every phase boundary.
4. Fast-forward only, blocker on anything else. Sequential execution means the integration head cannot move mid-issue except by operator action, which deserves a report, not a merge.
5. Branch and head are journaled at the worker's first commit boundary observed by the harness; a journal without the fields resumes by today's path, so pre-keystone journals are not stranded.
6. A branch left by a parked issue is checked out on resume, never recreated and never reset.
7. Landed as two commits within the hand-landed phase, per external review 2026-08-11: commit A — the harness cuts the branch and finalization merges it, worker behavior entirely unchanged (steps 1–2 and the merge half of step 5); commit B — workers commit, the compose pass retires, the verifier shim switches to the range (the rest). Three failures in two days at this seam argued for small steps; the split preserves a bisection point at the cost of one extra commit.

## Compatibility constraints

A repository with no remote finalizes as today, minus the push. Journals written before this change load and finalize by the current path. The branch guard still requires the integration branch at scheduler boundaries; its disposition logic gains the claimed-branch state rather than being weakened. Existing finalization tests asserting the committed tree keep passing where the tree is genuinely unchanged; tests asserting the staging mechanism are replaced with branch-merge equivalents, not deleted. `shortened()` and `validate_message()` keep their current tests byte-for-byte.

## Ordered steps

1. Add branch creation, merge-base, and fast-forward to the git client.
2. Cut `ortus/<issue-id>` at claim and hand the worker the branch; teach `BranchDisposition` the claimed state.
3. Narrow the worker contract: commit permitted on the issue branch only; close, push, integration-branch operations and branch switching stay forbidden.
4. Point the verifier shim at the `merge-base..head` diff.
5. Replace finalization's stage-and-commit with validate/amend, fast-forward, close, push; retire the compose pass from the path.
6. Journal branch and head; resume by checkout; report a missing recorded branch by name.
7. Regenerate the README state-graph if any journal phase changed.
8. Run `uv run pytest -m "fast or integration" -n auto -q` with `codegraph` masked from `PATH`.

## Dependencies

None in the graph — this is the keystone the rest of the programme points at. Consumers: `ortus-kdqt` and `ortus-6a0a.1` (branches to trigger on and gate), Phase L1 (the pipeline that replaces the shim).

## Edge cases

A worker that commits nothing parks an empty branch; finalization reports it rather than merging nothing. A worker that commits several times merges as a range, message validation applying to the head. An issue id illegal in a ref name is rejected at claim with an actionable message. A pre-existing `ortus/<issue-id>` branch from an earlier attempt is checked out and continued, never reset. A repository with no commits has no head to branch from. A killed run between commit and merge resumes by checkout and re-enters finalization. The deterministic-amend path must preserve the issue-id subject prefix.

## Plan-gap guidance

Stop and report rather than improvising if the fast-forward is ever impossible under sequential execution, if narrowing the commit prohibition would require weakening the close or push prohibitions, or if the verifier shim cannot express the branch range without contract changes larger than a diff-source swap. Never force-update or delete a branch, never let the worker touch the integration branch, and never ship this alongside any other change.
