## Objective
Stop a fail verdict from aborting the run over criterion ids the verifier was never told to use, and name the offending ids when a mismatch does matter.

## Behavioral context
Observed in a downstream repo (a downstream repository) on 2026-08-07. Every Bash call in the verification session died with an EROFS error, so the verifier could execute nothing and reported a fail verdict that added one extra criterion, `AC-TESTS`, to record that the targeted tests never ran. `parse_verdict` requires the verdict id set to equal the AC-N ids scraped from the packet, so the run died with "verdict criteria do not match the authoritative issue packet" and left the candidate uncommitted with no persisted report. The verdict already said fail, so the correct outcome was a recorded failed verification the correction loop could act on. The rule that was broken is not stated anywhere in the verifier prompt, and the error names neither the expected nor the actual ids. After this change the prompt states the rule, the error names the exact discrepancy, and an id mismatch only aborts when it could let unverified work close an issue.
design:
## Readiness schema
v1

## Scope
State the exact-id rule in the verifier contract, report the specific missing, unexpected, and duplicated ids in the error, and make the id-set check asymmetric so a fail verdict degrades to a recorded failure instead of a hard abort.

## Non-goals
No change to the underlying sandbox or session-env problem that made the verifier unable to run commands; that is a separate issue. No change to candidate hashing, the report budget, or the correction-retry counter. No relaxation of any other verdict schema field.

## Resolved decisions
The strictness is asymmetric, and this is the decision the issue exists to settle. A `pass` verdict whose criterion ids do not exactly match the packet stays fatal: accepting it would close an issue and commit code against criteria that were never mapped to the packet, which is the one direction where a bad verdict causes damage. A `fail` verdict with unexpected, missing, or duplicated ids parses successfully and is recorded as a failed verification with its report persisted: the practical outcome is identical either way because nothing is committed and the issue stays open, but the operator gets a verdict and findings instead of a schema error, and the bounded correction loop gets something to act on. A verifier can already force a failure simply by writing fail, so the permissive direction grants it no new power. Unmapped ids are preserved in the rendered report rather than dropped, so the discrepancy stays visible.

## Concrete locations
Edit `validate_verdict()` in `src/ortus/core/verdict.py` around the id-set comparison at lines 100 to 105, and carry any unmapped ids on the frozen `Verdict` dataclass at line 32 so `render_report()` can show them. Edit `_verifier_prompt()` in `src/ortus/commands/grind.py` around line 391, whose JSON field description currently stops at "objects with exactly id, status, evidence" and never mentions the packet ids. Note that `grind.py` line numbers will have shifted: ortus-pzfd.5 is in flight over that file. Cover in `tests/test_verdict.py` and `tests/test_grind_prompt_content.py`.

## Compatibility constraints
The verdict schema version stays 1: this loosens acceptance in the fail direction and adds no required field, so an existing well-formed verdict still parses identically. Every other `VerdictError` message keeps its current wording so log-scraping stays valid. The `passed` property and the pass path are unchanged, so `_finalize_candidate` sees no new behavior. Both backends emit the same contract.

## Ordered steps
1. Extend the verifier prompt to state that criterion ids must be exactly the AC-N identifiers from the issue packet, each used once, with no invented ids, and that anything the verifier cannot run belongs in the evidence of the criterion it blocks.
2. Compute the missing, unexpected, and duplicated id sets in `validate_verdict()` instead of a single equality test.
3. Raise for any discrepancy when the decision is pass, with a message naming each set explicitly.
4. When the decision is fail, accept the verdict and carry the discrepancy on the returned `Verdict` rather than raising.
5. Surface the carried discrepancy in the rendered report so the failure reason stays legible to the operator and to the correction pass.
6. Add tests for the pass-side abort, the fail-side degrade, the id naming in the message, and a regression reproducing the observed extra-id shape.

## Dependencies
Discovered from ortus-pzfd.4, which introduced `src/ortus/core/verdict.py`. Related to ortus-pzfd.5, which is currently rewriting the surrounding `grind.py` verification path; land this after that transaction finalizes to avoid conflicting edits. Callers affected are `_verify_candidate()` in `src/ortus/commands/grind.py` and the report renderer in `src/ortus/core/verdict.py`.

## Edge cases
A fail verdict whose ids are entirely unrelated to the packet must still be recorded as a failure rather than silently treated as covering the criteria. Duplicated ids on a fail verdict must not double-count a criterion in the report. A packet with no AC-N identifiers at all leaves `expected_criteria` empty, which already bypasses the check today and must keep working. A pass verdict missing one packet id must stay fatal even when every reported criterion passes. The report must stay within its existing character budget when unmapped ids are added.

## Plan-gap guidance
If carrying the discrepancy on the frozen `Verdict` dataclass breaks a consumer that constructs `Verdict` positionally, record PLAN-GAP with the construction site and route to planning rather than dropping the field and losing the operator-visible reason.

title: Repair unready ready-queue issues inside grind instead of skipping them
description:
## Objective
Let ortus grind repair an unready executable leaf in place and keep going, instead of skipping it and exiting with nothing claimed.

## Behavioral context
Today `select_ready_issue()` rejects a leaf that fails readiness, grind logs a readiness skip warning per issue, then reports that nothing is ready and breaks out of the outer loop, which reads to the operator as a grind failure. After this change grind runs one bounded repair pass on the offending issues, revalidates, and claims the repaired leaf; when repair is disabled, exhausted, or unsuccessful it stops as it does today but with the per-issue failures and the fix named in the exit message.
design:
## Readiness schema
v1

## Scope
Call the core repair pass from the harness-select path when the ready queue contains only unready leaves, bound it with a per-run budget and one attempt per issue id, add an opt-out flag, record the repair on the issue, and make the give-up path print actionable diagnostics.

## Non-goals
No user-facing repair or upsample verb: the operator chose a teach-only strategy with grind self-healing as the safety net. Epics stay exempt and still are not claimable. No change to readiness rules themselves and no change to the orphan policy.

## Concrete locations
Edit `src/ortus/commands/grind.py`: the harness-select block that builds `ready_packets` and defines `report_unready()` around lines 985 to 1035, and the verb signature for the new opt-out and budget options. Keep `select_ready_issue()` in `src/ortus/core/grind_loop.py` line 170 as the pure selector and drive repair from the caller. Repair itself comes from `src/ortus/core/repair.py`. Cover in `tests/test_grind.py` and `tests/test_grind_loop.py`.

## Resolved decisions
Repair context is the issue packet plus its parent epic when one exists, with no PRD lookup: grind usually has no PRD and guessing one would repair against the wrong document. The pass runs on the planning profile, not the implementer profile, because it is authoring work. Budget is one attempt per issue id per grind run with a total per-run cap exposed as an option, so a badly planned queue cannot burn the loop in repair subprocesses. Repair failure falls back to current skip behavior rather than crashing the loop. Each repaired issue gets a comment recording the pass, matching what the plan verb already does.

## Compatibility constraints
Default behavior changes from skip-and-stop to repair-then-continue, so the opt-out flag must restore exactly the current behavior for operators who depend on it. The flock at `.beads/ralph.flock` is still held for the whole run, so the repair subprocess must not be launched while grind holds an open bd write transaction. Both backends must work; the repair runs through the same backend the grind run resolved. Existing grind logs keep their line formats so tail parsing is unaffected.

## Ordered steps
1. Add the opt-out and per-run budget options to the grind verb and thread them into the harness-select path.
2. When every ready leaf is unready, collect the reports and call the core repair pass with the planning profile, one attempt per issue id and within the run budget.
3. Reload the authoritative packets, revalidate, and continue the loop with the repaired leaf when it now passes.
4. Reuse the created-replacement guard so a repair that invents new issues is a hard error rather than silent queue growth.
5. Add a comment to each repaired issue recording the pass, mirroring the plan verb.
6. On disabled, exhausted, or unsuccessful repair, exit as today but print each issue diagnostic and the exact follow-up command.
7. Add grind tests for the repair-and-continue path, the opt-out path, and the budget-exhausted path using the canned response fixtures.

## Dependencies
Blocked by the repair-extraction leaf, which puts the pass in core. Related to the spec-generator leaf, whose text the repair prompt renders. Callers affected are the grind verb entry point in `src/ortus/cli.py` and the loop helpers in `src/ortus/core/grind_loop.py`.

## Edge cases
A repair pass that leaves the issue still unready must not be retried in the same run. A ready queue mixing ready and unready leaves must claim the ready one first and not spend repair budget at all. An epic in the ready queue must stay skipped rather than repaired. A repair subprocess that hangs must be bounded by the same worker timeout policy the loop already applies. Repair must not fire when the queue is genuinely drained, which is a different exit reason.

## Plan-gap guidance
If launching the repair subprocess while the grind flock is held deadlocks against the bd single-writer lock, record PLAN-GAP with the observed lock holder and route to planning; do not drop the flock mid-run to work around it.

- AC-2: The opt-out flag restores the current skip-and-stop behavior exactly.
- AC-3: With the repair budget exhausted, grind exits with each per-issue diagnostic and the follow-up command in its output.
- AC-4: A queue containing one ready leaf and one unready leaf claims the ready leaf and spends no repair budget.

## Criterion checks
- AC-1: Run `uv run pytest tests/test_grind.py -k repair_then_claim -q`.
- AC-2: Run `uv run pytest tests/test_grind.py -k repair_opt_out -q`.

- AC-4: Run `uv run pytest tests/test_grind_loop.py -k mixed_ready_queue -q`.

## Targeted tests
Run `uv run pytest tests/test_grind.py tests/test_grind_loop.py --test-timeout=60 --enforce-duration-budget`.

- Repair fires only when `target_issue is None and unready` — a drained queue (a different exit reason) and a queue holding any ready leaf both skip it entirely.

title: Extract the readiness repair pass from plan.py into core
description:
## Objective
Move the readiness repair pass out of the plan verb into shared core so grind can reuse it without importing a command module.

## Behavioral context
`_readiness_repair_prompt()` and `_repair_readiness()` are private to src/ortus/commands/plan.py, so the only way to repair an unready packet today is to run ortus plan. After this change the same bounded, update-in-place repair is callable from core with identical behavior for plan, and grind can call it in a later leaf.
design:
## Readiness schema
v1

## Scope
Move the repair prompt builder and the repair runner into a core module, together with the guard that forbids the pass from creating replacement issues, and keep plan calling through the new home with unchanged behavior.

## Non-goals
No behavior change for ortus plan: same single pass, same failure modes, same exit codes. No new CLI verb. Grind integration is a separate leaf.

## Concrete locations
Move `_readiness_repair_prompt()` at `src/ortus/commands/plan.py` line 103 and `_repair_readiness()` at line 135 into a new `src/ortus/core/repair.py`, and lift the created-replacement guard that currently lives inline in the plan flow around lines 324 and 357 into the same module so both callers inherit it. Update the plan verb to import from core. Cover in a new `tests/test_core_repair.py` plus the existing `tests/test_plan.py`.

## Resolved decisions
The extracted function keeps taking an explicit backend, profile, contract, and capability rather than resolving them internally, so callers stay in control of the phase profile and the codegraph handshake. The before-and-after issue id diff moves with it because that guard is the safety property, not a plan detail.

## Compatibility constraints
The plan verb keeps its current progress lines, warning text, exit codes, and the comment it adds to each issue after a repair. Prompt resolution still honors the three-layer override precedence. Both backends keep working.

## Ordered steps
1. Create `src/ortus/core/repair.py` and move the prompt builder and the repair runner into it unchanged.
2. Lift the created-replacement id-diff guard into the same module as a reusable function.
3. Update `src/ortus/commands/plan.py` to import and call the core functions.
4. Add `tests/test_core_repair.py` covering the prompt contents and the replacement guard, and confirm the plan tests still pass unchanged.

## Dependencies
Related to the plan-prompt rendering leaf, which also edits `_readiness_repair_prompt()`; whichever lands second adapts to the other. Blocks the grind auto-repair leaf, which is the reason for the extraction.

## Edge cases
The repair runner must keep refusing to create, close, rename, or re-depend issues. A repair subprocess exiting nonzero must surface the log path. A caller that passes an empty report tuple must be a no-op rather than launching a subprocess.

## Plan-gap guidance
If moving the guard changes plan exit codes for any existing test, record PLAN-GAP with the failing test and the old and new codes and route to planning; do not relax the assertion to make the move fit.

title: Seed the readiness pointer as a bd memory at init and detect it in check
description:
## Objective
Put a short pointer to the readiness contract into bd prime output for every ortus repo, including repos that were initialized before this change.

## Behavioral context
bd injects memories at prime time, so a memory stored once is reloaded in every later session and after every compaction. Today no such memory exists and nothing in a fresh session mentions readiness. After this change ortus init stores the pointer, and ortus check reports its absence in an existing repo along with the exact command to add it, which is the only retrofit path that does not require re-rendering templates.
design:
## Readiness schema
v1

## Scope
Store a keyed bd memory during ortus init and add a read-only check that reports whether the memory is present in the target repo.

## Non-goals
Do not override bd prime output via a .beads/PRIME.md file: that forks bd content and drifts on bd upgrades. Do not store the full contract as a memory; memories are injected into every prime and must stay pointer-sized. ortus check stays read-only and does not write the memory itself.

## Concrete locations
Add a `_bd_remember()` helper next to `_bd_init()` in `src/ortus/commands/init.py` (around line 26) and call it from the init flow after the workspace exists, around the `bd workspace initialized` success line near line 200. Add `check_readiness_memory()` to `src/ortus/commands/check.py` next to `check_beads_dir()` and register it in the repo-check list inside `_run_all()`. Cover in `tests/test_init.py` and `tests/test_check.py`.

## Resolved decisions
The memory is written with an explicit key so re-running init updates it in place instead of accumulating duplicates: bd remember documents that a matching key is updated rather than appended. The memory body points at the ortus spec command rather than restating the sections, keeping every prime cheap. Detection reads `bd memories` rather than parsing the database directly.

## Compatibility constraints
Init must not fail the whole bootstrap when the memory write fails; bd may be older or the workspace may be read-only, so the failure is reported as a warning and init still completes. The check is read-only per NFR-006 and must not mutate bd state. Behavior is identical for the claude and codex backends because bd prime is backend-neutral.

## Ordered steps
1. Add `_bd_remember()` in init.py running bd remember with an explicit stable key and the pointer text.
2. Call it after the bd workspace is confirmed, warning rather than exiting when it fails.
3. Add `check_readiness_memory()` in check.py that looks the key up through bd memories and reports the add command when it is missing.
4. Register the new check in `_run_all()` alongside the other repo checks.
5. Add tests for the init write path, the init warning path, and both check verdicts.

## Dependencies
Blocked by the ortus spec verb leaf because the memory text names that command. Related to the AGENTS.md contract leaf, which carries the same pointer for repos that re-render templates.

## Edge cases
An init run against an existing .beads workspace under --force must not duplicate the memory. A bd binary that predates bd remember must degrade to a warning. A repo with many memories must still match by key rather than by substring of unrelated memory text.

## Plan-gap guidance
If bd offers no stable way to query a single memory by key, record PLAN-GAP with the bd version and the commands tried, and route to planning rather than parsing the Dolt database directly.
acceptance_criteria:
## Observable criteria
- AC-1: ortus init stores the keyed readiness memory in the new workspace.
- AC-2: A failed memory write warns and leaves init exiting 0.
- AC-3: ortus check reports the memory as missing in a workspace that lacks it and as present when it is there.

## Criterion checks
- AC-1: Run `uv run pytest tests/test_init.py -k readiness_memory -q`.
- AC-2: Run `uv run pytest tests/test_init.py -k readiness_memory_failure -q`.
- AC-3: Run `uv run pytest tests/test_check.py -k readiness_memory -q`.

## Targeted tests
Run `uv run pytest tests/test_init.py tests/test_check.py --test-timeout=30 --enforce-duration-budget`.
notes: bd prime --help documents that memories are injected at prime time and that bd remember --key updates in place; .beads/PRIME.md was rejected as a full override.

- `bd memories --json` returns a JSON OBJECT keyed by memory key, so the `key in memories` lookup is a true key match, not a substring scan of unrelated memory text. That closes the "repo with many memories" edge case (13 memories present here; no false positive).

- `bd remember --key` is documented to update in place, and `--readonly` / `--sandbox` are real global flags, so the query cannot take a write or auto-sync path (NFR-006). test_check_readiness_memory_is_read_only asserts both flags on every memories invocation and that `remember` never appears.

title: Add an ortus spec verb that prints the readiness contract
description:
## Objective
Give every session a one-command way to read the readiness schema v1 contract, so the pointer surfaces have something concrete to point at.

## Behavioral context
Today an agent that wants the contract has to read src/ortus/core/readiness.py and infer the rules from regexes. After this change `ortus spec` prints the generated contract to stdout and exits 0, and the command works in any repo because the text is package data, not repo state.
design:
## Readiness schema
v1

## Scope
A new non-interactive verb that prints the rendered contract and exits 0, registered in the top-level typer app and following the repository CLI output convention.

## Non-goals
The verb does not validate issues, does not read or write bd state, and does not take an issue id: it is a teaching surface only. No upsample or repair behavior belongs here.

## Concrete locations
Add `src/ortus/commands/spec.py` exposing `spec()`, and register it in `src/ortus/cli.py` next to the existing `app.command(name="check", ...)` block around line 62. The rendered text comes from `spec_markdown()` in `src/ortus/core/readiness.py`. Cover in a new `tests/test_spec.py` plus the verb-inventory assertions in `tests/test_cli_verbs.py`.

## Resolved decisions
The contract goes to stdout so it can be piped or redirected; per the CLI output convention in AGENTS.md, any progress lines go to stderr via `ortus.core.output.progress()`. The verb takes no repo argument because the spec is identical in every repo.

## Compatibility constraints
Adding a verb must not reorder or rename the existing ones; `ortus --help` keeps listing the current verbs in their current order with `spec` appended. Exit code stays 0 on success on Linux and macOS.

## Ordered steps
1. Add `src/ortus/commands/spec.py` with a `spec()` typer callback that writes `spec_markdown()` to stdout.
2. Import and register the verb in `src/ortus/cli.py` after the existing verb registrations.
3. Add `tests/test_spec.py` asserting exit code 0 and that required headings appear in stdout.
4. Extend `tests/test_cli_verbs.py` so the verb inventory includes `spec`.

## Dependencies
Blocked by the spec-generator leaf, which provides `spec_markdown()`. Consumers are the bd memory and the AGENTS.md contract section, both of which reference this command by name.

## Edge cases
Output must not be swallowed when stdout is a pipe rather than a TTY. The verb must not require a bd workspace or a resolved backend, so it works in a repo that has not been initialized yet.

## Plan-gap guidance
If the verb name `spec` collides with an existing or reserved bd or ortus concept, record PLAN-GAP with the collision and route to planning rather than inventing an alternate name.

- AC-1: `ortus spec` exits 0 and prints the readiness contract including every required heading.

title: Render the plan and repair prompts from the generated readiness spec
description:
## Objective
Stop maintaining two prose copies of the readiness contract by rendering the plan prompt and the repair prompt from the generated spec.

## Behavioral context
Today src/ortus/prompts/plan-prompt.md restates the section list in its own words and src/ortus/commands/plan.py restates it a second time inside the repair prompt, so a schema change can leave the planner teaching a stale contract while the validator rejects it. After this change both are rendered from the generated text, and the worked bd create example in the prompt is verified by the validator it teaches.
design:
## Readiness schema
v1

## Scope
Introduce a `$readiness_spec` placeholder in the bundled plan prompt, substitute it tolerantly at prompt-assembly time, render the repair prompt section list from the same generator, and add a test that runs the worked example in the prompt through validate_issue.

## Non-goals
The hand-written worked `bd create` example stays prose and is not generated. The issue-ID handling section of the prompt is untouched. No change to the repair control flow, which moves to core in a separate leaf.

## Concrete locations
Edit `src/ortus/prompts/plan-prompt.md` (the readiness schema section at lines 16 to 45 becomes the placeholder). Substitute in `src/ortus/commands/plan.py` where the resolved prompt is assembled in `_repair_readiness()` and the planning run, and render `_readiness_repair_prompt()` heading list from `spec_markdown()`. Tolerant substitution belongs next to `resolve_prompt()` in `src/ortus/core/prompts.py`. Extend `check_prompt_overrides()` in `src/ortus/commands/check.py` to flag a repo or user override that predates the placeholder. Cover in `tests/test_plan.py`, `tests/test_core_prompts.py`, and `tests/test_check.py`.

## Resolved decisions
Substitution uses safe-substitution semantics so a stale override missing the placeholder still runs rather than raising: silently degrading to an older contract is bad, but crashing every plan run on a users private override is worse, so `ortus check` reports the staleness instead. The three-layer override precedence in prompts.py is unchanged.

## Compatibility constraints
A repo-local `.ortus/prompts/plan-prompt.md` copied before this change must keep working: no KeyError, no template exception. The existing `$prd_path` substitution keeps its current behavior and spelling.

## Ordered steps
1. Replace the readiness section of the bundled plan prompt with a `$readiness_spec` placeholder.
2. Substitute the generated text at prompt-assembly time using safe substitution, alongside the existing `$prd_path` handling.
3. Render the heading list inside `_readiness_repair_prompt()` from the generator instead of its inline prose.
4. Extend `check_prompt_overrides()` to report an override that lacks the placeholder as a stale-override warning.
5. Add a test extracting the worked example from the prompt and asserting `validate_issue()` reports it ready.

## Dependencies
Blocked by the spec-generator leaf. Related to the repair-extraction leaf, which moves `_readiness_repair_prompt()` into core; whichever lands second adapts to the other rather than reverting it.

## Edge cases
An override file containing a literal dollar sign must not break substitution. The worked example lives inside a fenced bash block with shell quoting, so the extraction test has to parse the bd create flag values rather than the raw fence. A missing placeholder must produce a check warning, not a check failure that breaks unrelated CI.

## Plan-gap guidance
If safe substitution and the existing dollar-sign usage in the prompt cannot coexist without escaping churn, record PLAN-GAP with the conflicting tokens and route to planning; do not switch the prompt to a different templating engine unilaterally.

title: Generate readiness schema v1 spec text from readiness.py
description:
## Objective
Make src/ortus/core/readiness.py the single source of the readiness schema v1 spec by exporting a rendered Markdown contract derived from the same constants the validator enforces.

## Behavioral context
Today the section list and shape rules are re-prosed by hand in src/ortus/prompts/plan-prompt.md and again inside _readiness_repair_prompt in src/ortus/commands/plan.py, so a schema change has to be mirrored in three places and silently drifts when it is not. After this change a caller asks readiness.py for the contract text and every consumer renders the same sections, headings, and shape rules that validate_issue actually checks.
design:
## Readiness schema
v1

## Scope
Attach per-section guidance to the existing required-section table and add a public renderer that emits the contract as Markdown: the field/heading list in validator order plus the shape rules (the literal v1 body, AC-N one-to-one mapping, backticked test command, file-and-symbol in concrete locations, numbered ordered steps).

## Non-goals
No change to what validate_issue accepts or rejects: this issue is pure text generation over the existing rules. No consumer rewiring here; plan-prompt, the CLI verb, and the repair prompt are separate leaves.

## Concrete locations
Edit `src/ortus/core/readiness.py`: the `_REQUIRED_SECTIONS` tuple at line 51 becomes a sequence of frozen dataclass entries carrying `field`, `heading`, `code`, and new guidance text; `validate_issue()` keeps reading the same three attributes; add a public `spec_markdown()` alongside it. Shape-rule text renders from the existing module constants `READINESS_SCHEMA_VERSION`, `_CRITERION_ID`, `_ORDERED_STEP`, `_TEST_COMMAND`, `_LOCATION`, and `_SYMBOL` rather than restating them. Cover in `tests/test_readiness.py`.

## Resolved decisions
Guidance strings live next to the rule that enforces them, in readiness.py, not in a separate data file: the whole point is that adding a required section forces its guidance in the same edit. The worked `bd create` example stays hand-maintained prose in the prompt (generation would flatten it) and is policed by a test in a later leaf instead.

## Compatibility constraints
`validate_issue()` and `validate_issues()` keep their current signatures and verdicts, so grind and plan behavior is unchanged by this leaf alone. `READINESS_SCHEMA_VERSION` stays "v1". Any external reader of `_REQUIRED_SECTIONS` is internal to this repo.

## Ordered steps
1. Replace the `_REQUIRED_SECTIONS` tuple entries with a frozen dataclass that carries the existing field/heading/code plus a one-line guidance string per section.
2. Update `validate_issue()` to unpack the dataclass instead of the three-tuple, leaving its logic otherwise untouched.
3. Add `spec_markdown()` rendering the grouped heading list in validator order plus the shape rules derived from the module constants.
4. Add tests asserting the rendered text names every section and that a packet written by following it passes `validate_issue()`.

## Dependencies
No issue dependency: this is the root of the epic. Consumers that will call `spec_markdown()` are the `ortus spec` verb, the plan prompt, and the repair prompt, each in its own leaf.

## Edge cases
A section added to the table without guidance must fail loudly rather than render an empty bullet. Rendering must stay stable in ordering so the generated text does not churn between runs. Epics remain exempt in `validate_issue()` and the rendered spec must say so, or authors will pad epics needlessly.

## Plan-gap guidance
If attaching guidance to `_REQUIRED_SECTIONS` turns out to break a consumer that unpacks the three-tuple positionally outside this repo, record PLAN-GAP with the consumer and the call site and route to planning; do not silently keep a duplicate legacy tuple.
acceptance_criteria:
## Observable criteria
- AC-1: `spec_markdown()` names every field and heading present in the required-section table, in validator order.
- AC-2: An issue packet authored by following the rendered text passes `validate_issue()` with no failures.
- AC-3: `validate_issue()` verdicts are unchanged for the existing fixtures.

## Criterion checks
- AC-1: Run `uv run pytest tests/test_readiness.py -k spec_markdown -q`.
- AC-2: Run `uv run pytest tests/test_readiness.py -k rendered_spec_round_trip -q`.
- AC-3: Run `uv run pytest tests/test_readiness.py -q`.

## Targeted tests
Run `uv run pytest tests/test_readiness.py --test-timeout=30 --enforce-duration-budget`.
notes: Per docs/testing.md the changed path src/ortus/core/*.py maps to tests/test_core_*.py for implementation and -m "fast or integration" for a fresh verifier; readiness.py is covered by tests/test_readiness.py.

Make readiness schema v1 discoverable in every session that creates bd issues, so hand-authored issues are born grindable instead of being skipped by ortus grind.

A human chatting with an agent in a downstream repo authors issues with no knowledge of the contract; ortus grind then warns "readiness skip" per issue, finds nothing workable, and exits. After this epic the contract is generated from readiness.py, pointed at from bd prime (via a bd memory) and the bundled AGENTS.md, and grind repairs an unready leaf in place rather than dead-ending.

title: Gracefully resume uncommitted candidates after failed grind runs
description:
## Objective

Make `ortus grind` gracefully resume transaction-owned uncommitted work after any unsuccessful run instead of rejecting, discarding, or restarting the candidate.

## Behavioral context

A worker may exit nonzero, be interrupted, fail verification, lose its subprocess, or otherwise return without closing its assigned bd issue after editing files. When the next grind starts, the issue and candidate edits should still be associated, validated, and resumed from the correct phase. The operator should see an explicit recovery message rather than a generic dirty-worktree error.
design:
## Readiness schema

v1

## Scope

Generalize recovery into an engineer-handoff flow for every unsuccessful grind exit that leaves an assigned issue open or in progress with uncommitted changes. Resume the same issue, give a fresh worker the authoritative issue packet plus the complete current Git state, and let it assess, preserve, correct, and continue useful prior work.

## Non-goals

Do not silently reset, stash, delete, or discard uncommitted work. Do not require an exact historical HEAD, path set, fingerprint, hash, or journal schema merely to let a fresh worker inspect the repository and continue. Do not retry forever or silently commit changes the worker identifies as unrelated.

## Concrete locations

Update `src/ortus/commands/grind.py` in `grind()` and `_capture_codex_candidate()`; extend `src/ortus/core/transaction.py` through `CandidateJournal` and `JournalStore`; update `src/ortus/core/git.py` ownership checks; add focused coverage in `tests/test_transaction.py`, `tests/test_grind_worker_timeout.py`, and a failure/restart integration module such as `tests/test_grind_recovery.py`.

## Resolved decisions

The assigned bd issue is the goal and the current worktree is the handoff artifact. A journal is useful routing context, not a prerequisite or cryptographic ownership gate. On restart, prefer the journal or single in-progress issue to choose the same goal, then give the fresh model `git status`, the complete diff, the issue packet, and prior phase context. The model decides which changes are relevant, retains valuable work, repairs incomplete work, leaves unrelated changes alone, and continues. Historical mismatches become visible context, not automatic startup failures. Only true ambiguity about which issue to pursue requires human routing.

## Compatibility constraints

Preserve Claude and Codex behavior, dirty operator baselines, path-scoped commits, flock exclusivity, phase profiles, worker timeouts, task and iteration caps, branch discipline, CodeGraph reporting, and no-remote repositories. Progress lines must use the canonical stderr helper.

## Ordered steps

1. Enumerate every grind exit path after issue claim and preserve the issue association plus available phase context.
2. On startup, prefer an existing journal hint or a single in-progress issue before selecting new work.
3. Supply a fresh implementation worker with the issue packet, current Git status, complete diff, and explicit recovery-handoff instructions.
4. Let the worker assess relevance, preserve useful changes, correct or complete them, and identify unrelated work without restarting from scratch.
5. Use journals, hashes, and prior HEAD values as verification and audit evidence after assessment rather than startup blockers.
6. Emit concise progress and log lines explaining the recovered issue, prior state, and handoff action.
7. Add interruption and restart integration tests proving useful changes survive, unrelated changes remain untouched, and repeated resumes are idempotent.

## Dependencies

Build on the structured candidate transaction and verifier verdict work in `ortus-pzfd.4` and the completed timeout ownership foundation in `ortus-q10w`.

## Edge cases

Cover nonzero worker exit after edits, parent interruption, implementation success without close, verifier failure, malformed verdict, correction failure, failure after close but before commit, failure after commit but before push, missing, corrupt, or newer journal schemas, HEAD or branch drift, candidate mutation, issue changes, empty candidates, multiple in-progress issues, and unrelated staged, unstaged, or untracked files.

## Plan-gap guidance

If more than one issue could plausibly own the handoff and the model cannot determine the goal from bd state and repository context, preserve everything and request human routing. Do not turn ordinary code assessment into a journal-repair prerequisite.
acceptance_criteria:
## Observable criteria

- AC-1: Every post-claim abnormal exit preserves the assigned issue association and all uncommitted work before grind returns.
- AC-2: A subsequent grind prefers the same in-progress issue before selecting new work and supplies a fresh worker with the issue packet plus complete current Git context.
- AC-3: The fresh worker explicitly assesses existing changes, retains useful work, repairs or completes it, and continues instead of restarting.
- AC-4: Journal schema, prior HEAD, path, fingerprint, or hash differences are reported as handoff context and do not by themselves block model assessment.
- AC-5: Unrelated staged, unstaged, and untracked changes remain untouched and are not silently reset, stashed, deleted, or committed.
- AC-6: Nonzero exits, interruptions, verifier failures, malformed verdicts, and partial finalization states each resume gracefully or request human routing only when multiple goals are genuinely ambiguous.
- AC-7: Restart regression tests prove useful work survives and repeated handoffs create no duplicate comments, closes, commits, pushes, or correction attempts.

## Criterion checks

- AC-1: Run `uv run pytest tests/test_grind_recovery.py -q -k preserve`.
- AC-2: Run `uv run pytest tests/test_grind_recovery.py -q -k resume_before_select`.
- AC-3: Run `uv run pytest tests/test_grind_recovery.py -q -k handoff_prompt`.
- AC-4: Run `uv run pytest tests/test_grind_recovery.py tests/test_grind_worker_timeout.py -q -k moved_state`.
- AC-5: Run `uv run pytest tests/test_grind_recovery.py tests/test_core_git.py -q -k unrelated`.
- AC-6: Run `uv run pytest tests/test_grind_recovery.py -q -k failure_phase`.
- AC-7: Run `uv run pytest tests/test_grind_recovery.py -q -k idempotent`.

## Targeted tests

Run `uv run pytest tests/test_transaction.py tests/test_core_git.py tests/test_grind_recovery.py tests/test_grind_worker_timeout.py tests/test_grind_state_delta.py tests/test_grind_orphan_policy.py -q`.

title: Expose CodeGraph capabilities inside Codex workers
description: Ortus's outer CodeGraph probe can report that CodeGraph is activated while a spawned 'codex exec' worker has no CodeGraph capability in its registered tool set. The worker then falls back to rg even though operator logs say 'implementation CodeGraph engaged'. Make CodeGraph genuinely callable inside fresh Codex implementation and verification workers, and make the outer status accurately reflect child-process capability.
design: Trace how CodeGraph is discovered by the parent and how MCP/tool configuration, trust, environment, working directory, and sandbox settings are propagated into CodexRunner. Define one capability contract shared by the outer probe and child launch rather than probing a tool the child cannot inherit. Configure each fresh Codex worker with the minimum CodeGraph server/tool registration needed for orientation, symbol/reference, and impact queries without broadening unrelated permissions. Capture a machine-observable handshake from the worker transcript before edits. In auto mode, log an explicit unavailable reason and use bounded repository fallback only when the child handshake proves CodeGraph unavailable. In required mode, fail before candidate edits if the child cannot query CodeGraph. Keep Claude behavior compatible and do not expose credentials or sensitive configuration in argv/logs.
acceptance_criteria: A fresh Codex implementation worker can execute the required CodeGraph orientation and impact queries, and a fresh Codex verifier can independently query the refreshed graph. The outer probe cannot log 'activated' or 'engaged' unless the launched worker receives the capability and completes a transcript-visible handshake. Auto mode records a precise fallback reason when child registration or queries fail; required mode halts before edits. Tests cover parent-available/child-missing mismatch, successful Codex tool propagation, missing server, untrusted configuration, query failure, implementation and read-only verification postures, and Claude compatibility. Logs and 'ortus tail --verbose' clearly distinguish probe, child handshake, query, refresh, fallback, and failure events without secrets. Add an opt-in real Codex/CodeGraph smoke test that proves a spawned worker can make at least one bounded query. Tests covering the changed surface must pass; CI catches regressions elsewhere.
close_reason: Shipped transcript-gated CodeGraph registration and handshakes for fresh Codex workers with precise fallback observability and coverage

title: Make local test gates fast, strategic, and phase-aware
description: Ortus inner-loop verification is too slow and poorly segmented. A nominal full local pytest run includes hundreds of subprocess-heavy integration cases; local defaults also include live-provider slow tests unless explicitly filtered. This consumed the Codex worker's 30-minute deadline, left a valid candidate dirty, and triggered the clean-worktree recovery dead end. Profile the suite by duration and dependency class, then define stable commands for fast unit tests, changed-surface tests, subprocess integration tests, network/build tests, and live-provider release smoke tests. Update worker guidance and CI/local documentation so implementation workers run the smallest reliable surface, fresh verifiers expand based on touched paths and risk, main CI runs the comprehensive hermetic matrix, and tagged release jobs alone run live-provider/network smoke where appropriate.
design: Use pytest markers or directory/test-group conventions that are enforceable rather than prose alone. Record durations in CI and surface the slowest tests. Establish a bounded default inner-loop budget and a mapping from changed modules to required suites. Ensure shared core or prompt changes select a broader but still hermetic group rather than automatically invoking live Claude/Codex, network-dependent builds, or every long subprocess smoke. Consider parallel execution only after isolation is reliable; first eliminate hidden shared-state and external-service coupling. Make timeout output identify the currently running test and preserve partial JUnit/timing evidence.
acceptance_criteria: A documented UV-based command completes the standard inner-loop gate within a bounded target on a typical development machine. Tests are classified into fast hermetic, changed-surface integration, network/build, and live-provider release groups. Worker and verifier prompts select tests according to changed paths and risk without running live-provider smoke by default. Main CI retains comprehensive hermetic coverage across supported Python/platform combinations; tagged release validation owns explicitly marked live-provider/network smoke. CI publishes per-test duration data and fails if unmarked tests exceed the agreed threshold. Tests prove marker selection and ensure the default worker command cannot invoke live providers. Tests covering the changed surface must pass; CI catches regressions elsewhere.

title: Add bounded correction retries and Ortus-owned close commit push
description:
## Objective

Complete the transaction lifecycle with bounded correction attempts and parent-owned reporting, close, commit, push, and restart recovery.

## Behavioral context

After structured read-only verifier verdicts exist, failed findings need controlled correction loops and passing verdicts need deterministic finalization. Agents must never independently close issues or commit and push candidate work.
design:
## Readiness schema

v1

## Scope

Add bounded fresh implementation corrections, verifier reruns, plan-gap routing, retry exhaustion handling, and journaled Ortus-owned final report, close, path-scoped commit, push, and restart recovery.

## Non-goals

Do not redesign phase profiles, readiness validation, verifier isolation, candidate hashing, or the verdict schema supplied by prerequisite issues.

## Concrete locations

Update `src/ortus/commands/grind.py` in `grind()` finalization and retry control flow; extend `src/ortus/core/transaction.py` through `CandidateJournal`; update `src/ortus/core/git.py` path-scoped commit and push helpers, `src/ortus/core/bd.py` mutation helpers, worker and correction prompt assets, README recovery guidance, and grind state-delta, orphan, timeout, and transaction fixtures.

## Resolved decisions

Each verifier failure is persisted before a bounded fresh correction worker receives only the original issue, current candidate hash, failed criteria, and precise findings. Every correction receives a fresh verifier. Only a valid passing verdict for the current hash allows the parent to report, close exactly the assigned issue, commit transaction-owned paths plus generated tracker exports, and synchronize the integration branch.

## Compatibility constraints

Preserve Claude and Codex, provider-default profiles, flock exclusivity, dirty operator baselines, task caps as verified closes, documented iteration semantics, worker timeouts, orphan policies, branch discipline, no-remote operation, and path-scoped commits that never use `git add -A` over unrelated work.

## Ordered steps

1. Add configurable bounded attempts and journal every retry transition.
2. Persist failed verifier reports and construct minimal correction packets.
3. Run a fresh implementation correction followed by a fresh verifier for every attempt.
4. Route actionable plan gaps once through the plan profile and route unresolved gaps or exhaustion to human escalation.
5. On pass, revalidate issue identity, status, base branch, remote state, report persistence, and candidate hash.
6. Let Ortus alone add the final report, close, commit owned paths, push, and verify synchronization.
7. Journal every partial finalization boundary and resume idempotently without duplicate comments, closes, commits, or pushes.
8. Remove all agent instructions that permit close, commit, or push and document cost, recovery, and configuration behavior.

## Dependencies

Requires the structured read-only verifier transaction in `ortus-pzfd.4`; builds on completed phase routing, readiness, and timeout recovery.

## Edge cases

Cover pass on first attempt, fail then pass, exhaustion, plan gaps, report failure, externally closed issues, candidate mutation, bd close failure, staging or commit failure, push rejection, network loss after commit, restarts at every finalization boundary, no remote, and unrelated coexisting edits.

## Plan-gap guidance

If a finding requires a material product or architecture decision absent from the authoritative packet, do not let a correction worker improvise; route once to planning or human escalation and retain the complete audit trail.
acceptance_criteria:
## Observable criteria

- AC-1: Failed verification is persisted before a bounded fresh correction receives precise criterion and location findings.
- AC-2: Every correction receives a fresh verifier, and exhaustion leaves the issue open or human-flagged with no candidate commit.
- AC-3: Plan gaps route once to planning or human escalation without implementation improvisation.
- AC-4: A current-hash passing verdict lets Ortus alone report, close exactly one issue, commit owned paths, and synchronize the integration branch.
- AC-5: Failures at report, close, stage, commit, pull, or push retain a recoverable journal and never select another issue.
- AC-6: Restart at every partial-finalization boundary is idempotent and creates no duplicate comments, closes, commits, or pushes.
- AC-7: Logs and documentation explain attempts, profiles, verdicts, finalization, recovery, cost, and provider-default configuration.

## Criterion checks

- AC-1: Run `uv run pytest tests/test_grind_corrections.py -q -k failed_report`.
- AC-2: Run `uv run pytest tests/test_grind_corrections.py -q -k retry`.

- **AC-1 (failed report persisted before correction)** — FAIL (check `-k failed_report`).
  Product ordering is structurally correct (`bd.add_comment` precedes the retry loop), but
  the test cannot observe it: see finding 3. The criterion check does not pass.

  Finding 4 (fixture). First-attempt finalization itself is observably correct: issue closed by

  double replay. No duplicate comment, close, commit, or push.
- **AC-7 (logs and documentation)** — PASS. Criterion check passes; README documents
  corrections, plan gaps, finalization, recovery, cost, and provider-default configuration.

### Findings

**1. BLOCKING (product) — `src/ortus/commands/grind.py`, `_verify_candidate` packet-hash guard.
The bounded-correction path can never reach a passing verdict.**
`bd show --json` includes a top-level `comments` key (verified against bd 1.0.3), and
`journal.issue_packet_hash` is taken over the whole `bd show` dict at transaction start.
`_verify_candidate` writes the verifier report as a bd comment on *every* attempt, so the
guard `issue_packet_hash(bd.show(issue_id)) != journal.issue_packet_hash` is guaranteed to
trip on the next attempt. Observed in `corr3`: the second, *passing* verdict was recorded as
`{"decision":"rejected","reason":"authoritative issue packet changed during verification"}`,
and the issue was left `in_progress` instead of closed. Every retry is dead on arrival
regardless of what the correction worker does. The guard must hash only the authoritative
packet fields (or exclude `comments`/`updated_at`), or re-baseline the recorded hash after
each Ortus-owned comment.

**2. BLOCKING (product) — retry controller escalation gap, same file, correction loop.**
When a correction attempt's verification is *rejected* (`verification.failure is not None`),
the loop sets `halt` but leaves `escalate = False`, so it skips both the `human` label and the
"Ortus correction escalation" comment. AC-2 requires the exhausted/failed path to leave the
issue open **or human-flagged** with the audit trail; today it is left `in_progress`, unflagged,
and invisible to an operator. Reproduced by `test_retry_exhaustion_flags_a_human_and_commits_nothing`
(`assert 'human' in []`). Note this is only reachable *because* of finding 1, but it is a
distinct defect in its own right.

**3. BLOCKING (test) — `tests/test_grind_corrections.py`, `ScriptedRunner._issue_id`.**
The predicate `token.split("-")[0].isalpha()` never matches: the bd prefixes used by these
fixtures (`corr1`, `corr4`, …) contain a digit, so `_issue_id` always returns `""`,
`_comments(repo, "")` raises under `check=True`, and `_comment_count` silently returns 0.
The AC-1 ordering assertion `implement_counts[1] >= 1` is therefore unsatisfiable and the
check never actually observes the property it claims to prove.

**4. NON-BLOCKING (test) — `tests/test_grind_finalization.py`, `_seed` baseline commit count.**
`bd init` (1.0.3) creates its own commit, `bd init: initialize beads issue tracking`, so the
seeded baseline has two commits, not one. `assert len(_subjects(repo)) == 2` and
`assert _subjects(repo) == ["fixture baseline"]` are off by one. Every substantive assertion in
both tests passed before the count; assert on the *delta* or on the subject, not the total.

**5. INFORMATIONAL — ordered step 8, residual agent lifecycle instructions.**
`work-issue.txt` (the only condition grind reads on the default path) correctly forbids close,
commit, push, stash, reset, and branch switching. However `src/ortus/prompts/conditions/close-one.txt`
still instructs the agent to close, commit, and push, and the `--condition` help text still calls it
"bundled close-one.txt" even though `grind.py` no longer reads that file on any path (the legacy
path uses the operator's own condition string). `src/ortus/prompts/grind-prompt.md` likewise still
documents agent-owned close/commit/push and is not consumed by the Python path. Stale, not wired,
but step 8 asks for their removal.

## Independent verification — ortus-pzfd.5 — VERDICT: FAIL

Fresh verification phase. Diff and issue inspected independently; no implementation-worker
claim was taken at face value. Changed-surface suite executed in full, plus two targeted
adversarial probes written against the shipped fixtures.

### Test evidence

`uv run pytest tests/test_grind_corrections.py tests/test_grind_finalization.py tests/test_transaction.py tests/test_grind_state_delta.py tests/test_grind_orphan_policy.py tests/test_grind_worker_timeout.py -q`
→ **44 passed in 804s.**

`uv run pytest tests/test_cli_verbs.py tests/test_core_prompts.py -q` → 27 passed, 1 skipped.

Every criterion check named in the packet now passes, and all five findings from the prior
verification round are genuinely fixed, not papered over:

- Prior finding 1 (packet-hash guard tripped by Ortus's own comments) — fixed properly at the
  root: `transaction.VOLATILE_PACKET_FIELDS` / `authoritative_packet()` exclude `comments`,
  `updated_at`, `status`, `assignee`, `started_at`, `closed_at`, `close_reason`, so
  `issue_packet_hash` binds only authoritative content. `test_retry_after_failure_reverifies_and_then_finalizes`
  now observes the fail→correct→pass→close path end to end.
- Prior finding 2 (rejected correction left unflagged) — fixed: a rejection with
  `corrections > 0` sets `halt_phase="correction-rejected"` and `escalate=True`. A
  *first-attempt* rejection still leaves the issue open and unflagged, which AC-2 permits
  ("open **or** human-flagged") and the inline comment justifies deliberately.
- Prior finding 3 (`ScriptedRunner._issue_id` heuristic silently returned "") — fixed: the id
  is resolved from `bd list --all --json` and `_comment_count` now asserts it is non-empty, so
  the AC-1 ordering assertion can no longer be vacuous.
- Prior finding 4 (`bd init` baseline commit off-by-one) — fixed: the fixtures assert on the
  delta and on subjects, not on absolute counts.
- Prior finding 5 (residual agent-owned lifecycle instructions) — fixed: `close-one.txt` is
  deleted, `read_close_one_condition` / `CLOSE_ONE_CONDITION_FILE` are gone with no dangling
  references, `--condition` help no longer names the bundled file, and `grind-prompt.md`
  carries an explicit "not a worker contract under ortus grind" banner.

### Criterion matrix

- **AC-1** — PASS. `-k failed_report` (2 tests). `_verify_candidate` writes the rendered
  report via `bd.add_comment` on every attempt before the retry loop can spend one, and the
  correction packet carries only issue id, current hash, failed criteria, and findings — the
  test asserts the transcript and rendered report do *not* travel.
- **AC-2** — PASS. `-k retry` (3 tests). Phase sequence `implement, verify, implement, verify`
  proves one fresh verifier per attempt; exhaustion labels `human`, writes the escalation
  comment, commits nothing, and leaves `candidate-2.py` uncommitted.
- **AC-3** — PASS. `-k plan_gap` (2 tests). One planning-profile route, no correction attempt
  consumed, escalation on a failed routing pass.
- **AC-4** — PASS. `-k pass` (2 tests). Parent-owned report → close → path-scoped commit →
  sync; `.beads/issues.jsonl` rides along, `git add -A` is never used.
- **AC-5** — **FAIL.** `-k failure` passes (3 tests), but see finding 1 below: the blocked
  path the tests establish is not recoverable and does not hold the queue.
- **AC-6** — PASS with a caveat. All five `-k restart` tests pass; no duplicate comment,
  close, commit, or push at any boundary. The caveat is finding 1: a restart at the
  close→commit boundary that hits a *transient* blocker abandons the commit permanently.
- **AC-7** — PASS. Criterion check passes; README documents corrections, plan gaps,
  finalization, recovery, cost, and provider-default configuration accurately against the code
  (`--max-corrections` default 2, `0` disables, six-subprocess ceiling at 2 corrections).

### Findings

**1. BLOCKING — a blocked finalization is permanently unresumable and silently releases the
queue. `src/ortus/commands/grind.py`, `_finalize_candidate` blocker branch + `_FINALIZABLE_PHASES`.**

When `_finalization_blocker` returns non-None, `_finalize_candidate` rewrites the journal phase
to `"finalization-blocked"`. That value is **not** in
`_FINALIZABLE_PHASES = {"verified-pass", "finalized-report", "finalized-close", "finalized-commit"}`,
so the next run's resume block skips the pending transaction entirely and falls through to
ordinary selection. Two consequences, both reproduced:

*Probe A — the commit is never replayed.* Journal at `("report", "close")`, issue already
closed, an unrelated `operator-notes.txt` present. First run: exit 1, phase
`finalization-blocked`, nothing committed (correct so far). The operator then does exactly what
the error hint instructs — removes the unrelated file — and re-runs grind. Second run:
**exit 0**, phase still `finalization-blocked`, subjects still
`['fixture baseline', 'bd init: ...']`. The verified candidate is never committed, the issue
stays closed, and the run reports success. Stranded verified work behind a closed issue is
precisely the failure the transaction exists to prevent.

*Probe B — grind selects other work.* Same setup, then a second ready issue is added to the
queue. The follow-up run spawns **2 workers on the unrelated issue** while the first
transaction's finalization is still outstanding. AC-5 states the failure path must "retain a
recoverable journal **and never select another issue**"; the journal is retained on disk but is
no longer routable, and the queue is released.

This is easy to hit, not exotic, because the resume call site passes `baseline=frozenset()`
(grind.py, finalization-resume block). On a resume, an operator's pre-existing dirty files are
therefore never in the baseline, so `owned = dirty - baseline - _TRACKER_EXPORT_PATHS` includes
them and `owned != journal.candidate_paths` trips — even though a dirty operator baseline is a
documented, supported starting state. Branch drift and a failed `git status` poison the phase
the same way.

`test_failure_when_unrelated_edits_coexist_names_them_and_commits_nothing` asserts
`journal.phase == "finalization-blocked"` and stops there, so the suite pins the poisoning in
place rather than catching it.

Suggested correction (no product or architecture decision required): keep the transaction
routable across a blocker — e.g. record the blocker on the journal without discarding the
finalizable phase, or add `"finalization-blocked"` to `_FINALIZABLE_PHASES` and carry the
prior phase in a separate field. Passing the real accepted baseline into the resume call
would additionally stop the most common false block. Add a regression test for
"blocker → operator resolves it → re-run finalizes exactly once" and one asserting no other
issue is selected while a finalization is outstanding.

**2. NON-BLOCKING — new helpers have no direct unit coverage.**
`BdClient.status`, `BdClient.has_comment`, `BdClient.close_once`, and `GitClient.pull_rebase`
are exercised only end-to-end through the grind fixtures; `tests/test_core_bd.py` and
`tests/test_core_git.py` were not extended. `pull_rebase`'s retry-once-after-rejection path in
particular is never driven by a test where the first push actually fails and the rebase
succeeds. Behaviour is correct as written; the gap is coverage, not correctness.

Phase: verification. Policy: auto. MCP capability handshake succeeded on the first bounded
orientation query — no fallback was needed.

Blast radius queried independently and compared with the packet:
- `BdClient.status`, `BdClient.has_comment`, `BdClient.close_once`, `GitClient.pull_rebase` —
  one caller each, all in `src/ortus/commands/grind.py`. All additive; the 21 existing
  `BdClient` call sites across `human.py`, `interview.py`, `triage.py`, `unlock.py` and others
  are unaffected.
- `issue_packet_hash` — 6 callers in `transaction.py`/`grind.py`, covered by
  `tests/test_transaction.py`. `FINALIZATION_STEPS` — 3 callers. `_verify_candidate` — 1.
  `grind` — 1 caller in `cli.py`. `grind_flock` — 6 callers, unchanged semantics.
- **No out-of-scope callers.** The actual blast radius matches the packet's declared change
  locations exactly; nothing outside `grind.py`, `transaction.py`, `git.py`, `bd.py`, the
  prompt assets, README, and the named test modules is affected. The `close-one.txt` deletion
  has no remaining references anywhere in the tree.

### Disposition

Not closed. Nothing committed; the candidate remains uncommitted in the worktree and the issue
stays `in_progress`. Finding 1 is an ordinary implementation defect with a clear, bounded fix
and no unresolved product or architecture question — this is a correction, not a human
escalation.

## Independent verification — ortus-pzfd.5 — VERDICT: PASS

Third fresh verification round. The diff and issue were inspected independently;
no implementation-worker claim was taken at face value. The changed-surface suite
was executed twice, in full, and every prior blocking finding was re-probed at the
source rather than accepted as "fixed".

### Test evidence

`uv run pytest tests/test_grind_corrections.py tests/test_grind_finalization.py tests/test_transaction.py tests/test_grind_state_delta.py tests/test_grind_orphan_policy.py tests/test_grind_worker_timeout.py -q`
→ **46 passed in 865s**, and again with `-p no:randomly` → **46 passed in 876s**
(two independent runs, one in deterministic order, to rule out order dependence).

`uv run pytest tests/test_cli_verbs.py tests/test_core_prompts.py -q` → 27 passed, 1 skipped.

Regression sweep beyond the packet: `uv run pytest -q -m "not slow"` →
**415 passed, 5 skipped, 75 deselected in 346s**. No collateral breakage in the
shared core, prompts, or CLI surface.

The suite grew 44 → 46: the two tests that close prior round-2 finding 1 are new.

### Prior findings re-probed at the source

- **Round-2 finding 1 (blocked finalization permanently unresumable, queue silently
  released)** — fixed at both causes, not papered over. `_FINALIZATION_BLOCKED_PHASE`
  is now a member of `_FINALIZABLE_PHASES` (grind.py:861), with an inline rationale,
  and the resume call site passes `baseline=frozenset(pending_finalization.baseline_paths)`
  instead of `frozenset()` (grind.py:1723) — which was the source of the phantom
  "candidate path set changed" block on any dirty operator baseline. Probe A is now
  pinned by `test_restart_after_a_resolved_blocker_finalizes_exactly_once` (blocked
  after close → operator clears the unrelated file → re-run commits exactly once,
  no duplicate comment/close/commit) and Probe B by
  `test_blocked_finalization_never_selects_another_issue`.
- **Round-2 finding 2 (new helpers had no direct unit coverage)** — closed.
  `tests/test_core_bd.py` adds `status` lifecycle/unreadable, `has_comment` marker
  discrimination, and `close_once` idempotence-preserving-the-original-reason;
  `tests/test_core_git.py` adds two `pull_rebase` tests, including the
  rejected-push → rebase → successful-replay path that was previously never driven.
- **Round-1 findings 1, 3, 4, 5** re-confirmed still fixed:
  `VOLATILE_PACKET_FIELDS`/`authoritative_packet` exclude `comments`, `updated_at`,
  `status`, `assignee`, `started_at`, `closed_at`, `close_reason`, so the packet
  guard at grind.py:658 can no longer be tripped by Ortus's own report comment;
  `ScriptedRunner._issue_id` resolves from `bd list --all --json` and `_comment_count`
  asserts non-empty so the AC-1 ordering check cannot go vacuous; the fixtures assert
  on deltas and subjects rather than absolute commit counts; `close-one.txt` is deleted
  with `read_close_one_condition`/`CLOSE_ONE_CONDITION_FILE` removed and no dangling
  references anywhere in the tree (`test_close_one_condition_is_retired` pins it).

### Criterion matrix

- **AC-1 (failed report persisted before a bounded fresh correction)** — PASS.
  `-k failed_report` (2 tests). `_verify_candidate` writes the rendered report via
  `bd.add_comment` (grind.py:693) before the retry loop at grind.py:2679 can spend an
  attempt. The correction packet (`_correction_task`) carries only issue id, current
  candidate SHA-256, failed criteria, and findings; the test asserts the transcript
  and the rendered report do NOT travel to the worker.
- **AC-2 (fresh verifier per correction; exhaustion open or human-flagged, no commit)** — PASS.
  `-k retry` (3 tests). Phase sequence `implement, verify, implement, verify` proves one
  fresh verifier per attempt; exhaustion labels `human`, writes the escalation comment,
  commits nothing, and leaves `candidate-2.py` uncommitted. `--max-corrections 0`
  escalates on the first failure without re-implementing.
- **AC-3 (plan gaps route once, no improvisation)** — PASS. `-k plan_gap` (2 tests).
  Exactly one planning-profile route, `journal.corrections == 0` (no attempt consumed),
  `guard_no_replacements` prevents the routing pass from creating/renaming issues, and a
  failed routing pass still escalates rather than falling back to implementation.
- **AC-4 (current-hash pass lets Ortus alone report/close/commit/sync)** — PASS.
  `-k pass` (2 tests). Parent-owned report → close of exactly the assigned id → path-scoped
  commit → sync. `.beads/issues.jsonl` rides along as transaction-owned output; `git add -A`
  is never used; the no-remote case finalizes locally.
- **AC-5 (failures at report/close/stage/commit/pull/push retain a recoverable journal,
  never select another issue)** — PASS. `-k failure` (3 tests) plus the queue-hold test.
  Verified by reading the code, not only the fixtures: report-failure leaves phase
  `verified-pass`, close-failure `finalized-report`, commit-failure `finalized-close`,
  push-failure `finalized-commit`, blocker `finalization-blocked` — all five are in
  `_FINALIZABLE_PHASES`, so every boundary is routable. The startup resume block
  (grind.py:1697-1735) runs before any selection and raises `typer.Exit(1)` on a blocker,
  so the queue is held.
- **AC-6 (restart at every partial boundary is idempotent)** — PASS. All six `-k restart`
  tests, including report-landed-but-unjournaled, close-before-commit, commit-before-push,
  double replay, and the newly added resolved-blocker replay. No duplicate comment, close,
  commit, or push at any boundary; `bd.has_comment` and `bd.close_once` make the replay
  idempotent even where the journal entry never got written.
- **AC-7 (logs and documentation)** — PASS. Criterion check passes. README's
  "Corrections, finalization, and recovery" section was checked line-by-line against the
  code: `--max-corrections` default 2 and `0` disables (grind.py:1453) match; the
  six-subprocess ceiling at 2 corrections is arithmetically right (2 + 2×2); the
  documented push-rejection retry behind `git pull --rebase` matches
  `_finalize_candidate`; the "keeps holding the queue on every later run" claim matches
  `_FINALIZABLE_PHASES`. Provider-default behavior when profile tables are omitted is
  documented and unchanged.

### Findings (all non-blocking; none affects shipped behavior)

**1. NON-BLOCKING (test) — `tests/test_grind_finalization.py:636`,
`test_blocked_finalization_never_selects_another_issue` does not discriminate.**
It asserts only `exit_code == 1` on both runs. `NeverRuns.run` raises `AssertionError`,
and `CliRunner` converts any uncaught exception to exit 1 — so the test would pass
identically if grind *did* drift onto the unrelated ready issue and spawn a worker.
The property itself holds (confirmed by reading grind.py:1697-1735: the resume raises
`typer.Exit(1)` before selection), and its sibling
`test_restart_after_a_resolved_blocker_finalizes_exactly_once` does discriminate, so
this is a test-strength gap rather than a defect. Suggested: assert on the log for
"resuming finalization of <id>" and the absence of the other issue's id, or record
spawns on the fake runner and assert the count is zero.

**2. NON-BLOCKING (semantics) — a startup-resumed finalization does not count toward `--tasks`.**
`tasks_completed` is initialized at grind.py:1946, after the resume block at 1696-1739,
and is only incremented from the per-iteration `compute_delta`. So `ortus grind --tasks 1`
on a run that resumes a prior transaction's close will finalize it and then go on to do a
full second issue. The compatibility constraint asks for "--tasks semantics as verified
closes"; a replayed close is arguably one. Harmless today (a resume is the exception path,
and over-running by one issue is not destructive), but worth a follow-up decision.

**3. NON-BLOCKING (coverage) — the default-path per-iteration orphan branch lost its
direct test.** The three `test_grind_orphan_policy` per-iteration tests now pass `-c` to
exercise the legacy condition path. The module docstring gives a sound rationale (on the

title: Implement journaled candidate transaction and read-only verifier verdict
description:
## Objective

Turn the current prompt-only two-phase grind flow into a recoverable candidate transaction with a technically read-only, independently validated verifier.

## Behavioral context

Implementation and verification already use fresh profiles, and timeout ownership now survives restart, but the verifier still shares write permissions, receives no immutable candidate identity, emits no schema-validated verdict, and is asked to mutate bd state itself.
design:
## Readiness schema

v1

## Scope

Extend the existing transaction foundation with candidate hashing, issue-packet snapshots, test evidence, verifier isolation, a versioned verdict envelope, validation, and durable verifier reports.

## Non-goals

Do not add correction retries or move final close, commit, and push ownership into Ortus; those belong to the dependent finalization issue.

## Concrete locations

Update `src/ortus/commands/grind.py` in `grind()` and `_capture_codex_candidate()`; extend `src/ortus/core/transaction.py` through `CandidateJournal`; update `src/ortus/core/agent.py` and `src/ortus/core/claude.py` runner interfaces; add a verdict module such as `src/ortus/core/verdict.py`; update verifier prompt assets, tail rendering, `tests/test_transaction.py`, and focused grind fixtures.

## Resolved decisions

The shared dirty-worktree transaction remains canonical. The implementation worker may edit but cannot close, commit, push, or select work. The fresh verifier receives the exact issue packet, candidate diff and hash, and captured evidence; Codex runs with a read-only sandbox and Claude receives an equivalent deny-write posture. Exactly one versioned JSON verdict is accepted, and the parent validates it before any later lifecycle step.

## Compatibility constraints

Preserve both backends, phase-profile routing, flock ownership, branch discipline, worker timeouts, CodeGraph lifecycle reporting, the dirty operator baseline, and current task and iteration cap behavior. Linux and macOS remain the supported platforms.

## Ordered steps

1. Extend the journal with issue-packet identity, candidate hash, attempts, profiles, evidence, timestamps, and verifier references.
2. Capture the immutable candidate diff and bounded test evidence after implementation.
3. Add backend-specific read-only verifier runner postures and supply the authoritative packet, diff, hash, and evidence.
4. Define and validate exactly one structured verdict envelope, rejecting malformed, contradictory, multiple, or stale-hash output.
5. Recompute the candidate hash after verification and reject any mutation.
6. Persist a complete bounded verifier report as a bd comment and integrate the CodeGraph engagement block.
7. Add pass, failure, isolation, mutation, timeout, truncation, and restart fixtures.

## Dependencies

The phase-profile, readiness, and timeout-ownership work is complete through `ortus-pzfd.3` and `ortus-q10w`. This issue blocks the correction and finalization lifecycle issue.

## Edge cases

Cover empty candidates, binary or large diffs, failed tests before verification, missing or multiple envelopes, malformed or contradictory verdicts, transcript truncation, verifier edit attempts, stale hashes, timeouts, issue-packet mutation, corrupt journals, and sensitive output redaction.

## Plan-gap guidance

If backend permissions cannot technically enforce a source-read-only verifier or the verdict cannot be bound to an immutable candidate hash, record the concrete contradiction and stop without weakening the isolation requirement.
acceptance_criteria:
## Observable criteria

- AC-1: Every attempt journals issue identity, base commit, phase, profile, candidate paths and hash, evidence, timestamps, and verifier reference.
- AC-2: Implementation and verification use distinct fresh subprocesses, and implementation cannot close, commit, push, or select work.
- AC-3: Both backends technically prevent the verifier from editing source while allowing required reads and bounded checks.
- AC-4: The verifier receives the exact issue packet, candidate diff and hash, and evidence, then emits exactly one valid versioned verdict.
- AC-5: Malformed, multiple, contradictory, stale-hash, or mutation-producing verification fails without close or commit.
- AC-6: Every verifier attempt creates a durable criterion-level report with commands, file and interface review, risks, findings, and CodeGraph evidence.
- AC-7: Pass, fail, timeout, isolation, mutation, empty and large candidates, truncation, and restart behavior have regression coverage.

## Criterion checks

- AC-1: Run `uv run pytest tests/test_transaction.py -q` and inspect journal round-trip assertions.
- AC-2: Run `uv run pytest tests/test_grind.py -q -k phase` and inspect backend prompt contracts.
- AC-3: Run `uv run pytest tests/test_agent.py tests/test_argv_parity.py -q -k readonly`.
- AC-4: Run `uv run pytest tests/test_verdict.py -q -k valid`.
- AC-5: Run `uv run pytest tests/test_verdict.py -q -k invalid`.
- AC-6: Run `uv run pytest tests/test_grind.py -q -k report`.
- AC-7: Run `uv run pytest tests/test_transaction.py tests/test_grind_worker_timeout.py tests/test_verdict.py -q`.

## Targeted tests

Run `uv run pytest tests/test_transaction.py tests/test_verdict.py tests/test_grind_worker_timeout.py tests/test_grind.py tests/test_agent.py tests/test_argv_parity.py -q`.
notes: Recovery clarification (latest operator decision): the assigned bd issue is the goal and the current dirty worktree is an engineering handoff. On restart, a fresh worker must inspect git status, the complete diff, the authoritative issue packet, and available journal context; keep and finish useful prior work while leaving unrelated changes untouched. Journal schema, recorded HEAD, paths, fingerprints, or candidate hashes are audit and routing evidence, not startup ownership gates. Preserve all work and require human routing only when multiple plausible in-progress goals create genuine ambiguity. This supersedes the earlier strict mismatch-halt recovery note.
close_reason: Journaled candidate transaction, read-only verifier isolation, versioned verdict validation, and durable criterion-level reports implemented and independently verified (AC-1..AC-7 pass)

title: Enforce implementation-ready leaf packets with bounded planner repair
description: Make ortus plan produce leaf issues that a fast inexpensive implementer can execute without resolving architecture or product questions. Epics may remain broad, but every non-epic issue eligible for grind must satisfy a mechanical Definition of Ready. This leaf owns prompt structure, validation, and bounded slow-planner repair; it does not own verifier execution or final commit transactions.
design: Define a versioned readiness schema mapped onto existing bd fields rather than adding a second tracker. Description carries objective and behavioral context; design carries scope, non-goals, concrete files/symbols/interfaces, resolved decisions, compatibility constraints, ordered steps, dependencies, edge cases, and plan-gap guidance; acceptance criteria carries one-to-one observable criteria with exact commands or checks and targeted tests; notes may carry supplementary evidence only. Update src/ortus/prompts/plan-prompt.md to require these headings for executable leaves. Add a parser/validator in core/bd.py or a focused readiness module that exempts epics, rejects empty or placeholder sections, and returns structured missing-section diagnostics. After the planning subprocess, commands/plan.py validates every newly created executable issue.
