title: Keep an explicit priority 0 through packet assembly
description:
## Objective
Keep an explicit priority 0 in a drafted packet from being filed as priority 2.

## Behavioral context
Before: the assembler reads the priority with a falsy-or-default expression, so a
draft carrying 0 is filed at 2 and the most urgent bead lands mid-queue with no
warning. After: an explicit 0 survives assembly, and only an absent or
unparseable priority falls back to the bd default of 2.
design:
## Readiness schema
v1

## Scope
Change the priority coercion in `assemble_issue` so an explicit 0 is a value
rather than an absence, and cover it with a targeted test.

## Non-goals
No change to readiness schema v1, to the bd default for a genuinely absent
priority, or to `ortus ingest`, which already resolves its own priority.

## Concrete locations
`src/ortus/core/github_bead.py` in `assemble_issue()`; `_first_priority()` in
`src/ortus/commands/ingest.py` shows the intended reading; add coverage in
`tests/test_github_bead.py`.

## Resolved decisions
An explicit 0 wins. An absent or unparseable priority still resolves to 2, which
is what `BdClient.create` would have applied on its own.

## Compatibility constraints
Linux and macOS; no change to the bd CLI contract or to stored issue fields.

## Ordered steps
1. Replace the truthiness test in `assemble_issue` with an explicit empty check.
2. Keep the existing fallback to 2 for a value that will not parse as an int.
3. Add a test proving a draft carrying priority 0 assembles to 0.

## Dependencies
None — the only caller is the GitHub ingest path in the same module.

## Edge cases
Priority given as the string "0"; priority absent entirely; priority given as a
word that will not parse.

## Plan-gap guidance
If any caller relies on 0 meaning "unset", record PLAN-GAP and stop rather than
changing the meaning of the field.
acceptance_criteria:
## Observable criteria
- AC-1: a draft carrying priority 0 assembles to priority 0.
- AC-2: an absent or unparseable priority still assembles to priority 2.

## Criterion checks
- AC-1: Run `uv run pytest tests/test_github_bead.py -q -k priority`.
- AC-2: Run `uv run pytest tests/test_github_bead.py -q -k assemble`.

## Targeted tests
Run `uv run pytest tests/test_github_bead.py -q`.
close_reason: Explicit priority 0 survives assemble_issue; absent or unparseable still defaults to 2. Criterion checks passed.

comments.author: who
comments.text: An explicit priority 0 now survives packet assembly. The coercion in assemble_issue tests the drafted field for absence before it parses it, so 0 stays 0; None, an empty string, and an unparseable word still resolve to the bd default of 2. Two targeted tests cover both halves. AC-1: uv run pytest tests/test_github_bead.py -q -k priority — 2 passed. AC-2: uv run pytest tests/test_github_bead.py -q -k assemble — 3 passed. Whole file: 15 passed.

title: release: workflow_dispatch fails at Publish to TestPyPI (no trusted publisher)
description:
## Objective
The release workflow stops failing on every manual run: either the TestPyPI publish is configured to work, or the unused TestPyPI path is removed, so a workflow_dispatch does not always end red.

## Behavioral context
Before. `.github/workflows/release.yml` has a publish-test-pypi job that runs on workflow_dispatch (and on -test tags). Every manual dispatch fails at "Publish to TestPyPI" with a trusted-publishing error: "invalid-publisher: valid token, but no corresponding publisher (Publisher with matching claims was not found)". Confirmed on runs 33912028550, 33911979112, 33911707429 (build succeeds, TestPyPI fails, the rest skip). test.pypi.org has no trusted publisher registered for this repo workflow and its test-pypi environment, so the OIDC exchange is refused. The real tagged-release path (publish-pypi on a v* tag) works and is unaffected.
After. A release workflow_dispatch completes green: either the TestPyPI trusted publisher is registered so the publish succeeds, or the publish-test-pypi job and the workflow_dispatch test_pypi input are removed because TestPyPI dry-runs are not used.
design:
## Readiness schema
v1
## Scope
Resolve the persistently-red TestPyPI path in release.yml. Recommended: remove the publish-test-pypi job and the workflow_dispatch test_pypi input, since the path has never published successfully and real releases go through the tag path. Alternative if TestPyPI dry-runs are wanted: register the trusted publisher on test.pypi.org and document it.
## Non-goals
Do not touch the real PyPI publish (publish-pypi) or the github-release job; both work on a v* tag. Do not change the tag release triggers. Do not add secrets or long-lived tokens; trusted publishing is the mechanism either way.
## Concrete locations
.github/workflows/release.yml: the publish-test-pypi job and its if condition, and the workflow_dispatch inputs test_pypi block near the top. If keeping TestPyPI, the trusted-publisher registration is external (test.pypi.org project settings, environment test-pypi), recorded in a workflow comment.
## Resolved decisions
1. Recommended fix is removal: delete the publish-test-pypi job and the test_pypi workflow_dispatch input, because the job has failed on every dispatch since it was added and the real release path does not depend on it. This stops the red with no external config.
2. Alternative, if the maintainer wants TestPyPI dry-runs: add a trusted publisher on test.pypi.org for the repo, workflow release.yml, environment test-pypi, and leave the job; record the setup in a comment.
3. The maintainer picks removal vs configure; the bead ships removal unless told otherwise, since it needs no account access this repo can automate.
## Compatibility constraints
The tagged-release path (build, publish-pypi, github-release) is unchanged either way. Removing the TestPyPI job also removes the only use of the workflow_dispatch test_pypi input; keep the workflow_dispatch trigger only if something else needs it. No published artifact or install path changes.
## Ordered steps
1. Decide removal vs configure (default removal).
2. Removal: delete the publish-test-pypi job and the test_pypi input; if workflow_dispatch has no other purpose, drop it. Configure: register the TestPyPI trusted publisher and document it.
3. Assert with rg that release.yml no longer has a failing TestPyPI path (removal) or that it is documented (configure).
4. A manual dispatch or the next tag confirms green.
## Dependencies
Shares release.yml with ortus-3hef (release notes) and ortus-7dcf (action pins, landed); sequence edits so they do not touch the same lines.
## Edge cases
Something outside this repo relies on the TestPyPI dry-run: then choose configure, not removal. A -test suffixed tag also triggers publish-test-pypi via the contains(-test) branch; removal drops that path too, which is fine if unused. Keeping workflow_dispatch for a future manual real-PyPI run: leave the trigger, drop only the TestPyPI job and input.
## Plan-gap guidance
If the maintainer wants TestPyPI kept but cannot grant test.pypi.org access to register the publisher, stop and record PLAN-GAP: the job cannot be made green from inside the repo, so removal is the only in-repo fix.
acceptance_criteria:
## Observable criteria
- AC-1 (proves-new): a release workflow_dispatch no longer fails at a TestPyPI publish (the job is removed, or it succeeds with a registered publisher).
- AC-2 (guards-existing): the tagged-release path in release.yml (build, publish-pypi, github-release) is unchanged.
## Criterion checks
- AC-1: `rg -n "test-pypi|test_pypi|TestPyPI" .github/workflows/release.yml`
- AC-2: `rg -n "publish-pypi|github-release|tags:" .github/workflows/release.yml`
## Targeted tests
None - GitHub Actions and external TestPyPI configuration; verified by the criterion checks on the workflow and a green workflow_dispatch run.
close_reason: Removed the publish-test-pypi job and test_pypi dispatch input so a manual release run builds and stops green; tagged path unchanged

comments.author: who
comments.text: Shipped the removal the packet named as its default: the publish-test-pypi job and the test_pypi workflow_dispatch input are gone from release.yml, so a manual dispatch now builds the wheel and sdist and stops instead of failing the OIDC exchange against a publisher test.pypi.org never had. Kept the workflow_dispatch trigger as a build-only packaging smoke check, with a comment saying so. The tagged path is untouched: v* trigger, the real PyPI publish job, and github-release all unchanged, and the -test tag branch went away with the job that was its only consumer. AC-1: rg finds no test-pypi/test_pypi/TestPyPI in release.yml. AC-2: rg still finds publish-pypi, github-release, and the v* tags trigger.

title: release: put only the current version section in the GitHub release notes
description:
## Objective
The release workflow uses only the CHANGELOG section for the tag being released as the GitHub release notes, instead of the entire CHANGELOG.md file, so each release page shows just its own changes.

## Behavioral context
Before. The github-release job in .github/workflows/release.yml runs `gh release create` with `--notes-file CHANGELOG.md` when the file exists, so every future tagged release would use the whole changelog history as its notes. v0.3.0 shipped before CHANGELOG.md existed and used --generate-notes, and its notes were later set by hand, so this bites the next release (v0.3.1 / v0.4.0), which would otherwise get the full file. After. The job extracts the section for the tag being built (the block under `## [<version>]` up to the next `## [` or the link-reference footer) and passes only that to `--notes-file`. When CHANGELOG.md has no section for the tag, it falls back to --generate-notes rather than dumping the whole file.

## Design
See design field.
design:
## Readiness schema
v1
## Scope
Change the github-release job in .github/workflows/release.yml so the notes it passes to `gh release create` are the current tag version's CHANGELOG section, not the whole file. Extract the block between `## [<version>]` and the next `## [` (or the `[<version>]:` link footer) with awk/sed inline in the step, write it to a temp notes file, and use `--notes-file` on that. Fall back to --generate-notes when no matching section exists.
## Non-goals
Do not change the PyPI or TestPyPI publish jobs, the triggers, or the assets uploaded. Do not restructure CHANGELOG.md or its format. Do not backfill notes for already-published releases (v0.3.0 is done). Do not add a general changelog tool; a few lines of awk in the workflow is enough.
## Concrete locations
.github/workflows/release.yml: the `github-release` job's "Create GitHub release" step (the `notes_arg` / `gh release create` block, ~lines 84-99). CHANGELOG.md is the input format (## [x.y.z] headers, a `[x.y.z]:` link footer). No src/ change.
## Resolved decisions
1. Extraction is inline awk/sed in the workflow step, keyed on the tag: strip a leading `v`, match `## [<version>]`, print until the next line starting `## [` or `[<version>]:`, and trim trailing blanks. 2. Fall back to --generate-notes when the tag has no section, so a forgotten changelog entry still produces a release rather than failing. 3. The whole-file `--notes-file CHANGELOG.md` path is removed; it was never correct for a multi-version file. 4. Verification is an rg assertion on the workflow plus the next real tagged release, since a workflow step has no unit-test surface here.
## Compatibility constraints
The change is confined to the notes text of the github-release job; the tag triggers, publish jobs, and uploaded assets are unchanged. A tag whose version has a CHANGELOG section gets those notes; one without falls back exactly as an empty changelog would today. This bead and the Node-version bump both edit release.yml, so land them without overlapping the same lines.
## Ordered steps
1. Replace the `--notes-file CHANGELOG.md` branch with an extraction of the tag version's section into a temp file, used via --notes-file. 2. Keep the --generate-notes fallback for a missing section. 3. Assert with rg that the workflow extracts a section and no longer passes the whole file. 4. Confirm on the next tagged release that the notes carry only that version.
## Dependencies
Follows the CHANGELOG.md added for v0.3.0. Shares the release.yml file with the Node-action bump bead; sequence the two so they do not edit adjacent lines at once.
## Edge cases
A tag with no CHANGELOG section: fall back to --generate-notes. A version whose section is the only one in the file: extraction returns that whole section, no link footer leaks in. A tag name with a `v` prefix vs the bare `[x.y.z]` header: strip the `v` before matching. A CHANGELOG with an `## [Unreleased]` section on top: match the concrete version, not Unreleased.
## Plan-gap guidance
If the team wants the extractor unit-tested rather than inline awk, stop and record PLAN-GAP proposing a small tested `scripts/changelog-section.sh` the workflow calls, rather than shipping untested shell in the workflow.
acceptance_criteria:
## Observable criteria
- AC-1 (proves-new): release.yml extracts the tag version section from CHANGELOG.md and passes only that to `gh release create --notes-file`, not the whole file.
- AC-2 (proves-new): when CHANGELOG.md has no section for the tag, the workflow falls back to --generate-notes.
- AC-3 (guards-existing): the release triggers, publish jobs, and uploaded assets in release.yml are unchanged.
## Criterion checks
- AC-1: `rg -n "notes-file" .github/workflows/release.yml`
- AC-2: `rg -n "generate-notes" .github/workflows/release.yml`
- AC-3: `rg -n "pypi-publish|upload-artifact|release create" .github/workflows/release.yml`
## Targeted tests
None — this is a GitHub Actions workflow change with no unit-test surface; the criterion checks assert the workflow content and the next tagged release confirms the notes.
close_reason: release.yml now passes only the tag version's CHANGELOG section to gh release create, falling back to --generate-notes when no section exists

comments.author: who
comments.text: Completed: the github-release step in .github/workflows/release.yml now extracts the tag version's CHANGELOG section (heading matched literally after stripping the leading v, captured up to the next '## [' heading or the first link-reference footer line, trailing blanks trimmed) into a temp notes file for --notes-file, and falls back to --generate-notes when no section or no CHANGELOG exists. The whole-file --notes-file CHANGELOG.md path is removed. Criterion checks AC-1..AC-3 (rg on the workflow) pass; the extracted run script was also exercised with a stubbed gh against the real changelog, a missing version, a v0.3 prefix tag, no file, an Unreleased-on-top multi-version file, and an oldest-version section followed by footers. Publish jobs, triggers, and assets untouched; the Node-action bump bead's uses: lines were not edited.

title: agents: tell bead-authoring agents to run ortus validate after authoring
description:
## Objective
The agentic authoring surface tells an agent to run `ortus validate <repo> <id>` after it authors or repairs a non-epic bd issue, so a hand-authored bead is checked for grind eligibility at authoring time instead of being rejected later at claim. This wires the ortus-zjnb verb into the instructions agents actually read.

## Behavioral context
Before. Two surfaces teach the readiness contract and both only point at `ortus spec` (the rules), neither at a validation step: the managed AGENTS.md block section "Issue authoring contract (readiness v1)" (src/ortus/templates/blocks/agents.md) and the seeded readiness memory `ortus-readiness-contract` (readiness_memory_text() in src/ortus/core/readiness.py). So an agent authoring a bead by hand (for example via `claude -p "create a bd task ..."`) has no instruction to self-check, and the first signal it is unready is grind skipping it. After. Both surfaces add one step: after authoring or repairing a non-epic issue, run `ortus validate <repo> <id>`, which reports READY or the exact sections grind would reject. The step is advisory guidance, not a new gate: `ortus plan` already validates mechanically and grind still enforces at claim; this closes the manual-authoring path.

## Design
See design field.
design:
## Readiness schema

v1

## Scope

Add the `ortus validate` self-check step to the two authoring surfaces agents read: the managed AGENTS.md block "Issue authoring contract" section, and the seeded readiness memory text. Bump the agents block schema so the drift gate accepts the changed body, and update the tests that assert the block body and the memory text.

## Non-goals

Do not change readiness rules, `ortus spec`, or grind claim-time enforcement. Do not make validation a hard requirement or a hook; it is advisory guidance for the manual-authoring path. Do not touch the plan prompt's mechanical validation (plan already validates every new issue). Do not add the pointer to the CLAUDE.md pointer block (it stays a thin pointer to bd prime). Do not edit consumer repos' AGENTS.md directly; the template change propagates on the next `ortus init`.

## Concrete locations

src/ortus/templates/blocks/agents.md: the "Issue authoring contract (readiness v1)" section (~line 20-40), add the `ortus validate <repo> <id>` step beside the existing `ortus spec` pointer. src/ortus/core/agent_files.py: BLOCK_SCHEMAS, bump the `agents` block schema integer (the drift gate requires it when the body meaning changes). src/ortus/core/readiness.py: readiness_memory_text() (~1051) and READINESS_MEMORY_KEY (21), add the same one-line step. Tests: tests/test_init_render.py (agents block body + schema), tests/test_readiness.py (memory text), and any managed-block drift test in the suite.

## Resolved decisions

1. Update exactly the two surfaces an authoring agent consults: the managed AGENTS.md authoring-contract section and the seeded readiness memory. Both already name `ortus spec`; the validate step sits next to it.
2. Wording is advisory: "after authoring or repairing a non-epic issue, run `ortus validate <repo> <id>` to confirm it is grind-eligible." It does not claim to be a gate, because plan validates mechanically and grind enforces at claim.
3. Bump the `agents` block schema so re-init rewrites the block and the drift gate passes; the CLAUDE.md pointer block is unchanged.
4. This depends on ortus-zjnb: the instruction must name a verb that exists.

## Compatibility constraints

The managed-block change propagates only on re-init (`ortus init` / `--force`); existing consumer AGENTS.md files are untouched until then, and host prose outside the markers is preserved. Bumping the agents block schema is the mechanism that keeps the drift gate green; a body change without the bump fails the suite by design. The readiness memory is re-seeded by init; existing memories update when init runs `bd remember` again. No runtime behavior changes.

## Ordered steps

1. Add the validate step to the agents.md authoring-contract section and bump the agents BLOCK_SCHEMAS integer.
2. Add the same step to readiness_memory_text().
3. Update the tests that assert the agents block body/schema and the memory text.
4. Run the targeted tests.

## Dependencies

Blocked by ortus-zjnb (the `ortus validate` verb must exist before the instructions name it). Related to the human-facing pointer zjnb adds to grind/plan messages; this is the agent-facing counterpart.

## Edge cases

An agent in a repo re-initialized from an older Ortus sees the old block until re-init; that is the managed-block model, not a regression. A backend whose worker never authors issues (pure implementer) simply never runs the step; it is guidance on the authoring path, harmless elsewhere. If `ortus validate` is renamed before this lands, the instruction must match the shipped verb name.

## Plan-gap guidance

If bumping the agents block schema collides with an in-flight schema change on the same block, stop and record PLAN-GAP rather than guessing the integer; the two body changes must be sequenced.
acceptance_criteria:
## Observable criteria
- AC-1 (proves-new): the rendered agents block contains an `ortus validate` self-check step in the readiness authoring-contract section.
- AC-2 (proves-new): the seeded readiness memory text names `ortus validate` as the post-authoring check.
- AC-3 (guards-existing): the agents block schema is bumped so the managed-block drift gate passes, and the CLAUDE.md pointer block is unchanged.
## Criterion checks
- AC-1: `uv run pytest tests/test_init_render.py -k "agents_block_names_validate" -q`
- AC-2: `uv run pytest tests/test_readiness.py -k "memory_text_names_validate" -q`
- AC-3: `uv run pytest tests/test_init_render.py -q`
## Targeted tests
`uv run pytest tests/test_init_render.py tests/test_readiness.py -q`
close_reason: Agents block and readiness memory now name ortus validate as the post-authoring self-check; agents block schema bumped to 4

comments.author: who
comments.text: Added the ortus validate self-check to the agents block's authoring-contract section and to readiness_memory_text(), sitting after the ortus spec pointer as advisory guidance (plan still validates mechanically; grind still enforces at claim). Bumped the agents block schema to 4 and re-pinned the drift digest; CLAUDE.md pointer block untouched. New tests test_agents_block_names_validate_after_authoring and test_memory_text_names_validate_after_authoring. AC-1, AC-2, AC-3 criterion checks and the targeted tests all passed; ruff check clean on the changed files.

title: validate: a verb to check a bead against readiness before grinding
description:
## Objective
`ortus validate <repo> [<id>...]` reports whether one or more bd issues satisfy readiness schema v1, using the same validator `ortus grind` applies at claim, so an operator learns a bead is grind-eligible (or exactly why it is not) without launching a grind and waiting for the claim-time rejection.

## Behavioral context
Before. The only way to learn a bead fails readiness is to run `ortus grind` and read the skip message it prints at claim (for example "failing sections (2 of 15): acceptance_criteria/criterion checks, ..."). An operator who just authored a bead has no quick, local way to check it. After. `ortus validate .` with one or more ids validates exactly those issues; with no id it validates every open non-epic issue in the workspace as a pre-grind sweep. Each issue prints READY, EXEMPT (an epic), or the same `report.diagnostic()` grind would print. The command exits 0 when every named issue is ready or exempt and 1 when any is unready, so `ortus validate . && ortus grind .` gates a run. The readiness rules and grind's claim-time enforcement are unchanged; this only surfaces the existing verdict earlier.

## Design
See design field.
design:
## Readiness schema
v1
## Scope
Add a read-only `validate` verb that fetches the named issues (or all open non-epic issues) from bd, runs readiness.validate_issue on each, and prints READY / EXEMPT / the diagnostic, with an exit code that is 0 only when all are ready or exempt. Optional `--json` for scripting. Add a one-line pointer to `ortus validate` in the grind and plan ineligibility messages so the new verb is discoverable from the place the pain is felt.
## Non-goals
Do not overload `ortus check` (it is environment-scoped and its positional is a repo) or `ortus spec` (it prints the contract, needs no workspace). Do not change readiness rules, the schema, or grind's claim-time enforcement, which stays authoritative. Do not repair or edit issues; this reports, it does not fix (repair is plan's job). Do not validate epics beyond reporting them exempt. Do not add a new readiness code path; reuse the one grind and plan call.
## Concrete locations
New src/ortus/commands/validate.py (model it on src/ortus/commands/spec.py, but it takes a repo and ids and needs a bd workspace). Register the verb in src/ortus/cli.py. Reuse readiness.validate_issue (src/ortus/core/readiness.py:768), validate_issues (1058), failed_reports (1062), and ReadinessReport.diagnostic (50). Fetch issues via the bd client show/list (src/ortus/core/bd.py; cf. how plan.py _issue_reports gathers reports). Add the discoverability pointer where the diagnostic prints: src/ortus/commands/grind.py (~1821/1835) and src/ortus/commands/plan.py:293. Tests: new tests/test_validate.py; update whatever test asserts the grind/plan ineligibility message text.
## Resolved decisions
1. New verb, not `check` or `spec`. `check` validates the environment and its positional is a repo, so a bead id there is a domain and type overload; `spec` is the single-purpose contract printer that needs no workspace. A dedicated verb follows the `<repo> [<id>...]` convention the other verbs use.
2. It calls the exact readiness.validate_issue grind and plan use and prints the exact report.diagnostic(), so the preview never drifts from what grind says at claim. No second validation implementation.
3. No id given validates every open non-epic issue, so the verb doubles as a pre-grind queue sweep, not only a single-bead check.
4. Exit 0 when all named issues are ready or exempt, else 1, so it composes in a shell gate before grind.
5. The grind and plan ineligibility messages gain a one-line "run `ortus validate <id>` to see this before grinding" pointer, closing the discoverability gap a separate verb would otherwise open.
6. Verb name is `validate`. `ready` is rejected because it collides with `bd ready` (the unblocked queue); `lint` is rejected because it now also means the prototype-mode lint gate and code linting.
## Compatibility constraints
Read-only and additive: no existing verb changes behavior, and grind/plan only gain one line of pointer text (update the asserting test). The verb needs a bd workspace, unlike `spec`; run outside one it errors like the other repo verbs. Epics report exempt, matching validate_issue. Output on stdout stays pipe-clean under `--json` so it can feed another process.
## Ordered steps
1. Add validate.py: resolve repo, gather issues (named ids or all open non-epic), run validate_issue on each, render READY/EXEMPT/diagnostic, set the exit code.
2. Register the verb in cli.py and add `--json`.
3. Add the `ortus validate` pointer to the grind and plan ineligibility messages; update the asserting test.
4. Tests: a ready issue passes and exits 0; an unready issue prints the same diagnostic as grind and exits 1; an epic reports exempt; no-id validates the open queue; a missing id errors.
5. Run the targeted tests.
## Dependencies
No blockers. Consumes the readiness API (validate_issue/validate_issues/failed_reports/diagnostic) and the bd client. The pointer edit touches the grind/plan message a test asserts.
## Edge cases
A nonexistent id: named error, exit 1, and continue validating the rest rather than aborting on the first. An id that is an epic: exempt, does not fail the run. No open non-epic issues and no ids: exit 0 with a "nothing to validate" line, not an error. An issue whose fields are malformed enough that validate_issue raises: report it as unready with the exception text, never a traceback. `--json` and a nonexistent id: the JSON still lists the id with its error.
## Plan-gap guidance
If gathering "all open non-epic issues" cannot reuse an existing bd client method and would need a new query surface, scope this bead to explicit ids only and file the queue-sweep default as a follow-up, rather than adding a bd query path here.

title: docs: document the prototype verification mode in the README
description:
## Objective
The README documents the prototype verification mode from ortus-u8rp: the `.ortusrc` `verification` key, the `ortus grind --prototype` flag, and that prototype mode verifies with lint and syntax checks only instead of the behavioral test suite, so an operator can find and use it.

title: grind: a prototype verification mode that runs lint and syntax checks instead of tests
description:
## Objective
`ortus grind --prototype` (and a matching `.ortusrc` setting) runs a lightweight verification for high-velocity prototype projects: the worker proves an issue with the project's lint and syntax/compile checks only, not its behavioral test commands or the repo test suite, so an issue closes on a clean lint pass. Full mode is unchanged and stays the default.

## Behavioral context
Before. Verification is the issue's criterion-check commands. The composed worker condition (`_GOAL_POINTER` in src/ortus/commands/grind.py, ~line 487) states "The issue's criterion-check commands already ran during implement — they are the whole verification. Do not run pytest or the repo test suite." So the testing burden per issue is whatever behavioral tests the work spec's acceptance criteria declare, and there is no way to lower that bar for throwaway or exploratory work. After. With `verification = "prototype"` in `.ortusrc` (or `ortus grind --prototype`), grind composes a prototype verify instruction: implement the issue, then run the project's linter plus a syntax/compile gate chosen from `project_type` (for example `ruff check` plus `python -m compileall` for Python, `tsc --noEmit` for TypeScript, `go build ./...` for Go, `cargo check` for Rust), and treat a clean lint and syntax pass as sufficient to session-close. The worker does not run the issue's behavioral test commands or the repo suite. The done bar (issue closed and HEAD in sync with origin) is unchanged; only what the worker must prove before closing is lighter.

## Design
See design field.
design:
## Readiness schema

v1

## Scope

Add a `verification` mode to grind: a `.ortusrc` key `verification = "full" | "prototype"` (default `full`), a `ortus grind --prototype` flag that overrides it for one run, and the prototype verify instruction grind composes into the worker prompt. In prototype mode the verify instruction names the project lint + syntax/compile commands resolved from `project_type`/`linter` and tells the worker those are the whole verification. `ortus check` and the `.ortusrc` scaffold report the key. Docs note the mode and its lowered bar.

## Non-goals

Do not change what `ortus plan` authors into acceptance criteria — emitting lint-only ACs at plan time is a related follow-up, not this bead. Do not loosen readiness validation (it already accepts lint/syntax commands and a `None — <why>` Targeted tests). Do not change the done bar, session-close, or full-mode behavior. Do not add per-issue mode overrides. Do not touch the other backends' verify posture beyond the shared instruction text. Do not auto-detect "this looks like a prototype"; the mode is explicit.

## Concrete locations

src/ortus/core/config.py: DEFAULTS and the validator (add `verification`, default `"full"`, reject other strings). src/ortus/commands/grind.py: the grind() Typer options (add `--prototype`), the mode resolution (flag > `.ortusrc` > default), `_GOAL_POINTER` (~487) and `_compose_work_prompt` (~578) where the verify framing is set, and the phase-instruction path. src/ortus/prompts/goal-prompt.md: the verify step, which must read the mode via the composed instruction rather than hard-coding tests. Lint/syntax command resolution from `project_type` (cf. init's per-language linter defaults in src/ortus/commands/init.py). src/ortus/commands/check.py and the `.ortusrc` template/init_render: surface the key. Tests: tests/test_core_config.py, tests/test_grind.py, tests/test_grind_prompt_content.py.

## Resolved decisions

1. The mode is a single `.ortusrc` string `verification` plus a `--prototype` grind flag; flag wins, then `.ortusrc`, then default `full`. One switch, not a matrix.
2. Prototype verification is the project linter plus a syntax/compile gate, resolved from `project_type`: python -> `ruff check` + `python -m compileall`; typescript -> `tsc --noEmit` (+ the configured eslint if present); go -> `go build ./...`; rust -> `cargo check`; polyglot -> run each detected language's gate. The exact command set is data keyed by project_type, beside init's linter defaults.
3. The instruction replaces the "criterion checks are the whole verification" framing in prototype mode with "lint and syntax are the whole verification; do not run the behavioral test commands or the repo suite."
4. Readiness is untouched: an issue's AC test commands remain in the work spec as the record; prototype mode simply does not run them.
5. The mode is a property of the run, logged on the grind start line so a reader knows a prototype run held a lighter bar.

## Compatibility constraints

Full mode is byte-identical to today, and `verification` absent from `.ortusrc` resolves to `full`, so every existing project is unaffected. The `--prototype` flag is off by default. The done bar, orphan handling, CodeGraph policy, and session-close are unchanged. Claude's 4,000-character `/goal` condition cap still applies: the prototype instruction must fit or be injected as a phase instruction rather than inflating `_GOAL_POINTER`.

## Ordered steps

1. Add the `verification` config key and validation with tests.
2. Add the `--prototype` grind flag and the flag>config>default resolution.
3. Add the project_type -> lint/syntax command map and the prototype verify instruction, composed into the worker prompt; log the mode on the grind start line.
4. Report the key in `ortus check` and the `.ortusrc` scaffold.
5. Document the mode in the README.
6. Run the targeted tests.

## Dependencies

Related follow-up (separate bead): `ortus plan --prototype` authoring lint-only acceptance criteria so a prototype project is light end to end. No blockers. Touches the verify-framing text asserted by tests/test_grind_prompt_content.py.

## Edge cases

A `project_type` with no obvious lint/syntax gate (or `linter = none`): prototype mode runs the syntax/compile gate alone, and if none exists it records that verification is syntax-parse only, never silently a no-op. polyglot: run each detected language's gate. An issue whose AC are already lint-only: prototype and full modes verify identically. `--prototype` with `verification = "full"` pinned: the flag wins for that run and the start line says so. A lint gate that is itself slow or unbounded: it is a bounded lint command, not the test suite, so the unbounded-suite concern does not apply.

## Plan-gap guidance

If prototype mode cannot express the lint/syntax gate as bounded commands for some project_type without running that language's full toolchain, stop and record PLAN-GAP naming the project_type rather than shipping a gate that quietly runs the whole build.

- AC-2 (proves-new): the config validator accepts `"full"` and `"prototype"` and rejects any other value with a named error.
- AC-3 (proves-new): the grind start line records the resolved verification mode.
- AC-4 (guards-existing): full mode composes the exact worker condition it does today, and the existing grind prompt-content tests pass.

title: init: let the operator pick from the served models at an interactive terminal
description:
## Objective
When `ortus init --backend local` (or `--backend opencode`) omits `--local-model` AND stdin is an interactive terminal AND the server lists models, prompt the operator to pick one from the served list and continue init with it — instead of listing and exiting. When stdin is not a TTY, behavior is unchanged: list and exit 1, so scripts stay predictable.

## Behavioral context
Before. ortus-14tc made the missing-model error list the served ids (init.py:457 -> _served_models_hint at ~482 -> list_served_models), then exits 1 regardless of context; an operator at a terminal must copy an id and re-run. After. At an interactive terminal, init renders the served ids as a numbered menu, reads the operators choice, sets that id as the local model, and proceeds through the normal render/probe path — no re-run. Non-interactive stdin (piped, closed, CI without a TTY) keeps the exact list-and-exit-1 behavior, honoring the standing lesson that init must not block on stdin (see the askuserquestion-replacement memory).

## Design
See design field.
design:
## Readiness schema
v1
## Scope
At the missing-model branch, gate on sys.stdin.isatty(): when interactive and list_served_models returns >=1 id, present a numbered menu, read and validate a choice, set table["model"], and fall through to the existing parse/render path. Non-interactive, unreachable, auth-demanded, or zero-models all keep 14tc behavior (list/curl hint, exit 1). Add a _select_served_model helper and tests for both stdin modes.
## Non-goals
Do NOT prompt when stdin is not a TTY — this is the critical constraint; a script or CI run must still fail fast with the list, never hang. Do not silently auto-select when multiple models are served (an explicit pick is required). Do not build a fuzzy-search or full TUI; a numbered read is enough. Do not touch the pinned --local-model path, other backends, or probe_models/list_served_models internals. Do not change the exit code on the non-interactive path (stays 1).
## Concrete locations
src/ortus/commands/init.py: the `if "model" not in table:` branch (~457) and _served_models_hint (~482); add _select_served_model(base_url, api_key_env) -> str | None beside it and sys.stdin.isatty() gating. Reuse src/ortus/core/local_backend.py list_served_models (337) and the LocalServerError kinds. Prompt via typer/click (typer.prompt or click.Choice/IntRange); menu text goes to stderr through output, not stdout. Tests: tests/test_init.py (the two message-asserting tests around test_init_local_requires_local_model / test_init_opencode_requires_local_model).
## Resolved decisions
1. The interactivity gate is sys.stdin.isatty(); nothing else (no new flag) — matching how a shell tool decides to prompt, and keeping every existing non-interactive caller (scripts, tests, CI) on the list-and-exit path. 2. A single served model is still offered as a prompt with it as the default (Enter accepts), not auto-pinned, so the operator always confirms which model is written. 3. Invalid input (non-number, out of range) re-prompts up to 3 times, then exits 1 with the list; EOF/KeyboardInterrupt during the prompt exits 1 cleanly, never a traceback, never a hang. 4. The chosen id is fed into the same table["model"] slot --local-model would fill, so the downstream render/probe/opencode.json path is identical whether the model was typed on the CLI or picked here. 5. Menu/prompt output is stderr (like output.error), so stdout stays clean for any caller capturing it.
## Compatibility constraints
Non-interactive init is byte-for-byte unchanged (same list, same exit 1) — the two existing message-asserting tests must still pass when isatty is False. --local-model still bypasses this branch entirely. probe_models/list_served_models signatures and their error identities (used by check.py/grind.py) are untouched. No behavior change for claude/codex/grok.
## Ordered steps
1. Add _select_served_model: fetch via list_served_models, render a numbered menu to stderr, read/validate a choice (bounded retries, clean EOF/interrupt handling), return the id or None. 2. In the missing-model branch, when sys.stdin.isatty() and a selection is returned, set table["model"] and continue; otherwise keep the current error+exit. 3. Tests: TTY (monkeypatched isatty True + fed stdin) selects and init proceeds; non-TTY lists and exits 1; invalid-then-valid input; unreachable degrades to curl hint. 4. Run the targeted tests.
## Dependencies
Follows ortus-14tc (closed) — reuses its list_served_models and the missing-model branch it shaped. Callers of list_served_models/probe_models (check, grind, init) must be unaffected. No blockers.
## Edge cases
stdin a TTY but the server unreachable/auth-demanded: no menu (nothing to list) -> current curl-hint error, exit 1. Exactly one served model at a TTY: prompt with it as default. stdout redirected while stdin is a TTY: still prompt (gate is stdin), menu to stderr. A served id with odd characters: it is copied verbatim into the table, same as --local-model would. Non-TTY with a served list: unchanged list + exit 1 (never prompt).
## Plan-gap guidance
If any existing non-interactive caller (a test harness, CI, or ortus internal) runs init with an attached pseudo-TTY where a prompt would block, stop and record PLAN-GAP: the gate needs a stricter signal (an explicit --non-interactive/assume flag) rather than isatty, decided before shipping a prompt that could hang automation.
acceptance_criteria:
## Observable criteria
- AC-1 (proves-new): with stdin a TTY and models served, init prompts, and the selected id is written as the local model and init proceeds (no re-run, no exit 1).
- AC-2 (guards-existing): with stdin not a TTY, init does not prompt and keeps the 14tc list-and-exit-1 behavior byte-for-byte.
- AC-3 (guards-existing): --local-model still bypasses the prompt, an unreachable server still degrades to the curl hint, and other backends are unaffected.
## Criterion checks
- AC-1: `uv run pytest tests/test_init.py -k "interactive_selects_served_model" -q`
- AC-2: `uv run pytest tests/test_init.py -k "non_tty_lists_and_exits" -q`
- AC-3: `uv run pytest tests/test_init.py tests/test_core_local_backend.py -q`
## Targeted tests
`uv run pytest tests/test_init.py tests/test_core_local_backend.py -q`

A single id is offered as the Enter default, not auto-pinned. Invalid answers re-prompt within LOCAL_MODEL_PROMPT_RETRIES (3); exhaustion, EOF, and Ctrl-C fall through to the existing missing-model error with the list, exit 1, no traceback. The listing is fetched once and shared: _served_models fetches, _served_models_hint now takes the ids. Plan-gap check: no ortus internal spawns init, and the closed-stdin subprocess test uses DEVNULL, so no non-interactive caller attaches a pseudo-TTY. title: init: list the served models when --backend local omits --local-model
description:
## Objective
When `ortus init --backend local` (or `--backend opencode`) is run without `--local-model`, and the configured base_url is reachable, the error lists the model ids the server actually serves so the operator can copy one, instead of telling them to curl the endpoint themselves.

## Behavioral context
Before. init.py raises LOCAL_MODEL_REQUIRED_MESSAGE with a hint `list the served ids with: curl {base_url}/models` (src/ortus/commands/init.py:456-461). The operator must run curl by hand and read raw JSON to find a valid id. After. init probes `{base_url}/models` itself and prints the served ids as a copyable list in the error, e.g. `served models at http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1: - 0bserverx/Qwen3.8-...`. When the server is down or demands a key, it falls back to the current curl hint unchanged. The exit code stays 1 (a model is still required) — this improves the message, it does not auto-pick a model.

## Design
See design field.
design:
## Readiness schema
v1
## Scope
At the missing-model raise site, resolve base_url (from the [local]/--local-base-url the same way the code already does) and fetch the served ids to render them in the error. Reuse the existing endpoint fetch: extract the id-listing half of probe_models into a reachability-tolerant helper (base_url in, ids out, or a typed unreachable/auth signal) so no model is required to list. On any LocalServerError kind (unreachable, auth-demanded), fall back to the current curl hint. Update the two tests that assert the old message.
## Non-goals
Do not add interactive numbered selection: init runs non-interactively (in scripts, closed stdin) and this project already treats stdin-in-headless as a hazard (see askuserquestion-replacement memory); a TTY-gated picker can be a later follow-up. Do not auto-select a single served model (explicit is safer; the operator pins the id). Do not change probe_models validation behaviour for the pinned-model path. Do not touch codex/claude/grok. Do not change the exit code (still 1).
## Concrete locations
src/ortus/commands/init.py:456-461 (the `if "model" not in table:` raise site, LOCAL_MODEL_REQUIRED_MESSAGE at ~228), src/ortus/core/local_backend.py:338 probe_models and its `_served_ids(payload)` helper and LocalServerError kinds (unreachable/auth-demanded), the base_url resolution (`table.get("base_url", DEFAULT_LOCAL_BASE_URL)`), and the --local-base-url flag (init.py:638). Tests: tests/test_init.py (test_init_local_requires_local_model:691, test_init_opencode_requires_local_model:882) and tests/test_core_local_backend.py.
## Resolved decisions
1. Extract a `list_served_models(base_url, *, api_key_env=None, timeout)` helper from probe_models so listing needs no LocalConfig/model; probe_models then calls it and adds the model-membership check, keeping one fetch path. 2. Listing is best-effort: any unreachable/auth failure degrades to the existing curl hint, so a down server never turns a clear "pick a model" error into a stack trace. 3. Timeout is the short LOCAL_PROBE_TIMEOUT (3s) — this runs on a hot init path and is informational. 4. The rendered list is plain ids, one per line, under a line naming the base_url; no numbering (no selection implied).
## Compatibility constraints
The exit code stays 1 and a model is still required — scripts that depend on the failure are unaffected. probe_models keeps its exact signature and semantics for the pinned path; only its internals are refactored to share the fetch. When the server is unreachable the message is byte-for-byte the current one. Other backends init unchanged.
## Ordered steps
1. Extract list_served_models() from probe_models; have probe_models call it. 2. At the raise site, on missing model, try list_served_models(base_url) and render the ids; on LocalServerError fall back to the curl hint. 3. Update the two message-asserting tests to accept the list (reachable) and the hint (unreachable), with a fake server. 4. Run the targeted tests.
## Dependencies
Follows the opencode pivot (epic ortus-t2kn, closed). Callers of probe_models: check.py, grind.py, init.py — the refactor must not change what they see. No blockers.
## Edge cases
Server reachable but serves zero models: print "no models served at {base_url}" plus the curl hint. Auth-demanded: fall back to the curl hint (listing would need the key). A very long served list: print all — the operator needs the exact id. base_url from --local-base-url vs the [local] default: resolve the same value the pinned path would.
## Plan-gap guidance
If extracting list_served_models cannot preserve probe_models exact unreachable/auth/model-missing error identities that check.py and grind.py assert on, stop and record PLAN-GAP rather than changing those error semantics to make listing convenient.
acceptance_criteria:
## Observable criteria
- AC-1 (proves-new): init --backend local without --local-model, against a reachable server, prints the served model ids in the error.
- AC-2 (proves-new): with the server unreachable or demanding a key, init falls back to the existing curl hint and still exits 1 with no traceback.
- AC-3 (guards-existing): supplying --local-model still initializes normally, and probe_models callers in check/grind see unchanged error semantics.
## Criterion checks
- AC-1: `uv run pytest tests/test_init.py -k "requires_local_model and lists_served" -q`
- AC-2: `uv run pytest tests/test_init.py -k "requires_local_model_unreachable_falls_back" -q`
- AC-3: `uv run pytest tests/test_init.py tests/test_core_local_backend.py -q`
## Targeted tests
`uv run pytest tests/test_init.py tests/test_core_local_backend.py -q`

comments.author: who
comments.text: Implemented. An unpinned local/opencode init now lists the served ids from {base_url}/models as the missing-model hint: one id per line under a line naming the server; 'no models served at <base_url>' plus the curl line when the list is empty; the unchanged curl line on unreachable, auth-demanded, or a base_url that is not a URL. Exit code stays 1 and nothing is written. Core: list_served_models(base_url, *, api_key_env=None, timeout) is the unpinned listing; it and probe_models share a private _fetch_served_ids rather than probe_models calling list_served_models, because the latter would replace the pinned alias with the <model> placeholder in the unreachable remediation that test_probe_models_unreachable_names_serving_command asserts equals serving_hint(config). The shared fetch keeps one request path and every pinned verdict (kind, message, remediation) byte-identical for check and grind. _is_http_url carries the table URL rule for parse_local_table and the listing, and also rejects an unclosed IPv6 bracket or a non-numeric port, which urlsplit/.port raise ValueError on, so both report a verdict instead of raising from a later reader. Init forwards a recorded api_key_env so a keyed server still lists. Not done, by the Non-goals: no interactive picker, no auto-select of a single served id. Criterion checks passed: AC-1 (uv run pytest tests/test_init.py -k 'requires_local_model and lists_served' -q: 3 passed), AC-2 (-k requires_local_model_unreachable_falls_back: 2 passed, parametrized unreachable and auth-demanded), AC-3 (tests/test_init.py tests/test_core_local_backend.py: 122 passed). ruff clean on the changed files. Rendered by hand against a throwaway loopback models server and a closed port.

title: opencode: carry the verify denial at agent scope so no config scope re-allows write tools
description:
## Objective

Make the opencode verify posture hold against every configuration scope: `OpenCodeRunner.launch_env(readonly=True)` also delivers the bash, edit, and write denial at agent scope for the agent a verify run uses, and `ortus check` reports that posture, so an agent-scoped allow in a project or user config can no longer hand a verifier the write tools.

## Behavioral context

Before. The verify launch exports only `OPENCODE_PERMISSION`, a global-table denial. bd memory opencode-q1-permission-scopes (the ortus-t2kn.12 probe, opencode 1.18.27) proves that an `agent.build.permission` allow in project `opencode.json`, in the user-level config, in `OPENCODE_CONFIG_CONTENT`, or in a `build.md` agent file re-advertises bash, edit, and write, and the live model rewrote a guard file. opencode resolves permissions as an ordered ruleset in which agent-scoped rows follow the global rows and the last match wins. The `ortus check` posture row resolves only the project table and the variable, so it reports a read-only posture that a project can silently undo.

After. A verify launch also exports `OPENCODE_CONFIG_CONTENT` carrying `{"agent":{"build":{"permission":{"bash":"deny","edit":"deny","write":"deny"}}}}`, merged over any object the operator already has in that variable. The same probe shape shows the three tools absent and the guard intact under every scope tested. The posture row names both the global and the agent-scope denial for the verify phase. The implement phase is unchanged.
design:
## Readiness schema

v1

## Scope

`OpenCodeRunner.launch_env` in src/ortus/core/agent.py: when `readonly`, export `OPENCODE_CONFIG_CONTENT` with the agent-scoped denial for the `build` agent, deep-merged over an operator-provided `OPENCODE_CONFIG_CONTENT` JSON object so unrelated keys survive. `OpenCodeRunner.preflight_readonly`: refuse, with a message naming the variable, when the operator value is present but is not a JSON object, instead of silently replacing it. `_opencode_posture_row` in src/ortus/commands/check.py: report the verify posture as the global denial plus the agent-scope denial. Tests in tests/test_agent.py and tests/test_check.py.

## Non-goals

No reimplementation of opencode configuration resolution to detect allows in every scope: the agent-scope denial makes the tested scopes moot, and a detector would have to mirror five scopes and still miss the next one. No change to the implement-phase environment. No change to the shape of `OPENCODE_READONLY_PERMISSION` or to exporting `OPENCODE_PERMISSION`, which stays as belt and braces. No opencode version bump. No Windows.

## Concrete locations

src/ortus/core/agent.py (`OpenCodeRunner.launch_env`, `OpenCodeRunner.preflight_readonly`, `OPENCODE_READONLY_PERMISSION`, `OPENCODE_PERMISSION_ENV`); src/ortus/core/claude.py (`ReadOnlyExecutionBlocked`, the refusal type the Claude preflight raises); src/ortus/commands/check.py (`_opencode_posture_row`, `OPENCODE_POSTURE_TOOLS`); tests/test_agent.py; tests/test_check.py. Evidence: bd memory opencode-q1-permission-scopes.

## Resolved decisions

1. Harden rather than only detect. The agent-scope denial through `OPENCODE_CONFIG_CONTENT` beat the project agent allow live and every other allow placement in the recorder (bd memory opencode-q1-permission-scopes), so it is the guard; detection alone would leave the verifier writable until a check ran.
2. The denial targets `build`, the agent `opencode run` uses when no `--agent` is passed; `OpenCodeRunner.build_argv` never passes one.
3. Merge, never replace. An operator `OPENCODE_CONFIG_CONTENT` object keeps its other keys; only `agent.build.permission.bash`, `.edit`, and `.write` are overwritten with deny.
4. `OPENCODE_PERMISSION` keeps being exported: it is proven, cheap, and still holds if a later opencode drops agent-scope precedence.

## Compatibility constraints

Linux and macOS. opencode 1.18.27 is the proven version and the finding pins it. Implement-phase launches and every other backend keep their argv, environment, decoder, and tests. No stored data changes. `ortus check` gains detail in one row and changes no exit code for a provisioned project.

## Ordered steps

1. Add a constant naming the verify agent (`build`) and a helper that builds the agent-scoped denial document from `OPENCODE_READONLY_PERMISSION`.
2. In `launch_env(readonly=True)`, read `OPENCODE_CONFIG_CONTENT` from `extra_env` first and the process environment second, parse a present value as a JSON object, deep-merge the denial into it, and export the result.
3. In `preflight_readonly`, refuse with a clear message when the operator value is present but not a JSON object.
4. Extend `_opencode_posture_row` so the verify posture names the agent-scope denial beside the global one.
5. Add tests: denial exported with no operator value; denial merged over an operator object with unrelated keys surviving; a non-JSON value refused; posture row wording.
6. Run the targeted tests.

## Dependencies

Parent ortus-t2kn. Follows ortus-t2kn.12, the spike whose memory is the evidence. Code callers: `OpenCodeRunner.run` consumes `launch_env`; the grind verify launch and `check` consume the posture.

## Edge cases

A project or user config that selects a different default agent, or a future grind that passes `--agent`, would sidestep a `build`-only denial: if opencode exposes the resolved agent name, deny for that name too; otherwise keep `build` and say so in the posture row. An operator value that already denies is idempotent. An empty string in the variable counts as absent. The variable must never carry key material; the denial document contains none.

## Plan-gap guidance

If a re-probe with the recorded shape shows opencode 1.18.27 no longer lets `OPENCODE_CONFIG_CONTENT` win over a project agent allow, stop and record PLAN-GAP instead of adding a detection layer here.
acceptance_criteria:
## Observable criteria

- AC-1 (proves-new): `launch_env(readonly=True)` exports `OPENCODE_CONFIG_CONTENT` with the bash, edit, and write denial under `agent.build.permission`, merged over an operator-provided object.
- AC-2 (proves-new): `preflight_readonly` refuses a non-JSON operator `OPENCODE_CONFIG_CONTENT`.
- AC-3 (guards-existing): the check posture row names the agent-scope denial and the existing opencode check rows pass.

## Criterion checks

- AC-1: `uv run pytest tests/test_agent.py -k opencode_agent_scope_denial -q`
- AC-2: `uv run pytest tests/test_agent.py -k opencode_preflight_config_content -q`
- AC-3: `uv run pytest tests/test_check.py -k opencode_posture -q`

## Targeted tests

`uv run pytest tests/test_agent.py tests/test_check.py -q -n auto`
close_reason: Verify launches export the write-tool denial at agent scope in OPENCODE_CONFIG_CONTENT, merged over the operator's document; check reports it and a non-object value is refused before launch

comments.author: who
comments.text: Verify launches now export the write-tool denial twice: OPENCODE_PERMISSION as before, plus OPENCODE_CONFIG_CONTENT carrying agent.build.permission bash/edit/write=deny, deep-merged over whatever JSON object the operator already exports in that variable so unrelated keys survive (extra_env first, process environment second). A present value that is not a JSON object is refused by read_opencode_config_content with ReadOnlyExecutionBlocked, surfaced by OpenCodeRunner.preflight_readonly before launch and by launch_env itself; the implement phase is unchanged. The check posture row reports the verify posture as the global denial plus the agent-scope denial for agent build and turns an unmergeable operator value into a posture-unknown failure. README posture paragraph gained the second export. Criterion checks AC-1..AC-3 passed; tests/test_agent.py, tests/test_check.py, tests/test_core_agent.py green under -n auto.

title: opencode spike: can another permission scope re-allow write tools under the verify denial
description:
## Objective

Record whether any opencode configuration scope other than the project `permission` table — `agent.<name>.permission` in `opencode.json`, the user-level opencode config, or `OPENCODE_CONFIG_CONTENT` — can re-allow `edit`, `write`, or `bash` for the agent a verify run uses after `OPENCODE_PERMISSION` has denied them, so the verify posture's non-writability rests on evidence for every scope rather than on the global-table merge alone.

## Behavioral context

Before. `OpenCodeRunner.launch_env(readonly=True)` exports `OPENCODE_PERMISSION={"edit":"deny","write":"deny","bash":"deny"}`, proven (bd memory opencode-q1-sandbox) to remove those tools when the project `permission` table is the only other permission source. The `ortus check` posture row resolves only that table plus the variable. Whether an agent-scoped block or another scope takes precedence over the merged global table is unverified; a scope that wins would let a verifier write, which the grind contract treats as a correctness failure, not a WARN.

After. bd memory opencode-q1-permission-scopes exists, starting with a verdict token (OK / HOLE / PLAN-GAP), naming each scope tested and whether the verify launch kept or lost the denial. A HOLE verdict names the guard to build (a check in `OpenCodeRunner.preflight_readonly`, a check row, or both) as a new leaf; this spike does not build it.
design:
## Readiness schema

v1

## Scope

An operator-run, host-side probe (opencode cannot run in the dev sandbox). In a scratch repo with the `ortuslocal` provider block and a guard file, launch `opencode run --format json` with `OPENCODE_PERMISSION` set to the verify denial while, in turn: (1) `opencode.json` carries `agent.<default>.permission` allowing bash, edit, and write; (2) the user-level opencode config carries the same; (3) `OPENCODE_CONFIG_CONTENT` carries the same. Each time ask the model to overwrite the guard file and record whether the tools were advertised and whether the file changed. Record findings via bd remember. No Ortus code changes.

## Non-goals

No runner, check, or preflight change here — findings only. Do not change the shape of the verify denial. Do not probe Windows. Do not benchmark the model.

## Concrete locations

src/ortus/core/agent.py (`OpenCodeRunner.launch_env`, `OPENCODE_READONLY_PERMISSION`), src/ortus/commands/check.py (`_opencode_posture_row`, which resolves only the project table and the variable), bd memory opencode-q1-sandbox (the global-table finding this extends). bd memory to write: opencode-q1-permission-scopes.

## Resolved decisions

1. Same server, model, and opencode version as opencode-q1 unless the host has moved on; the finding pins whatever version ran.
2. Verdict tokens: OK (no scope re-allows a denied tool), HOLE (a scope does; name it and the tool), PLAN-GAP (opencode cannot be driven to answer).
3. A HOLE files a guard leaf under ortus-t2kn; this spike records, it does not build.

## Compatibility constraints

Findings-only: no shipped behavior changes, every backend keeps its argv, decoder, and tests. The probe writes only to a scratch repo, a scratch user config directory, and bd memory — never to the real project or the operator's live opencode config.

## Ordered steps

1. Scratch repo with the provider block, the codegraph mcp entry, and a guard file with known contents.
2. Baseline: the verify denial alone; confirm the write tools are absent and the guard file is intact.
3. Add the agent-scoped allow to `opencode.json`; repeat the write attempt.
4. Move the allow to a scratch user-level config; repeat.
5. Move it to `OPENCODE_CONFIG_CONTENT`; repeat.
6. `bd remember --key opencode-q1-permission-scopes` with the verdict token, the version, and one line per scope.

## Dependencies

Parent ortus-t2kn. Extends bd memory opencode-q1-sandbox. Blocks nothing today; a HOLE verdict creates the guard leaf.

## Edge cases

opencode may name its default agent something other than `build`; record the name it reports and test that one. A version that ignores `OPENCODE_PERMISSION` entirely is a HOLE for the whole posture, not a per-scope result — record it as such and stop.

## Plan-gap guidance

If opencode cannot be launched headless on the host at all, stop and record PLAN-GAP in the memory; do not infer precedence from reading opencode source alone.
acceptance_criteria:
## Observable criteria

- AC-1 (proves-new): bd memory opencode-q1-permission-scopes exists, starts with a verdict token, and records each scope tested with its result.

## Criterion checks

- AC-1: `bd memories opencode-q1-permission-scopes`

## Targeted tests

None — spike findings are recorded in bd memory; no repository code changes.
close_reason: HOLE: an agent-scoped permission allow in project opencode.json, the user-level config, OPENCODE_CONFIG_CONTENT, or a build.md agent file re-allows bash, edit, and write under the verify denial (advertised tools and a live guard rewrite); global-table allows do not. Recorded in bd memory opencode-q1-permission-scopes; guard leaf ortus-t2kn.15 filed.

comments.author: who
comments.text:
Verdict HOLE, recorded in bd memory opencode-q1-permission-scopes (opencode 1.18.27, llama-server [redacted]2:8080, the reference 27B, default run agent build). Method: for each scope, one run against a recording OpenAI-compatible server that captured the tools[] opencode advertised, and one live run asking the model to overwrite a guard file, both under the exact OPENCODE_PERMISSION denial launch_env exports. Controls behaved: no denial advertises bash/edit/write and the model wrote via bash; the denial alone advertises neither and the model answered NO-WRITE-TOOL with the guard intact.

Every agent-scoped allow re-allowed the tools: project opencode.json agent.build.permission, the user-level config agent.build.permission, and OPENCODE_CONFIG_CONTENT agent.build.permission each advertised bash, edit, and write and the live model rewrote the guard (write tool; bash plus write for the env scope). A build.md agent file with frontmatter allows, project or user, also re-advertised them. Global permission-table allows in any scope did not re-allow: the env denial wins the global merge as the check posture row assumes. Mechanism per opencode agent list: an ordered ruleset, last match wins, agent-scoped rows appended after the global rows.

Guard evidence: an agent-scoped denial delivered through OPENCODE_CONFIG_CONTENT beat the project agent allow live and every allow placement in the recorder, including both build.md files. Filed ortus-t2kn.15 to harden launch_env(readonly=True) with that agent-scope denial and report it in the check posture row. Untested and noted there: default_agent or --agent selecting an agent other than build, the OPENCODE_CONFIG path scope, and .opencode/opencode.json. No repository code changed; the probe ran from the worker sandbox against a scratch repo and a scratch HOME, and the operator live opencode config was never touched.

title: opencode audition: drive the reference 27B through a full grind loop and record the verdict
description:
## Objective
The pivoted opencode local backend drives the reference 27B (0bserverx/Qwen3.8-27B-Heretic-Abliterated-Uncensored-GGUF:Q4_K_M on llama-server) through a full grind loop — claim, implement with tool use and CodeGraph MCP, verify under the read-only posture, close — on a scratch repo, and the verdict (tool-call fidelity, MCP composition, close honesty, tokens/sec, context fit) is recorded, replacing the abandoned codex audition (ortus-d333.11).

## Behavioral context
Before. The codex+shim audition (ortus-d333.11) was abandoned mid-run at the context wall; the 27B was proven to make chat-completions tool calls but never completed a codex loop. After. The same model, driven by opencode, closes at least one real issue end to end (or the verdict names exactly where it stalls), and bd memory opencode-q3 records the outcome.
design:
## Readiness schema
v1
## Scope
Operator-run audition on the GPU host (labelled human: GPU, a large local model, and a terminal-launched grind). Configure a scratch repo for --backend opencode against the running llama-server, plan a tiny fixture issue, run ortus grind --backend opencode, and record the verdict. The only repo change is one README What-to-expect paragraph.
## Non-goals
No fine-tuning, no model eval beyond the worker contract, no Ortus code changes beyond the doc paragraph, no retry-logic design (record 5xx behavior only).
## Concrete locations
A scratch repo on the host; tests/fixtures/sample-prds/tiny-3-task.md as the issue source; README What-to-expect paragraph; bd memory opencode-q3. Reference: the closed ortus-d333.11 audition spec and its carried-forward evidence.
## Resolved decisions
1. Runs on opencode, not codex — the whole point of the pivot. 2. Success is defined at the pipeline level (a real close, or a precise stall report), separable from model quality. 3. Context/perf numbers are recorded for the docs What-to-expect paragraph.
## Compatibility constraints
No shipped behavior changes except the doc paragraph. The audition uses the operators server and does not alter the real project.
## Ordered steps
1. Confirm t2kn.2-.6 shipped and check --backend opencode is green. 2. Scratch repo + opencode.json; plan the tiny fixture. 3. ortus grind --backend opencode; observe claim/implement/verify/close. 4. Record opencode-q3 with the verdict token and numbers; add the README paragraph.
## Dependencies
