title: Grind progress lines carry no timestamp, so console output cannot be correlated with anything
description:
## Objective
Prefix every progress line with a `yyyymmddhhmmss` timestamp so an operator can tell when a phase happened and line the console up against the grind log.

## Behavioral context
Grind progress lines are emitted as `[ortus grind] <phase>` with no time on them. For a verb that finishes in two seconds this is fine; grind runs for hours, and the operator question is always the same — how long has it been sitting on that line. The answer is currently unavailable without scrolling to a log file and hoping the phase text matches.

The correlation problem is worse than the missing clock. This project stamps time in three different ways already: the grind log writes `[2026-08-08 12:55:52]` in local time, the transaction journal writes `2026-08-08T19:56:03+00:00` in UTC, and the console writes nothing at all. Reading the same run through two of those on 2026-08-08 produced a seven-hour discrepancy that had to be reasoned about before either number could be trusted.

After this change every progress line begins with a compact timestamp on the same clock the grind log uses, so the console and the log can be read side by side.
design:
## Readiness schema
v1

## Scope
Add a `yyyymmddhhmmss` timestamp to the progress line format in the shared output helper, and update the documented convention to match.

## Non-goals
Do not change the grind log file format, which already carries `[YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS]` and is parsed by tooling. Do not change the journal timestamps, which are ISO-8601 UTC by design because they are data rather than display. Do not touch `warn` or `error`, which are single events rather than progress. Do not add a flag to turn this off.

## Resolved decisions
The verb tag is kept and the timestamp is added ahead of it, giving `[20260808132845] [ortus grind] <phase>`, because the tag is what identifies the emitting verb when several ortus processes share a terminal and the request was for a timestamp rather than only the tag.

The timestamp is local time, not UTC, so it matches the clock the grind log already prints. Correlating the console against the log is the entire point of the change, and an operator forced to shift seven hours between two views of one run is the failure this is fixing.

The change goes in the shared helper and applies to every verb rather than to grind alone. Grind motivates it, but a per-verb branch would mean two documented formats and a conditional in a five-line function, and the short verbs lose nothing by carrying a timestamp. This is deliberately slightly wider than the reported symptom; the alternative is a convention that is true for seven verbs and false for one.

## Concrete locations
Edit `progress()` in `src/ortus/core/output.py` around line 35, whose format string is `[ortus <verb>] <phase>` and whose docstring cites the convention. Update the `CLI output convention` section of `AGENTS.md` around line 18, which states the format verbatim. Cover in `tests/test_core_output.py` and `tests/test_cli_verbs.py`.

## Compatibility constraints
Progress lines stay on stderr so machine-readable stdout is untouched. Existing assertions in `tests/test_cli_verbs.py`, `tests/test_plan.py` and `tests/test_spec.py` test for the verb tag as a substring and must keep passing, which a prefix preserves; any that anchor to the start of a line must be updated rather than the format bent to suit them. The markup escaping already applied to the verb and phase must be preserved, since the timestamp is generated rather than user-supplied but the surrounding string is still rendered as markup. Grind log lines keep their current shape so nothing that reads them breaks.

## Ordered steps
1. Add the timestamp to the format string in the shared helper, generated in local time.
2. Confirm the verb tag and the existing markup escaping are both intact.
3. Update the documented convention in AGENTS.md to show the new format.
4. Run the verb-level suites and fix any assertion that anchors to the start of a line rather than matching a substring.
5. Add a test asserting the prefix shape and that it precedes the verb tag.

## Dependencies
No issue dependency. Related to the ortus-0udo dashboard epic, which solves the same underlying complaint — an operator unable to tell a live run from a stalled one — at a larger scale; this is the cheap fix that helps immediately and stays useful afterwards, since the console remains the surface people actually watch.

## Edge cases
Two ortus processes sharing a terminal must remain distinguishable, which is why the verb tag stays. A phase emitted either side of midnight must roll the date, which a full `yyyymmdd` handles and a bare time would not. A host whose timezone changes mid-run is not worth defending against; local time is read by a human sitting at that host. A phase string containing markup characters must still be escaped as it is today.

## Plan-gap guidance
If a test elsewhere anchors on the exact line start in a way that cannot be updated without changing unrelated behaviour, record PLAN-GAP naming the test rather than dropping the prefix.

title: Dashboard warnings panel and postmortem replay of a finished run
description:
## Objective
Surface the failure modes that actually end runs while they are still developing, and let the same view be pointed at a finished run to explain why it ended.

## Behavioral context
Three conditions ended runs repeatedly in one session: the watchdog killing a worker mid-flight, correction attempts exhausting into a human label, and a verifier unable to execute any command and returning every criterion blocked. Each was diagnosed only afterwards, by reading logs by hand — one investigation required extracting a job log from a CI API and comparing passing sets across runs.

A stopgap script that surfaced these markers immediately produced seven false positives, because it matched the agent transcript rather than the ortus lines. That discrimination now lives in the run-state model and this panel consumes it.

After this change the panel shows live warnings with the evidence that produced them, and `ortus dashboard --replay <log>` renders the same view over a finished run including its terminal state.
design:
## Readiness schema
v1

## Scope
The warnings region driven by the models warning counts, and a replay mode that renders a finished run from its log and journal.

## Non-goals
No remediation actions. No alerting, notification or exit codes based on warnings. No aggregation across runs, which would be a fleet feature.

## Resolved decisions
Warnings show the evidence line that produced them, not just a count, because a bare count is what made the stopgap script untrustworthy and an operator needs to judge the claim. Replay reuses the same panels rather than a separate renderer, so a run explains itself the same way whether it is live or finished, and there is one code path to keep correct. Replay is a flag on the same verb rather than a new verb, since the view is identical and only the source differs.

## Concrete locations
Fill the warnings region in `src/ortus/commands/dashboard.py` from the warning counts and evidence in the snapshot from `src/ortus/core/runstate.py`. Add a replay flag to the `dashboard()` callback accepting a log path, and resolve the journal alongside it. Cover in `tests/test_dashboard.py`.

## Compatibility constraints
Live mode must be unchanged by the addition of replay. A replayed run must never write to the repository, exactly as live mode does not. A log from an older run whose vocabulary has since changed must render what it can rather than raising. The warning vocabulary must come from the shared model so live and replay agree.

## Ordered steps
1. Render warning counts with the ortus line that produced each, from the model.
2. Show a live warning as it appears rather than only at the end of a run.
3. Add the replay flag resolving a log path and its journal.
4. Render the terminal state of a replayed run: how it ended and at which phase.
5. Add tests for a clean run showing no warnings, a run whose agent content quotes the vocabulary showing none, a run with a real watchdog kill showing one, and a replay of a finished run.

## Dependencies
Blocked by the run-state leaf and the shell leaf. Related to every other panel leaf, which replay renders unchanged; whichever lands last inherits the others.

## Edge cases
A run that ended cleanly has no terminal failure and replay must say so rather than inventing one. A log still being written must be replayable, showing progress up to the current end. A log for a run whose journal has since been deleted must render from the log alone. Two runs sharing a log directory must be distinguishable by filename.

## Plan-gap guidance
If a warning cannot be attributed to an ortus line with certainty, record PLAN-GAP naming the marker and route to planning rather than reintroducing transcript matching, which produced seven false positives the first time.
acceptance_criteria:
## Observable criteria
- AC-1: A run with a real watchdog kill shows one warning with the ortus line as evidence.
- AC-2: A run whose agent content quotes the warning vocabulary shows no warnings.
- AC-3: Replay renders a finished run through the same panels, including how it ended.
- AC-4: Live mode is unchanged by the presence of the replay flag.

## Criterion checks
- AC-1: Run `uv run pytest tests/test_dashboard.py -k warning_real_timeout -q`.
- AC-2: Run `uv run pytest tests/test_dashboard.py -k warning_no_false_positive -q`.
- AC-3: Run `uv run pytest tests/test_dashboard.py -k replay_finished_run -q`.
- AC-4: Run `uv run pytest tests/test_dashboard.py -q`.

## Targeted tests
Run `uv run pytest tests/test_dashboard.py --test-timeout=30 --enforce-duration-budget -q`.
notes: The false-positive lesson is concrete: a stopgap health script reported 7 phantom timeouts and 6 phantom escalations because the worker under observation was editing the recovery code containing those strings. Ortus writes plain lines into the grind log; the agent writes JSON.

title: Dashboard verdict panel: criteria as they are judged
description:
## Objective
Show each acceptance criterion and its outcome as the verifier produces them, so an operator sees whether a run is passing before it ends.

## Behavioral context
Verdicts are the most informative artifact a run produces and the least visible. In one session a verifier passed every criterion and then ended without emitting its envelope, so a sound candidate was rejected and the operator learned only from a terse error after the run had exited. In another, a verifier failed a criterion whose own prescribed check passed, on the strength of a wider sweep, and that reasoning sat unread in a bd comment.

The data is available: verifier reports are written under `logs/grind-transactions/` as markdown named by candidate hash and attempt, and the verdict envelope appears in the log. After this change the panel lists each criterion with pass, fail, running or not-yet-reached, and shows the decision once emitted.
design:
## Readiness schema
v1

## Scope
The verdict region: per-criterion status and the overall decision, sourced from the verifier report artifacts and the verdict envelope in the log.

## Non-goals
No re-running of criterion checks. No rendering of the full verifier report, which can run to many kilobytes. No judgment of its own about whether the verdict is correct.

## Resolved decisions
Criteria are listed from the issue packet so the panel can show not-yet-reached ones, rather than only those the verifier has already reported; an operator watching a seven-criterion issue needs to know four are outstanding. The overall decision is shown as pending until an envelope is emitted, because the absence of an envelope is itself a failure mode that cost a run and should be visible while it is happening rather than after.

## Concrete locations
Fill the verdict region in `src/ortus/commands/dashboard.py`, reading verifier report artifacts under `logs/grind-transactions/` referenced by verifier_refs in the journal, and the verdict envelope from the log events surfaced by `src/ortus/core/runstate.py`. Criterion identifiers come from the issue packet, validated by `src/ortus/core/readiness.py`. Cover in `tests/test_dashboard.py`.

## Compatibility constraints
A run with no verifier report yet shows criteria as not-yet-reached rather than as failing. A verdict whose criterion identifiers do not match the packet must render both sets rather than dropping either, since that mismatch is a real condition the verdict validator already reports. A report too large to display must be summarised rather than truncated mid-criterion.

## Ordered steps
1. Read the criterion identifiers from the issue packet.
2. Render each as not-yet-reached before any verdict exists.
3. Update statuses from the verifier report artifacts as they are written.
4. Show the overall decision once an envelope is emitted, and show pending until then.
5. Add tests for no verdict, a partial verdict, a passing verdict, and a criterion-identifier mismatch.

## Dependencies
Blocked by the run-state leaf and the shell leaf. Related to the verdict contract in `src/ortus/core/verdict.py`, which defines the envelope this panel reads.

## Edge cases
A correction round produces a second verifier report for the same issue and the panel must show the latest rather than merging them. A verdict emitted for a stale candidate hash must be shown as stale rather than as current. An issue whose packet has no criterion identifiers is a readiness failure and must render as such rather than as an empty verdict.

## Plan-gap guidance
If verifier reports cannot be attributed to an attempt from their filenames and the journal alone, record PLAN-GAP naming what is available and route to planning rather than showing a verdict from the wrong attempt.

- AC-1: Criteria from the issue packet are listed as not-yet-reached before any verdict exists.
- AC-2: Statuses update from a verifier report artifact.
- AC-3: The overall decision shows pending until an envelope is emitted, then the decision.
- AC-4: A criterion-identifier mismatch renders both sets rather than dropping either.

## Criterion checks
- AC-1: Run `uv run pytest tests/test_dashboard.py -k verdict_not_yet_reached -q`.
- AC-2: Run `uv run pytest tests/test_dashboard.py -k verdict_from_report -q`.
- AC-3: Run `uv run pytest tests/test_dashboard.py -k verdict_pending_then_decided -q`.

## Targeted tests

title: Dashboard candidate panel: owned, inherited and disowned paths
description:
## Objective
Show what the run will commit if it passes, and what it is deliberately leaving alone, so an operator can see a wrong candidate before it is committed rather than after.

## Behavioral context
Candidate composition caused several failures in one session and was invisible in all of them. A worker inherited seven paths belonging to its own issue and declared them unrelated, which would have committed five paths and silently abandoned seven. Separately a verifier was rejected for candidate drift because disowned paths were counted as unexplained. In both cases the facts were in the journal — candidate_paths, handoff_paths, unrelated_paths, baseline_paths, base_head — and nobody was looking.

After this change the panel shows owned, inherited and disowned counts with the paths themselves, plus the base commit the candidate is measured against.
design:
## Readiness schema
v1

## Scope
The candidate region: owned paths, inherited handoff paths, disowned paths, and the base commit, sourced from the journal.

## Non-goals
No diff rendering, which belongs to git. No editing or disowning from the dashboard, which is read-only. No hashing or verification of the candidate, which the transaction already does.

## Resolved decisions
Disowned paths are shown alongside owned ones rather than hidden, because the operator question they answer is whether the worker judged ownership correctly, and that judgment failed once already in a way that would have discarded real work. Counts lead and paths follow, so a large candidate stays readable in a fixed region. The base commit is shown because a candidate is only meaningful against the tree it was captured on, and a moved base is a real failure the transaction checks for.

## Concrete locations
Fill the candidate region in `src/ortus/commands/dashboard.py` from candidate_paths, handoff_paths, unrelated_paths, baseline_paths and base_head in the snapshot from `src/ortus/core/runstate.py`, which reads them from the journal written by `JournalStore` in `src/ortus/core/transaction.py`. Cover in `tests/test_dashboard.py`.

## Compatibility constraints
A journal with no handoff or disowned paths, which is the common case, must render cleanly rather than showing empty sections. A candidate larger than the region must truncate with a count rather than scroll the layout. An absent journal shows no candidate rather than an empty one.

## Ordered steps
1. Render owned path count and paths from the journal.
2. Add inherited and disowned counts and paths, labelled distinctly from owned.
3. Show the base commit the candidate is measured against.
4. Truncate long path lists with a remaining count.
5. Add tests for a plain candidate, a candidate with inherited and disowned paths, and a truncated long candidate.

## Dependencies
Blocked by the run-state leaf and the shell leaf. Related to the ortus-9ljd and ortus-8nzp handoff fixes, whose behaviour this panel makes visible; this leaf does not depend on them landing.

## Edge cases
A path appearing in both handoff and disowned lists must render once, as disowned. A journal from a finalized run shows the candidate that was committed rather than blanking. Paths with unusual characters must not break the layout. A very large candidate must not slow the refresh.

## Plan-gap guidance
If owned and inherited paths cannot be distinguished for a given journal schema, record PLAN-GAP naming the schema version and route to planning rather than labelling them all owned.
acceptance_criteria:
## Observable criteria
- AC-1: Owned paths and their count are shown from the journal.
- AC-2: Inherited and disowned paths are shown, labelled distinctly from owned.
- AC-3: The base commit the candidate is measured against is shown.
- AC-4: A candidate longer than the region truncates with a remaining count rather than breaking the layout.

## Criterion checks
- AC-1: Run `uv run pytest tests/test_dashboard.py -k candidate_owned -q`.
- AC-2: Run `uv run pytest tests/test_dashboard.py -k candidate_inherited_and_disowned -q`.
- AC-3: Run `uv run pytest tests/test_dashboard.py -k candidate_base_commit -q`.
- AC-4: Run `uv run pytest tests/test_dashboard.py -k candidate_truncates -q`.

## Targeted tests
Run `uv run pytest tests/test_dashboard.py --test-timeout=30 --enforce-duration-budget -q`.

title: Dashboard current-action panel: what it is doing and how long it has been blocked
description:
## Objective
Distinguish a worker that is thinking from one blocked on a subprocess from one that has stalled, which is the single question `ortus tail` cannot answer.

## Behavioral context
While a worker waits on a test suite it issues one blocking tool call and then nothing. The log still grows, but only with progress heartbeats that carry no content, so `ortus tail` prints nothing for ten or twenty minutes. An operator watching that stream cannot tell a healthy suite run from a hang, and asked three times in one session whether silence meant death. Measured on one turn: 61 percent of the elapsed time was spent blocked on tests, across 29 invocations and 35 polling calls, because suites exceeding the tool cap get backgrounded and then polled.

After this change the panel names the current action, shows how long it has been current, and reports the observable evidence that work is happening underneath it.
design:
## Readiness schema
v1

## Scope
The current-action region: the latest action description, its age, an explicit blocked indicator once that age passes a threshold, and a progress signal for a running test suite.

## Non-goals
No rendering of the full agent transcript, which is what `ortus tail` is for. No parsing of pytest output. No attempt to predict completion.

## Resolved decisions
Blocked duration is the age of the latest action rather than a parsed subprocess state, because the log is the only signal available to a read-only observer and the age is exactly the quantity an operator uses to judge a stall. The pytest temp workspace count is shown as corroborating evidence when present, since it moves while the suite runs and is the signal an operator was reduced to watching by hand; it is presented as evidence rather than as a progress bar, because the total is unknown. A threshold marks the transition from thinking to blocked so the two are visually distinct.

## Concrete locations
Fill the current-action region in `src/ortus/commands/dashboard.py` from the latest-action and blocked-duration fields of the snapshot in `src/ortus/core/runstate.py`. The workspace signal is the entry count under the pytest temporary root. Cover in `tests/test_dashboard.py`.

## Compatibility constraints
An idle run shows no action rather than a stale one from a finished run. The panel must not shell out on every refresh in a way that competes with a CPU-bound grind, so the workspace count is a directory listing and nothing heavier. A missing pytest root is normal and must render as absent rather than zero.

## Ordered steps
1. Render the latest action and its age from the snapshot.
2. Mark the action as blocked once its age passes the threshold, keeping the two states visually distinct.
3. Add the pytest workspace count as corroborating evidence when the directory exists.
4. Show an idle state when no run is in flight.
5. Add tests for thinking, blocked, idle, and a missing pytest root.

## Dependencies
Blocked by the run-state leaf and the shell leaf. Related to the warnings leaf, which escalates a blocked action into a warning once it exceeds a much longer bound.

## Edge cases
A log whose latest event is a heartbeat rather than an action must keep showing the last real action, not blank. An action age computed across a timezone boundary must not go negative. A worker that finishes while the panel shows blocked must clear on the next tick. A pytest root shared by two concurrent grinds inflates the count and must be labelled as evidence rather than as this run progress.

## Plan-gap guidance
If heartbeats prove indistinguishable from real actions in the log, record PLAN-GAP with a sample and route to planning rather than showing an age that resets on every heartbeat.
acceptance_criteria:

title: Dashboard header: phase, iteration, correction budget and watchdog countdown
description:
## Objective
Show at a glance which issue is being worked, which phase it is in, how much correction budget remains, and how long before the watchdog kills the worker.

## Behavioral context
Two failures in one session were invisible until they were fatal. A worker was killed at the 1800 second cap while holding finished work, stranding a candidate that a human then recovered by hand; nothing on screen counted down to it. Separately, correction attempts were consumed silently, and escalation to a human label arrived as a surprise after the budget was already spent.

Both facts are on disk. The journal carries attempt, attempts and corrections, and the worker start time is derivable from the phase timestamps. After this change the header shows the claimed issue with its priority, the current phase, the iteration, corrections spent against the cap, and remaining watchdog headroom as a countdown.
design:
## Readiness schema
v1

## Scope
The header region: issue identity and priority, phase, iteration, corrections spent over the cap, elapsed run time, and watchdog headroom remaining.

## Non-goals
No candidate, verdict or warning content; those are their own leaves. No editing of the timeout or the budget. No projection of when the run will finish, which is not knowable.

## Resolved decisions
The watchdog headroom is rendered as remaining time rather than elapsed, because the operator decision it informs is whether to intervene before a kill. The cap is read from the run rather than assumed, since it is a flag whose default changed once already. Issue title and priority come from a read-only bd query rather than the journal, which stores only the id, and a failed query degrades to showing the id alone rather than blanking the header.

## Concrete locations
Fill the header region defined by the shell in `src/ortus/commands/dashboard.py`, reading phase, attempt, attempts, corrections and the phase timestamps from the snapshot provided by `src/ortus/core/runstate.py`. The watchdog cap is the `--worker-timeout` option declared in `src/ortus/commands/grind.py`. Cover in `tests/test_dashboard.py`.

## Compatibility constraints
An idle repository shows an idle header rather than a fabricated phase. A bd query failure must not take down the view. The countdown must never render negative; a worker past its cap is shown as overdue. Terminal width changes must not truncate the phase or the budget, which are the two fields an operator scans for.

## Ordered steps
1. Render issue id, phase, iteration and elapsed run time from the snapshot.
2. Add corrections spent over the cap, sourced from the journal.
3. Compute watchdog headroom from the worker start time and the configured cap, clamped at zero.
4. Enrich with title and priority from a read-only bd query, degrading to the id when that query fails.
5. Add tests for a live header, an idle header, an overdue watchdog and a failed bd query.

## Dependencies
Blocked by the run-state leaf and the shell leaf. Related to the warnings leaf, which surfaces the same watchdog once it has fired rather than while it approaches.

## Edge cases
A resumed run inherits a journal whose start timestamps predate this worker, so headroom must be computed from the current worker rather than the transaction. A cap of zero disables the watchdog and must render as no limit rather than as expired. A phase the model does not recognise must render verbatim rather than as unknown.

## Plan-gap guidance
If the worker start time cannot be distinguished from the transaction start time on a resume, record PLAN-GAP naming the fields available and route to planning rather than showing a countdown that is wrong.

title: Add the ortus dashboard verb with a read-only Textual shell
description:
## Objective
Add `ortus dashboard` as a Textual application whose layout hosts the panels, and make its read-only posture a property the tests enforce rather than a convention.

## Behavioral context
The dashboard observes a repository while a worker owns it. A grind computes its candidate as the dirty set minus the baseline captured at claim time, so anything written into the tree after that claim silently becomes the worker work and is judged by its verifier. That is not hypothetical: during one session an operator assistant edited two files while a worker held the tree and had to unpick its own hunks an hour later to keep the candidate coherent. A tool whose whole purpose is to watch a live run must be incapable of that.

After this change `ortus dashboard [repo]` opens a live view, refreshes without re-reading the whole log, exits cleanly on q, and cannot write to the repository, to bd, or to git.
design:
## Readiness schema
v1

## Scope
The CLI verb, the Textual application shell with the panel layout, the refresh loop driven by the run-state snapshot, and tests that enforce read-only access.

## Visual contract
Dark ground by default, with colour used to carry meaning rather than decoration: one accent for healthy motion, one for attention, one for failure, and dim text for everything static. No emoji anywhere in the interface — the audience is a terminal on a developer machine, glyph support is uneven across fonts, and a coloured rule or a filled bar reads faster than a pictograph. The intended feel is an instrument panel: box-drawing rules, monospaced alignment, and at least one element that visibly moves every refresh — the watchdog bar draining, the blocked timer counting, the workspace count climbing — so a healthy run looks alive at a glance and a stalled one is obvious by its stillness. Aesthetics are load-bearing here: an operator watched a silent tail for hours unable to tell progress from death.

## Non-goals
No panel content; each panel is its own leaf. No actions of any kind — no claiming, no unlocking, no clearing labels, no stopping a run. No fleet or multi-repo mode.

## Resolved decisions
Read-only is enforced, not documented: every bd invocation passes `--readonly --sandbox`, the same flags `check.py` already uses for its memory query, and a test asserts the argument vector of every bd call the dashboard makes. Refresh is on a timer reading the incremental snapshot rather than a filesystem watcher, because a watcher on a repo under active test churn wakes constantly for paths the dashboard does not display. The verb takes an optional repo argument defaulting to the current directory, matching every other ortus verb. Dark is the default rather than following the terminal, because the palette is chosen for contrast against a dark ground and a light terminal would wash out the accent colours; a light variant is a later concern. The no-emoji rule is asserted in a test rather than left to reviewer discipline, since a single decorative glyph added later would pass every other check.

## Concrete locations
Add `src/ortus/commands/dashboard.py` exposing a `dashboard()` typer callback, and register it in `src/ortus/cli.py` alongside the existing verbs. Add `textual` to the dependencies in `pyproject.toml`; `rich` is already present and Textual builds on it. Read state through `read_snapshot()` from `src/ortus/core/runstate.py`. Cover in a new `tests/test_dashboard.py`.

## Compatibility constraints
Adding a verb must not reorder or rename the existing ones, so `ortus --help` keeps its current listing with dashboard appended. The application must start and exit cleanly against a repository with no grind log and no journal, showing an idle state rather than an error. It must not require a bd workspace to start. Both backends are irrelevant here because the dashboard reads state rather than launching anything.

## Ordered steps
1. Add the textual dependency and confirm the suite still collects.
2. Add the verb and register it, with an optional repo argument defaulting to the current directory.
3. Build the application shell with named placeholder regions matching the agreed layout: header, current action, candidate, verdict, warnings.
4. Drive refresh from the incremental snapshot on a timer, carrying the offset between ticks.
5. Add a test asserting every bd invocation carries `--readonly --sandbox`, and a test asserting the dashboard performs no write to the repository during a refresh cycle.
6. Add a test that the application starts and exits against an idle repository.

## Dependencies
Blocked by the run-state leaf, which provides the snapshot the shell refreshes from. Blocks every panel leaf, which fill the regions this shell defines.

## Edge cases
A repository with no logs directory must show idle rather than raise. A terminal too small for the layout must degrade rather than crash. A grind that starts after the dashboard is already open must be picked up on the next tick. A grind that ends while the dashboard is open must show a terminal state rather than freezing on the last frame.

## Plan-gap guidance
If enforcing read-only bd access proves impossible for some query the panels need, record PLAN-GAP naming the query and route to planning rather than dropping the flags.
acceptance_criteria:
## Observable criteria
- AC-1: `ortus dashboard` is registered and appears in the CLI help without disturbing the existing verb order.
- AC-2: Every bd invocation the dashboard makes carries the read-only and sandbox flags.
- AC-3: A refresh cycle performs no write to the repository worktree.
- AC-4: The application starts and exits cleanly against a repository with no grind log.
- AC-5: The rendered interface contains no emoji, defaults to a dark theme, and carries at least one element that changes between refreshes.

## Criterion checks
- AC-1: Run `uv run pytest tests/test_cli_verbs.py -q`.
- AC-2: Run `uv run pytest tests/test_dashboard.py -k readonly_bd_flags -q`.
- AC-3: Run `uv run pytest tests/test_dashboard.py -k performs_no_writes -q`.
- AC-4: Run `uv run pytest tests/test_dashboard.py -k starts_idle -q`.
- AC-5: Run `uv run pytest tests/test_dashboard.py -k visual_contract -q`.

## Targeted tests
Run `uv run pytest tests/test_dashboard.py tests/test_cli_verbs.py --test-timeout=30 --enforce-duration-budget -q`.

title: Derive a run state model from the journal and an incremental log tail
description:
## Objective
Provide one read-only model of a grind run that every dashboard panel reads, built from the transaction journal plus an incrementally tailed log.

## Behavioral context
The facts an operator needs are already on disk but scattered. `logs/grind-transaction.json` carries issue_id, phase, attempt, attempts, corrections, candidate_paths, handoff_paths, unrelated_paths, baseline_paths, base_head, candidate_hash, plan_gap_routed and per-phase timestamps. The grind log carries what the worker is doing right now. Nothing joins them.

Two properties matter more than the join. The log reached 1.5 MB in a single session, so re-reading it on every refresh would burn CPU on a host already spending most of a turn on tests. And the log interleaves two writers: ortus emits plain lines such as `iter 1: worker TIMEOUT after 1800s`, while the agent emits JSON whose content quotes that same vocabulary whenever a worker edits the recovery code. A reader that cannot separate them invents failures, as a stopgap script did.

After this change a caller gets a snapshot of the run — phase, current action, how long the current action has been blocked, candidate composition, correction budget, warnings — refreshed by reading only bytes appended since the last call.
design:
## Readiness schema
v1

## Scope
A core module exposing a run-state snapshot and an incremental tailer: parse the journal, follow the log from a byte offset, classify each line by writer, and derive phase, latest action, blocked duration, and warning counts.

## Non-goals
No rendering, no Textual, no CLI verb; those are separate leaves. No writes of any kind. No bd or git access — panels that need those query them separately, so this module stays a pure function of two files and is testable without a workspace.

## Resolved decisions
Writer classification keys on whether a line parses as JSON: ortus writes plain text into the log and the agent writes JSON, so a failed parse identifies an ortus line. Guessing by substring is what produced the phantom timeouts, and any future reader inherits the same trap unless the rule lives in one place. The tailer returns a new offset with each snapshot and the caller passes it back, so the module holds no file handle and a truncated or rotated log is detected by a shrinking size rather than by an open descriptor going stale. Journal absence is a valid state meaning no transaction is in flight, not an error.

## Concrete locations
Add `src/ortus/core/runstate.py` exposing a frozen snapshot dataclass and a `read_snapshot()` that accepts a repo path and a byte offset. Parse the journal written by `JournalStore` in `src/ortus/core/transaction.py`, whose fields are listed above. Phase vocabulary must match what `src/ortus/commands/grind.py` writes. Cover in a new `tests/test_core_runstate.py`.

## Compatibility constraints
The module must not import Textual, so the model is usable headless and in tests. It must tolerate a journal written by an older schema by ignoring unknown fields and defaulting absent ones. It must never open the repo for writing, and must work while a grind holds the flock. A partially written log line, which happens because the log is appended live, must not raise.

## Ordered steps
1. Define the snapshot dataclass covering issue, phase, attempt, corrections, candidate composition, latest action, blocked duration, and warning counts.
2. Parse the journal into that shape, defaulting every field so an absent or older journal is valid.
3. Implement the incremental tailer returning parsed events plus the next offset, detecting truncation by size.
4. Classify each line by writer and count warnings only from ortus lines.
5. Derive the latest action and how long it has been the latest, which is the blocked duration.
6. Add tests including a mixed log whose agent content quotes the warning vocabulary, asserting zero warnings.

## Dependencies
No issue dependency; this is the root of the epic. Blocks every panel leaf and the replay leaf, which all read this snapshot.

## Edge cases
A log whose final line is half written must be skipped and re-read once complete. A log that shrinks between calls indicates rotation and must reset the offset rather than seek past the end. A journal present with no log, or a log with no journal, are both valid. A run that has finalized leaves a journal whose phase is terminal, which the model must report rather than treat as live. Timestamps are UTC in the log and local in some journal fields, so the blocked duration must not go negative.

## Plan-gap guidance
If the log turns out to interleave writers within a single line, so JSON parsing cannot separate them, record PLAN-GAP with a sample line and route to planning rather than reintroducing substring heuristics.
acceptance_criteria:
## Observable criteria
- AC-1: A snapshot reports issue, phase, attempt, correction count and candidate composition from a journal fixture.
- AC-2: A second call with the returned offset parses only bytes appended since the first.
- AC-3: Agent content quoting the warning vocabulary produces zero warnings, while an ortus line produces one.
- AC-4: A truncated final line, a rotated log, and an absent journal are each handled without raising.

## Criterion checks
- AC-1: Run `uv run pytest tests/test_core_runstate.py -k snapshot_from_journal -q`.
- AC-2: Run `uv run pytest tests/test_core_runstate.py -k incremental_offset -q`.
- AC-3: Run `uv run pytest tests/test_core_runstate.py -k warning_writer_discrimination -q`.
- AC-4: Run `uv run pytest tests/test_core_runstate.py -k degraded_inputs -q`.

title: ortus dashboard: one live view of a grind run
description:
## Objective
Give an operator a single screen that answers, without reading a log: is the run alive, what is it doing, is it about to fail, and where is the time going.

## Behavioral context
Watching a grind currently means stitching together three surfaces, none of which answers the question alone. `ortus tail` renders agent events, so while a worker blocks on a test suite it prints nothing at all and a healthy run is indistinguishable from a hang; an operator asked three times in one session whether a silent tail meant a dead process. The grind stdout shows phase transitions but no progress inside a phase. Everything else lives in places nobody watches: the journal at `logs/grind-transaction.json`, bd issue state, the git worktree, verifier reports under `logs/grind-transactions/`, and pytest temp directories.

A stopgap shell script written during that session covered the gap and immediately demonstrated the central hazard: it grepped the grind log for `worker TIMEOUT` and `correction escalation` and reported seven phantom timeouts, because the worker under observation was editing the recovery code that contains those strings. Ortus writes plain lines into that log and the agent writes JSON; anything that reads the log must tell them apart.

After this epic `ortus dashboard` replaces all three surfaces with one read-only Textual view, live or replayed over a finished run.
design:
Umbrella container; leaves carry the readiness v1 packets.

Operator decisions, settled before decomposition: single-run deep view rather than a fleet table, strictly read-only, live plus postmortem replay, and sequenced behind the handoff fixes that unblock a downstream repository.
acceptance_criteria: Epic closes when every child leaf is closed.
close_reason: milestone rollover: all child issues closed

title: Make tail smoke test terminate the full subprocess group

The descendant tail process can retain the pipe file descriptors, causing communicate to wait indefinitely after both configured timeouts. This caused the local full-suite verification to hang after the seeded tail content test began.
design: Launch the smoke subprocess in its own session or process group and terminate the group on timeout, mirroring the production runner cleanup. Preserve cross-platform behavior on supported Linux and macOS. The test must retain its assertion that seeded log content is flushed before termination.
acceptance_criteria: The tail smoke test finishes within a bounded time on Linux and macOS even when ortus tail is still polling. Timeout cleanup leaves no uv or ortus tail descendant and communicate returns without hanging on inherited pipes. The seeded log content assertion still passes. Tests covering the changed surface must pass; CI catches regressions elsewhere.

title: grind: per-iteration worker watchdog to auto-recover from stuck workers
description:
ortus grind drives the queue via a subprocess-per-task `claude -p /goal` loop, blocking on the worker subprocess until it exits. orphan-policy (revert/escalate) and idle-sleep only run AFTER the worker exits. So a worker that is stuck-but-alive hangs the ENTIRE loop indefinitely with no automatic recovery — the only fix is a human manually killing the `claude -p /goal` process.

Observed twice in a single real build run (prdpad):
1. Cancel-loop: the worker picked/hallucinated a non-existent bd id and put the failing `bd show <id>` in a PARALLEL tool batch alongside other calls. The harness cancels the whole batch when one call errors, so it thrashed indefinitely (every tool result: "Cancelled: parallel tool call Bash(bd show ...) errored"). CPU climbing, never exits. (Note: also a violation of the prompt's own "bd must be its own unwrapped call" rule — but the loop should be resilient to it.)
2. Hung-after-close: the worker successfully closed its issue (bd close OK, committed + pushed), but then did NOT end the session per the prompt; it kept issuing post-close `bd` commands (one appeared to hang on dolt) and ran ~25 min, blocking the next iteration.

In both cases bd state showed the truth (issue still in_progress, or already closed), but grind couldn't act on it because the worker never returned. A manual `kill <worker_pid>` let grind immediately recover (orphan-revert in case 1; counted the close + advanced in case 2).
design:
Add a worker watchdog to the grind orchestrator, surfaced as CLI options:
- `--worker-timeout <secs>`: hard cap on a single iteration's worker; on exceed, SIGTERM then SIGKILL the worker (and its process group), then run the existing post-iteration logic (bd-state delta + orphan-policy). Default off or a generous value (e.g. 900s).
- `--worker-stall-timeout <secs>` (optional, smarter): kill the worker if there's been no progress for N secs, where "progress" = a change in `bd` state OR the worker's stream-json log mtime advancing. This distinguishes a legitimately long task (log actively advancing) from a true hang.

Implementation notes:
- Run the worker with a timeout (e.g. subprocess timeout / a watchdog thread), kill the whole process group so child build/bd/dolt processes die too.
- After kill, treat exactly like a normal exit: recompute bd-state delta; if an issue moved to closed, count it; if claimed-but-unclosed, apply --orphan-policy. Log the timeout kill explicitly (e.g. "iter N: worker TIMEOUT after <secs>, killed (rc=143)").
- Ensure the kill releases any dolt locks the worker held (relevant to case 2).
acceptance_criteria:
DONE WHEN:
1. A grind worker that exceeds --worker-timeout (or stalls past --worker-stall-timeout) is automatically SIGTERM/SIGKILLed by the orchestrator without human intervention.
2. After the kill, grind applies normal recovery: orphan-policy on a claimed-but-unclosed issue, or counts the close if bd state already shows it closed, then spawns the next iteration.
3. The timeout kill is logged distinctly in the grind log.
TEST: with a synthetic worker that sleeps/loops forever (and one that closes its issue then hangs), confirm grind kills it within the timeout, logs it, recovers via bd-state + orphan-policy, and proceeds to the next iteration — all hands-off.
close_reason: Add --worker-timeout watchdog to grind: hard-caps each iteration's worker, SIGTERM/SIGKILLs its process group on exceed, logs TIMEOUT distinctly, then runs normal bd-state+orphan-policy recovery

title: ortus tail: also follow plan logs (extend PREFIXES; reconcile timestamped vs fixed-name)
description:
`ortus tail` currently follows only `grind-*.log`, `goal-*.log`, and `ralph-*.log` (see `src/ortus/commands/tail.py:PREFIXES`). Plan logs are invisible to it, so an operator watching grind via `ortus tail` will not see plan activity.

**Filename mismatch to reconcile:** `ortus plan` writes to a FIXED filename `<repo>/logs/plan.log` (no timestamp), unlike grind/goal/ralph which use `<verb>-YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS.log`. This has two consequences:

1. The current `PREFIXES = ("grind-", "goal-", "ralph-")` tuple won't match `plan.log` — adding a `plan-` prefix wouldn't help.
2. The fixed name means each new `ortus plan` invocation overwrites (or truncates) the prior plan log — no history.

The implementer should pick one consistent shape:

- **(a)** Change `ortus plan` to write `plan-YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS.log`. Then add `"plan-"` to `PREFIXES` and the existing tail logic just works. Bonus: preserves plan history across runs (matches grind's pattern).
- **(b)** Keep `plan.log` fixed and special-case it in `tail.py` (match either `plan.log` or `plan-*.log`). Smaller change, but preserves the historical-overwrite footgun.

Recommend **(a)** — small change to plan, consistency win across all four log producers, no per-verb special-casing needed in tail.

**Out of scope:**
- Interactive vs non-interactive tail modes (covered elsewhere).
- Per-verb log retention/rotation policy (separate concern if it ever becomes one).
acceptance_criteria:
**Approach (a) — change plan to timestamp + extend tail's PREFIXES.**

1. In `src/ortus/commands/plan.py`, change the log-path construction from:
   ```python
   log_path = log_dir / "plan.log"
   ```
   to a timestamped version:
   ```python
   ts = datetime.now().strftime("%Y%m%d-%H%M%S")
   log_path = log_dir / f"plan-{ts}.log"
   ```
   (mirror whatever timestamp helper grind already uses — there's likely a shared util; don't duplicate.)

2. In `src/ortus/commands/tail.py`, add `"plan-"` to the PREFIXES tuple. Update the module docstring's `{grind,goal,ralph}` glob mention to include `plan`.

3. Verify:
   - `ortus plan <repo> <prd>` writes `<repo>/logs/plan-<ts>.log`.
   - `ortus tail <repo>` picks up that file in its rotation/listing.
   - Re-running `ortus plan` creates a NEW file (not overwriting the prior one) — confirm via `ls logs/`.

**Tests:**
- `tests/test_tail.py` (or a new tail-prefix test): assert PREFIXES contains `"plan-"`.
- `tests/test_plan.py`: assert the log file produced matches `plan-*.log` glob with a timestamp component.
- Per ortus-4ni7: targeted tests only (`uv run pytest tests/test_plan.py tests/test_tail.py`); skip the full suite.

**If choosing approach (b) instead:** justify in the issue's design field why the fixed-name footgun is acceptable; tail.py changes become slightly larger (regex or two-prefix match).

Standard close: commit on main (small change, low blast radius); `git push`. Commit message must not contain the protected term.
close_reason: plan writes timestamped plan-<ts>.log; tail PREFIXES includes plan-; preserves plan-log history

title: ortus init: restore --package-manager, --framework, --linter flags (driven by --project-type)
description:
The copier-era `copier.yaml` collected three conditional template variables that the Python rewrite of `ortus init` dropped entirely. Restore them as CLI flags with the same per-language conditional choices and defaults copier used.

**Scope (operator-confirmed): exactly these three flags. Nothing else from the copier list is in scope.**

| Flag | Choices (gated on `--project-type`) | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `--package-manager` | python: uv/pip/none · typescript: bun/npm/pnpm/yarn/none · go: gomod/none · rust: cargo/none · polyglot: none | per-language: python=uv, typescript=npm, go=gomod, rust=cargo, polyglot=none |
| `--framework` | python: fastapi/flask/django/none · typescript: nextjs/express/none · go: gin/none · rust: actix/axum/none · polyglot: none | none (operator opts in) |
| `--linter` | python: ruff/none · typescript: eslint/none · go: golangci/none · rust: clippy/none · polyglot: none | per-language: python=ruff, typescript=eslint, go=golangci, rust=clippy, polyglot=none |

The conditional shape comes directly from the `package_manager`, `framework`, and `linter` blocks in the historical `copier.yaml` (still reachable in git history at the last commit that contained it; reference, don't re-vendor).

**Naming note (out of scope here but worth flagging):** the existing `--project-type` flag's values (`python|typescript|go|rust|polyglot`) are actually what copier called `language_profile` (sandbox allowedDomains). The "what kind of project" axis (api/cli/library/fullstack from copier's `project_type`) does not exist in the new CLI and is intentionally not being added per operator direction. Operator OK'd "keep the project-type driving language." If the misnomer becomes confusing later, file a separate rename issue.

**Explicitly NOT in scope (operator already trimmed):**

- `project_name`, `project_description` — derived from target dir
- `author_name`, `author_email` — defer to `git config user.name` / `user.email`
- `github_username`
- `license`
- `has_prd`, `prd_path` — covered by separate `ortus plan` flow
acceptance_criteria:
**Part 1 — add the three flags to `ortus init`.**

In `src/ortus/commands/init.py`, add three typer options:

1. `--package-manager TEXT` (validation: must be one of the per-`--project-type` choices listed in the description, OR `none`)
2. `--framework TEXT` (same validation pattern; defaults to `none` for all languages)
3. `--linter TEXT` (same pattern, with per-language defaults)

Resolution order for each flag:
1. CLI value if explicitly passed
2. Per-language default (from the table)
3. Reject with a helpful error if the value isn't valid for the current `--project-type`

Validation error format follows existing ortus patterns (e.g. `ortus check`'s pass/fail style).

**Part 2 — propagate to the template render context.**

In `src/ortus/core/init_render.py` (or wherever RenderContext lives), add the three new fields to `RenderContext`. Templates that reference `package_manager`, `framework`, `linter` (some `.jinja` files under `template/` likely still do from the copier era) should pick up the values automatically. Audit `template/**/*.jinja` for these var names; update any that became broken when the rewrite dropped the inputs.

**Part 3 — tests.**

- Add unit tests in `tests/test_init.py` (or a new `tests/test_init_flags.py`) covering:
  - Default resolution per language (e.g. `ortus init <tmpdir> --project-type=python` → package_manager defaults to `uv`)
  - Explicit override (`--package-manager=pip`)
  - Invalid combination (e.g. `--project-type=python --package-manager=bun` → error)
- Per ortus-4ni7 convention: run **targeted tests only** (`uv run pytest tests/test_init*.py`), not the full suite — CI handles the matrix.

**Part 4 — help text.**

`ortus init --help` should show the three new flags with one-line descriptions. No need to enumerate all per-language choices in the help text; mention "choices depend on --project-type" and let `--help` for a specific verb be terse.

**Out of scope:**
- Interactive prompts when stdin is a TTY (file separately if wanted — related to ortus-jni5/ortus-s60a progress-output work)
- The other 9 copier prompts the operator explicitly dropped
- Renaming `--project-type` to `--language-profile`

Standard close: commit on main (small additive change, low blast radius); `git push`. Commit message must not contain the protected term.
close_reason: Added --package-manager/--framework/--linter flags to ortus init with per-project-type choices, defaults, and validation; threaded through RenderContext; new tests cover defaults, overrides, invalid combos, help text

title: grind-prompt: Verification step pushes full-suite runs; should prefer targeted tests + rely on CI for the full sweep
description:
**Observed cost:** the inner claude agent in `ortus grind` keeps running `uv run pytest` (the full 231-test suite, ~4m40s) as the Verification step for every issue, regardless of blast radius. For small/cosmetic changes (UX tweak in `ortus init`, doc edits, single-file refactors) this is ~5 minutes of blocking work per task with little marginal safety.

**Root cause, two layers:**

1. `src/ortus/prompts/grind-prompt.md` step 6 ("Verify") and the Verification section both say to "run tests, linting, and builds." Agents read this conservatively and default to the full suite.
2. Acceptance criteria writers (including this session's recent issues like ortus-jni5) explicitly say `uv run pytest must pass`. That convention forces the full run even when targeted tests would suffice.

**Preferred shape (operator direction):**

Trust the **GitHub Actions matrix** (`.github/workflows/test.yml` — Linux+macOS, Python 3.10/3.11/3.12) as the comprehensive-coverage gate. Inside a grind iteration, run the *targeted* subset that exercises the changed surface. Full-suite breakage in unrelated areas is CI's job to catch — the agent should commit + push, then let CI surface anything missed.

This trades a small risk of a red CI run for a roughly 10x speedup in per-task wall time, and recovers grind budget for actually making progress through the queue.

**Out of scope:** pre-commit hooks (different surface), linting policy (separate concern).
acceptance_criteria:
**Part 1 — update `src/ortus/prompts/grind-prompt.md`.**

Reword the Verify step (step 6) and the Verification section to:
1. **Prefer targeted tests.** Recommend running pytest scoped to the files/directories actually touched by the issue (e.g. `uv run pytest tests/test_init.py tests/test_init_render.py` when only `init` changed). The agent should reason from the affected paths to the relevant test files.
2. **Explicitly defer full-suite coverage to CI.** Add a one-line note: "The GitHub Actions matrix at `.github/workflows/test.yml` runs the full suite across all supported platforms on push; do not rerun it locally for confidence."
3. **Keep a backpressure clause for high-blast-radius changes.** If the change touches `src/ortus/core/` (shared infrastructure) or `src/ortus/prompts/` (affects every future iteration), the full local `uv run pytest` is still appropriate. Otherwise, targeted is the default.

**Part 2 — update AC-writing convention (template/example) so future bd issues don't re-introduce the regression.**

The right wording for ACs going forward is "**tests covering the changed surface must pass; CI will catch regressions elsewhere**" — not "uv run pytest must pass." Either add a sentence to AGENTS.md (or a docs/ section) noting this convention, OR add a short comment block at the top of `grind-prompt.md` reminding agents to interpret AC test instructions in scope.

**Part 3 — verify.**

Run targeted tests: `uv run pytest tests/test_grind_prompt_content.py` (which asserts grind-prompt structure) and any tests under `tests/test_grind*.py` that exercise the verify-step parsing. Skip the full suite per the new convention this issue is establishing.

Standard close: commit on main (small prompt edit, low blast radius); `git push`. Commit message must not contain the protected term.
close_reason: Reworded grind-prompt Verify/Verification to prefer targeted tests + defer full-suite to CI matrix; added AC convention to AGENTS.md; grind test cohort (70 tests) green

title: grind orchestrator should exclude --label=human from bd ready
description:
The ortus-grind shell currently surfaces issues labeled 'human' (e.g. ortus-tper) to agent loops, even though they require manual human action and cannot be agent-completed. Three consecutive grind sessions all picked up ortus-tper, did the same re-verification, and reverted/closed without progress.

Fix: in ortus/grind.sh (or wherever ready-queue selection happens), filter out issues with the 'human' label before handing them to /goal sessions. Equivalently, teach 'bd ready' to honor a default --exclude-label set, or pass --exclude-label=human at the orchestrator layer.

Reference: ortus-tper was closed in grind session #3 (2026-05-17) with reasoning documenting this loop.
close_reason: grind orchestrator now filters EXCLUDED_LABELS=('human',) from open/in_progress snapshots so human-only queues drain instead of spinning; bd CLI gains exclude_labels kwargs on count_by_status + in_progress_ids

title: Configure PyPI trusted publishing for who/ortus (publish-pypi job failed on v0.1.0)
description:
The v0.1.0 release workflow (run 25997780366) succeeded for build + github-release jobs (release exists with install.sh), but publish-pypi failed with:

  invalid-publisher: valid token, but no corresponding publisher
  sub: repo:who/ortus:environment:pypi
  repository: who/ortus
  workflow: .github/workflows/release.yml
  environment: pypi

PyPI has no trusted publisher configured for this project. Two-step fix:

1. On PyPI, create a project (or claim 'ortus' if available) and add a trusted publisher with:
   - Owner: who
   - Repository: ortus
   - Workflow: release.yml
   - Environment: pypi
2. On GitHub, ensure the 'pypi' environment exists on the repo (Settings -> Environments). Add protection rules if desired (e.g., required reviewers).

Until configured, every v* tag push will leave the workflow in a 'failure' state (github-release still succeeds independently).
acceptance_criteria:
1. PyPI trusted publisher record exists for who/ortus, workflow release.yml, environment pypi.
2. 'pypi' environment exists on the GitHub repo.
3. On the next v* tag push, publish-pypi job completes successfully and the package appears on https://pypi.org/project/ortus/.
4. Decide what to do about the orphaned v0.1.0 (republish as v0.1.1 once trusted-publishing is configured, or leave v0.1.0 as GitHub-release-only).
notes:
[2026-05-17 grind session #2] Re-verified: (1) The 'pypi' GitHub Environment DOES already exist on who/ortus (gh api repos/who/ortus/environments returns it, created 2026-05-17, no protection rules) — acceptance criterion #2 is already satisfied. (2) PyPI trusted publisher still appears missing (curl pypi.org/pypi/ortus/json returns Not Found; Cloudflare-challenged HTML page prevents richer probe) — criterion #1 still requires manual action by the PyPI account owner. (3) Criteria #3 and #4 depend on #1. Re-flagging for human; reverting to open.
[2026-05-17 grind session #3] Encountered again by an agent loop; still blocked on human (PyPI trusted-publisher record on pypi.org). No agent-completable acceptance criteria remain — root fix is to make the grind ready-queue exclude --label=human so agents don't re-pick this. Reverting to open.
close_reason: Agent loop cannot complete — requires PyPI account owner to register trusted publisher at pypi.org (Owner=who, Repository=ortus, Workflow=release.yml, Environment=pypi). GitHub-side pypi Environment already exists (criterion #2 met). Re-open or file a follow-up when PyPI is configured, then verify criteria #3-#4 on next v* tag push. Closing to prevent recycling through agent ready-queue (3rd grind session). Root fix: have grind/bd-ready exclude --label=human.

title: Cut initial v0.1.0 release so /releases/latest/download/install.sh resolves
description:
Follow-up to ortus-g54s (README install.sh URL 404 — short-term unbreak landed via raw.githubusercontent.com).

The README now points at `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/who/ortus/main/install.sh` (always-current, follows main HEAD). That works today but isn't the canonical install path documented in the PRD (prd/PRD-ortus-global-cli.md FR-028: `releases/latest/download/install.sh`).

To make the canonical URL resolve, cut the initial release:

1. Tag v0.1.0 from main: `git tag v0.1.0 && git push origin v0.1.0`
2. The release workflow at `.github/workflows/release.yml` should fire automatically on v* tag push.
3. Verify with `gh release view v0.1.0` — install.sh should be attached as an asset.
4. Verify the canonical URL resolves: `curl -fsSL https://github.com/who/ortus/releases/latest/download/install.sh | head -5`.
5. Optionally revert the README change in ortus-g54s back to the canonical `/releases/latest/...` form so the documented install path matches what's published.

Why P2 and not P1: the immediate user-facing breakage is fixed (raw URL works). This is the proper long-term fix that aligns the README, PRD, and CI release pipeline.
acceptance_criteria:
1. `git tag v0.1.0 && git push origin v0.1.0` triggers the release workflow.
2. `gh release view v0.1.0` shows install.sh attached as an asset.
3. `curl -fsSL https://github.com/who/ortus/releases/latest/download/install.sh | head -5` returns the install script (not 404).
4. (Optional) README reverted to canonical /releases/latest/download/install.sh URL in both Quick Start and Install sections.
notes:
Blocked on human decision before release tag is pushed.

Issue's steps assume pyproject.toml is at version 0.1.0, but it is currently 0.1.0.dev0. Pushing v0.1.0 tag now would:

1. Trigger publish-pypi job that publishes 'ortus-0.1.0.dev0' to PyPI (permanent — version strings on PyPI are immutable, even .dev pre-releases consume the slot).
2. Create GitHub release v0.1.0 whose attached wheel is named ortus-0.1.0.dev0-py3-none-any.whl, mismatching the tag.

Two paths forward — human should pick:

(a) Bump version: edit pyproject.toml 'version = "0.1.0"', commit, push, then tag. (Recommended — matches the issue intent.)
(b) Defer the release and let me unrelease the trusted-publishing slot first.

Additional check the human should confirm before unblocking:
- Is the 'pypi' GitHub Actions environment configured with trusted publishing to PyPI? If not, publish-pypi will fail (github-release will still succeed since they share only 'needs: build', so acceptance criteria 1-3 can still be met).
close_reason: v0.1.0 release cut: tag pushed, workflow ran, GitHub release published with install.sh+wheel+sdist, canonical /releases/latest/download/install.sh URL resolves (302 to asset), README reverted to canonical URL. PyPI publish step failed (trusted-publishing not configured on PyPI) — tracked separately as follow-up.

title: README.md: restructure Quick Start (beads-style, install in code block + structural Note) + delete duplicate mechanism paragraph
description:
Two coupled changes to the README opener.

**1. Restructure Quick Start in the beads style** — currently the Quick Start is a single bash block that uses absolute paths (`~/code/myproj`) and lacks the install line up top. The beads pattern at https://github.com/gastownhall/beads/blob/v1.0.4/README.md is a single consolidated code block that includes the install one-liner, uses `cd your-project && <verb> .` everywhere, and is followed by a bold **Note:** clarifying the key conceptual point. This issue brings ortus's Quick Start to that shape.

**2. Delete the duplicate mechanism paragraph** — the README opener currently has two paragraphs after the etymology line: the action-oriented headline (shipped by ortus-8bot) and a redundant mechanism paragraph (shipped by ortus-vk86 before it was superseded). The mechanism paragraph restates `/goal` and the Ralph Loop concept already covered by the headline. Delete it.

**Operator decisions encoded in the AC:**
- Install section stays as-is (long-form reference below Quick Start; some duplication of the curl line is acceptable, matches beads).
- Note callout is structural only ("global CLI, install once, doesn't get cloned into your project, only adds these per-project files") — does NOT re-state /goal or Ralph Loop (already in the headline).
- Path style: `cd your-project && <verb> .` (beads-style; single cd then `.` everywhere).
- Keep `ortus check` in the Quick Start (operator's call — opposite of beads, which omits it).
- Keep the `--tasks 5` bounded grind example in Quick Start.
- Drop the `-c "auth migration ships cleanly"` bounded grind example from Quick Start (discoverable via `ortus grind --help`; was distracting in the main demo).
- No emoji on the section header.
- Quick Start header stays `## Quick start` (existing lowercase-s capitalization).
acceptance_criteria:
Two exact edits to README.md. No other changes.

**Edit 1: Delete the duplicate mechanism paragraph.**

Delete the entire paragraph (and its trailing blank line) currently sitting between the headline and the `## Install` header:

```
Ortus uses Claude Code's `/goal` directive as the per-task completion signal: each bd-tracked task runs in a fresh `claude -p` subprocess, and `/goal`'s managed Stop hook judges when the task is done from the conversation itself rather than from sentinel strings. The loop shape is inspired by the Ralph Loop concept — one task, one fresh window, drive the queue to zero.
```

After the deletion, the README opener should read (etymology → headline → `## Install`):

```
*Ortus* (Latin: "rising, origin, birth") — the point from which something springs into being.

Ortus autonomously closes a backlog of bd-tracked issues using Claude Code, one fresh subprocess per task. Inspired by the Ralph Loop concept: fresh window per task, drive the queue to zero, no context drift.

## Install
```

**Edit 2: Replace the entire `## Quick start` section.**

Find the existing section, which begins with `## Quick start` and currently contains a single bash code block ending with the `-c "auth migration ships cleanly"` line. Replace EVERYTHING from `## Quick start` (inclusive) through the closing ``` of that bash block (inclusive) with this:

````
## Quick start

```bash
# Install Ortus globally (system-wide — don't add ortus as a project dependency)
curl -fsSL https://github.com/who/ortus/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sh

# Bootstrap YOUR project
cd your-project
ortus init .

# Verify prereqs (bd, claude, jq, hooks, sandbox)
ortus check .

# Decompose a PRD into bd issues
ortus plan . path/to/feature.md

# Or run the idea→interview→PRD→tasks flow with no PRD path
ortus plan .

# Drive the bd queue to zero — one task per fresh /goal subprocess
ortus grind .

# Bounded: stop after N tasks
ortus grind . --tasks 5
```

**Note:** Ortus is a global CLI you install once and use everywhere. You don't clone this repository into your project — `ortus init` only adds a small set of per-project files (`.beads/`, `.claude/settings.json`, `AGENTS.md`, `.ortusrc`, `.gitignore`) to an existing directory. It is not a Python dependency.
````

Constraints:
- The `## Install` section above and the `## The eight verbs` section below must remain UNTOUCHED (only Quick Start gets replaced).
- Do NOT add an emoji to the `## Quick start` header.
- Do NOT change the section's capitalization (`Quick start`, lowercase 's', matches existing).
- The `-c "..."` form is intentionally absent from Quick Start; do NOT add it back. It remains discoverable via `ortus grind --help` and the verb table.
- Standard close: commit on the current feature branch, `bd dolt push`, `git push`. Do NOT push to main.
close_reason: README opener cleaned: removed duplicate mechanism paragraph; Quick Start restructured beads-style with install one-liner + cd-then-dot paths + structural Note callout

title: scripts/ + src/: strip PRD § refs per project principle (keep intent inline)
description:
Apply the Ortus principle (bd memory `ortus-principle-do-not-reference-prd-sections-e`) to code: PRD § refs in comments, docstrings, and runtime output strings must go. PRD section numbers rot as specs evolve and add noise for readers without the spec context. Preserve the operative facts (threshold values, defaults, the actual decision) inline so the reader still has the *why*.

title: grind-prompt.md: delete step 10 (Compact + reorient); renumber step 11 → 10
description:
grind-prompt.md step 10 ("**Compact + reorient**") instructs the model to run `/compact` then re-read AGENTS.md "before the next task begins." This is meaningless under ortus grind's actual execution model.

**Why it's a no-op:**

ortus grind runs one task per fresh `claude -p` subprocess (subprocess-per-task — see ortus-3ico). `/compact` is an *in-session* shrinkage operation: it summarizes the current process's prior messages and replaces them inline within the same claude process. It does NOT write any hand-off artifact for the next process.

Since step 11 (Exit) immediately follows step 10, the in-memory savings from compaction are discarded a beat later when the process terminates. The next grind iteration spawns a brand-new claude process that has no access to any summary the prior process generated.

The same was true of `ralph.sh`, which also ran one fresh `claude -p` per iteration (`while true; do claude -p "$(cat prompts/ralph-prompt.md)" ...; done`). The step has never been meaningful in any shipped Ortus loop.

**Principle this codifies:**

Every Ortus claude invocation runs with a fresh context window populated by good specs + bd state + codegraph activity reads. Persistence belongs in bd comments, codegraph v1 blocks, and git — not model-generated summary chains.

See bd memory: `ortus-design-principle-no-compaction-compaction-is-a`.

**Scope notes:**

- `ralph-prompt.md` has the same step but is NOT in scope here — it is slated for deletion in Phase 5 (ortus-dcr4).
- Related: ortus-ylv1 (port content from ralph-prompt → grind-prompt) should strip any `/compact` references during the port rather than carry them across.

**Out of scope (separate issue if desired):** add a one-line guardrail in AGENTS.md noting that Ortus does not use `/compact`.

3. No other changes to grind-prompt.md.
4. ralph-prompt.md is NOT modified.
5. Run `pytest` (and any other repo test commands defined in pyproject.toml or Makefile); confirm no regression.
6. Standard close sequence: commit on the current feature branch, `bd dolt push`, `git push`. Do NOT push to main.

title: Port richer per-task content from legacy ralph-prompt.md into grind-prompt.md (Python source of truth)
description:
**TL;DR**: The legacy bash-era `ortus/prompts/ralph-prompt.md` (23KB) contains substantial per-task content — orient/select/claim/investigate/implement/verify/log/close/commit/push instructions, subagent strategy guidance, Issue Plan JSON schema, completion-comment format with CodeGraph v1 block, etc. — that was authored over many iterations and reflects hard-won operator preferences. The Python-side `src/ortus/prompts/grind-prompt.md` is a newer, narrower file that doesn't carry all of that content. Operator wants ralph-prompt.md to remain the *intellectual source of truth* for what claude should do per task, while `ortus grind` (Python) is the *execution vehicle*. Port the missing content from ralph-prompt.md into grind-prompt.md so the Python orchestrator runs with the full instruction set the bash era was using.

**Why this matters:**
- **Quality of every grind iteration.** Each iteration claude runs is driven by grind-prompt.md. If grind-prompt is leaner than ralph-prompt, every iteration is operating with less guidance — degraded subagent strategy, missing completion-comment structure, etc.
- **Pre-Phase-5 readiness.** Phase 5 (sod1.*) will eventually delete `ortus/prompts/ralph-prompt.md`. If grind-prompt doesn't carry forward all the content first, that deletion silently loses ~23KB of accumulated wisdom.
- **Operator-recognized preference**: ralph-prompt is the spec the operator was iterating on for months. The Python pivot rewrote the per-task body from scratch but didn't carry forward all the accumulated rules. This task closes that gap.

**What stays the same and what changes between the two prompts:**

Same (port verbatim):
- The per-task loop body: orient → select → claim → investigate → implement → verify → log → close → commit/push
- Subagent Strategy table (Reads/Writes/Validation/Reasoning rows; "main = scheduler only" rule)
- Issue Plan JSON schema (`has_enough_info`, `missing`, `implementation_steps`, `verification_steps`, `closure_reason`)
- Completion comment format (`**Changes**:`, `**Verification**:`, optional `**CodeGraph v1**:` block)
- CodeGraph integration steps (1.5, 4, 6.5, 7, 7.5) gated on `codegraph_available`
- "Important Rules" section (one task per invocation, no partial work, no placeholders, verify acceptance criteria, descriptive commits)
- Steering section (upstream = issue is spec; downstream = tests/lints/builds are guardrails)
- Context Management section (40-60% smart zone discipline, etc.)

Different (adapt during port):
- **Termination signal**: ralph-prompt emits `<promise>COMPLETE|EMPTY|BLOCKED</promise>` sentinels for shell-side parsing. grind-prompt uses `/goal` evaluator + bd-state-delta verification. Replace sentinel-emit instructions with: "End the turn after `bd close`. The /goal evaluator + outer-shell bd state delta will verify completion. `<promise>BLOCKED</promise>` is retained as a transcript marker only if you cannot complete (claimed-but-blocked semantics) — see FR-017."
- **Per-iteration shape note**: ralph-prompt says "one task per invocation"; grind-prompt should clarify that the Python outer loop spawns a fresh subprocess per task (matches ralph.sh's shape, NOT goal.sh's long-session shape; the pivot landed in ortus-3ico).
- **Queue exhaustion**: ralph-prompt says emit EMPTY; grind-prompt should say "if bd ready is empty, end the turn; outer shell handles queue exhaustion via `bd count --status=open`."

**Predecessor context**: ralph-prompt.md is currently orphan code (no Python code references it; legacy bash goal.sh/ralph.sh shim still load it but those are slated for Phase 5 deletion). After this port, grind-prompt becomes the single source of truth for per-task instructions in the Python world.
design:
**Step 1 — diff the two prompts to identify what's missing.**

```bash
diff -u src/ortus/prompts/grind-prompt.md ortus/prompts/ralph-prompt.md | head -200
```

Lines marked `+` (present in ralph, absent in grind) are the porting targets. Lines marked `-` (present in grind, absent in ralph) are grind-specific adaptations to preserve (mostly the /goal evaluator integration).

**Step 2 — section-by-section port.**

For each section in ralph-prompt.md (numbered list below), one of three actions:

1. **Verbatim copy** into grind-prompt.md — content is shape-agnostic (subagent strategy, issue plan schema, completion comment format, codegraph integration, important rules, steering, context management, glossary).
2. **Adapt during copy** — content references the legacy termination mechanism; substitute the /goal+bd-state-delta semantics.
3. **Skip** — content is specifically about the bash subprocess-per-iter shape that's already covered by the Python outer-loop logic (e.g., the BLOCKED/COMPLETE/EMPTY sentinel grep).

**Sections to port (per the description's same/different lists):**

| Section | Action |
|---|---|
| Per-task loop body (orient→select→claim→investigate→implement→verify→log→close→commit/push) | Verbatim copy |
| Subagent Strategy table | Verbatim copy |
| Issue Plan JSON schema | Verbatim copy |
| Completion Comment format (Changes/Verification + CodeGraph v1 block) | Verbatim copy |
| CodeGraph integration steps 1.5, 4, 6.5, 7, 7.5 | Verbatim copy |
| Important Rules (one task per invocation, no partial work, etc.) | Verbatim copy |
| Steering (upstream/downstream) | Verbatim copy |
| Context Management | Verbatim copy |
| Termination signal instructions | Adapt: replace "emit `<promise>X</promise>` sentinel" with "end the turn; /goal evaluator + outer-shell bd-state-delta verifies." Keep `<promise>BLOCKED</promise>` as a transcript marker per FR-017. |
| Queue exhaustion instructions | Adapt: replace EMPTY-emit with "if bd ready is empty, end the turn; outer shell handles." |
| Glossary | Verbatim copy if grind-prompt doesn't have one |

**Step 3 — verify the port doesn't break /goal evaluation.**

The /goal evaluator (Haiku) reads the conversation each turn. If grind-prompt becomes much larger, the evaluator's per-turn cost goes up slightly. Verify:
- grind-prompt total size after port is reasonable (≤ original ralph-prompt size of 23KB; ideally smaller since we drop sentinel sections)
- The /goal condition string itself remains narrow (still "close one bd issue"; not affected by prompt body size)
- One smoke run via `uv run ortus grind . --tasks 1` against a seeded fixture; verify behavior matches expectations

**Step 4 — regression test.**

Add `tests/test_grind_prompt_content.py` that asserts grind-prompt.md contains key markers from each ported section:

```python
def test_grind_prompt_has_subagent_strategy_table():
    content = (PROMPTS / "grind-prompt.md").read_text()
    assert "Subagent Strategy" in content
    assert "main context = scheduler only" in content
    # ... other markers
```

This catches regressions where future edits accidentally strip sections.

**Step 5 — update ralph-prompt's status note.**

Add a one-line preamble at the top of `ortus/prompts/ralph-prompt.md` indicating it's superseded:

```markdown
> **NOTE 2026-05-17**: This file is the bash-era predecessor of `src/ortus/prompts/grind-prompt.md`.
> Active behavior is in grind-prompt.md. This file is retained until Phase 5 sunset (ortus-sod1.3)
> deletes the bash sources. Do NOT edit this file; edit grind-prompt.md instead.
```

Prevents future drift between the two during the deferred Phase 5 window.

**Acceptance (local-verify per ortus-ctun protocol):**

(1) Step 1 diff captured (comment on this bd issue or save in notes).

(2) grind-prompt.md contains the same key sections as ralph-prompt.md (per the table above) — verified by static greps for section markers.

(3) Termination/queue-exhaustion sections are correctly adapted (no leftover instructions to emit `<promise>COMPLETE</promise>` etc. that would confuse the /goal evaluator).

(4) `tests/test_grind_prompt_content.py` added and passing.

(5) `ortus/prompts/ralph-prompt.md` has a "superseded by grind-prompt.md" preamble.

(6) Optional smoke: one real `uv run ortus grind . --tasks 1` against a fixture closes one issue cleanly (verifies the ported prompt doesn't break /goal flow).

(7) Branch in sync.

**Don't wait for CI.** Close on local-verify + push.
