- Parse and understand the idea context

### Question Generation
- Use prd/PRD-PROMPT.md as the prompt template for generating discovery questions
- Generate 3-7 focused questions that help clarify:
  - User needs and pain points
  - Scope and constraints
  - Success criteria
  - Technical considerations
  - Edge cases

### Subtask Creation
For each generated question:
- Create a subtask using `bd create -t task --parent <idea-id>`
- Set assignee to human (or configurable)
- Title should be the question itself (truncated if needed)
- Description should include:
  - Full question text
  - Context from the original idea
  - Instructions: "Answer by editing this description or adding a comment, then close when done"

### Dependency Setup
- Each Q&A subtask should block the parent idea: `bd dep add <idea-id> <subtask-id>`
- This ensures the idea cannot be closed until all Q&A is complete

## Implementation Notes
- Create as a function/module that can be called from prd-pipeline.sh
- Use `bd show <id> --json` to read bead details
- Return list of created subtask IDs for tracking

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Reads idea description successfully
- [ ] Generates relevant discovery questions using PRD-PROMPT.md
- [ ] Creates subtasks with proper structure
- [ ] Sets up blocking dependencies correctly
- [ ] Handles edge cases (empty description, etc.)

title: Widen the concurrent-grind lock bound for the workers beside it
description:
## Objective

Make the second-grind lock assertion measure the lock path rather than how busy
the machine was, by taking its wall-clock bound from the helper that already
exists for that purpose.

## Behavioral context

Before: the test asserts a hard `elapsed < 0.5` around a `FlockBusy` raise.
Under the distributed gate that half second is shared with every other worker
on the runner, so the assertion reports contention as a slow lock. Observed
failing 2026-09-25 in a `-m "fast or integration" -n auto` run whose only other
failure was elsewhere, and passing in the same selection on neighbouring runs.

After: the bound is widened the way `tests/conftest.py` already widens other
elapsed-seconds assertions, so the test still proves a second grind fails fast
without failing because three other workers shared the core.
design:
## Readiness schema

v1

## Scope

- Route this test's 500ms bound through the existing wall-clock helper.
- Check the sibling elapsed-seconds assertions in the same module and route any
  with the same defect.

## Non-goals

- Do not delete, skip, xfail or re-mark the test, and do not drop an assertion.
- Do not remove the bound or replace it with an unbounded wait; a second grind
  still has to fail fast, which is the whole point of the test.
- Do not change `grind_flock` or `FlockBusy` themselves.
- Do not touch the judge-log lock probe; ortus-uvn2 owns that one.

## Concrete locations

- `tests/test_grind_logic.py` —
  `test_second_concurrent_grind_raises_flockbusy_under_500ms` and its
  `elapsed < 0.5` assertion.
- `tests/conftest.py` — `wall_clock_budget()`, written for exactly this and
  used today only by `tests/test_init.py`.
- `src/ortus/core/grind_logic.py` — `grind_flock()` and `FlockBusy`, the
  behavior under test, unchanged by this work.

## Resolved decisions

1. The helper is the contract for an elapsed-seconds bound in this suite; a
   test that hand-rolls one is the defect, not the helper.
2. The test keeps a bound. Widening is not removing.

## Compatibility constraints

Linux + macOS. The spawn start context and the five-second acquisition wait
stay as they are; only the measured bound is routed through the helper.

## Ordered steps

1. Read what `wall_clock_budget()` returns for a half-second bound.
2. Route the assertion through it and keep the failure message naming both the
   measured milliseconds and the budget applied.
3. Scan the module's other elapsed assertions for the same pattern.
4. Run the module alone and under distribution.

## Dependencies

None. `wall_clock_budget()` already exists and has a consumer.

## Edge cases

- A quiet single-worker machine must still hold the tight bound, so the helper
  has to widen for contention rather than raise the floor unconditionally.
- A bound widened past the three-second hold the child process takes would stop
  proving anything; keep it well under that.

## Plan-gap guidance

If `wall_clock_budget()` cannot express this bound without changing what the
test proves, record PLAN-GAP rather than loosening the number by hand.
acceptance_criteria:
## Observable criteria

- AC-1 (proves-new): the lock bound is taken from the shared helper rather than
  written as a bare literal.
- AC-2 (guards-existing): the module passes under distribution, where the
  contention that exposed this lives.
- AC-3 (guards-existing): the module passes serially, where the tight bound
  still has to hold.

## Criterion checks

- AC-1: `uv run pytest tests/test_grind_logic.py -k flockbusy -q`
- AC-2: `uv run pytest tests/test_grind_logic.py -n auto -q`
- AC-3: `uv run pytest tests/test_grind_logic.py -q`

## Targeted tests

`uv run pytest tests/test_grind_logic.py -q`

title: Give the judge-log lock probe a contention-proof start wait
description:
## Objective

Stop the judge-log multi-process append probe from failing the hermetic gate when the runner is saturated, without weakening what it proves about the lock.

## Behavioral context

Before: the probe spawns three `spawn`-context child processes while holding an exclusive flock, and asserts each one reaches its start event within a flat 5 seconds. On 2026-09-25 the gate run `-m "fast or integration" -n auto` on a 32-worker WSL box failed on the first of those waits; the same file passed in 1.16s run alone, and the immediately following identical gate run was green. A `spawn` child re-imports the interpreter, so its startup time scales with how many other workers are competing for the machine — exactly the condition the gate creates.

After: the wait is derived from the contention the run is under rather than being a flat constant, so the probe still fails when the lock is genuinely not held and stops failing when the box is merely busy. Every assertion about lock ordering and record completeness is kept.
design:
## Readiness schema

v1

## Scope

- Replace the flat start-event timeout in the probe with one scaled the way the suite already scales its other timing expectations.
- Leave the lock assertions, the record-completeness assertions and the process count exactly as they are.

## Non-goals

- No skip, xfail or marker change to reach green; a flaky test is fixed or explained, never silenced.
- No change to `judge_log`'s own locking or record format.
- No move away from the `spawn` context, which is what makes the probe meaningful on macOS.

## Concrete locations

- `tests/test_core_judge_log.py` — `test_process_appends_take_the_lock_and_remain_complete`, the `started.wait(5)` call and the `_append_in_process` helper beside it.
- `tests/conftest.py` — `_DURATION_BUDGET_SCALE` and `wall_clock_budget`, the existing convention for a timing expectation that has to survive a contended runner.

## Resolved decisions

1. Scaling, not raising: a flat larger constant would hide a real lock regression behind a long wait.
2. The suite already has a contention scale factor; the probe should use it rather than inventing a second one.

## Compatibility constraints

Linux + macOS, Python 3.10-3.12, and the probe must stay correct under `-n auto` where dozens of workers share one machine.

## Ordered steps

1. Reproduce by running the gate under `-n auto` on a loaded box and confirm the wait is what fails.
2. Read how `wall_clock_budget` and `_DURATION_BUDGET_SCALE` express a contended expectation.
3. Apply the same scaling to the start wait.
4. Run the file alone and then inside the full gate under `-n auto`.

## Dependencies

None. Observed during ortus-87rz's acceptance run; that issue's changes do not touch this file or `judge_log`.

## Edge cases

- A child that never starts at all must still fail the probe, not hang it.
- The scale factor is configurable through the environment, so a nonsense value must not make the wait unbounded.

## Plan-gap guidance

If the start wait turns out not to be the flaky step — for instance the flock itself is being lost — record PLAN-GAP naming what actually failed rather than widening a timeout that was never the cause.
acceptance_criteria:
## Observable criteria

- AC-1 (proves-new): the probe passes inside the full hermetic gate under `-n auto`.
- AC-2 (guards-existing): the judge-log file's own tests all still pass, none skipped.
- AC-3 (guards-existing): the suite's timing-convention tests still hold.

## Criterion checks

- AC-1: `uv run pytest tests/test_core_judge_log.py -m "fast or integration" -n auto -q`
- AC-2: `uv run pytest tests/test_core_judge_log.py -q`
- AC-3: `uv run pytest tests/test_test_policy.py -q`

## Targeted tests

`uv run pytest tests/test_core_judge_log.py tests/test_test_policy.py -q`

title: Read the budget probe's Ubuntu duration on three green main runs
description:
## Objective

Confirm on main that the scaled-down budget probe reached its goal — `tests/test_test_policy.py::test_over_budget_is_rejected_under_verification_flags` under 2 seconds on the Ubuntu leg — across three consecutive green main runs after the change, and record the numbers or name the shortfall.

## Behavioral context

Before: every measurement of the scaled probe comes from a developer host (11.92s before the change, 1.05s after, same machine and same command). No CI leg has reported the test's duration since, so the 2-second goal is asserted rather than observed; the pre-change Ubuntu median was 11.4s.

After: three consecutive green main runs of the test workflow have that testcase's Ubuntu `time` read out of the gate's JUnit report and recorded on this issue with run ids, next to the 11.4s pre-change median, and the goal is either met or the shortfall is named and scoped.
design:
## Readiness schema

v1

## Scope

- Read the `time` attribute of the `test_over_budget_is_rejected_under_verification_flags` testcase from the JUnit report the gate step writes on the Ubuntu leg of three consecutive green main runs.
- Record those durations, with run ids, in a comment on this issue.
- State the verdict against the 2-second goal and against the 11.4s pre-change median.

## Non-goals

- No change to the probe, its scale constant, the budget hook, its message or the slow marker: a miss is recorded and scoped, never absorbed by shrinking the scale further.
- No re-running of CI to manufacture a green run, and no averaging a slow leg away.
- No machine names, user names or host paths in anything recorded.

## Concrete locations

- `tests/test_test_policy.py` — `_PROBE_BUDGET_SCALE`, `_PROBE_SLEEP` and `test_over_budget_is_rejected_under_verification_flags`, the test whose duration is the measurement.
- `tests/conftest.py` — `ci_gate_budget_scale()` and `pytest_runtest_makereport()`, the contract the inner probe session drives.
- `.github/workflows/test.yml` — the gate step's `--junitxml` output and the artifact carrying it.
- `gh run list` and `gh api` against this repository's Actions history for runs and artifacts.

## Resolved decisions

1. The measurement is the testcase's JUnit `time` on the Ubuntu leg, not a local run: the goal is stated about CI, and a developer host has neither the runner's cores nor its contention.
2. Three consecutive green runs, so one lucky or one unlucky runner does not settle it.
3. A miss is recorded here with numbers and routed to a new bead; the probe's scale stays where this change put it.

## Compatibility constraints

Needs `gh` authenticated against this repository's Actions history and the gate step still writing `junit.xml`. Ubuntu leg only, across the unchanged Python 3.10-3.12 matrix on Linux and macOS.

## Ordered steps

1. List the most recent green main runs of the test workflow.
2. For three consecutive ones, fetch the Ubuntu leg's JUnit report.
3. Read the probe testcase's `time` attribute from each.
4. Record the three numbers with their run ids in a comment on this issue and state the verdict.

## Dependencies

Needs the scaled-probe change merged to main and at least three green runs after it. Sibling of the gate wall-clock reading bead, which measures the whole step rather than this one test. Consumers: none — this bead changes no code.

## Edge cases

- Fewer than three green main runs exist yet: wait for them rather than counting a red, cancelled or in-progress run.
- A run whose gate step was retried or cut short by the step timeout is not one of the three.
- The JUnit artifact expired or was never uploaded: read the step log's `--durations` output instead and say so in the record.
- A known runner incident inflating one leg is named in the record rather than averaged away.

## Plan-gap guidance

If `gh` cannot read the run history or artifacts — no auth, no network, workflow renamed — record PLAN-GAP naming the command and its exact error and flag human, rather than estimating a CI duration from a local sweep.
acceptance_criteria:
## Observable criteria

- AC-1: The three most recent consecutive green main runs of the test workflow are identified by id and date. `gh run list --workflow test.yml --branch main --status success --limit 3`
- AC-2: Each of those runs' Ubuntu JUnit report is read for the probe testcase's time, compared against the 2-second goal, and recorded with its run id in a comment on this issue. `gh api repos/{owner}/{repo}/actions/runs`

## Targeted tests

None — this bead reads CI history and records numbers; it changes no code.

title: Read the grind-family CI wall clock after the bd-call cut
description:
## Objective

Read the first green main run carrying the bd-snapshot change and record whether the grind-family JUnit total dropped at least 30% per Ubuntu leg from the audit baseline.

## Behavioral context

Before: the bd-call budget is proved locally by `tests/test_grind_bd_budget.py`, which counts invocations rather than seconds. The wall-clock claim the audit made — that the grind-family suites hold a large share of the Ubuntu per-leg total because almost all of their time is inside real bd subprocesses — has no post-change reading yet.

After: one Ubuntu leg of a green main run has been read, the per-file JUnit durations for `tests/test_grind*.py` plus `tests/regression/test_grind_no_stream_leak.py` are recorded on this bead, and the 30% target is answered yes or no against the audit baseline (test_grind.py 136s, test_grind_completion_contract.py 33s, test_grind_reap.py 19s, test_grind_orphan_policy.py 25s).
design:
## Readiness schema

v1

## Scope

Read the JUnit artifact of one green main run that already contains the snapshot change, sum the grind-family durations on its Ubuntu leg, compare with the audit baseline, and record the numbers on this bead.

## Non-goals

Do not change product code to hit a number. Do not delete, skip, xfail or re-mark a test to reach a time target. Do not re-run the local bd-budget tests; they are already the invocation proof, and this bead measures wall clock only.

## Concrete locations

- `.github/workflows/` — the workflow whose Ubuntu leg publishes the JUnit artifact.
- `tests/test_grind.py`, `tests/test_grind_completion_contract.py`, `tests/test_grind_reap.py`, `tests/test_grind_orphan_policy.py`, `tests/regression/test_grind_no_stream_leak.py` — the files summed.
- `tests/test_grind_bd_budget.py` — the invocation ceilings this reading follows up on.

## Resolved decisions

1. The invocation budget is already proved and is not re-litigated here.
2. A miss is recorded as a finding with the per-file numbers, never repaired by relaxing a ceiling.

## Compatibility constraints

The run read must be a green main run on the Ubuntu leg, taken after the commit that added the snapshot read path.

## Ordered steps

1. Find the newest green main run containing the snapshot change.
2. Download its Ubuntu-leg JUnit artifact.
3. Sum the grind-family durations and compare with the audit baseline.
4. Record the result as a comment on this bead, with the per-file numbers.

## Dependencies

Depends on the bd-snapshot change having landed on main. No code consumer.

## Edge cases

An expired or missing artifact: read the next green main run instead. A leg whose contention differs markedly from the audit's: record that alongside the numbers rather than adjusting them.

## Plan-gap guidance

If no green main run carrying the change has a readable JUnit artifact, record PLAN-GAP with the runs inspected rather than estimating the durations.
acceptance_criteria:
## Observable criteria

- AC-1 (proves-new): a green main run carrying the change is identified, so its Ubuntu-leg artifact can be read.
- AC-2 (proves-new): the per-file grind-family durations and the percentage change from the audit baseline are recorded as a comment on this bead.

## Criterion checks

- AC-1: `gh run list --branch main --status success --limit 10`
- AC-2: `bd comments ortus-6c86 --json`

## Targeted tests

None — this bead changes no code; the reading recorded on it is the whole verification.

title: Split the cache-write bucket by TTL so its price is not assumed
description:
## Objective

Report Claude's 5-minute and 1-hour cache writes as separate buckets, so the
estimated dollar figure weights each at the rate it was actually billed.

## Behavioral context

Before: `UsageBuckets` carries one `cache_write_tokens` bucket, and the price
table in `src/ortus/core/cost.py` weights it at the one-hour rate (2x input),
because every cache write in this repository's own worker logs arrives in
`usage.cache_creation.ephemeral_1h_input_tokens`. Measured against two windows
that reported `total_cost_usd`, that rate lands within 1.5% of the provider's
figure while the 5-minute rate (1.25x) lands about 10% under. A repository whose
workers run the 5-minute TTL is therefore overstated on that bucket by 60%, and
nothing in the report says so.

After: the two TTLs are separate buckets end to end, each weighted at its own
documented multiplier, so an estimate is correct under either TTL rather than
correct under the one this repository happens to use.
design:
## Readiness schema

v1

## Scope

- Add the 5-minute and 1-hour cache-write buckets to `UsageBuckets`, keeping
  `cache_write_tokens` as their sum so every existing reader and JSON key still
  answers what it answers today.
- Read `usage.cache_creation.ephemeral_5m_input_tokens` and
  `ephemeral_1h_input_tokens` in `_claude_facts` and `_claude_message_facts`.
- Give `ModelPrice` a rate per TTL and weight each bucket with its own in
  `estimate_cost`.
- Document the split in `docs/cost.md` beside the estimate's other caveats.

## Non-goals

- No change to Codex, Grok or OpenCode parsing; none of them reports a TTL.
- Do not drop `cache_write_tokens`: the dashboard and the eval report read it.
- Do not change which figure wins when the provider reported dollars.

## Concrete locations

- `src/ortus/core/cost.py` — `UsageBuckets`, `ModelPrice`, `PRICES`,
  `estimate_cost`, `_claude_facts`, `_claude_message_facts`.
- `tests/test_cost_telemetry.py` — the reaped-window fixture already carries a
  `cache_creation` object with both TTL fields.
- `docs/cost.md` — the "Where a window's dollars come from" section.

## Resolved decisions

1. A write whose TTL the stream does not state keeps the one-hour rate, which is
   what the current table assumes for every write.
2. `cache_write_tokens` stays the sum, so no consumer has to change to keep
   working.

## Compatibility constraints

Linux and macOS, Python 3.10-3.12. Existing `ortus cost --json` keys stay and
new keys are additive. Old logs keep parsing, with their writes landing in
whichever TTL bucket they named.

## Ordered steps

1. Run `uv run pytest tests/test_cost_telemetry.py -q` for a green baseline.
2. Add the buckets and a failing test that a 5-minute write is priced at 1.25x.
3. Split the rate in `ModelPrice` and weight each bucket.
4. Update the docs and re-run the targeted tests.

## Dependencies

Follows ortus-fva5, which added the price table this refines. Consumers are
`ortus cost`, `ortus eval` and the dashboard.

## Edge cases

- A `cache_creation` object that names neither field, with a non-zero
  `cache_creation_input_tokens`: the total stands and takes the default rate.
- The two TTL fields disagreeing with the total: trust the total for the sum and
  the fields for the split.
- A window with only per-message readings: the same split is available there.

## Plan-gap guidance

If the published 5-minute and 1-hour multipliers cannot be confirmed from the
provider documentation available in the repository, record PLAN-GAP naming them
rather than picking a ratio.
acceptance_criteria:
## Observable criteria

- AC-1 (proves-new): a window whose cache write is a 5-minute write is priced at
  the 5-minute rate, and a one-hour write at the one-hour rate.
- AC-2 (guards-existing): `cache_write_tokens` still reports the total and the
  existing rollups are unchanged.

## Criterion checks

- AC-1: `uv run pytest tests/test_cost_telemetry.py -k cache_write_ttl -q`
- AC-2: `uv run pytest tests/test_cost_telemetry.py tests/test_dashboard.py -q`

## Targeted tests

`uv run pytest tests/test_cost_telemetry.py tests/test_harness_eval_report.py tests/test_dashboard.py -q`
close_reason: The five-minute and one-hour cache writes are separate buckets priced at their own documented multipliers, with the flat total unchanged for existing readers

comments.author: who
comments.text: Claude's two cache-write TTLs are now separate buckets end to end. UsageBuckets carries cache_write_5m_tokens and cache_write_1h_tokens beside the flat cache_write_tokens total, filled from the cache_creation object where the stream states a TTL; the total stays the bucket of record, so every existing reader and JSON key answers what it answered before and the new keys are additive. ModelPrice carries a rate per TTL, derived from the documented multipliers (1.25x input for the five-minute TTL, 2x for the one-hour), and estimate_cost weights each stated bucket at its own rate. A write whose TTL nothing in the stream names sits in the total alone and keeps the one-hour rate, which is what the table weighted every write at before this change, so an older log is priced exactly as it was. The multipliers were confirmed against the provider caching documentation available in this environment rather than picked as a ratio, so the plan-gap branch did not apply. Criterion checks pass: AC-1 (pytest tests/test_cost_telemetry.py -k cache_write_ttl) reports 2 passed, 29 deselected, and AC-2 (pytest tests/test_cost_telemetry.py tests/test_dashboard.py) reports 118 passed. The spec's targeted set adds test_harness_eval_report.py for 139 passed, and the two remaining suites that import the cost module, test_worker_failure_class.py and test_prompt_prefix.py, report 33 passed. No leftover work: the scope's four pieces (buckets, parsing, per-TTL rates, docs) all landed.

title: Record the pre-turn gate's truncated fields on its decision row
description:
## Objective

Carry `truncated_fields` on the pre-turn gate's decision row as well as the
semantic-readiness one, so every judgment in the decision log says whether it
read full issue text or a shortened slice.

## Behavioral context

Before: `pack_state` truncates oversized issue text in both phases and reports
each cut field as an `OmissionReason.TRUNCATED` omission, and `DecisionEvent`
carries a validated `truncated_fields` list. Only `evaluate_readiness` fills
it. The two pre-turn callers in `src/ortus/commands/grind.py` take `.state`
off the packed result and drop the omissions, so a pre-turn row for a bead
whose description was cut is indistinguishable from one that read the whole
field.

After: both pre-turn decision writes pass the truncated field names they
already have in hand, and a replay can separate full-text from truncated-text
judgments for every phase rather than for semantic readiness alone.
design:
## Readiness schema

v1

## Scope

- Keep the `PackedState` at both pre-turn sites in `src/ortus/commands/grind.py`
  instead of immediately taking `.state`, derive the sorted truncated field
  names from its omissions, and pass them to `DecisionEvent`.
- Reuse the existing logger validation; no new payload field and no schema bump.

## Non-goals

- No change to what `truncate_field` keeps or to the caps.
- No change to the decision payload shape, the replay reader, or readiness
  schema v1.
- No new log file and no second event kind.

## Concrete locations

- `src/ortus/commands/grind.py` — the two `pack_state(...).state` calls that
  feed `write_decision(... DecisionEvent(...))`.
- `src/ortus/core/judge_log.py` — `DecisionEvent.truncated_fields` and
  `_truncated_fields`, already validated and already written.
- `src/ortus/core/judge_state.py` — `OmissionReason.TRUNCATED`, the omissions
  the packer already returns.
- `src/ortus/core/judge_readiness.py` — `evaluate_readiness` is the worked
  example of deriving the list from a packed state.
- `tests/test_grind_judge.py` and `tests/test_core_judge_log.py` — where the
  pre-turn row is asserted today.

## Resolved decisions

1. The field already exists and is already validated; this issue only fills it
   at the remaining call sites.
2. The list stays sorted, so the pre-turn row and the semantic row order their
   names the same way.
3. A row with nothing truncated keeps the empty list it writes today.

## Compatibility constraints

Python 3.10-3.12 hermetic gate. Logs written before this change still load:
the reader already treats the field as optional for decision rows.

## Ordered steps

1. Run the pre-turn gate tests for a green baseline.
2. Keep the packed result at both grind sites and derive the sorted names.
3. Pass them to `DecisionEvent` at both sites.
4. Assert the pre-turn row carries the names, and run the targeted tests.

## Dependencies

Follows the truncating packer. Consumers are `ortus judge export` and
`ortus judge replay`, which already accept the field.

## Edge cases

- Issue text disabled or a judge-private label produces omissions that are not
  truncations; the list stays empty.
- A field both screened out and over the cap is omitted, never truncated, so it
  must not appear in the list.

## Plan-gap guidance

If a pre-turn site turns out not to have the packed omissions in scope without
restructuring how grind builds its judge state, record PLAN-GAP with the call
site named rather than threading a new parameter through unrelated helpers.
acceptance_criteria:
## Observable criteria

- AC-1 (proves-new): a pre-turn decision row for a bead whose issue text was
  truncated names the cut fields in `truncated_fields`.
- AC-2 (guards-existing): a pre-turn row for a bead inside its caps still
  writes an empty list, and replay accepts both rows.

## Criterion checks

- AC-1: `uv run pytest tests/test_grind_judge.py -k truncated -q`
- AC-2: `uv run pytest tests/test_core_judge_log.py tests/test_judge_replay.py -q`

## Targeted tests

`uv run pytest tests/test_grind_judge.py tests/test_core_judge_log.py tests/test_judge_replay.py -q`
close_reason: Both pre-turn decision writes carry the packer's truncated field names, so every phase's row says whether it judged full issue text or a slice

comments.author: who
comments.text:
Both pre-turn decision writes now carry the packer's truncated field names, so every phase in the decision log says whether it judged full issue text or a shortened slice. The shadow observation and the enforcing gate each keep the PackedState instead of taking .state immediately, and a shared helper derives the sorted TRUNCATED omission names the logger already validates. No payload field, no schema bump, no change to the caps or to what the packer keeps.

AC-1: a pre-turn row for a bead whose objective and acceptance were cut names both fields, asserted on the shadow path and the enforcing path. AC-2: a row inside its caps still writes an empty list and replay accepts both rows. Criterion checks passed: uv run pytest tests/test_grind_judge.py -k truncated -q (4 passed); uv run pytest tests/test_core_judge_log.py tests/test_judge_replay.py -q (122 passed). Targeted set passed together: 171 passed.

title: Drop the unused triage import that fails the orchestrator lint
description:
## Objective

Make `uv run ruff check src/ortus/commands/grind.py` pass again. It reports one
F401 on a clean checkout of HEAD.

## Behavioral context

Before: `TriageClass` is imported from `ortus.core.judge_triage` at the top of
`src/ortus/commands/grind.py` and used nowhere in the module, so ruff fails the
file with F401 and any lint gate over the package is red.

After: the lint passes and the triage route still behaves as it does today.
design:
## Readiness schema

v1

## Scope

- Establish whether the name is genuinely unused in `src/ortus/commands/grind.py`.
- Remove it from the import, or use it where the module was meant to.

## Non-goals

- Do not change how a parked bead is routed or classified.
- Do not remove `TriageClass` from `ortus.core.judge_triage`; other callers and
  its own tests own it.
- No unrelated lint fixes in the same change.

## Concrete locations

- `src/ortus/commands/grind.py` — the `from ortus.core.judge_triage import (...)`
  block, which also imports `pin_directive_section` and `triage_parked_bead`.
- `src/ortus/core/judge_triage.py` — where `TriageClass` is defined.

## Resolved decisions

- A red lint gate is a defect even when every test passes.
- Whichever way it goes, the routing behaviour is unchanged by this bead.

## Compatibility constraints

Linux and macOS. No behaviour change: this is either a deleted import line or a
name put to the use it was imported for.

## Ordered steps

1. Search the module for every use of the name.
2. Remove it from the import if it has none.
3. Run the lint and the grind suites that cover the triage route.

## Dependencies

None. The name arrived with the triage route that reads a parked bead's evidence.

## Edge cases

If the name is used only inside a string, a comment or a type annotation that
`from __future__ import annotations` defers, it is still needed and the fix is
to keep it and silence the rule at that line instead.

## Plan-gap guidance

If removing it breaks a caller outside this module, stop and record PLAN-GAP
rather than re-exporting a command module's imports.
acceptance_criteria:
## Observable criteria

- AC-1 (proves-new): the orchestrator module lints clean.
- AC-2 (guards-existing): the triage route still behaves as it does today.

## Criterion checks

- AC-1: `uv run ruff check src/ortus/commands/grind.py`
- AC-2: `uv run pytest tests/test_judge_triage.py -q`

## Targeted tests

`uv run pytest tests/test_judge_triage.py -q`
close_reason: TriageClass had no reader in grind.py; dropping it from the judge_triage import makes ruff pass with the triage route unchanged

comments.author: who
comments.text: TriageClass occurred exactly once in src/ortus/commands/grind.py — the import itself — with no string, comment, or deferred-annotation use, so the edge case that would have kept it did not apply. Dropped it from the judge_triage import block, leaving pin_directive_section and triage_parked_bead, the two names the orchestrator actually calls. The enum stays defined and exported in ortus.core.judge_triage for the callers and tests that own it. AC-1: uv run ruff check src/ortus/commands/grind.py — All checks passed. AC-2: uv run pytest tests/test_judge_triage.py -q — 17 passed. The module still imports cleanly, and no routing or classification behaviour changed.

title: Measure the stuck-decision priors and set their values
description:
## Objective

Replace the authored constants in the stuck-claim vector with values measured
from real grind runs, or record that the authored ones survive contact.

## Behavioral context

Before: `decide_stuck_claim` shapes its continue/replan/escalate vector with
four hand-chosen numbers — how much continue mass each burned window moves,
the ceiling on that movement, how much of it lands on escalate rather than
replan, and how much a spent re-plan shifts toward escalate. They were picked
to satisfy the mapping the issue that introduced them specified, not from a
run. After: each is either kept with recorded numbers behind it or moved to a
measured value, and the stuck-decision log is what settles it.

The decision log already carries everything the comparison needs: every record
has the vector, the action, the window count, whether the branch advanced, and
whether it failed open. What is missing is a run long enough to have opinions
about and a pass that reads those records against what the claims actually did
afterwards.
design:
## Readiness schema

v1

## Scope

- Collect stuck-decision records from grind runs with `post_turn` enabled.
- Compare each decision against the claim's observed fate: closed in the next
  window, closed later, escalated, or still burning.
- Keep or move each of the four constants, recording the numbers on this issue.

## Non-goals

- No change to the three actions or to which outcome maps to which class;
  that mapping is settled.
- No new confidence floor and no needs_human gate; low confidence stays a
  flattening of the vector.
- No change to the fail-open baseline or to the marker comment formats.
- No change to the decision-log record shape.

## Concrete locations

- `src/ortus/core/judge_stuck.py` — the four constants and the vector rule.
- `src/ortus/core/judge_replay.py` — the record shape the comparison reads.
- `tests/test_judge_post.py` — where changed values are pinned.

## Resolved decisions

- The metric is whether the action taken preceded a close, not whether the
  vector agreed with the model's choice; agreement with Jev is not the goal.
- A null result keeps the authored values and is recorded as a null result.

## Compatibility constraints

Linux and macOS. Changing a constant changes behavior for every repository
with `post_turn` enabled, so the change lands with its numbers in this issue.

## Ordered steps

1. Collect stuck-decision records from runs with the phase enabled.
2. Join each record to the claim's fate in the windows that followed.
3. Compare the taken action against what the claim went on to do.
4. Keep or move each constant, pinning any change in tests.
5. Record the numbers, nulls included, on this issue.

## Dependencies

Needs the stuck decision and its log record, which landed with ortus-uy3w.
Reads the same log the other post-turn analysis reads.

## Edge cases

- A corpus in which every decision failed open has no vector to score and
  settles nothing; name it rather than reading it as agreement.
- Too few escalate decisions to compare is a null result for that constant
  alone, not for all four.

## Plan-gap guidance

If no repository has run long enough with the phase enabled to produce a
corpus, stop and record PLAN-GAP: moving a constant on a handful of records
would be re-authoring it, not measuring it.
acceptance_criteria:
## Observable criteria

- AC-1 (proves-new): the four constants are each kept or moved with the
  numbers behind the call recorded on this issue. `bd comments ortus-uy3w`
- AC-2 (guards-existing): the mapping from outcome to action and the
  fail-open baseline are unchanged by whatever the constants become.
  `uv run pytest tests/test_judge_post.py -k decide_stuck -q`
- AC-3 (guards-existing): the decision record still replays after any change.
  `uv run pytest tests/test_judge_replay.py -q`

## Criterion checks

- AC-1: `bd comments ortus-uy3w`
- AC-2: `uv run pytest tests/test_judge_post.py -k decide_stuck -q`
- AC-3: `uv run pytest tests/test_judge_replay.py -q`

## Targeted tests

`uv run pytest tests/test_judge_post.py tests/test_judge_replay.py -q`

comments.author: who
comments.text:
PLAN-GAP: there is no corpus to measure, so the four constants cannot be moved by measurement this window. This is the condition the packet's own plan-gap guidance names.

Evidence gathered this window:

1. Decision logs. Thirteen real jev-decisions.jsonl files exist outside this repository's test fixtures, holding 50 records between them. Every one is a pre-turn 'decision' (26) or an 'outcome' (24). There are zero 'post_turn' records and therefore zero 'stuck_decision' records anywhere. log_stuck_decision only writes when config.post_turn is set, and JudgeConfig.post_turn defaults to False; this repository has no .ortusrc, so the phase has never been on.

2. Run logs. _decide_stuck calls write_log unconditionally, so any real no-close window would leave a '[timestamp] stuck decision for <id>: ...' line in the grind run log whether or not post_turn was enabled. Across all 179 grind run logs in this repository, spanning 2026-05-16 to 2026-09-24, that line appears zero times, as does the wedged-claim counter line. An earlier grep appeared to find 37 hits in today's log; all 37 were the f-string source of that very log call, echoed into a captured worker transcript, not emitted lines.

3. Why the corpus is empty by construction rather than by sampling. judge_stuck.py has exactly one commit: ortus-uy3w, 2026-09-24 14:52. The most recent grind run began at 14:06 the same day, before the constants existed. No grind run has ever executed with decide_stuck_claim present, so this is not a thin corpus or an all-fail-open corpus; the decision has never been taken.

This is distinct from the null result the packet's resolved decisions describe. A null result keeps the authored values after a corpus failed to discriminate between them, and the edge cases scope it that way: an all-fail-open corpus 'settles nothing', and too few escalate decisions is 'a null result for that constant alone'. Both presuppose records. With n=0 the measurement never ran, and keeping the four constants on that basis would record a verdict the evidence does not contain.

The four constants are therefore left exactly as authored: _WINDOW_STEP 0.25, _WINDOW_CAP 0.75, _ESCALATE_SHARE_STEP 0.34, _ADVANCED_PULL 0.5, _REPLAN_STEP 0.6. Nothing in this repository changed.

What unblocks this bead: grind runs with post_turn enabled, long enough that claims actually burn no-close windows, from a terminal rather than from inside an agent session. That is the same prerequisite the sibling measurement beads carry, and they sit in the human queue for it. Once such runs exist, steps 2 through 5 of this packet can proceed against a real corpus.

Flagging human rather than closing: the work this bead describes has not been done, and closing it would retire a measurement that was never taken.

title: Tail: render the Grok usage event the rollup now bills
description:
## Objective

Show a per-turn usage line for a Grok worker on `ortus tail`, the way the
Claude and Codex renders already do.

## Behavioral context

Before. `_render_grok_object` returns nothing for `{"type":"usage"}`, so a Grok
run streams thought, text and tool lines but never reports what a turn billed.
The cost rollup now decodes that same event into the shared buckets, so the
numbers exist and only the live view omits them.

After. A Grok usage event renders one line naming input, cached and output, so
an operator watching a Grok run sees the same information class the other
backends show.
design:
## Readiness schema

v1

## Scope

Render the Grok usage event in the tail view using the field names the rollup
decoder reads, in the shape the Claude and Codex branches already print.

## Non-goals

Do not change the cost rollup or any bucket it fills. Do not change how any
other backend renders. Do not add a price table or infer dollars.

## Concrete locations

- `src/ortus/commands/tail.py` — `_render_grok_object`, the `usage` early
  return, and the existing `[USAGE]` line the result branch prints.
- `tests/test_tail.py` — where the Grok render is proven.

## Resolved decisions

1. Grok `input_tokens` excludes the cached read; the render must not add or
   subtract the two.
2. Unreported fields are shown as unreported, never as zero.

## Compatibility constraints

Linux and macOS. The Grok golden fixture is shared with the cost tests, so it
must keep its current lines.

## Ordered steps

1. Render the usage event beside the other Grok kinds.
2. Prove it against the golden Grok stream.

## Dependencies

Discovered while decoding the same event for the cost rollup.

## Edge cases

A usage event missing a field renders that field as unreported rather than as
a zero.

## Plan-gap guidance

If the Grok usage event field names diverge from what the cost rollup decoder already reads (input_tokens / cached read / output_tokens) or from the Claude [USAGE] shape in _render_object (tail.py ~352: input/cached/output), or if rendering the event forces a change to the shared Grok golden fixture lines the cost tests pin, stop, record PLAN-GAP naming the mismatched fields and fixture path, preserve candidate edits, and route to human — do not invent dollars, do not zero-fill missing fields, and do not alter Claude or Codex renders.
acceptance_criteria:
## Observable criteria

- AC-1 (proves-new): the golden Grok stream renders a usage line naming input,
  cached and output.
- AC-2 (guards-existing): the Claude and Codex tail renders are unchanged.

## Criterion checks

- AC-1: `uv run pytest tests/test_tail.py -k grok -q`
- AC-2: `uv run pytest tests/test_tail.py -q`

## Targeted tests

`uv run pytest tests/test_tail.py -q`
close_reason: Grok usage event renders input/cached/output on tail; AC-1 and AC-2 criterion checks pass

title: Measure the prompt-audit A/B and set its default
description:
## Objective

Decide whether `prompt_audit` should default on, from the frozen evaluation
set's numbers rather than from taste.

## Behavioral context

`prompt_audit` serves the audited prompt variants to every phase and defaults
to false, so today it is a flag an operator turns on without evidence either
way. The evaluation set already defines a `prompt-audit` arm beside the
control for both fixtures, and the report already carries cost per closed bead
with close rate, worker errors, turns, wall time, and cache hit rate beside
it. What is missing is the run and the verdict. After this issue the default
is whatever the measurement supports, the numbers are recorded, and a null
result is recorded as a null result rather than quietly dropped.
design:
## Readiness schema

v1

## Scope

- Run both fixtures under the control arm and the `prompt-audit` arm using the
  frozen recipe.
- Record the emitted report, including every null metric, where the other A/B
  issues record theirs.
- Set or leave the `prompt_audit` default according to the primary metric,
  with the guardrails as veto conditions.

## Non-goals

- No change to what the treatment does. This issue measures `prompt_audit`; it
  does not edit the audited prompt variants.
- No new fixture and no large application fixture; the set is frozen at the
  two small PRDs in `ortus.evalpack`.
- No change to the report schema or to which metrics are collected.
- No verdict on the other two treatments; they have their own issues.

## Concrete locations

- `src/ortus/core/harness_eval.py` — `TREATMENTS`, the `prompt-audit` entry
  and its `measured_by` back-reference.
- `src/ortus/core/prompt_audit.py` — `AUDIT_CONFIG_KEY`, `audit_enabled()`.
- `src/ortus/core/config.py` — the `prompt_audit` default.
- `tests/test_prompt_audit_flag.py` — where a changed default is pinned.

## Resolved decisions

- The primary metric is cost per closed bead; a treatment that wins on cost
  while losing on close rate, worker errors, turns, wall time, or cache hit
  rate does not ship as the default.
- A null primary metric is a null result and is recorded as one: it does not
  become an argument for either default.
- The arm definition lives in the evaluation set, not in this issue, so both
  A/B issues and this one are measuring the same thing.

## Compatibility constraints

- Linux and macOS only.
- Changing the default changes behavior for existing projects that never set
  the key, so the change lands with its numbers in the issue's notes.

## Ordered steps

1. Run the control and `prompt-audit` arms for both fixtures via the recipe.
2. Collect the report and record it, nulls included.
3. Compare the primary metric; check every guardrail for a veto.
4. Set or leave the `prompt_audit` default accordingly and pin it in tests.
5. Point the treatment's `measured_by` back at this issue.

## Dependencies

Depends on the fixture pack and report in ortus-4ji7, and reads better after
ortus-5yjr makes the sweep one command. Sibling of ortus-nudo and ortus-p810,
which measure the other two treatments the same way.

## Edge cases

- A backend that reports no dollars leaves the primary metric null; the
  comparison is then inconclusive and the default does not move.
- The two fixtures disagreeing about the winner: record both and do not move
  the default on a split.
- A guardrail regressing while cost improves: no default change.

## Plan-gap guidance

If the arm cannot be run without a credential or budget this repository does
not already provide, stop and record PLAN-GAP. If the evaluation set's
`prompt-audit` arm no longer matches what `prompt_audit` switches on, stop and
record PLAN-GAP rather than measuring a treatment the report misnames.
acceptance_criteria:
## Observable criteria

- AC-1: The `prompt-audit` treatment's `measured_by` names this issue, so the arm and its consumer point at each other. `uv run pytest tests/test_harness_eval_report.py -k treatments -q`
- AC-2: The `prompt_audit` default matches the recorded verdict and is pinned by a test rather than left implicit. `uv run pytest tests/test_prompt_audit_flag.py -q`

## Targeted tests

`uv run pytest tests/test_harness_eval_report.py tests/test_prompt_audit_flag.py -q`

title: Execute the evaluation matrix instead of printing it
description:
## Objective

Turn the evaluation matrix `ortus eval --matrix` prints into one the verb
executes, so a before/after comparison is a single command rather than eight
copy-pasted command blocks.

## Behavioral context

Today `ortus eval <root> --matrix` prints, per fixture and arm, the `ortus
init` / `.ortusrc` / `ortus plan` / `ortus grind` sequence the operator runs by
hand; `ortus eval <root>` then reads the grind logs those runs left and prints
the comparison. The recipe and the report are therefore already frozen and
already tested, but the hours in between are manual, and a mistyped seat name
or a forgotten config line silently produces two arms that were never
comparable. After this change `ortus eval <root> --run` builds every seat,
applies each arm's config line, plans its fixture, grinds it to zero, and
prints the same report at the end, with one progress line per cell so a long
run is legibly alive.
design:
## Readiness schema

v1

## Scope

- A `--run` mode on the `eval` verb that executes each cell of `matrix()` in
  order and then emits the existing report.
- Per-cell progress lines and a per-cell wall-clock timeout.
- Resume: a cell whose seat already holds a grind log is skipped, so an
  interrupted sweep continues instead of paying for the finished arms twice.
- A per-cell execution record (exit status, skipped or run) carried into the
  report beside the metrics.

## Non-goals

- No new metrics and no schema change: the report stays
  `harness-eval-report/v1`, primary metric plus the five guardrails.
- No third fixture, and no large application fixture — the set is frozen at
  the two small PRDs shipped in `ortus.evalpack`.
- No CI wiring. A run spends real model budget and stays operator-invoked.
- No provider or seat selection beyond the existing `--backend`.

## Concrete locations

- `src/ortus/commands/eval.py` — `evaluate()` gains the run mode.
- `src/ortus/core/harness_eval.py` — `arm_commands()`, `matrix()`,
  `build_report()`, `EvalCell`.
- `src/ortus/core/output.py` — `progress()` for the per-cell lines.
- `tests/test_harness_eval_report.py` — the pack's existing test module.

## Resolved decisions

- The run mode executes the very strings `arm_commands()` already emits rather
  than building its own argv. A second construction path would drift from the
  documented recipe, and the recipe is the artifact operators copy.
- Treatments stay `.ortusrc` keys appended to the seat's config; none of the
  three is a grind flag, so one appended line remains the whole difference
  between arms.
- Execution is injected so tests drive it without spawning a backend.

## Compatibility constraints

- Linux and macOS only, in line with AGENTS.md.
- `--matrix` output and the report schema are unchanged; this adds a mode and
  breaks no existing caller.

## Ordered steps

1. Add an injectable command executor to `ortus.core.harness_eval`.
2. Add `--run` to `evaluate()`, iterating `matrix()` in order.
3. Skip a cell whose seat already holds a grind log; report it as skipped.
4. Record each cell's exit status and surface it beside its metrics row.
5. Cover execution order, resume, and a failing cell in the pack's tests.

## Dependencies

Depends on the fixture pack and report in ortus-4ji7. Consumed by ortus-p810
and ortus-nudo, which need both arms of their treatment run the same way.

## Edge cases

- A seat directory that already exists, with or without logs.
- `ortus grind` exiting nonzero: the sweep continues and the cell is marked.
- An interrupted sweep resumed later.
- A backend CLI that is not installed: fail that cell, not the sweep.

## Plan-gap guidance

If executing a cell turns out to need a credential, network service, or seat
layout this repository does not already configure, stop and record PLAN-GAP
rather than inventing one. If the frozen report schema cannot carry the
per-cell execution record without a breaking change, stop and record PLAN-GAP
rather than renaming existing metrics.
acceptance_criteria:
## Observable criteria

- AC-1: `--run` executes each cell's recorded commands, in matrix order, through the injected executor. `uv run pytest tests/test_harness_eval_report.py -k run_executes -q`
- AC-2: A cell whose seat already holds a grind log is skipped rather than re-run. `uv run pytest tests/test_harness_eval_report.py -k run_resumes -q`
- AC-3: A nonzero exit from one cell leaves later cells running and is recorded against that cell. `uv run pytest tests/test_harness_eval_report.py -k run_cell_failure -q`
- AC-4: The run mode ends by emitting the unchanged `harness-eval-report/v1` report. `uv run pytest tests/test_harness_eval_report.py -k run_emits_report -q`

## Targeted tests

`uv run pytest tests/test_harness_eval_report.py -q`
close_reason: Implemented: ortus eval --run executes every matrix cell through an injected executor, skips seats that already hold a grind log, records each cell's exit status, and ends in the unchanged harness-eval-report/v1 report. All four AC criterion checks pass.

comments.author: who
comments.text:
Done. `ortus eval <root> --run` now executes the matrix it used to only print, then emits the same report at the end.

What landed. `run_matrix` walks `matrix()` in declaration order and hands every command string straight to an injected executor, so there is still exactly one construction path for a cell's commands: the strings an operator copies from `--matrix` are the strings the sweep issues. The default `shell_executor` runs them through a shell because a treatment arm applies itself with a `printf ... >> .ortusrc` redirect, and it returns 124 for a command its cell's wall clock cut short. The budget is per cell rather than per command, so a slow init cannot buy the grind that follows it an extra hour. `cell_has_run` makes resume cheap: a seat that already holds a grind log is recorded skipped and issues nothing, which is what keeps an interrupted sweep from paying twice for the arms that finished. A cell that exits nonzero stops at that command, keeps its exit status and the command that produced it in a `CellExecution`, and the sweep moves on to the next cell.

Report shape. `build_report` takes the sweep's records and carries them into the report as an `executions` list beside the existing rows; no metric was added, renamed, or changed meaning, and the schema stays harness-eval-report/v1. A report rebuilt from logs has no records and renders the table it always had; a swept report gains one trailing status column so a null metric can be read against whether its cell failed, was skipped, or ran and reported nothing.

Verification (AC criterion checks, all passing):
- AC-1: uv run pytest tests/test_harness_eval_report.py -k run_executes -q
- AC-2: uv run pytest tests/test_harness_eval_report.py -k run_resumes -q
- AC-3: uv run pytest tests/test_harness_eval_report.py -k run_cell_failure -q
- AC-4: uv run pytest tests/test_harness_eval_report.py -k run_emits_report -q

Changed-surface group also green: uv run pytest tests/test_harness_eval_report.py tests/test_cost_telemetry.py tests/test_cli.py tests/test_cli_verbs.py -q -n auto --test-timeout=30 (76 passed).

Note for the consumers of this verb: a sweep still spends real model budget and stays operator-invoked, so the two A/B measurement packets waiting on both arms need an operator shell to run `--run`; nothing here lets a sandboxed worker produce those numbers.

title: Prune spilled output files under logs/ortus-output
description:
## Objective

Give spilled command output a retention rule so `logs/ortus-output/` does not grow without bound across grind runs.

## Behavioral context

ortus-6gz3 made oversized check output, tracker-comment quotes, and packet fields spill to a file under a spill directory (`logs/ortus-output/` beside the grind logs, or the system temp dir when no repository is known) and injected a path, a byte size, and a tail in place of the body. Nothing deletes those files. `logs/` is gitignored so they never reach a commit, but a long-lived seat accumulates one file per oversized capture forever, and a comment that names a pruned path must still read sensibly.
design:
## Readiness schema

v1

## Scope

- Decide and implement a retention rule for the spill directory (age, count, or total bytes).
- Keep a reference readable after its file is gone: the comment already carries the size and the tail.

## Non-goals

- Changing the reference format.
- Deleting grind logs or transaction artifacts.
- Pruning the system temp fallback, which the OS already owns.

## Concrete locations

- src/ortus/core/spill.py — default_spill_dir, _write.
- src/ortus/core/checks.py — run_checks passes the repository's spill directory.

## Resolved decisions

- Spilled bodies are disposable artifacts, not evidence of record: a pruned file is acceptable, a missing size or tail is not.

## Compatibility constraints

Linux + macOS. The prune must never remove a file a live run is still writing.

## Ordered steps

1. Choose the retention rule and its default.
2. Prune at spill time or at grind start, whichever keeps the run's own captures.
3. Test that a fresh capture survives a prune and that the directory stays bounded.

## Dependencies

Needs ortus-6gz3 landed.

## Edge cases

A spill directory shared by two concurrent grind seats must not have one run prune the other's live captures.

## Plan-gap guidance

If no rule keeps a run's own captures without a lock, record PLAN-GAP rather than pruning by wall-clock age alone.
acceptance_criteria:
## Observable criteria

- AC-1 (proves-new): a spill directory over the retention bound is pruned and the current run's captures survive.
- AC-2 (guards-existing): a spilled reference still renders path, size, and tail.

## Criterion checks

- AC-1: `uv run pytest tests/test_large_output_spill.py -k prune -q`
- AC-2: `uv run pytest tests/test_large_output_spill.py -k helper -q`

## Targeted tests

`uv run pytest tests/test_large_output_spill.py -q`
close_reason: Spill directory now bounded by file count and byte budget, pruned at spill time with a grace window that keeps live and concurrent captures; criterion checks AC-1 and AC-2 pass.

comments.author: who
comments.text:
Retention rule: newest-first, bounded by a file count (SPILL_RETAINED_FILES=200) and a byte budget (SPILL_RETAINED_BYTES=256 MiB), with a grace window (SPILL_MIN_AGE_SECONDS=6h) below which no capture is pruned whoever wrote it.

Pruning runs at spill time, inside the write path, after the body has landed — so the run's own captures sort to the front of both bounds and survive by construction, with no grind-start hook and no lock. The grace window is what makes a shared directory safe between two concurrent seats: it is longer than the 5400s worker watchdog, so no seat can still be writing a body another seat reads as abandoned. Age only protects; the caps alone drive deletion, so this is not a wall-clock-age prune and the PLAN-GAP guidance did not apply.

The temp-directory fallback is excluded, per the non-goal: the OS owns it. The reference format is unchanged — size and tail travel inside the reference, so a comment naming a pruned path still reads sensibly.

Criterion checks: AC-1 'uv run pytest tests/test_large_output_spill.py -k prune -q' 4 passed; AC-2 'uv run pytest tests/test_large_output_spill.py -k helper -q' 4 passed; targeted 'uv run pytest tests/test_large_output_spill.py -q' 16 passed. Spill consumers 'uv run pytest tests/test_core_checks.py tests/test_grind_loop.py -q' 59 passed.

title: Surface worker failure classes on the tail and dashboard reads
description:
## Objective
Render the worker-failure class an operator can already see in the grind log on the two live surfaces that read those logs, and map it into the judge post-turn outcome reasons.

## Behavioral context
`ortus-jlxt` landed the closed taxonomy (`src/ortus/core/worker_failure.py`), the grind marker line, and the per-backend/model rates in `ortus cost`. `ortus tail` and `ortus dashboard` render the marker as a plain ortus line today, which is readable but not distinguished: a window that died on a sandbox EPERM looks like any other progress line. `judge_replay` still carries its own outcome reasons (`worker_timeout`, `auth`) with no relation to the taxonomy.
design:
## Readiness schema
v1

## Scope
Give `classify_crumb` and the tail failure rendering a case for the failure marker so the class is visibly a failure, and record the class alongside the existing judge post-turn outcome reason without changing the replay schema incompatibly.

## Non-goals
Do not change the taxonomy or its precedence. Do not rewrite the judge outcome enum. Do not re-classify from the surfaces; read the class the marker already carries.

## Concrete locations
`src/ortus/commands/tail.py`, `src/ortus/commands/dashboard.py` (`classify_crumb`), `src/ortus/core/judge_replay.py` (`OUTCOMES`), `src/ortus/core/worker_failure.py` (`FAILURE_LINE` is the parse).

## Resolved decisions
1. The marker is the single source; no surface re-derives a class.
2. Replay keeps its own reasons; the class travels beside them.

## Compatibility constraints

Linux/WSL2 and macOS grind hosts. The FAILURE_LINE regex and WorkerFailure enum in src/ortus/core/worker_failure.py (landed by ortus-jlxt) are the contract: surfaces parse the marker, they do not invent classes. An unknown class name on the marker renders as the ortus_harness_bug bucket. judge_replay.OUTCOMES stays the closed set {done, plan_gap, flake, auth, needs_human, continue}; the worker-failure class travels beside those reasons as a side field so older replay consumers keep working without a schema bump.

## Ordered steps
1. Parse the marker with `FAILURE_LINE` on each surface.
2. Render it as a failure crumb and a tail event.
3. Record the class beside the post-turn outcome reason.
4. Run the tail, dashboard, and replay suites.

## Dependencies
Depends on ortus-jlxt (the taxonomy and marker).

## Edge cases
An older log has no marker: the surfaces must render exactly as they do today. A marker naming a class this Ortus does not know renders as the harness-bug bucket.

## Plan-gap guidance

If classify_crumb (dashboard.py) cannot accept an ortus FAILURE_LINE marker without breaking the Grok-only GROK_CRUMB_TYPES path, or if recording the class on a judge post-turn outcome requires widening OUTCOMES rather than a side field next to the existing reason, stop, record PLAN-GAP naming the exact call site and the conflicting type, preserve candidate edits, and route to human — do not re-derive a class from the worker stream and do not change the OUTCOMES enum.
acceptance_criteria:
## Observable criteria
- AC-1 (proves-new): a log carrying a failure marker renders the class on the dashboard crumb.
- AC-2 (proves-new): the same log renders the class in tail output.
- AC-3 (guards-existing): a log with no failure marker renders unchanged.

## Criterion checks
- AC-1: `uv run pytest tests/test_dashboard.py -k failure -q`
- AC-2: `uv run pytest tests/test_tail.py -k failure -q`
- AC-3: `uv run pytest tests/test_dashboard.py tests/test_tail.py -q`

## Targeted tests
`uv run pytest tests/test_dashboard.py tests/test_tail.py tests/test_judge_replay.py -q`
